title: Security Deposit Maximum (Landlord Reference)
bodyText:
Colorado law caps the security deposit you can charge at two months' rent (C.R.S. section 38-12-102.5(1)). From January 1, 2027, the cap does not apply where you bought the home from the tenant and the two of you signed a post-closing occupancy agreement under the purchase contract (38-12-102.5(2)); every other Colorado tenancy stays capped.

This is a ceiling on what you're allowed to collect - it's not something your lease needs to tell the tenant, since stating the legal maximum only gives them a number to hold you to. The actual deposit amount you're charging this specific tenant is already captured in your lease through the Security Deposit clause.

Use this as a guardrail when entering the deposit amount for a Colorado lease: outside that one exception, if you type in more than two months' rent, that number is not enforceable.

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited
bodyText: Colorado law prohibits taking action against a tenant - raising rent, cutting services, declining to renew, or starting an eviction - because they reported an unsafe condition, exercised a right under the lease, or joined a tenant organization (C.R.S. section 38-12-509). This applies whether or not your lease mentions it, so there's no need to include it in tenant-facing text. What matters practically: if you have an independent, legitimate reason to raise rent or not renew (the lease naturally ending, a real violation, etc.), document that reason - having a clear paper trail is what protects you if a tenant later claims a decision was retaliatory.

title: Rent Can't Be Raised More Than Once a Year
bodyText: No matter what your lease says, you cannot raise a tenant's rent more than once every 12 months in Colorado (C.R.S. section 38-12-702). This applies to month-to-month tenancies as much as fixed terms. Keep this in mind if you ever build a rent-escalation or annual-increase clause - the 12-month floor overrides anything the lease tries to specify.

title: For-Cause Eviction Rules (After 12 Months)
bodyText: Once a tenant has lived in a property for 12 months or more, Colorado generally requires you to have a specific legal reason - 'cause' (like nonpayment or a lease violation) or a defined 'no-fault' reason (such as selling the property or doing major renovations, with 90 days' notice) - before you can end the tenancy or decline to renew (C.R.S. section 38-12-1301 et seq.). This does NOT apply if the property is your own primary residence or directly adjacent to it, a short-term rental, a mobile home lot, or employer-provided housing. Check which of your properties fall into an exempt category - this determines which version of the month-to-month termination clause applies.

title: Never Waive a Tenant's Right to Call Police
bodyText: Colorado law makes it void for any lease to contain language that waives, discourages, or penalizes a tenant for calling police or emergency services (C.R.S. section 38-12-402). This mainly matters if you're ever tempted to add a 'crime-free housing' or repeated-nuisance-call type clause - that pattern is exactly what this law targets, and any such clause would be unenforceable.

title: Confidentiality Duty for a Tenant Who Is a DV/Stalking Victim
bodyText: If a tenant, or a qualified third party acting for them, tells you the tenant is a victim-survivor of unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse, you must not disclose that information to anyone, including a co-tenant, without the tenant's express written consent, unless a court order requires it. If the tenant ends the lease for that reason and gives you a new address, the same rule protects the address. One duty runs the other way: if the tenant has given you written or actual notice of their status and consents to your sharing it with the court, you must disclose it to the court in any civil action, with the complaint and the return of service, or whenever you become aware of their status. You also may not ask a rental applicant about victim-survivor status, consider it, or require them to disclose it (C.R.S. 38-12-402(4), (5)). This applies whatever the lease says, and a violation carries the statutory damages described in the domestic-violence termination note.

title: Never Ask About Immigration or Citizenship Status
bodyText: Colorado's Immigrant Tenant Protection Act prohibits asking a tenant about their immigration or citizenship status, disclosing or threatening to disclose it, or using it to harass, intimidate, or deny housing (C.R.S. section 38-12-1201 et seq.). Violations carry real penalties - up to $2,000 per violation plus attorney's fees. Any lease provision attempting to waive these protections is void, even if the tenant agrees to it in writing. You may still ask every applicant for the same information or documents needed to verify financial qualifications, including a Social Security number or taxpayer identification number, and a landlord who is also the tenant's employer may collect what employment forms require. The rules also give way to what federal, state or local law (including a government rent-assistance program), a subpoena, a warrant or a court order requires.

title: Attorney Fee Clauses Must Work Both Ways
bodyText: Two Colorado rules work together here, and between them they decide whether you ever see a dollar of attorney fees. First, a clause that only lets the landlord recover attorney fees and court costs - but not the tenant, if the tenant wins - is void under C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(II), and any fee-shifting clause must award fees to the prevailing party once the court finds the party prevailed and the fee is reasonable. Second, and less well known: under 13-40-123 a prevailing residential landlord or tenant is not entitled to recover attorney fees at all "unless the residential rental agreement between the parties contains a provision for either party to obtain attorney fees". So silence costs you the fees, and a landlord-only clause costs you the fees too, because it is void. The only version that works is a mutual prevailing-party clause - which is why the Default by Tenant clause has one, and why it is worth checking any clause you write yourself for the same thing.

title: If a Tenant Dies During the Lease
bodyText: Colorado's 'Letty's Act' (C.R.S. section 38-12-801(3.5)) prohibits charging liquidated damages, accelerating rent beyond the end of the month (or 10 business days after the unit is vacated, whichever is later), clawing back move-in concessions, or any other early-termination penalty when a lease ends because a tenant died. You can retain enough of the security deposit to cover any damage related to the death, and you can take possession without filing an eviction once the estate's representative surrenders the unit, or automatically 30 days after death if rent is unpaid or the unit has been cleared out.

title: Notify Tenants If Your Identity or Agent Changes
bodyText: If you (or your authorized agent) change - for example, a property changes management companies, or ownership transfers - Colorado law requires the new landlord or agent to notify each tenant within 1 business day, either in writing/electronically or by posting the new information conspicuously at the property (C.R.S. section 38-12-801(2)). This is an ongoing operational duty, not something that needs to be in the lease itself.

title: Don't Charge for a Service You Don't Actually Provide
bodyText: Colorado's Honest Pricing law prohibits charging a fee for any service you don't actually provide (C.R.S. section 6-1-737). This is a good general check for any fee-based clause you write yourself: make sure the fee corresponds to something real.

title: Offer at Least One Fee-Free Way to Pay Rent
bodyText: You can't charge a rent payment processing fee unless you also offer at least one payment method with no fee attached (C.R.S. section 6-1-737). When you list your accepted payment methods in the lease, make sure at least one of them is genuinely free to the tenant.

title: Advertised Rent Must Show the Full Price
bodyText: When you advertise or list a property, Colorado's Honest Pricing law requires showing a single all-in price including mandatory fees, displayed more prominently than any broken-out fee amounts - not itemized separately (C.R.S. section 6-1-737). This applies to marketing and listings, not lease text, and becomes relevant if Steinoak ever adds a listing/marketing feature.

title: Utility Billing Rules Are Still Being Clarified
bodyText:
If you use a shared or master utility meter and allocate costs among tenants by formula (RUBS), Colorado now has a statutory safe harbor (C.R.S. 6-1-737(4.5), added by HB26-1013).

You may allocate utility costs this way if:
- The total you bill across all tenants does not exceed what the utility provider charged for the whole premises.
- You add no markup, surcharge, or administrative fee beyond what C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(VI) allows (either 2% of the billed amount or a flat $10 per month, not both).
- Common-area and shared-facility costs are excluded from the allocation.
- The allocation method is clearly disclosed in the lease or an addendum.

This replaces the interim Attorney General enforcement guidance issued in late 2025.

title: Radon Disclosure Risk Changes With Lease Length
bodyText:
The radon disclosure itself is required before every lease is signed, whatever its length. What changes with length is the tenant's escape hatch.

Under C.R.S. 38-12-803(3)(a) a tenant may void the lease and vacate under 38-12-507 if you fail to give the required written disclosures, or if you fail to make a reasonable effort to mitigate within 180 days after being notified that a radon measurement professional found 4 picocuries per liter or more (3)(a)(II).

From January 1, 2026 that whole subsection (3) stops applying to a lease of one year or less (3)(b). Read the line carefully: a standard 12-month lease is "one year or less", so it escapes; a 13-month lease or a longer renewal does not.

If you offer a term over a year, the void-and-vacate remedy is live, and the 180-day mitigation clock is the thing to diary.

title: You Must Accept Housing Vouchers
bodyText:
Colorado law requires most residential landlords to accept applicants using a housing voucher. Two small-landlord exemptions remain: a landlord with three or fewer units for rent, and, for the single-family homes, an owner of five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five rental units in total (C.R.S. 24-34-502(1.5)(a), (1.7)).

Outside those exemptions, refusing an applicant solely because they use a voucher is source-of-income discrimination, and it is expensive. A court that awards the tenant damages must award at least $5,000 (24-34-505.6(6)(a)). On top of that, the Colorado Civil Rights Commission must order a civil penalty of at least $5,000, and up to $10,000 for a first violation, $25,000 for a second within five years and $50,000 for two or more earlier violations within seven years (24-34-508(1)(f)).

You can still decline a voucher applicant for legitimate, consistently-applied reasons - credit, income, rental history - just never because of the voucher itself. You also can't refuse to cooperate with the approval process (inspection, paperwork) as a way of avoiding this duty, and the duty to cooperate with a rental assistance application has no small-landlord exemption (24-34-502(1)(r)).

title: How the Voucher Approval Process Actually Works
bodyText: A voucher applicant doesn't move in until the unit is inspected and the Housing Assistance Payment contract is signed - you're not required to let someone occupy the unit before that happens. If a tenant does move in early anyway, standard guidance puts them on the hook for full, unsubsidized rent until the contract is finalized - you're not left holding the shortfall. The multi-year wait some landlords worry about is the tenant's wait to be issued a voucher in the first place; once a voucher holder actually applies to your specific unit, the approval process itself typically takes days to a few weeks, not years.

title: Security Deposit Rights Can Never Be Waived
bodyText: A tenant cannot waive their rights regarding return of the security deposit, whether orally or in writing - any lease provision attempting this is unenforceable (C.R.S. section 38-12-103(7)). Keep this in mind for any custom security deposit language you write yourself.

title: Alternate Housing May Be Required During Major Repairs
bodyText: This is triggered by the TENANT'S REQUEST, not automatically. If a condition materially interferes with a tenant's life, health, or safety (or is a condition under C.R.S. 38-12-505(4)(l)), and the tenant requests it, you must provide - within 24 hours of that request, at no cost to the tenant - either a comparable dwelling unit or a hotel room, your choice which. Requirements: at least as many beds as the tenant uses; habitable; accessible if the tenant has a disability; within 5 miles of the unit unless the tenant consents otherwise (you may go 5-10 miles if substantially cheaper, and if nothing is available within 10 miles, the nearest available). If the stay runs past 48 hours, the place must have a refrigerator with a freezer and a range stove or oven - OR you pay each tenant a per diem for meals and incidentals at least equal to the Colorado state employee intrastate travel per diem, paid when you first reasonably expect the stay to exceed 48 hours and every 24 hours after. Beyond the per diem, you pay only reasonable relocation costs such as storage and transportation. Two things that protect you: the tenant still owes rent during the relocation and for the rest of the term; and if you put a tenant in a hotel and the condition cannot be fixed within 60 consecutive days for reasons outside your reasonable control, you can cap the hotel at 60 consecutive days - but only if you give written notice at the earliest opportunity stating that it cannot be fixed in 60 days, the end date for hotel coverage (no earlier than 60 days in), and that the tenant may terminate the lease with no liability or penalty, AND you return the tenant's full security deposit on or before you give that notice.

title: Pet Deposit and Pet Rent Limits
bodyText: Colorado caps what you can charge for a pet: the pet security deposit can't exceed $300 and must be fully refundable - you can no longer charge a non-refundable 'pet fee.' Pet rent can't exceed $35 per month or 1.5% of the monthly rent, whichever is greater (C.R.S. section 38-12-106, HB 23-1068). The actual amounts you charge a specific tenant are entered in your lease's Pets clause - use these numbers as the ceiling when entering them for a Colorado property.

title: Carpet Damage Has a Special Rule
bodyText:
You can't deduct from a security deposit for carpet being "substantially and irreparably damaged" unless the carpet has not been replaced with new carpet within the ten years preceding the end of the lease or surrender of the premises (C.R.S. 38-12-103(11)(c), as amended by HB25-1249, effective January 1, 2026).

Even then, you may retain only the minimum amount necessary to replace the carpet - or to repaint - in the specific area that is damaged, not the full room or unit and not the full replacement cost (C.R.S. 38-12-103(11)(a)-(b)).

Keep this in mind at move-out before assuming worn or stained carpet justifies a deduction.

title: What Counts as "Bad Faith" When Withholding a Deposit
bodyText: If you retain 125% or more of a tenant's actual documented damages from their security deposit, Colorado law presumes you did so in bad faith (HB 25-1249). Bad-faith withholding also includes retaining a deposit without cause, or for an unlawful, retaliatory, or discriminatory reason. Bad-faith withholding exposes you to treble damages - document your actual costs carefully before making a deduction.

title: Either Party Can Request a Move-Out Walkthrough
bodyText: Either you or the tenant can request a walkthrough inspection near the end of the lease (in person or by video) to identify anything beyond normal wear and tear before move-out (HB 25-1249). Doing a walkthrough does not legally lock you out of charging for genuine damage discovered afterward - the law's definition of 'wrongfully withheld' doesn't reference walkthrough completeness at all. That said, missing something during a walkthrough could still work against you if a dispute goes to court, since a tenant could argue you'd have caught it if it were real damage.

title: Never Charge a Tenant for Normal Wear and Tear or Preexisting Issues
bodyText: Any lease provision assigning a tenant a fee or charge for repairs, cleaning, or other work due to normal wear and tear, or for damage/defective conditions that existed before their tenancy began, is void under Colorado law (HB 25-1249). Keep this in mind for any custom deposit-related language you write yourself.

title: Federal ESA Enforcement Changed in 2026 - Colorado Law Did Not
bodyText:
Federal and Colorado law have pulled apart on emotional support animals, and it would be easy to read the federal news and get this wrong.

On September 17, 2025 HUD withdrew its assistance-animal guidance, and on May 22, 2026 it went further: HUD's Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity now says it will pursue Fair Housing Act accommodation complaints only for animals individually trained to do work or tasks for a disability - the ADA service-animal standard - and will no longer expect landlords to automatically accommodate untrained emotional support animals. HUD says it intends to go through formal rulemaking.

Here is what that does NOT change for you in Colorado.

- It is a change in how one agency prioritizes enforcement, not a change in the Fair Housing Act itself; the statute and its regulations are unchanged, and a tenant can still bring a private FHA claim, as can the Department of Justice.
- **Colorado has its own law.** C.R.S. 24-34-502 makes it a discriminatory housing practice to refuse a reasonable accommodation that a person with a disability needs to use and enjoy a dwelling, and that covers assistance animals including ESAs. That statute never depended on HUD guidance and was not affected by any of this.

So in Colorado, continue to treat a documented ESA as an assistance animal, not a pet: no pet deposit, no pet rent, no breed or size restriction, and no demand for details about the nature or severity of the disability. The tenant stays responsible for actual damage, and you may still deny where the specific animal is a direct threat or would cause substantial property damage that cannot be otherwise addressed.

Watch for HUD's rulemaking, but do not change your Colorado practice on the strength of the enforcement memo alone.

title: Habitability: Your Operational Duties Beyond the Repair Itself
bodyText:
Repair clock (C.R.S. 38-12-503(6)(a)): begin remedial action within 24 hours of having notice of a condition that materially interferes with the tenant's life, health or safety, and within 72 hours for a condition that makes the property uninhabitable or otherwise requires repair.

Before entering to start or continue that work, give the tenant at least 24 hours' written notice, unless the condition imminently threatens life, health or safety or is an active and ongoing threat of substantial damage to the property.

C.R.S. 38-12-503 imposes several duties that have nothing to do with the repair work itself, and missing them can independently establish a breach.

- **Communication:** Contact the tenant within 24 hours of having notice (72 hours if the premises are inaccessible due to an environmental public health event), stating what you intend to do and when it will start and finish - and you must affirmatively tell the tenant about your obligation to provide a comparable unit or hotel room at no cost.
- **Records:** Keep all written notices, correspondence, and documentation about the condition and your remedial action for the entire tenancy plus 3 years, and produce any of it to the tenant within 10 calendar days of a request.
- **Mold and dampness:** Within 72 hours of notice you must install containment, stop active water sources, and install HEPA filtration, then maintain containment through remediation, dry and decontaminate affected materials, test after remediation, and reassemble to prevent recurrence.
- **Gas:** You must hire a professional (as defined in C.R.S. 38-12-104(3)) for any hazardous condition involving gas piping, facilities, appliances, or equipment.
- **Timelines to watch:** A rebuttable presumption that you failed to act on time attaches at 7 days for life/health/safety conditions and 14 days for uninhabitable conditions.

title: Nothing in the Habitability Rules Can Be Waived
bodyText: C.R.S. 38-12-503(10): except as Part 5 itself allows, any agreement waiving or modifying ANY right, remedy, obligation, or prohibition in Part 5 is void as contrary to public policy. This is broader than the other non-waiver rules already tracked - it is not limited to a specific right, it covers the entire habitability regime. Practical effect: no lease language can shorten the 24/72-hour response windows, waive the relocation obligation, disclaim the warranty of habitability, or contract around the record-keeping and notice duties. Also note the reverse: 38-12-503(3)(f)(II) says designating a verbal notice method in the lease waives YOUR right to insist on written notice - one of the few places where lease language can cost you something under Part 5.

title: Rules on Application Fees and Tenant Screening
bodyText: Colorado's Rental Application Fairness Act (C.R.S. 38-12-901 et seq.) constrains the application stage, before any lease exists. In short: an application fee must reflect your actual cost to process the application, must be the same for every applicant for that property, and must be itemized on request. If an applicant provides a portable tenant screening report, you generally may not charge them an application fee at all - and you must tell applicants whether you accept portable reports. When screening, you generally may not consider rental or credit history older than 7 years, or criminal history older than 5 years, except for certain enumerated offenses (methamphetamine manufacture, offenses requiring sex-offender registration, homicide, and stalking). From January 1, 2027, every rental application must also include a notice of the information and data you will try to access when screening, a general description of the factors you will consider (such as credit history, rental history, income and, if applicable, criminal background), and whether you use a third-party screening service and, if so, its name; you do not have to adopt or disclose fixed disqualifying criteria (C.R.S. 38-12-904(1.7)). None of this belongs in the lease itself, but it governs how you get to a lease.

title: Small-Landlord Exemption Applies to the Statement, Not the Duty
bodyText:
Colorado's source-of-income rules have three small-landlord limits, and they do not line up, so check each one separately.

- **Printing the statement:** A written lease must say that Colorado prohibits source-of-income discrimination, unless you have five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five rental units in total (C.R.S. 38-12-801(2.5)).
- **Accepting the income:** The source-of-income discrimination rules (C.R.S. 24-34-502(1)(l) to (1)(p)) do not apply to a landlord with three or fewer units for rent. Separately, a landlord who owns five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five rental units in total is not required to accept federal Housing Choice Vouchers for those single-family homes (24-34-502(1.5)(a), (1.7)). These exemptions were not removed in 2025; the 2025 act added to the rules without touching them.
- **Cooperating with rental assistance:** Since May 29, 2025, every landlord, with no small-landlord exemption, must make reasonable efforts to respond on time to requests for information and documents needed for a tenant's rental assistance application, and must cooperate in good faith with a tenant applying for rental assistance, including by providing documents a government agency or other administering entity requires (24-34-502(1)(r)).

Getting the voucher or assistance rules wrong is costly: where a court finds discrimination based on a tenant's use of a housing subsidy under these rules and awards damages, it must award at least five thousand dollars (24-34-505.6(6)(a)), and the Colorado Civil Rights Commission must add a civil penalty of at least five thousand dollars, up to fifty thousand for repeat violations (24-34-508(1)(f)).

Being exempt from one rule is not being exempt from the others, and the exemptions turn on what you own, so recheck them whenever you add a property.

title: You Cannot Push Habitability Repairs Onto the Tenant's Renter's Insurance
bodyText: C.R.S. 38-12-503(13): you may not require a tenant to submit a claim to their renter's insurance carrier to cover a cost or expense related to remedial action you are responsible for paying, and you may not file a claim against a tenant's renter's insurance policy at all without the tenant's express written permission given at the time the claim is submitted. Requiring renter's insurance in the lease remains fine - what you cannot do is treat that policy as a funding source for repairs Part 5 makes your responsibility.

title: Habitability Notice Must Be Written - and Your Lease Can Accidentally Give That Up
bodyText:
Colorado requires WRITTEN notice before the habitability clock starts against you, and the courts enforce that strictly: Anderson v. Shorter Arms Investors, LLC, 2023 COA 71, 537 P.3d 831 holds that substantial compliance does not apply and that a tenant's oral notices are insufficient as a matter of law. That is a real protection - but C.R.S. 38-12-503(3)(f)(II) lets you throw it away by accident: if your lease or your property rules say a tenant may or must give notice verbally, you have waived your right to written notice.

Never designate a phone number or any verbal method as the habitability-notice channel.

Note also that 'written notice' is broad and does not have to come from the tenant - notice from a government entity, a third party, another tenant about a condition affecting multiple units, tenant correspondence with maintenance, or your own written observations can all count under (3)(e).

Anderson also held that notice of mold or dampness not presently interfering with life, health, or safety must include permission to enter in order to be sufficient.

title: Colorado's Self-Help Eviction Penalty Is Severe
bodyText: Colorado makes it unlawful to remove or exclude a tenant from a dwelling unit without going through court process, and the penalty is one of the harshest in this library. Under C.R.S. § 38-12-510, a landlord who willfully and unlawfully removes a tenant — or willfully and unlawfully cuts off heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas, or other essential services — owes the tenant statutory damages equal to the tenant's ACTUAL damages PLUS the greater of three times the monthly rent or $5,000, plus attorney fees and costs. The court may also order possession restored to the tenant. That means changing the locks, pulling the meter, or hauling belongings to the curb can cost you five figures on a unit renting for a fraction of that, and can put the tenant back in the property. A writ of restitution executed by an officer is the only lawful route.

title: Colorado Has No Holdover Rent Multiplier - and No Fees Without a Lease Clause
bodyText:
Colorado gives landlords no doubled or trebled rent remedy against a holdover tenant. Article 40 of title 13 sets no holdover damages measure at all, and Colorado courts have measured the recovery as the reasonable rental value of the premises for the period of unlawful detention. So your recovery for a holdover period is ordinary rental value plus costs, not a penalty multiple.

The section that does matter is C.R.S. 13-40-123, and it is about fees rather than holdover: the prevailing party in an eviction action recovers damages, reasonable attorney fees and costs of suit, "except that a residential landlord or tenant who is a prevailing party shall not be entitled to recover reasonable attorney fees unless the residential rental agreement between the parties contains a provision for either party to obtain attorney fees". Read that together with 38-12-801(3)(a)(II), which voids a one-way fee clause and requires any fee-shifting provision to run to the prevailing party.

The combination is a trap worth knowing: with no fee clause you get no fees, and with a landlord-only fee clause you get no fees either, because the clause is void. A mutual prevailing-party clause is the only version that pays, and the lease's Default by Tenant clause contains one.

title: Colorado Gives You No Storage Duty — and Broad Immunity
bodyText: Colorado is unusually protective of landlords once a writ of restitution is executed. Under C.R.S. § 13-40-122(3) you have no duty to store or maintain a tenant's personal property removed from the premises, and even if you choose to store it you have no duty to inventory it, to determine who owns it, or to note its condition. Storing it creates neither an express nor an implied bailment, and the statute makes you immune from liability for loss or damage. A landlord who follows the lawful directions of the officer executing the writ is immune from both civil and criminal liability for acts or omissions involving the removed property. If you do elect to store, § 13-40-122(4) lets you charge the tenant reasonable storage costs, recovered either through your lien rights under title 38 or by requiring payment before the tenant reclaims the property. If you do not store it, the property must remain available for the tenant to reclaim from the public right-of-way. Two timing rules bind the officer, not you, but affect your schedule: a writ may only be executed between sunrise and sunset, no earlier than ten days after judgment — and no earlier than thirty days if the tenant receives SSI or Social Security disability benefits.

title: Pets Are the One Post-Eviction Duty Colorado Does Impose
bodyText: Colorado relieves you of almost every duty toward a tenant's belongings after a writ is executed — but pet animals are the exception, and the duties are affirmative. Under C.R.S. § 13-40-122 you must give the local animal control authority access to the premises to remove or secure any pet animals in a timely manner, and provide the tenant's name and contact information if you have it. You must post notice at the premises, in a visible place, naming the organization the animals were taken to and how to contact it, and give the tenant that same information on request. No pet animal may be removed from the premises during execution of the writ and left unattended on public or private property. This is a genuine carve-out from the broad immunity elsewhere in the section: the statute treats leaving a pet on the curb the way it does not treat leaving furniture there.

title: You Can No Longer Skip Notice Just Because the Lease Ends on a Set Date
bodyText: Colorado used to excuse both parties from giving notice where the lease term ended at a time certain. Since the 2024 amendments, only the tenant is excused: no written termination notice is necessary from a tenant with a fixed-term tenancy that ends at an agreed time. As a landlord, electing not to renew a fixed-term tenancy is something you must do by written notice that expires at the end of the term, with the notice period scaled to how long the tenancy has run -- which for a tenancy of a year or longer is at least 91 days.

title: Deposit Documentation on Tenant Request
bodyText: From January 1, 2026, a Colorado tenant may make a written request for the documentation behind any amount you retained from a security deposit, and you must provide it within 14 days. The duty covers documentation in your possession relevant to the retention - photographs, inspection forms or reports, receipts, invoices, and estimates. Keep this material as you go rather than assembling it after a dispute starts: the same statute deems a withholding wrongful where your written statement fails to list exact reasons, and the landlord carries the burden of proving both that a retention was not wrongful and what the actual damages were.

title: You Must Give the Tenant a Signed Copy Within Seven Days
bodyText: If there is a written rental agreement, you must give the tenant a copy signed by both you and the tenant no later than the seventh day after the tenant signs. An electronic copy is sufficient unless the tenant asks for a paper copy, in which case you must provide one on paper. The agreement must also state the name and address of the landlord or the landlord's authorized agent.

title: No Penalty Clause Tied to an Eviction
bodyText: A Colorado written rental agreement must not include a clause that assigns a penalty to a party stemming from an eviction notice or an eviction action resulting from a violation of the rental agreement. Any provision included in violation of this rule is void and unenforceable. This is separate from the rent and damages a court may award in an eviction proceeding - what is prohibited is a lease term imposing its own penalty because a notice was served or an action was filed.

title: Fire or Casualty Damage: What Colorado Requires
bodyText: Colorado has no fire-or-casualty statute; after a fire the warranty of habitability (C.R.S. 38-12-501 to 38-12-511) decides what happens, and no lease term can change it (38-12-503(5), (10)). IF THE TENANT DIDN'T CAUSE IT: damage that makes the home uninhabitable or threatens life, health or safety is a condition you must fix at your own expense. You must start remedial action within 72 hours of notice (24 hours where it threatens life, health or safety), keep at it, and finish within a reasonable time (38-12-503(2)(b), (4), (7)). If the tenant asks, you must provide a comparable unit or a hotel room within 24 hours, at no cost to them; after 48 hours it must have a fridge with freezer and a stove, or you pay a daily meal allowance at the state employee rate (38-12-503(4)(a)-(b)). The tenant still owes rent. If repairs can't be finished within 60 consecutive days for reasons outside your control, you can end the hotel duty after 60 days by written notice and by returning the full security deposit; the tenant may then end the lease without penalty (38-12-503(4)(c)). THE TENANT CAN'T SIMPLY LEAVE: the tenant's termination right arises only once you are in breach (you didn't start, stopped, or didn't finish in a reasonable time), and then on 10 to 60 days' written notice (38-12-507(1)(a)). While you are repairing promptly, the lease continues. YOU CAN'T SIMPLY LEAVE EITHER: a lease term giving you a right to end the lease after an ordinary fire would modify your Part 5 duties and is likely void. Your one statutory exit is for a sudden environmental public health event (a disaster or environmental event such as a wildfire or flood affecting nearby homes) or government action, and only if the lease includes it (38-12-503(11); the optional clause "Termination After an Environmental Public Health Event"). Whether a single-house fire counts as such an event is unsettled. IF THE TENANT CAUSED IT: a condition substantially caused by the misconduct of the tenant, their household, guests or invitees is not a breach of the warranty (38-12-503(9)), so none of the above applies and your ordinary lease remedies do; the victim of domestic violence, abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking is excepted. ENDING THE LEASE BY AGREEMENT: after a major fire, you and the tenant can agree in writing to end the lease. Prorate rent to move-out, refund rent paid for later periods, and return the deposit on Colorado's normal schedule. Don't include a release of the tenant's habitability claims (a hotel you owed, rent for uninhabitable days, the deposit): an agreement waiving Part 5 rights is void as to that waiver (38-12-503(5), (10)). The statute doesn't address mutual termination directly; for a large loss, have an attorney review the agreement.

title: Late Fee Limits
bodyText:
Colorado limits residential late fees (C.R.S. 38-12-105) and backs the limits with real money.

- You can't charge a late fee until rent is at least 7 days late, and it can't exceed the greater of $50 or 5% of the past-due rent.
- The fee has to be disclosed in the rental agreement, which your lease's Late Fee clause does by stating your amount.
- You must give the tenant written notice of a late fee within 180 days after the rent it relates to was due, or you cannot charge it.
- You may not charge a late fee more than once for the same late payment unless the total still fits under the cap, may not charge interest on a late fee, and may not recoup a late fee out of a rent payment - which is why the lease applies payments to rent first.
- A late fee is not rent, so an unpaid late fee on its own can neither support an eviction nor terminate the tenancy. And none of the subsidy-paid portion of rent can carry a late fee at all.

The consequences of getting it wrong: a non-complying lease provision is void and unenforceable, you owe the tenant a $50 penalty for each violation, you have 7 days from written notice to cure, and if you don't the tenant can sue for damages plus a penalty of $150 to $1,000 per violation plus attorney fees - and can raise the violation as a defense in your eviction.

Treat these as hard guardrails when you enter the amount for a Colorado lease.

title: Returned Payment Fees
bodyText:
Colorado sets no dollar cap on a landlord's returned-payment fee, but the charge should be reasonable under the dishonored-instrument statute (C.R.S. 13-21-109), and you may add the actual bank charges you incur.

Don't call it rent or treat it as rent: it isn't subject to a rent late fee and can't be the basis of a remedy for nonpayment of rent.

Your lease's Returned Payments clause states your fee.

title: Domestic Violence and Stalking: Tenant's Right to End the Lease
bodyText: A Colorado tenant who is a victim-survivor of unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse, and who intends to move out because of fear of imminent danger to themselves or their children, may end the lease and move out without further obligation except the limited payment described below. The tenant, or a qualified third party acting for them, gives you written notice with one of the four qualifying documents: a self-attestation affidavit, a letter from a qualified third party, a police report from the prior 120 days, or a valid protection or restraining order (C.R.S. 38-12-402(2)(a), (a.5); see the separate note on qualifying documents, which also covers what you may and may not ask for). What you may recover is narrow: at most one month's rent, and only if you incurred economic damages as a direct result of the early termination and gave the tenant documentation of them within 30 days after the agreement terminated. Separately, you must give a written statement of your actual damages within 30 days after the date the tenant vacates, or you lose the right to charge or collect any future rent. Those are two different clocks; work to the earlier one. If another tenant remains on the lease, you may not collect the month's rent from the victim-survivor at all, and you may never charge the victim-survivor for damage caused by the abuse (see the separate note on deposits after a domestic-violence termination, which also covers debt collection). You may not end a tenancy or evict solely because a tenant is a victim-survivor, and your lease may not let you end the tenancy, penalize the tenant or take any adverse action for calls for police or emergency help about these situations. A tenant can sue for a violation and recover actual damages plus the greater of three months' rent or five thousand dollars, with punitive damages, attorney fees and costs (38-12-402(1), (3), (8)). You also owe the tenant confidentiality and must allow safety lock changes (see the separate notes).

title: Tenants' Right to Install EV Charging
bodyText:
Colorado gives tenants the right to install a Level 1 or Level 2 electric vehicle charging system at their own expense for their own use (C.R.S. 38-12-601).

- You can't charge a fee for placing or using it, other than reimbursement for the electricity actually used or a reasonable access fee in place of metering (plus a reasonable fee to reserve a space in a shared parking area).
- You also can't restrict a tenant's parking because the vehicle is a plug-in hybrid or electric vehicle.

What you may require (registration within 30 days, safety and appearance requirements, insurance naming you, reimbursement if you install it) is in the lease's EV charging clauses.

title: No Late Fee on the Subsidy Portion of Rent
bodyText: If a housing subsidy pays part of the rent, you can't charge the tenant a late fee for late payment or nonpayment of any portion the subsidy provider is responsible for paying (C.R.S. 38-12-105(1)(f)). A late fee can apply only to the tenant's own share.

title: Subsidized Tenancies: Rent Proration When Part of the Unit Is Uninhabitable
bodyText: If a housing subsidy pays part of the rent and the property becomes partly uninhabitable, rent is reduced in proportion to the part affected, calculated on the total rent including the subsidy-paid portion. Rent already paid for that period is refunded pro rata (C.R.S. 38-12-507, as amended by HB25-1240). Whether the proration covers the subsidy-paid portion rests on the Division of Real Estate's summary of the bill, not the enrolled text.

title: Bed Bugs: Disclosure on Request and Entry Notice
bodyText:
Two Colorado bed-bug rules.

- Disclosure (C.R.S. 38-12-1005): when a prospective tenant asks, you must disclose whether the unit has had a known bed-bug infestation in the previous eight months and the date of the most recent bed-bug inspection, if any. The duty is owed on request and before the lease is signed, so putting it only in the lease can come too late; the lease's optional Bed Bug Disclosure clause records what you disclosed.
- **Entry (38-12-1004(1)(a)):** Before you, an inspector or a pest-control agent enters for a bed-bug inspection or treatment, give the tenant at least 48 hours' written or electronic notice, unless the rental agreement sets a different minimum; your lease's Access clause states your period.

title: Termination Notice Periods and Contents
bodyText:
Colorado sets minimum notice to end a periodic tenancy, or to decline to renew a fixed term, scaled to how long the tenancy has run (C.R.S. 13-40-107):
- At least 91 days for a tenancy of one year or longer.
- 28 days for six months to a year.
- 21 days for one to six months.
- 3 days for one week to one month, or a tenancy at will.
- 1 day for less than a week.

These are minimums, so a lease period can be longer but never shorter.

The notice must be in writing, expire at the end of the period or term, describe the property and the date the tenancy ends, and be signed by the party giving it or their agent or attorney.

Once a tenancy has run 12 months, a covered landlord also needs a legal reason to end it (see the for-cause eviction note).

Your lease states your chosen notice period; use these minimums as the guardrail.

title: Two Habitability Statements Your Colorado Lease Must Carry
bodyText:
Since January 1, 2025 every Colorado residential lease must carry two separate statements, both in at least twelve-point bold-faced type (C.R.S. 38-12-505(3)(c) and (3)(d)).

- The first says the tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing under the warranty of habitability and that you may not retaliate for reporting unsafe conditions, requesting repairs or asserting that right.
- The second must appear in both English and Spanish, and must give an address where the tenant can mail or hand-deliver written notice of an uninhabitable condition and an email address or online tenant portal for the same notice - both, not either.

Two practical points.

- If you offer an online tenant portal, the same English-and-Spanish statement must also be posted conspicuously inside the portal (38-12-505(3)(e)).
- **Whatever channels your lease names become channels that count:** A tenant notice is sufficient if it uses any method the rental agreement permits (38-12-503(3)(f)(I)), so you have to actually monitor the mailbox, the inbox and the portal. Never name a phone number or any verbal method - a lease that lets the tenant give habitability notice verbally waives your right to written notice entirely (38-12-503(3)(f)(II)).

title: In Colorado, Only the Monthly Rent Is Evictable Rent
bodyText:
Colorado bars you from writing a lease that treats anything except the set monthly payment for occupancy as "rent" with all the rent-collection remedies, eviction included (C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(V)). Utility and service charges are named in the statute, and so is "any other charge that is not rent". A provision that breaks this rule is void and unenforceable (38-12-801(3)(b)), and a late fee gets the same treatment in its own section (38-12-105(7)).

The practical consequence is the part landlords most often get wrong: you can charge pet rent in Colorado, up to the 38-12-106(2) cap, but you cannot evict for it. Online guidance that says unpaid pet rent is grounds for a 10-day demand and an eviction is wrong here. Same for unpaid utility charges, late fees and returned-payment charges: they are real debts you can sue for, but not a basis for a possession action.

Two carve-outs: subsection (3)(a)(V) does not apply to a mobile home in a mobile home park (38-12-801(4)) or to a duplex, triplex or accessory dwelling unit where you live in one of the units or on the same lot (38-12-801(8)).

title: Electronic Notices: What Colorado Will Not Let You Email
bodyText:
Colorado's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act carves residential landlords out of exactly the notices that matter most. It does not apply to any notice of default, acceleration, repossession, foreclosure or eviction, or of the right to cure, under a rental agreement for an individual's primary residence (C.R.S. 24-71.3-103(3)(b)(II)), nor to a notice cancelling or terminating utility service including water, heat and power (3)(b)(I).

So a 10-day demand for payment or compliance, a notice to terminate and a notice of default get no help from the electronic-records statute: email or portal delivery of one of those rests on ordinary proof that it actually reached the tenant, not on a statutory rule that electronic counts as writing.

Three more limits.

- The Act only applies between parties who have each agreed to transact electronically, and a party who agrees once may refuse the next transaction - a right that cannot be waived by agreement (24-71.3-105(2), (3)).
- An electronic record satisfies a writing requirement only if the recipient can retain it at the time of receipt, and if your system stops the tenant printing or storing it the record is not enforceable against them (24-71.3-108(1), (3)).
- Those requirements cannot be varied by agreement (24-71.3-108(4)), so no lease clause fixes any of this.

Send default, cure, termination and eviction notices the way article 40 of title 13 requires, and keep habitability notices separate - those the law positively requires you to accept by email or portal.

title: Mandatory Mediation Before Filing, and the Waiver You Cannot Put in the Lease
bodyText: Before filing an eviction against a residential tenant who receives SSI, Social Security disability insurance under Title II, or Colorado Works cash assistance, you must have gone through mandatory mediation and had it fail, and your complaint must carry an affidavit saying so (C.R.S. 13-40-110(1)(a)). You are exempt if you are a 501(c)(3) that offers tenants mediation, or a landlord with five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five total rental units including any single-family homes. The tenant can also take you out of it by not disclosing, or declining to disclose in writing, that they receive one of those benefits in response to your written inquiry - which is a good reason to make that written inquiry. Mediation is free to the tenant; you pay only your share; the Office of Dispute Resolution must schedule it within 14 days of your request. Getting this wrong is fatal to the case: non-compliance is an affirmative defense and the court "shall dismiss the case without prejudice" (13-40-110(1)(d)). The part that touches your lease: a tenant may voluntarily waive mandatory mediation, "but a waiver must not be in any lease agreement or other agreement" (13-40-110(1)(b)), and 38-12-801(3)(a)(III)(E) separately voids a lease waiver of it. A lease clause also may not let you recoup mediation costs from the tenant (38-12-801(3)(a)(VII)). So the waiver has to be a separate, later, voluntary document - never a lease term.

title: When the Tenant Causes the Damage
bodyText: Colorado handles this in one place rather than remedy by remedy, and it handles it in your favour. If a condition is substantially caused by the misconduct of the tenant, a member of the tenant's household, a guest or invitee, or someone under the tenant's direction or control, that condition "does not constitute a basis for a breach of the warranty of habitability" (C.R.S. 38-12-503(9)). Because every tenant remedy in 38-12-507 - the 10-to-60 day termination right, the recurrence termination right, repair-and-deduct, appliance replace-and-deduct, the damages claim including any reduction in fair rental value, and injunctive relief - is predicated on a breach of that warranty, tenant-caused damage switches all of them off at once. You also stop being the one who pays: 38-12-503(7) makes the landlord responsible for remedying at the landlord's own expense "except as described in subsection (9)". There is one exception to the exception: it is not misconduct if the condition resulted from domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking against the tenant and you have notice of it. Colorado has no casualty or untenantability statute in article 12 giving a tenant a separate right to walk away after a fire, so there is no second door for them to leave by; the only casualty termination is yours, under 38-12-503(11), and it needs your lease to permit it. Recovering the money runs through ordinary channels - the tenant's maintenance obligations, the deposit (38-12-103(1)(b) allows retention for repair of damage beyond normal wear and tear) and a contract claim for lost rent. No special Colorado clause is needed or offered, and a clause purporting to strip abatement rights more broadly than 38-12-503(9) does would be void under 38-12-503(10).

title: Colorado Regulates AI That Prices or Screens Housing
bodyText: Colorado has no rent-setting-cartel statute of the kind some states have passed, but it does have something broader that reaches the same software. The Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act (C.R.S. 6-1-1701 et seq.) regulates systems that make, or substantially contribute to, a "consequential decision" - and housing is one of the listed domains (6-1-1701(3)(f)). If you deploy an AI or algorithmic tool to set rents, score applicants or decide renewals, you are a deployer, with duties to avoid algorithmic discrimination, run a risk-management programme, disclose the system to the consumer and report discovered discrimination (6-1-1702 to 6-1-1705). Violating part 17 is itself a deceptive trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act (6-1-105(1)(hhhh)), which carries treble damages, so the exposure is not theoretical. Watch the date: SB 26-189 repealed and reenacted part 17, and the new version applies to consequential decisions made on or after January 1, 2027, with a narrower "covered domain" structure and express carve-outs for low-stakes and routine decisions. Until then the 2024 version governs. Separately, the Colorado Privacy Act gives consumers an opt-out of profiling in decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects, which it defines to include the provision or denial of housing.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix a Tenant's Neglect and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Colorado gives a landlord no statutory self-cure right of the kind several states have - there is no provision letting you notice a tenant's neglect, do the work yourself and add the cost to the next rent payment. Two Colorado rules get in the way of writing one into the lease. Entry for repairs is governed by the habitability sections rather than a general access statute, so a self-cure entry has no statutory authorisation to rest on. And you could not bill the cost "as rent" even if you did the work: 38-12-801(3)(a)(V) reserves rent, and the remedies that go with it, to the set monthly payment for occupancy. The routes that do work are the ordinary ones - a 10-day demand for compliance or possession under 13-40-104(1)(e), the tenant's maintenance obligations, the security deposit for damage beyond normal wear and tear, and a money claim. Nothing stops you contracting for the right to do the work and recover the cost as a debt rather than as rent, but you would be drafting that from scratch and should take advice first.

title: No Blank-Space Rule, But a Real Copy Duty
bodyText: Colorado has no statute of the kind some states have requiring every blank space in a written lease to be completed, and no consumer-protection provision making a blank-filled-after-signing lease an unlawful practice. What Colorado does have is a copy duty with a deadline: you must give the tenant a copy of the written agreement signed by both of you no later than the seventh day after the tenant signs, and it may be electronic unless the tenant asks for paper (C.R.S. 38-12-801(1)). Colorado also prescribes specific content the agreement must contain - the landlord or agent name and address (38-12-801(2)), the source-of-income statement for a non-exempt landlord (38-12-801(2.5)), and the two bold-faced habitability statements (38-12-505(3)(c) and (3)(d)). So the discipline still applies even without a blank-space statute: fill or strike every bracket and placeholder before anyone signs, because an unfilled habitability-notice address or a missing identity statement is a missing required disclosure, not just an untidy lease.

title: Quiet Enjoyment Is Non-Waivable, With One Carve-Out You May Use
bodyText: Colorado does not spell out a covenant of quiet enjoyment, but it does something more useful to know about: it makes a lease waiver of the implied covenant void. A written rental agreement must not include a waiver of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment, or of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and any provision included in breach of that is void and unenforceable (C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(III)(C), (D) and (3)(b)). The same subsection then hands you a narrow permission: "a written rental agreement may provide that the landlord is not responsible for any violation of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment that is committed by a third party acting beyond the reasonable control of the landlord". That is worth using, and it is the only quiet-enjoyment disclaimer Colorado allows - a broader one is void. Two carve-outs from the prohibition itself: it does not reach a mobile home in a mobile home park (38-12-801(4)) or an owner-occupied duplex, triplex or accessory dwelling unit (38-12-801(8)). Quiet enjoyment also shows up as a limit on entry, which is why the Colorado access clause ties the notice period to it.

title: Statutory Forms in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado prescribes no form of lease, but it does prescribe text and forms you have to use. The radon warning statement is given in the statute's own words and must appear in bold-faced type "in substantially the same form" (C.R.S. 38-12-803(2)(a)(I)), inside a separate document the tenant signs. The source-of-income statement is set out in 38-12-801(2.5)(a) and the two habitability statements in 38-12-505(3)(c) and (3)(d) are prescribed by content, language and type size. On the court side, an eviction is commenced "using the standard form of eviction complaint and affidavit for a residential tenancy that is available online through the judicial department's website" (13-40-110(1)(a)), though the court must accept a different form that meets the section's requirements (13-40-110(1)(f)). The Judicial Branch also publishes the JDF demand, notice, summons, answer and writ forms; those are court forms, not statutory text, and are worth using because they are kept current. No form is prescribed for the 10-day demand itself - what matters is that its content matches 13-40-104.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Colorado statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells. The lease governs, through its alteration and installation terms and its rules on fixing things to the building. If you do allow one, remember that a doorbell camera is an alteration to the property for which the no-alterations clause requires your written consent, and that Colorado's wiretap, eavesdropping and privacy-tort law is the place any recording question gets answered.

title: The Radon Disclosure Cannot Live in the Lease
bodyText:
Colorado does not let the lease carry this one.

Before the lease is signed, you must give the tenant a separate written radon disclosure "in a document that the tenant signs to acknowledge receipt" (C.R.S. 38-12-803(2)(a)), and that document has to contain three things:
- The radon warning statement in bold-faced type, clearly legible and in substantially the form the statute sets out.
- Everything you know about radon at the property - whether a test has been done, the current records and reports, any concentrations detected, any mitigation or remediation performed, and a description and documentation of any mitigation system.
- A copy of the most recent radon brochure the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment publishes.

The tenant acknowledges receipt by signing that document, not the lease (38-12-803(2)(b)).

Your lease's Radon Disclosure Acknowledgment says the tenant received all of that - so if you never produced the separate document, you have had the tenant sign a statement that is not true, which helps them and not you. Produce the document first, get it signed, then sign the lease.

One thing to watch: the statute says "a copy of" the brochure, so emailing a link may not be enough; attach the brochure itself.

title: The Repayment Plan You Must Offer a Victim-Survivor
bodyText: This one is a three-business-day clock that can end your eviction case, and it is easy to miss because it sits in the eviction statute rather than the domestic-violence part. If a tenant tells you they are a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking and backs it with any one of the accepted documents - a police report, a valid protection or restraining order, a self-attestation affidavit, or a letter from a qualified third party such as a victim-service worker, attorney, social worker, medical professional, faith leader or mental health provider - then you shall offer a repayment plan no later than three business days after you serve a demand for unpaid rent, or three business days after you receive the documentation, whichever is later (C.R.S. 13-40-104(4)(e)(I)(A)). Not offering one is an affirmative defense to your unlawful-detainer action. The plan is structured at the tenant's discretion, must require full repayment of all lawfully owed rent in monthly payments of at least $25, and cannot run more than nine months. You may not charge any fees, interest or penalties connected to it (4)(e)(I)(C). The protections cannot be waived in the lease or any other agreement (4)(c). Two things that run in your favour: the tenant waives the affirmative defense if they neither accept your plan nor propose a conforming alternative within seven days of receiving yours; and if they miss a payment or make three or more late ones, you can serve a notice of default demanding all remaining rent and then move for judgment. None of this stops you seeking possession against a different tenant who is the one responsible for the abuse (4)(d).

title: The Terms Colorado Will Not Let Your Lease Contain
bodyText: Colorado gives you a closed list of terms a written rental agreement "must not include", and anything on it that ends up in your lease is void and unenforceable (C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a) and (3)(b)). The list, in the statute's order: a penalty on either party stemming from an eviction notice or an eviction action that results from a lease violation; a one-way fee-shifting clause - any fee-shifting provision must award attorney fees to the prevailing party once the court finds they prevailed and the fee is reasonable; a waiver of the right to a jury trial, except that the parties may agree to waive a jury in a hearing to determine possession; a waiver of the ability to pursue, bring, join, litigate or support any joint, class or collective claim arising from the tenancy; a waiver of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; a waiver of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment, except that the lease may say you are not responsible for a third party's violation of it beyond your reasonable control; a waiver of the mandatory mediation required by 13-40-110(1); a fee, damages or penalty for a tenant failing to give notice of nonrenewal before the end of the agreement, except your actual losses from the missing notice; characterising any amount other than the set monthly payment for occupancy as "rent" with rent remedies including eviction; requiring the tenant to pay a markup or fee on a service a third party bills you, beyond either 2% of what you were billed or $10 a month, but not both; letting a voucher or subsidy provider pursue possession based solely on unpaid utilities; and recouping the cost of mandatory mediation from the tenant. Two practical warnings. The class-action waiver is the one most often imported by accident - it is boilerplate in form leases from other states, and in Colorado it is simply void, so do not paste a lease in from elsewhere without checking. And the nonrenewal item is narrow rather than absent: you cannot charge a fee or a set amount for a missing nonrenewal notice, but your actual losses are still recoverable, so there is nothing to gain from a fee clause and something to lose. Who is exempt: 38-12-801(4) switches off the jury, good-faith, quiet-enjoyment, nonrenewal, fees-as-rent, markup and voucher items for a mobile home in a mobile home park, and 38-12-801(8) switches off the whole waiver group and those same items for a duplex, triplex or accessory dwelling unit where you live in one of the units or on the same lot. The eviction-penalty and fee-shifting items have no exemption and apply to everyone.

title: After You File for Nonpayment, You Must Accept Full Payment Until Judgment
bodyText: If you gave the tenant proper notice of nonpayment, you must accept the tenant's full payment of all amounts lawfully due under that notice, plus any rent that has since come due under the lease or under a repayment plan, at any time until the judge enters judgment for possession (C.R.S. 13-40-115(4)). The tenant can pay you or pay the court. Once the court confirms the full amount was timely paid, it must vacate any judgments already issued and dismiss your case with prejudice, so refusing a full payment to keep the case going does not get you possession. No written agreement can waive this right (13-40-115(5)), which is why the lease leaves the cure period on nonpayment to applicable law rather than stating or limiting it.

title: Colorado Gives You a Landlord's Lien, Not an Abandoned-Property Procedure
bodyText:
Nothing in Colorado's landlord-tenant statutes or its courts title tells you how to notify a tenant about belongings left behind at the end of a tenancy, how long to hold them, or when you may throw them out. The old statute that used to do that was repealed in 1975.

What Colorado gives you instead is a landlord's lien: once the tenant owes you unpaid rent, you have a lien on the household furniture, goods, appliances and other personal property of the tenant and the tenant's household that is on the premises. The lien does not reach pet animals, small kitchen appliances, cooking utensils, beds, bedding, necessary clothing, personal or business records and documents, or personal effects, and it cannot include your attorney fees.

If the tenant has moved out, you must let the tenant and the household back in, at a reasonable time and in a reasonable manner, to take away anything the lien does not cover. If the tenant is still in the unit you may assert the lien, but asserting it in a way that substantially interferes with the tenant's right to occupy and enjoy the unit is itself unlawful, forfeits the lien and exposes you to a damages claim.

To turn the lien into money you normally have to sue to foreclose it within sixty days of the charges falling due, and if you sell without substantially complying with the statute the tenant recovers the value of the property, never less than one hundred dollars, plus attorney fees.

There is a shortcut: if the owner of the property has not contacted you for at least thirty days and you have no good-faith reason to think the owner still wants it, the property is presumed abandoned, you do not have to sue, and you may sell or otherwise dispose of it after sending fifteen days' written notice of the manner and date of disposal to the last address you have, by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested; if that comes back unclaimed you must publish the notice once in a county newspaper. Keep the notice and the receipt or proof of non-delivery for a year.

Two traps.

- **Do not use any of this while the tenant is still in possession:** Locking a tenant out or seizing a home without court process costs actual damages plus the greater of three months' rent or five thousand dollars.
- Property removed during or after a sheriff's execution of a writ of restitution follows a different and much friendlier set of rules.

Because Colorado prescribes nothing for an ordinary move-out, the cautious course is to put your own procedure in the lease, send written notice of where the property is and how to claim it, keep a dated photo inventory even though no statute makes you inventory anything, hold the property for at least thirty days before disposing of it, and send the fifteen-day disposal notice anyway.

Charging the tenant for removal or storage is now governed by Colorado's 2026 fee rules: pass through only the actual third-party charge for handling the tenant's own goods, add no markup, no administrative fee and no escalation, never charge for anything you are obliged to do anyway, never add a charge for paying it late, and never call it rent. Charge nothing at all if the tenancy ended because the tenant died.

Your city or county may impose more, so check local rules. Mobile home parks are governed by Part 2 of Colorado's mobile home law and are not covered here.

Take advice before selling a tenant's belongings.

title: Colorado Has No Re-Letting or Mitigation Statute After a Tenant Walks Out
bodyText: Nothing in Colorado's landlord-tenant statutes or its courts title tells you what to do when a tenant abandons the unit partway through a fixed term. There is no statutory duty to re-let, no statutory deadline for trying, no formula for the damages you may keep claiming, and no statute saying the lease survives the demand you served or the eviction you filed. All of that is left to your lease and to Colorado's general contract law, which only the courts can settle; treat the common-law position as unresolved. What that means in practice is that the lease has to do the work. Say in it that the tenant stays liable for rent as each instalment falls due for the rest of the term, that you may re-enter and re-let for the tenant's account without releasing the tenant, and that anything you collect from a new tenant is credited against what the old tenant owes. Then behave as though a mitigation duty exists: start advertising at the same rent promptly, keep dated evidence of every listing, showing and application, and do not leave the unit sitting while the rent meter runs, because a court applying ordinary contract principles may well cut your claim down to what you could reasonably have avoided. Two drafting traps are statutory and real. You cannot write a clause that penalises the tenant for an eviction notice or an eviction action arising from a lease violation, so an acceleration-of-all-remaining-rent clause or a liquidated-damages clause triggered by the default you are evicting on is void. And you cannot charge a fee, damages or penalty for the tenant failing to give notice that they will not renew, beyond the losses you actually incur. If the tenancy ended because the tenant died, you may not accelerate rent beyond the end of that month or ten business days after the unit is emptied, whichever is later, and you may not charge liquidated damages or any other early-termination penalty at all.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit in Colorado
bodyText:
Colorado backs you up if you want to rent out an accessory dwelling unit, but only in part of the state.

In what the statute calls a subject jurisdiction, the local government has had to allow one accessory dwelling unit as an accessory use to a single-unit detached dwelling, anywhere it allows single-unit detached dwellings, since June 30, 2025, and it must decide the application through an administrative process against objective standards with no public hearing. More importantly for you as a landlord, that local government may not require the accessory dwelling unit, or any other dwelling on the same lot, to be owner-occupied. It may still ask you to show you live on the parcel when you apply to build or convert the unit, and it may still require that when you apply for a short-term-rental licence, and it keeps a long list of other powers: parking in limited cases, size limits, non-restrictive design standards, impact fees, historic-district standards, life-safety and building codes, short-term-rental rules, and a water or wastewater capacity statement.

A subject jurisdiction is a municipality of at least a thousand people inside a metropolitan planning organization, or the part of a county inside both a census designated place of at least forty thousand and a metropolitan planning organization, and the rules do not apply to an exempt parcel - no domestic water and sewage treatment or a well that cannot serve another unit, a historic property outside a historic district, or a floodway or hundred-year floodplain. Outside a subject jurisdiction your local zoning still controls, and the state rules do not help you; check your city or county code.

If the property is in a homeowners' or condominium association, a declaration, bylaw or rule that restricts creating an accessory dwelling unit in a way the state statute forbids is void as a matter of public policy, whether it was adopted before or after May 13, 2024, though reasonable restrictions survive.

Two things change inside your lease once the unit is an accessory dwelling unit on a lot where the owner lives, or where the owner's primary residence is on the same lot.

- **Several of Colorado's prohibited lease terms stop applying to you:** The bans on waiving a jury trial, class claims, good faith and fair dealing and quiet enjoyment, on nonrenewal-notice penalties, on treating non-rent amounts as rent, on third-party-billing markups, and on voucher-provider possession actions for unpaid utilities. That is an exemption in your favour, not a limit on you, but the clauses here are still drafted to the stricter standard, and the ban on eviction-penalty clauses and on one-way attorney fee clauses still applies to you.
- Colorado's for-cause eviction rules do not apply at all, so you are not confined to the statutory list of causes after twelve months.

Record the lot layout, the shared areas and who occupies the primary residence in the lease, because those are the facts that prove both exemptions if they are ever questioned.

title: Colorado Will Not Let Your Lease Invent a Notice Method
bodyText:
Colorado has no statute letting you and your tenant agree on an extra or substitute way of giving a notice the law requires, and no general "actual notice is enough" rule for tenancies. For the notices that start an eviction - a demand for possession or compliance, a notice to vacate, or a no-fault eviction notice - the statute names the only ways to serve: hand the copy to a known tenant occupying the premises, or leave it with a person or family member older than fifteen who lives on or is in charge of the premises, or, if nobody is there after attempts at personal service on at least two separate days, post it in a conspicuous place on the premises. A text message, an email, a note under the door or an app notification is not one of those methods, and a lease clause saying it is will not make it one.

Colorado does use the phrase actual notice in two places, and neither helps you give a statutory notice a new way.

- **The first runs against you rather than for you.** Since 6 August 2025, if a tenant gives you written or actual notice that they are a victim-survivor of unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse, you must make all reasonable efforts to serve that tenant personally, and only if personal service fails after three attempts may you fall back on posting plus certified mail or a commercial courier with a receipt or other proof of delivery. Note what "actual notice" means there: the tenant does not have to put it in writing, so a spoken word to you or your manager counts, and you cannot require a form. If the tenant tells you and consents to your telling the court, you must disclose it on the complaint or with the return of service. So train whoever takes your calls to record any such disclosure the day it is made.
- **The second is about the security deposit, not about serving notices:** From 1 January 2026 you are deemed to have delivered the deposit statement, payment and documentation by sending them to the tenant's last-known address or to any email address for the tenant that you have actual notice of, so an email address the tenant gave you verbally can satisfy that duty.

Separately, Colorado's habitability rules do treat electronic and digital records as writing, but that definition expressly does not reach the notice and demand requirements in the eviction article.

The cautious course is to serve statutory notices only by the statutory methods, keep a dated affidavit of how each was served, and treat any extra method your lease allows - email, text, a portal message - as a courtesy copy that never replaces statutory service.

title: Colorado Does Not Make You Tell Your Tenant About a Foreclosure
bodyText:
Nothing in Colorado law requires you to tell a tenant that the property is being foreclosed, condemned, taken by eminent domain, sold at a tax sale or put into receivership, and nothing requires you to disclose a pending or threatened lawsuit about the property before or during a tenancy.

Colorado handles the foreclosure case differently: the notice goes to the property rather than through you. The mailing list the foreclosing party gives the public trustee or sheriff must include the occupant of the property, addressed simply to "occupant" at the property address, and for a public trustee sale it must include a lessee with an unrecorded possessory interest, at the premises and at the property address, where the lender wants the foreclosure to wipe out that possessory interest. That notice goes by regular mail and is complete on mailing. So your tenant will usually be told, by someone other than you, and often before you have said anything. If the tenant's residential lease is recorded, the tenant keeps separate rights under the foreclosure article; most residential leases are not recorded.

The practical consequences are worth planning for.

- A tenant who opens an "occupant" letter and learns the building is in foreclosure, from a stranger, is a tenant who stops paying and starts looking. If the property is at risk, tell them yourself first, in writing, and tell them what it means for their lease.
- Make sure your lease requires the tenant to forward anything that arrives at the premises from a court, sheriff, public trustee, lender, association or agency, because if you do not live at the property that may be your only warning.

Colorado does impose a real adverse-proceeding notice duty in one place only: a mobile home park landlord must notify home owners of an intent to sell the park within fourteen days of a triggering event, and receiving a notice of election and demand or a lis pendens about a foreclosure of the park, or notice that a certificate of levy has been filed, is one of the listed triggering events; a change of use needs twelve months' notice. That regime is Part 2 of Colorado's mobile home law and does not reach ordinary site-built rentals.

FEDERAL: federal law can give a tenant extra notice rights when a federally related property changes hands after foreclosure, which is separate from Colorado law.

title: Colorado Legislates Carbon Monoxide Alarms, Not Smoke Alarms
bodyText:
Colorado's alarm statute covers carbon monoxide only. The Colorado Revised Statutes mention a "smoke alarm" or "smoke detector" only twice, both in the definition of a carbon monoxide alarm. So your smoke-alarm obligation does not come from the landlord-tenant statutes; it comes from whatever building, housing and fire codes apply where the property is, and the warranty of habitability then makes a code violation a habitability problem if it would materially interfere with the tenant's life, health or safety. Treat smoke alarms as a code question, check the codes your jurisdiction has adopted, and do not assume the absence of a statute means the absence of a duty.

Carbon monoxide is different and precise. It bites on a rental in two situations: when interior alterations, repairs, fuel-fired appliance replacements or additions requiring a building permit happen, or a sleeping room is added, and separately on any change in tenant occupancy. That second trigger is the one landlords miss - every turnover brings the unit under the rule. It applies if the dwelling has fuel-fired appliances or an attached garage. Fuel means coal, kerosene, oil, fuel gases or other petroleum or hydrocarbon products such as wood.

When it applies, an operational alarm must sit within fifteen feet of the entrance to every room lawfully used for sleeping, or wherever the adopted building code specifies. In a rental multi-family building with a centralized alarm system or another way for a responsible person to hear the alarm at all times, you may instead put an operational alarm within twenty-five feet of each fuel-fired heater or appliance, fireplace or garage.
