The alarm must be listed by a recognised testing laboratory, be audible and distinct, and be battery powered, plugged in with battery backup, wired in with battery backup, or connected through an electrical panel; a combined smoke and carbon monoxide unit is allowed if it meets both sets of law and clearly differentiates the two hazards.

The duties split.

- Before a new tenancy you must replace any carbon monoxide alarm that was stolen, removed, found missing or found not operational after the last occupancy, and you must provide the tenant with any batteries needed to make it work at the time they take residence.
- During the tenancy the tenant must keep, test and maintain the alarms in good repair and must notify you in writing if batteries need replacing, if an alarm is stolen, removed, missing or not operational, or of any deficiency they cannot correct; you must then replace the alarm or fix the deficiency. Outside those four duties the statute says you are not responsible for maintenance, repair, replacement or batteries.

Nobody - you, the tenant or anyone else - may remove batteries from or otherwise disable a carbon monoxide alarm except while inspecting, maintaining, repairing or replacing it or its batteries.

There is a real shield if you comply: no one has a claim against a property owner, their authorised agent, a person in possession or an installer for damages resulting from the operation, maintenance or effectiveness of a carbon monoxide alarm installed in accordance with the manufacturer's published instructions and the statute. So document the make, model, location and install date, keep the manufacturer's instructions, and photograph each alarm at every turnover.

Finally, the statute is a floor, not a ceiling: any municipality, city and county or county may impose stricter installation and maintenance requirements, so check yours.

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee in Colorado - Charge the Actual Damage Instead
bodyText: Colorado forbids anyone from removing the batteries from, or in any way rendering inoperable, a carbon monoxide alarm except while inspecting, maintaining, repairing or replacing it or its batteries. What it does not do is attach any consequence. There is no fee, no penalty, no fine and no criminal offence anywhere in Colorado law for tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and nothing authorises you to put a tampering fee in your lease. Do not try. Colorado's 2026 fee rules bar you from requiring a tenant to pay a charge for a good, service or property necessary to comply with your own obligations, and replacing a carbon monoxide alarm that a tenant reports as removed, missing or not working is your obligation under the alarm statute. They also bar a charge above the actual total price of the thing charged for, a charge for something you do not actually provide, and any charge for the late payment of a non-rent amount. A fee that breaks those rules is a prohibited lease clause, void and unenforceable, and charging it is treated as a deceptive, unfair and unconscionable act, with a fourteen-day demand route and eighteen percent interest on top of actual damages. The route that does work is ordinary damage recovery. If the tenant, or someone the tenant lets in, breaks, defaces or destroys an alarm, that is tenant-caused damage beyond normal wear and tear, and you recover the actual documented cost of repair or replacement the same way as any other damage - from the deposit with the itemised written statement the deposit statute requires, or as a damages claim. Keep the evidence: photograph each alarm at move-in and move-out with the date, log every alarm report the tenant makes, and keep the invoice for any replacement. Do not bill a flat sum, do not add a markup or an administrative charge, do not add a late charge to it, and do not call it rent. And remember the split of duties: you must supply working alarms and the batteries at move-in and replace or fix an alarm the tenant reports, while the tenant must keep, test and maintain them and report problems in writing. A tenant who disables an alarm is breaching the lease, which is a cleaner lever than a fee.

title: Colorado Gives You No Right to Enter for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText:
There is nothing in Colorado law that lets you into a tenant's home to feed, water, care for or take away the tenant's animal, however obvious the emergency looks. Colorado's statutes mention a landlord and an animal in only three places, and none of them is about entry: the pet deposit and pet rent limits, the landlord's lien, which expressly does not attach to pet animals, and the rules about pets when a sheriff executes a writ of restitution. That last one is the only time Colorado tells anyone to take charge of a tenant's pet, and it is the officer who does it, not you: the officer must inspect for pet animals, hand them to the tenant if the tenant is there, and otherwise contact the local authority in charge of animal control, while you must give that authority access to remove or secure the animals, post a notice at the premises saying where they were taken, and give the tenant the same information on request. Outside that, entering without consent is just entering without consent, with all the exposure that carries, including Colorado's severe unlawful-removal penalties if the entry shuts the tenant out.

So do two things instead.

- **Get the tenant's consent in advance, in the lease:** Ask for every animal in writing, ask for a named emergency carer and phone number, and take the tenant's permission to let that person in for that purpose only if the tenant cannot be reached. That consent is what makes the entry lawful, so keep the contact details current and record every attempt to reach the tenant before you use it.
- When there is no reachable carer, call the local authority in charge of animal control or local law enforcement and let them act. If you report suspected cruelty in good faith to a local law enforcement agency or to the state bureau of animal protection, Colorado gives you immunity from civil liability for making the report; that immunity does not cover a report you know to be false, which is a civil infraction.

Note that the tenant's consent ends at the tenant's death, after which you deal with the animals through the personal representative or heirs, or as the law otherwise allows.

Your city or county may have its own animal rules; check local rules.

title: You Need Not Supply an Appliance, But You Cannot Disclaim One You Do
bodyText:
Colorado settles this in a single definition, and it cuts both ways. Nothing in the habitability rules requires you to provide any appliance at all. But those rules apply to an appliance to the extent it is part of a written agreement with the tenant or is otherwise actually provided to the tenant by you, at the start of or during the tenancy, for the length of the lease.

So the lease cannot disclaim an appliance you actually hand over. Leaving a working fridge in the kitchen and writing "landlord does not maintain the refrigerator" does not work: you provided it, so it is in, and a functioning appliance maintained in good working order is one of the listed habitability characteristics. Nor can the tenant agree otherwise, because nothing in the habitability rules can be waived.

Note how narrow the statutory word is. "Appliance" there means a refrigerator, range stove, oven, air conditioner, permanent cooling device or portable cooling device included in the premises by a landlord. A dishwasher, washing machine, dryer, microwave, garbage disposal or freezer is not on that list, so the appliance characteristic does not reach it. That is not a free pass: a premises can still be uninhabitable because it is otherwise unfit for human habitation, or because of a code violation that materially interferes with life, health or safety, and a leaking dishwasher or a dryer vented into a closet will get you there by another route.

So the exclusion you can actually rely on is narrow. Use it for items the tenant owns and brings, and for items you genuinely do not provide and will remove on request. The clean way to handle a non-listed item you do not want to maintain is to take it out before the tenancy starts rather than leave it with a disclaimer.

Whatever you exclude, do not charge for it: Colorado's 2026 fee rules bar you from requiring a tenant to pay for a good, service or property not actually provided, and from charging for anything necessary to meet your own obligations.

Two more things.

- Write down, with photos and dates, exactly what is at the property at move-in and who owns each item, because the argument later is always about what was provided.
- If the property is a single-family residence and you receive no government subsidy, Colorado does allow one narrow way to shift repair work to the tenant: a good-faith written agreement separate from the lease, signed, supported by adequate consideration, covering specified repairs, only where the tenant has the requisite skills - and never where the work would endanger the tenant's health or safety. That is a separate document, not a lease clause.

title: Colorado Has No Asbestos Disclosure Duty - But Abatement Rules Catch Rentals
bodyText: No Colorado statute requires you to test a rental for asbestos, to tell a tenant that asbestos is or may be present, or to put an asbestos warning in the lease. What Colorado regulates is the work itself, and that is where rentals get caught. Asbestos abatement in an area of public access must be done under a state certificate, by certified workers, supervised by a certified trained supervisor who is on site at all times while work is in progress, with an air pollution permit. The definition of an area of public access expressly includes a single-family residential dwelling, and the only way out is an opt-out available to a homeowner who lives in the single-family dwelling as their own primary residence, on a form from the state division. A landlord is not that homeowner. So the homeowner exemption that lets an owner-occupier strip their own basement pipes does not cover you, and neither does the separate exemption for an individual doing abatement on their own primary residence. Treat every asbestos job at a rental as a regulated project. The state rules bite above a floor: for a single-family residential dwelling, fifty linear feet on pipes, thirty-two square feet on other materials, or the equivalent of a fifty-five gallon drum; for anything larger, a higher threshold. Below the floor the certification and permit scheme does not apply, but the material is still what it is and your habitability and general duties do not go away. Separately, when you apply for a permit to renovate or demolish, the local permitting authority must ask you to disclose on the application whether you know if the property has been inspected for asbestos, so an inspection you commissioned becomes a document you will be asked about. That disclosure goes to the permitting office, not the tenant. Practical course, since the state leaves this to you: in a building likely to contain asbestos, have a survey done before any work that disturbs material, keep the report, use a certified abatement contractor, and tell tenants in writing before work starts what will happen and when, because a disturbance that makes the unit unfit to live in becomes a habitability problem and could entitle the tenant to remedies even though no asbestos statute applies. Do not volunteer a vague asbestos warning in the lease with nothing behind it; if you do disclose, disclose what you actually know and can document. Note that Colorado's asbestos part is scheduled to be repealed effective September 1, 2027 subject to legislative review, so check whether it has been continued before relying on it. Your city or county may add requirements. FEDERAL: federal asbestos rules, including the rules for schools and for worker protection, apply independently of Colorado law and are not restated here.

title: No Colorado Rule Makes You Disclose the Association's Documents - But You Cannot Bill the Tenant for Them
bodyText:
Colorado requires nothing here. If you rent out a condominium, townhome or a house in a covenanted subdivision, no statute makes your lease disclose the association's obligations, attach its declaration, bylaws or rules, or give the association a copy of the lease. The association's own disclosure duties run to unit owners, which means to you, not to your tenant: the association must make its identity, agent, budget, assessments, financial statements, audit, insurance and bylaws available to unit owners on reasonable notice, and its responsible-governance policies cover inspection and copying of records by unit owners. Fines and enforcement work the same way - the association notices and fines the unit owner, with its own cure periods and a bar on daily fines, so a covenant violation by your tenant lands on you.

There is one exception that gives a tenant rights directly: if the declaration requires votes on specified matters to be cast by lessees rather than unit owners, then lessees get notice of meetings, access to records and the other rights on those matters as if they were unit owners, and you lose your vote on them. Read your declaration before assuming you control the vote.

Because the state says nothing, the lease has to do the work, and it is worth doing: hand over the rules before signing, list what you handed over, bind the tenant to comply, and pass on amendments.

The part to get right is money. Colorado's 2026 fee rules bar you from requiring a tenant to pay any fee, charge or amount for the maintenance of common areas, and "common areas" is defined broadly enough to include the grounds, areas and facilities held out for tenants generally - which is what association assessments mostly pay for. They also bar a charge for anything necessary to comply with your own obligations, a charge above the actual price of the thing charged for, a charge for something not actually provided, and any charge for the late payment of a non-rent amount. So do not add an "HOA fee", an "amenity fee" or an assessment pass-through to the rent as a separate line; set the rent at a level that covers the assessments instead, because rent itself is not a fee.

A fine caused by the tenant is closer to the line. The cautious course is to treat it as your actual documented loss from the tenant's breach rather than as a lease fee: give the tenant a copy of the association's notice and a real chance to cure, charge only what the association actually charged you, add no markup and no late charge, charge nothing if the association withdraws or reduces it, and never call it rent. Getting a fee wrong here is expensive, because a prohibited fee clause is void and charging it counts as a deceptive, unfair and unconscionable act with a fourteen-day demand route and eighteen percent interest on top of actual damages.

title: Automatic Renewal: Colorado's Consumer Statute May Reach Your Lease
bodyText:
Colorado has no statute about automatically renewing a lease. Nothing requires an auto-renewal clause, nothing forbids one, and nothing sets the notice you must give before a rollover. So if you want the lease to roll over rather than end on its last day, the clause is yours to write - but three bodies of Colorado law shape it, and one of them is easy to miss.

- **The one that is easy to miss is Colorado's consumer automatic-renewal statute.** It covers an arrangement in which a paid subscription or purchasing agreement renews automatically at the end of a definite term, and when it applies the person offering it must present the renewal terms clearly and conspicuously before the contract is signed, keep any renewal term to a year or less without the consumer's express written consent for longer, give a retainable written acknowledgment with the cancellation policy and how to cancel, provide a simple, cost-effective, timely, easy-to-use and readily accessible way to cancel, give notice of any material change, and send a reminder at least twenty-five and no more than forty days before each renewal. Does it reach a residential lease? Nobody can say for certain. A lease is not obviously a paid subscription or a purchasing agreement, and the statute never mentions a landlord, a tenant or a dwelling. But the definition of consumer covers a person who acquires something by purchase or lease, and from 16 February 2026 it no longer has to be for personal, family or household purposes, because that limit was deleted. A 2025 act also replaced the cancellation-mechanism rules with tighter one-step online cancellation requirements. Only a court or the attorney general can settle whether leases are in. The cautious course is to write the clause so that it complies whether or not the statute applies: that costs you a reminder letter and a cancellation route, and it buys certainty. One comfort - enforcement of that statute rests exclusively with the attorney general and the district attorneys, so there is no private right of action for a tenant under it.
- **The second body of law is the ban on nonrenewal penalties.** Your lease must not impose any fee, damages or penalty on a tenant for failing to give notice that they will not renew, beyond the losses you actually incur because the notice was missing. A flat "failure to give 60 days' notice" charge is void.
- **The third is Colorado's own notice and cause regime.** A fixed-term lease ending on a set date no longer lets you skip notice, you cannot raise the rent more than once in any twelve-month period of consecutive occupancy whatever the form of the tenancy, and once a tenant has been in place twelve months the for-cause rules may mean you need a statutory reason to refuse to renew at all. Auto-renewal can help you there, because the tenancy simply continues.

Keep the renewal term to a year or less, send the reminder, honour the cancellation route, and never charge for a non-renewal.

title: Colorado Has No Balcony Inspection Law - Your Duty Comes From Habitability
bodyText: Several states now require a licensed inspection of balconies, decks and elevated walkways on a fixed cycle, with a written report and a deadline for repairs. Colorado has nothing like it. Searching the entire Colorado Revised Statutes turns up no inspection, survey, certification or engineer's report requirement for a balcony, deck, landing, stair or elevated walkway, and no inspection interval. That is not the same as having no duty. Colorado's warranty of habitability makes a rental uninhabitable if it substantially lacks floors, stairways, elevators and railings maintained in good repair, or if it fails to comply with an applicable building, housing or health code where the violation would materially interfere with the tenant's life, health or safety, or if it is otherwise unfit for human habitation. A rotting balcony or a loose railing lands in all three. The warranty is non-waivable, you have to make sure the premises is fit before you lease it, and once a tenant gives you written notice of an uninhabitable condition your repair clock starts. Inaccessible fire exits or egress are separately presumed to interfere materially with life, health and safety, which matters where a balcony is part of an egress route. So treat inspection as risk management rather than compliance. Walk every balcony, deck, exterior stair and elevated walkway at least once a year and after any heavy snow load, freeze-thaw cycle or storm; look at the ledger connection to the building, the flashing, the fasteners, the decking and the railing height and rigidity; write down and date what you found and what you did; and get a structural engineer or qualified contractor to look at anything you are not sure about, because the cost of the inspection is trivial next to a collapse. Keep the records: with no statutory inspection standard, your own documented programme is the best evidence that you met your habitability duty. If the property is in a common interest community, the balcony may be a limited common element that the association maintains under the declaration, so read the declaration before you assume the work is yours - or that it is not. Your city or county may impose inspection requirements of its own, and we do not research local codes, so check.

title: Bed Bugs: What the Tenant Must Do, and the Clock You Are On
bodyText:
Colorado's bed bug law is unusual in that it tells the tenant what to do, not just you. The tenant must promptly notify you in writing or electronically when they know or reasonably suspect their unit has bed bugs - and if they do it electronically they must send it to the email address, phone number or portal your rental agreement specifies. So specify one. If the lease is silent, the tenant may use any channel you have previously used to contact them, which is how a bed bug report ends up in a text thread nobody reads. The tenant must also keep proof of delivery.

Then your clock starts, and it is short.

- Within ninety-six hours of receiving notice of bed bugs or their possible presence, after giving the tenant entry notice, you must obtain an inspection of the unit by a qualified inspector.
- If that inspection confirms bed bugs, you must have all contiguous units inspected as promptly as reasonably practical - contiguous meaning next-door units you own, manage, lease or sublease.
- You must tell the tenant in writing within two business days after any inspection whether the unit has bed bugs; if the inspector finds none, that notice must also tell the tenant they may contact the local health department if still concerned.
- If bed bugs are found, the inspector reports to you within twenty-four hours and you must commence reasonable treatment measures within five business days of the inspection date.

On entry, you give at least forty-eight hours' written or electronic notice before you, the inspector or the pest control agent try to enter - but the statute expressly lets the rental agreement set a different minimum, and the tenant may waive the notice altogether, so this is one of the few places Colorado invites you to write your own number. Once noticed, the tenant may not unreasonably deny access. The inspector may do an initial visual and manual inspection of bedding and upholstered furniture, may inspect other items where that is necessary and reasonable, and if bed bugs are found may have whatever further access to the tenant's belongings is necessary and reasonable.

On money, read the split carefully.

- You pay all costs of inspection and treatment.
- The tenant pays all costs of preparing the unit for inspection and treatment.
- A tenant who knowingly and unreasonably fails to comply becomes liable for the cost of treating their unit and the contiguous units where the need arose from that non-compliance - a narrow exception, keyed to non-compliance, not to who brought the bugs in.

Do not write a clause making the tenant pay for treatment because the infestation was their fault: Colorado puts that cost on you, and a fee that contradicts the statute is a prohibited lease term and void, and charging it counts as a deceptive, unfair and unconscionable act.

If a tenant stonewalls, the statute gives you a court route: you may seek injunctive relief against a tenant who refuses reasonable access or fails to comply with a reasonable request for inspection or treatment, and the court may order access, order treatment measures, or assess the tenant with costs and damages; any such order must be served on the tenant at least twenty-four hours before entry.

Two more points worth having.

- You must not offer for rent a unit you know or reasonably suspect has bed bugs, and on request you must disclose whether the unit had bed bugs in the previous eight months and the last date it was inspected and found clear.
- **Compliance pays:** A landlord who complies with the bed bug part is deemed to have satisfied the warranty of habitability on bed bug matters.
- Nothing requires you to provide alternative lodging or to replace the tenant's property, and nothing displaces disability accommodation law.

title: Why This Library Does Not Give You an Arbitration Clause for Colorado
bodyText: Colorado has a general arbitration act and no statute saying a residential lease may or may not contain an arbitration clause. Under that act a written agreement to arbitrate an existing or future dispute is valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on grounds that would let you revoke any contract, the court rather than the arbitrator decides whether an arbitration agreement exists and covers the dispute, and certain protections cannot be waived in advance - among them the right to a lawyer at the hearing, the right to notice that an arbitration has been started, the arbitrator's duty to disclose conflicts, and the rules on vacating an award. So in the abstract you could write one. In a Colorado residential lease you should not, for four reasons. First, your lease must not waive the tenant's right to a jury trial, with one exception: the parties may agree to waive a jury in a hearing to determine possession of the dwelling unit. An arbitration clause takes every dispute away from a jury, so the most natural reading is that it does what the statute forbids. Second, your lease must not waive the ability to pursue, bring, join, litigate or support any joint, class or collective claim arising from or relating to the term of the tenancy - which is the class-action waiver that is the main commercial reason landlords want arbitration in the first place. Third, your lease must not waive the mandatory mediation required before filing an eviction against certain tenants receiving disability or public assistance, and it must not let you recoup the costs of that mediation. Fourth, any fee-shifting in the clause has to run to the prevailing party, not to you alone, and a court has to find both that the party prevailed and that the fee is reasonable. Three further traps. A mobile home park agreement must not bind a home owner to arbitration instead of a civil trial at all; such a provision is against public policy, unenforceable and void. Since 19 May 2026, a predispute arbitration agreement and a predispute joint-action waiver are not valid or enforceable at the election of a person alleging sexual harassment or sexual misconduct, and the court, not the arbitrator, decides that even if your clause says otherwise. And Colorado's for-cause eviction rules cannot be contracted around by any provision of a rental agreement. Note one place the prohibitions do not reach you: the jury-waiver, class-waiver, mediation-waiver, nonrenewal-penalty, fees-as-rent, third-party-markup and voucher-utilities prohibitions do not apply to a mobile home in a park, nor to a duplex, triplex or accessory dwelling unit where you use the premises or one of the units as your own primary residence or your primary residence is on the same lot. That is an exemption in your favour, so for those small owner-occupied properties an arbitration clause with a class waiver is not caught by the prohibited-clause list - but the sexual-harassment carve-out and the mobile-home ban still apply, and this library does not offer the clause. If you want arbitration anyway, add your own clause and take advice first. FEDERAL: the Federal Arbitration Act also bears on the enforceability of arbitration clauses and may preempt parts of state law; it is federal and is not restated.

title: Colorado's Constitution Lets You Ban Cannabis Outright
bodyText:
Colorado legalised adult-use marijuana in its constitution, and in the same breath protected you. The amendment says nothing in it stops a person, employer, school, hospital, detention facility, corporation or any other entity who occupies, owns or controls a property from prohibiting or otherwise regulating the possession, consumption, use, display, transfer, distribution, sale, transportation or growing of marijuana on or in that property. That list is wide enough to cover a total ban, not just a smoking ban, and it applies to your rental. Nothing in Colorado's statutes cuts it back: there is no housing protection anywhere in the code for a medical marijuana cardholder or for any other cannabis user, and no statute telling you what a lease may or may not restrict. The medical amendment exempts only health insurers and employers, and says nothing at all about landlords.

So you choose. You may ban smoking and vaping only, or ban growing only, or ban possession and use in every form.

Three practical points.

- **Growing is where your ground is firmest:** Even for a lawful adult user, home growing is legal only up to six plants with no more than three mature and flowering, only in an enclosed locked space, not openly or publicly, and not for sale - so a cultivation ban in the lease protects you against the mould, humidity, electrical load and odour problems that a grow in a rental actually causes, and against the risk that the tenant exceeds those limits.
- **Get the restriction into the lease at signing.** A rule you add later binds the tenant only if you change the terms lawfully, which for most Colorado tenancies means notice and, after twelve months of tenancy, the constraints of the for-cause rules.
- The constitutional definition of marijuana excludes industrial hemp and some hemp-derived products, so a clause worded only against marijuana may not catch a hemp or CBD product; say what you mean.

Two things to handle carefully rather than by blanket rule.

- A tenant who asks for a disability-related accommodation involving cannabis is making a fair-housing request, and that has to be considered on its own merits rather than refused by pointing at the lease; take advice.
- A cannabis restriction is best enforced as an ordinary lease breach, not by treating cannabis as criminal activity, since adult use within the constitutional limits is not a crime in Colorado.

FEDERAL: marijuana remains federally controlled and that bears on federally assisted housing and on lenders and insurers, and it is not covered here.

Mobile home parks have their own regime.

title: A Mandatory Carpet Cleaning Clause Is Now Void in Colorado
bodyText:
If your Colorado lease says the tenant must have the carpets professionally cleaned at move-out, or charges a carpet cleaning fee, that provision is void from 1 January 2026.

Colorado made two changes at once and together they close the door.

- Any provision in or pertaining to a rental agreement that assigns a fee or charge to a tenant for repairs, cleaning or other necessary work due to normal wear and tear, or for any damage or defective condition that preexisted the tenancy, is against public policy and void - and so is any provision that waives or modifies, for the tenant's benefit, anything in the security deposit part.
- "normal wear and tear" was rewritten to mean deterioration, damage or uncleanliness arising from the use for which the unit is intended or reasonably and typically used, without negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse. Carpet that is simply soiled from a family living on it is now squarely normal wear and tear.

There is one opening, and it is narrow: normal wear and tear expressly does not include uncleanliness that renders the dwelling unit substantially less clean than it was when the lease began. So you may recover cleaning cost where the tenant leaves the place materially dirtier than they found it - a pet-urine-soaked carpet, not a faded traffic lane. Charge the actual documented cost of restoring it, not a flat fee, and nothing else.

Two related rules reinforce this.

- The list of things you may retain a deposit for was narrowed, and the old entry for "cleaning contracted for by the tenant" was deleted, so a cleaning charge now has to survive as a lawful charge listed in the lease or as necessary repair work exceeding normal wear and tear that did not preexist the tenancy.
- **Carpet replacement has its own limits:** No retention for replacing carpet throughout the unit unless there is substantial and irreparable damage beyond normal wear and tear that did not preexist the tenancy, replacement of only the damaged portion otherwise, the same approach for interior painting, and carpet may not be deemed substantially and irreparably damaged at all if it has not been replaced with new carpet within the ten years before the lease ended or the premises were surrendered.

Getting this wrong is expensive. Wrongfully withholding a deposit, which now includes retaining an amount that unreasonably exceeds your actual damages - presumed where you keep 125 percent or more of them - forfeits your right to withhold anything and exposes you to treble the withheld amount plus attorney fees and costs, with the burden on you to prove both the amount of your actual damages and that you complied.

So document instead of charging: photograph the carpets at move-in and move-out with dates, note the carpet's age and last replacement date, offer the walk-through inspection either party may now request before the lease ends and after furniture is out, and keep the receipts and invoices you will have to hand over on a written request.

If the property is a mobile home in a mobile home park, the walk-through right and the carpet and paint rules do not apply.

title: Which Casualty and Re-Renting Rules Your Colorado Lease Can Change
bodyText: Colorado splits this in two. The casualty side you cannot change: fire, flood, wildfire, a toxic release or any other event that makes the home unfit to live in is handled by Colorado's habitability rules, and any lease term that waives or modifies a right, remedy, obligation or prohibition in those rules is void. So you cannot shift the cost of casualty repairs to the tenant, cannot write away the relocation and per diem duties that arise when a condition makes the home unsafe, and cannot make the tenant give up habitability remedies in exchange for a lower rent. One casualty power does depend on your lease: where a sudden environmental public health event or a government action makes continued occupancy impossible or unlawful, you may end the lease without further liability only if your lease says you may, and only if you meet every condition the statute attaches, including thirty days' written notice, returning the full deposit by the termination date, giving access to retrieve belongings, and prorating rent for the uninhabitable period. If your lease is silent, you do not have that power at all, so put it in writing. The re-renting side is the opposite: Colorado has no statute that makes you mitigate your loss by re-renting after a tenant walks out, and no statute stopping your lease from dealing with it. That leaves it to your lease and to general Colorado contract law, where a court may still expect a landlord to act reasonably. The cautious course is to write the lease so the tenant stays liable for rent until the home is re-rented or the term ends, whichever comes first, to re-rent promptly anyway, and to keep records of what you did — a clause that tells the tenant you may leave the home empty and collect full rent to the end of the term is the one most likely to be cut down. Do not write a liquidated-damages or accelerated-rent charge into the lease for an early move-out without advice: separate Colorado rules void such charges when the tenancy ends because the tenant died, and bar fees tied to an eviction.

title: No Certificate-of-Occupancy Disclosure Duty in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado puts no certificate-of-occupancy duty on you as a landlord. There is no state statute telling you to show a tenant the certificate, to say in the lease whether the home has one, or to prove one exists before you rent, and no state statute says a lease is void or rent uncollectable because the certificate is missing. That is because certificates of occupancy are issued by your city or county building department under local code, not by the state. So the real question is a local one: many Colorado municipalities and counties require a certificate of occupancy before a dwelling may be lawfully occupied, and some require a rental licence or an inspection on top of it, with their own penalties. Check with the building department where the property sits before you advertise, and keep the certificate and any inspection records in your file. Two practical points follow. First, a missing certificate does not reduce what you owe the tenant: your habitability duty runs from the day the tenant moves in whatever the paperwork says, and a condition that makes the home unfit is a breach no matter how the unit was permitted. Second, renting a space that was never approved for living in, such as a basement or garage conversion, is where this usually goes wrong — the local enforcement action, not a state disclosure rule, is the risk. If you want to put something in the lease, the safe version is a statement that the home is approved for residential occupancy and that the tenant will use it only as a home; do not promise a certificate you have not seen. Colorado does require two other rental disclosures that landlords often confuse with this one: a written elevated-radon disclosure and warning, and bed bug history if the tenant asks for it.

title: Children in the Household: A Protected Class, Not a Lease Term
bodyText: Colorado requires nothing in your lease about children, and that silence is deliberate — children are handled as a discrimination question instead. Familial status is a protected class, which in Colorado means one or more people under eighteen living with a parent or someone with legal custody or parental responsibilities, and it also covers a pregnant applicant and someone in the process of getting custody. So you may not refuse to rent, refuse to show, or make a home unavailable because the household includes children; you may not set different terms, rent, deposit, rules or facilities for a household with children; you may not advertise a preference against children; and — the one that catches landlords out — you may not ask about children or make a record of it. That last point means you should not put a question about children on your application, and should not write a clause that counts children separately or forbids them. If you want to know who will live in the home, ask for the names of all occupants without asking their ages or relationships, which is what a straightforward permitted-occupants clause does. What you may still do is set a neutral occupancy limit: Colorado's discrimination rule expressly does not override a reasonable state, local or federal cap on the maximum number of occupants, so a limit written per bedroom or per unit and applied to every household alike is lawful. Pick the number from the local building or health standard, keep it the same for everyone, and never apply it only to families. Your city or county cannot help you tighten it either: since mid-2024 a Colorado local government may not limit how many people live together based on their family relationship, and may base an occupancy limit only on demonstrated health and safety standards or affordable-housing program rules. Two narrow Colorado exemptions from the familial-status rule exist — for a private individual owner renting a single-family house who owns no more than three such houses and uses no broker or agent and no advertising, and for a building of no more than four independent households where the owner actually lives in one of them — but they are easy to lose and they do not exempt you from federal fair housing law. Treat them as a last resort and take advice before relying on one. Federal fair housing law applies to children independently of Colorado law.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice Rule in Colorado
bodyText: Some states make a tenant tell the landlord before leaving a home empty in winter, so the pipes can be protected. Colorado has no such rule — nothing in Colorado law requires that notice, sets a temperature or a number of days, or gives you a remedy for not getting it. In a state where a hard freeze will split a supply line in a day, that leaves a real gap you have to close yourself, by lease and by habit. What you can do: put a plain term in the lease requiring the tenant to tell you in writing before the home will be empty for more than a set number of days, to keep the heat at or above a set temperature through the winter months, and to let you in to protect the plumbing if a freeze is forecast while they are away. Those are ordinary tenant duties and ordinary access terms, and Colorado leaves them to your lease. Keep two limits in mind. You may not charge the tenant a fee for failing to give the notice unless the charge reflects an actual loss you really incurred, and you cannot dress the charge up as rent. And if the heating itself fails, that is your problem, not the tenant's: working heat is part of what you must provide, and you may not charge the tenant for anything you need in order to meet that duty. Also be careful about reading an empty home as an abandoned one. Colorado lets you treat a unit as abandoned without going to court only on real evidence that the tenant has permanently given up possession — keys returned, belongings substantially removed, the tenant's own notice, or a long absence while rent goes unpaid — and getting that judgment wrong is expensive, because an unlawful removal costs you the tenant's actual damages plus the greater of three months' rent or five thousand dollars, with fees and costs. A tenant on a ski holiday with rent paid is not an abandoning tenant. The cautious course is to use your lease notice term, document what you see, and go to court if you are unsure.

title: Collection Fees Are Not Collectable in Colorado
bodyText: Do not put a collection fee in a Colorado lease, and do not add one to a tenant's ledger. Colorado blocks it from three directions at once. First, your lease may not contain any clause that puts a penalty on a party arising out of an eviction notice or an eviction action brought over a lease violation, and a clause like that is void and unenforceable — a fee you add once you have served a demand for rent or started a case is exactly that penalty. Second, you may not require a tenant to pay any fee, charge or amount tied to the overdue payment of something that is not rent, so a collection charge stacked on an unpaid utility bill, pet fee, late fee or damage charge is unlawful on its own. Third, almost nothing in Colorado law gives a landlord the power to pass collection costs to a tenant in the first place: the statutes that let collection costs be added to a debt are for homeowner associations recovering assessments and for public bodies collecting money owed to the state, and neither reaches a landlord. The one real exception is narrow and is about bounced payments, not about lateness. If a rent cheque or other payment order is not paid on presentment, Colorado gives the holder a civil claim for the face amount plus a reasonable posted or contractual charge of up to twenty dollars, and, if the item has been assigned to a licensed collection agency, twenty percent of the face amount as costs of collection with a twenty-dollar floor; if you give the statutory written notice and the total is still unpaid after fifteen days, you may instead claim three times the face amount with a hundred-dollar floor, subject to the defences the statute lists. That is a court remedy you pursue, not a fee you may simply add to a ledger, it applies only to the dishonoured item, and your lease's own returned-payment charge still has to fit Colorado's limits. Two more traps sit alongside this. You cannot relabel the charge as rent: only the set monthly payment for occupancy may be treated as rent with rent remedies behind it, including eviction, and a late fee in particular is distinct from rent and cannot be classified as rent for the nonpayment ground. And attorney fees follow their own rule: in an eviction case a residential landlord recovers no attorney fees at all unless the lease provides for them, and if your lease does provide for them the clause must award them to whichever party prevails, after the court finds that party prevailed and that the fee is reasonable — a one-way clause is prohibited. So what can you actually do? Keep a lawful late fee, disclosed in the lease and inside the statutory limits. Pursue the unpaid rent itself, with interest only if the lease provides for it and the law allows. If you hire a collection agency, pay it out of what you recover rather than billing the tenant: the agency is separately barred from collecting any amount incidental to the debt unless the agreement creating the debt expressly authorises it or the law permits it, and since your lease cannot lawfully authorise a collection fee, the agency has nothing to stand on. Charging anyway is costly — a tenant can demand reimbursement, and if you do not pay within fourteen days you owe actual damages plus eighteen percent interest a year compounded annually, and the conduct counts as a deceptive, unfair and unconscionable practice. Take advice before adding any charge to a delinquent account.

title: Common-Area Lighting Is Your Duty and Your Bill
bodyText: In Colorado the lights in the hallways, stairwells, entries, laundry room, parking area and other shared spaces are yours to keep working and yours to pay for. Two separate rules get you there. The habitability rules treat the whole property as what you must keep fit to live in — the unit, the structure it sits in, and the common areas — and they list working electrical lighting, with wiring and equipment that met the law when it was installed, as one of the things the property must not substantially lack. Stairways, floors and railings in good repair, and shared areas kept clean and free of debris, are on the same list. A defect confined to a shared area only makes the property uninhabitable if it materially affects the tenant's use of their own home, so one dead bulb in a laundry room is not a habitability breach — but an unlit stairwell or a dark entry the tenant has to use at night very likely is, and the clock on it is short once you have written notice. Then there is the money. You may not require a tenant to pay any fee, charge or amount for the maintenance of common areas, and you may not charge for anything you need in order to meet your own obligations, including habitability. You also may not charge for utilities above what the provider actually billed for service to that tenant's unit, and for this rule the tenant's unit expressly does not include the common areas. If you allocate utilities among tenants using a ratio system, common-area and shared-facility utility costs must be left out of the allocation altogether, the total billed to all tenants cannot exceed what the utility charged for the whole property, no markup or administrative fee may be added, and the method has to be disclosed clearly in the lease or an addendum. So the Massachusetts-style arrangement — common-area lights wired to one tenant's meter, with the lease making that tenant pay — does not work here. If a shared light is on a tenant's meter, fix the wiring or credit the tenant; do not write a clause making them absorb it. Practical habits: replace shared-area bulbs on a schedule rather than on complaint, keep the written record of when you were told and when you acted, and check whether your city or county requires more, since local housing codes often set minimum light levels for stairs and exits and a code violation that materially interferes with life, health or safety is itself a habitability breach.

title: No Government Approval Needed for a Colorado Lease
bodyText: Some jurisdictions will not let a lease of land take effect until a government officer signs off on it, because the land is held communally or by a family or clan rather than individually. Colorado has nothing like that. There is no communal, family or homestead land tenure in Colorado law, and no Colorado statute makes any lease wait for a governor's, commissioner's or agency's approval before it is valid. Your residential lease is effective when you and the tenant sign it, and the only statewide paperwork duty attached to signing is handing the tenant a signed copy within seven days. Two things can still sit on top of a private lease and are worth checking before you sign. If the property is in a common interest community, the declaration, bylaws and rules of the association may restrict leasing — a minimum lease term, a cap on the number of rented units, a registration or approval step with the association, or a requirement that the tenant acknowledge the rules. That is a private contract restriction, not a government approval, but breaching it can cost you, so read the governing documents and build any association requirement into your lease and your timeline. And if the land is tribal land, you are outside Colorado landlord-tenant law and outside this library: leases of land held in trust for the Southern Ute Indian Tribe or the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, or of allotted land in Indian country, are governed by tribal law and by federal law, and both the approval question and the eviction question can be answered only there. Get specialist advice before you lease or try to recover possession of such property. Separately, a city or county may require a rental licence, registration or inspection before you may lawfully rent, and some require a certificate of occupancy; that is a local permission, not a lease-approval rule, and you should check it where the property sits.

title: Rent After a Condemnation or Vacate Order in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado has no statute that says in so many words that you may not collect rent once a dwelling is condemned, closed or posted as unfit. Do not read that as permission. Colorado gets to a harsher place by another route, and the practical answer is that rent for a condemned unit is usually worth nothing and chasing it is dangerous. Here is why. A property that fails to comply with applicable building, housing and health codes in a way that materially interferes with a tenant's life, health or safety is uninhabitable by statute, and so is a property that is otherwise unfit for human habitation — which is what a condemnation says about it. Once a court finds a breach of the warranty of habitability, the fair rental value of the home is presumed to be zero dollars for the whole period the condition went unremedied where it materially interfered with the tenant's life, health or safety, and fifty percent of the lease rent where it did not. The tenant can raise that as a defence to your action for possession or for rent, and the court must then reduce the rent, order you to repay the difference between the reduced value and what was actually paid, award the tenant's costs and fees, and order the repairs. A tenant may also simply end the lease on ten days' written notice with no liability, or deduct repair costs from rent after notice. And if the tenant leaves after an injunction, you may not re-rent the home until it complies. So the sequence to follow when a unit is condemned or ordered vacated is: stop billing and stop accepting rent for the period the home is unusable; refund or credit the rent already paid for that period; comply with the relocation duties, which can mean a comparable unit or a hotel room at your cost with a meal per diem, triggered by the tenant's request within twenty-four hours; and either repair and document the repair or end the tenancy properly. If the order came from a government authority and makes continued occupancy impossible or unlawful, you may end the lease without further liability only if your lease gives you that power, and only on at least thirty days' written notice, with the full deposit returned by the termination date, access for the tenant to retrieve belongings, and a prorated refund of rent for the uninhabitable period. Keep in mind too that you may not charge the tenant for anything you need in order to meet your habitability duty, and that the condemnation itself may come with local relocation or licensing obligations your city or county imposes — check local rules, and take advice before invoking any termination.

title: Confession of Judgment: No Colorado Ban, and No Reason to Use One
bodyText: A confession-of-judgment clause has the tenant agree in advance that judgment may be entered against them without a hearing. Colorado does not have a statute voiding that clause in an ordinary residential lease, which can read like permission. It is not. Colorado does ban the clause in two neighbouring places — a mobile home park rental agreement may not authorise a third person to confess judgment on a claim arising from the agreement, and any such provision is against public policy, unenforceable and void; and a consumer may not authorise anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of a consumer credit transaction, with the authorisation void. A home rental is not a consumer credit transaction on the better reading of the statute, because the consumer credit code reaches leases of goods rather than leases of a home, but that gap is a drafting accident rather than a policy choice, and no Colorado court decision was available to settle it. More importantly, the clause cannot do the one thing a landlord would want it for. You may not remove or exclude a tenant without going through court process, and the penalty for trying is the tenant's actual damages plus the greater of three months' rent or five thousand dollars, with fees and costs. So a confessed judgment cannot give you possession; you would still have to bring an eviction case. And the clause sits badly beside the terms Colorado does void: your lease may not waive the tenant's right to a jury trial except in a hearing to determine possession, may not waive the ability to bring or join a class or collective claim, may not waive the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and may not assign a penalty arising from an eviction notice or action. A clause that strips notice and hearing is the kind of term a court is invited to read against you, and it would be void as to anything it indirectly waived. This library therefore does not offer a confession-of-judgment clause for Colorado. If you want one anyway, nothing in this library stops you adding your own, but take legal advice first — and check the Colorado Rules of Civil Procedure, which are not part of the source set used here and which govern whether a court will enter such a judgment at all. The practical alternative is to make your default and notice terms clear and lawful, and to use the eviction process when you need possession.

title: Habitability Rules Other States Have That Colorado Does Not
bodyText: Colorado's habitability law is among the most demanding in the country, so the gaps are not the places to relax — they are the places where you decide the standard yourself and where a lease term or a good habit is worth having. Four gaps are worth knowing. First, Colorado has no smoke-alarm statute at all. Not one word about smoke alarms or smoke detectors appears anywhere in Colorado's statutes, and the list of things that make a home uninhabitable does not include an alarm or detector of any kind. Colorado does regulate carbon monoxide alarms in rentals, and those duties are real but narrow: they bite when a permitted alteration, repair, fuel-fired appliance replacement or added sleeping room happens, or on a change of tenant, and then you must replace an alarm that is missing or not working before the new tenancy, supply the batteries at move-in, and replace or fix an alarm when the tenant tells you it is missing or faulty — while ongoing testing and upkeep sit with the tenant. Smoke alarms are left to your local building code and to you. Install and maintain them anyway, document it at every move-in, and make the tenant's testing and reporting duty an express lease term. Second, there is no minimum indoor temperature in Colorado. Your duty is functional rather than numeric — heating facilities that met the law when installed and are kept in good working order — with a presumption against you from October through April if they are not. So you cannot point to a number to prove compliance; you prove it with a working system and a prompt response. Third, Colorado gives tenants no rent-escrow or rent-withholding procedure. That sounds like good news and is not: instead of a tenant parking rent with the court, Colorado lets a tenant deduct the cost of repairs from rent after notice, end the lease on ten days' notice with no penalty, and raise habitability as a defence to your claim for possession or rent — after which the court can value the home at zero for the whole unremedied period. The practical lesson is that there is no neutral holding account to buy you time; fix it on the clock. Fourth, you are never required to supply an appliance, and never required to supply cooling. The habitability rules reach only the appliances you actually provided or promised. But once you provide one, it must work, and you may not charge the tenant for repairing it; and you may not stop a tenant from installing or using a portable cooling device except on the narrow grounds the statute lists, in which case you must disclose the restriction in writing and tell the tenant about cooled common spaces or nearby community cooling spaces. One more absence worth naming: Colorado imposes no duty to change or re-key locks, for domestic violence or any other reason, though working locks on exterior doors and openable windows are themselves a habitability requirement. A city or county may require more than the state does on any of these points; check local rules.

title: Other Rules Colorado Does Not Have
bodyText: Colorado regulates residential tenancies heavily, which makes its gaps easy to miss. Four are worth knowing, because each is a place where your lease, not the statute, decides the outcome. Subletting and assignment: Colorado has no statute on either. Nothing gives your tenant a right to sublet or to hand the lease to someone else, nothing requires you to be reasonable about refusing, and nothing sets a deadline for you to answer a request. That cuts your way, but only if your lease says so — write a clear term requiring your written consent before any sublet, assignment or additional occupant, and say what happens if the tenant does it anyway. Say in the same place that your consent, if you give it, does not release the original tenant. Double letting: Colorado has no provision about letting the same home to two tenants, no remedy for the tenant who is shut out, and no offence. If it happens through a scheduling error, you are in ordinary contract and possession territory, which is slow and expensive, so the real protection is process — one calendar, one signed lease per unit, and no keys released until the lease and the money are in. Rental application fraud: Colorado tightly regulates what you may charge for an application and what you may consider in it, but says nothing at all about a tenant who lies on one. There is no statutory termination ground and no statutory remedy for it. If you want to be able to act on a false application, your lease has to say that the accuracy of the application is a term of the lease and that a material false statement is a breach — and even then, how you end a tenancy is governed by Colorado's notice rules, and for a tenant past twelve months in a covered property the grounds for eviction are fixed by statute and a lease cannot add to them. Rent grace periods: Colorado sets none. Rent is due when your lease says it is due, and the well-known seven-day rule is not a grace period at all — it is the point before which you may not charge a late fee. So do not describe seven days as a grace period to your tenant, and do not assume you must wait a week to treat rent as unpaid. Colorado case law is not covered here on any of these points, so where the stakes are high take advice before acting.

title: Squatters and Other Questions Outside the Landlord-Tenant Law
bodyText: Three things landlords ask about are not in Colorado's landlord-tenant article, so each answer below draws on the whole Colorado code and the constitution. Two exist, in places you would not look. First, Colorado does have a fast squatter remedy, and it sits in the courts title rather than the property title. If someone is occupying a vacant home with no agreement and no permission, you can file a complaint and a verified motion in county court for a temporary mandatory injunction, and the court holds a hearing within one court day; if it finds the occupant is an unauthorized person it must issue the injunction and a writ of restitution before adjourning, and a sheriff must act within twenty-four hours of receiving the order, removing the person and ordering them to stay off for fourteen days or face arrest for trespass. The limits are strict and they are the whole point: this route is closed if the occupant is your relative, if you or your agent ever accepted money or anything of value from them, or if they were ever given permission to be there — in which case you are in ordinary eviction territory. You must also have demanded that they leave, told them you were going to court, and served the motion and the hearing notice, and you swear the motion under penalty of perjury, with sanctions, contempt and perjury prosecution on the table if you swear falsely. Never use it against a former tenant or a holdover. Second, Colorado does have a rent receipt duty. If a tenant hands you cash or a money order in person, you must give a receipt at that moment showing the amount and the date. For any other payment, you must give a receipt within seven days of the tenant asking, showing the amount, the recipient and the date, unless you already have a procedure that gives the tenant that record — an online portal statement normally does. Electronic receipts are fine unless the tenant asks for paper. A receipt can be part of a billing statement. Third, there is no statewide landlord registration or rental licence in Colorado, and nothing in the landlord-tenant law makes registration a precondition to getting a judgment for possession. But two general business filings can stop you suing for rent. If you rent under any name other than your own true name, a statement of trade name must be on file with the Secretary of State, and until it is you may not maintain a court case to collect a debt, such as unpaid rent, from anyone you dealt with under that name (C.R.S. §§ 7-71-101, 7-71-102). And an out-of-state company that transacts business here must file a statement of foreign entity authority naming a Colorado registered agent, and until it does it may not sue to collect its debts and the court may stay its case (C.R.S. §§ 7-90-801, 7-90-802, 7-90-803). Owning property "without more" is not transacting business, but whether renting it out is more is a case-law question, so file before you need to sue. Neither failure voids the lease or stops you defending a case. But your city or county very likely has its own rental licence, registration or inspection scheme, and some make an unlicensed landlord's position much worse; mobile home parks are separately registered with the state. Check local requirements where the property sits before you rent and before you file anything.

title: Liens for Work a Colorado Tenant Orders - the Five-Day Notice
bodyText:
In Colorado, work done on your property with your knowledge is treated by the lien statute as having been done at your request — and the statute says so expressly about a landlord who has authorised improvements by lease or contract. Your interest in the property is then exposed to a contractor's or supplier's lien for that work.

There is a way out, and it is short. Within five days after you learn of the work, or of intended work, you must give written notice that your interest will not be subject to any lien, either by serving it personally on every person performing labour or furnishing labourers, materials, machinery or fixtures for the work, or by posting a written notice in a conspicuous place on the land or the building and keeping it posted.

Five days is the whole game, which makes two practical consequences follow.

- You need to hear about tenant work immediately, so build that into your lease as a notice duty on the tenant and into your habits — act on any sign of work, a skip in the driveway, a permit notice, a contractor's van, by starting the clock and posting.
- Prepare the notice in advance and keep posting materials on hand; a posted notice that you keep posted is usually more practical than personally serving every trade on a job you did not commission.

Two things will not save you.

- A lease clause saying the tenant may not allow liens, or that the tenant is not your agent, binds only the tenant: Colorado says an agreement to waive or refrain from enforcing a lien is binding only between the parties to it, so it does nothing against the contractor who files.
- The statute itself deems whoever has charge of the work your agent for lien purposes, so reciting the opposite in a lease does not change it.

Note too that the escape route is not available where your interest is already exposed because you actually contracted for the work — so if you authorise and arrange the job, the notice will not help. Where a lien does get filed, your remedies are against your tenant under the lease, and the statute's other machinery — substitution of a bond, the release procedure and the penalty for an excessive claim — may be worth taking advice on. Keep in mind that the lien statute is interpreted liberally in favour of claimants.

The practical posture is: consent to tenant work only in writing and only when you know who is doing it, require advance notice, post the notice anyway, and do not rely on lease words alone.

title: The Colorado Consumer Protection Act Reaches Your Lease
bodyText: Renting out a home in Colorado is a consumer transaction, and the Consumer Protection Act applies to how you advertise it, price it and talk about it. That matters because the Act's remedies are much harsher than ordinary contract damages. Two routes bring a landlord inside it. The first is the Act's catch-all, which makes it a deceptive trade practice to knowingly or recklessly engage in any unfair, unconscionable, deceptive, deliberately misleading, false or fraudulent act or practice in the course of your business — broad enough to reach a misleading advertisement, a misdescribed unit, a fee presented as something it is not, or a claim about the property you knew was wrong. The second is the Act's own landlord section, which forbids a list of landlord fees outright and says in terms that breaking it is a deceptive, unfair and unconscionable act or practice. Two more listed practices are worth knowing: failing to disclose material information about property that you knew when you advertised or let it, where the silence was meant to induce the tenant to go ahead; and misrepresenting the price. What is not in the Act is the pair of things landlords often expect: leaving blank spaces in a lease at signing is not a listed practice, and failing to hand over a copy at signing is not either — the copy-at-signing practice in the Act is limited to installment sales of goods and services. Your copy duty comes from the landlord-tenant statute instead, which gives you seven days from the tenant's signature. Then the exposure. A tenant who is an actual or potential consumer of your property and is injured may sue, and the Act gives the greater of actual damages with prejudgment interest, five hundred dollars, or three times actual damages where bad faith is shown by clear and convincing evidence, plus costs and reasonable attorney fees — and these claims can be brought as class actions, where a successful class recovers actual damages, injunctive relief, costs and fees. The attorney general and district attorneys can also enforce the Act with civil penalties. There is one real limit in your favour: the Act does not apply to conduct in compliance with the orders or rules of, or a statute administered by, a federal, state or local agency. Colorado courts have also read into the Act an element about the practice's effect on the public, but that is a judicial gloss rather than statutory text and the source set used here contains no case law, so do not plan around it. The practical takeaways: advertise the total price as a single number and more prominently than anything else; never charge a fee on the prohibited list; disclose what you know about the property; keep your advertising and your lease consistent; and if a tenant complains about a fee in writing, deal with it inside fourteen days, because ignoring the demand adds eighteen percent interest a year compounded annually on top of damages. A bad-faith finding can treble the award, so take advice early.

title: Converting a Colorado Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText:
Colorado has a condominium conversion notice rule, and it is simpler than most states' but has sharp edges. When a developer converts an existing multiple-unit dwelling into condominium units, then on recording the declaration the developer must notify every residential tenant of the building of the conversion. The notice has to be in writing, sent by certified or registered mail with postage prepaid and a return receipt, or delivered to the tenant in person; the return receipt is prima facie evidence that the tenant got it.

The notice does double duty: it also counts as the notice terminating the tenancy. But it cannot cut a tenancy short. A tenancy cannot end before the existing lease expires unless both the tenant and the developer agree; and if the lease has fewer than ninety days left when the notice goes out, or there is no written lease at all, the tenancy cannot end sooner than ninety days after the notice, again unless both agree. A tenant whose lease runs out inside that window may hold over for the rest of the ninety days on the same lease terms, provided they keep paying rent on time and keep to the lease.

Inside the ninety days you can only get the tenant out two ways: by agreement, in exchange for paying all of the tenant's moving expenses or some other consideration you both settle on, or because the tenant fails to pay rent on time.

Two things to plan for before you record.

- From the moment the declaration is recorded, anyone applying to rent must be told about the recording at the time of application — so change your application process, not just your lease.
- A lease signed after the recording may provide for termination on fewer than ninety days, but only if the lease itself conspicuously discloses that you intend to convert the property. Build that disclosure in before you sign, not later.

Be careful about one overlap. Colorado's for-cause eviction rules apply to a tenant who has been in the property at least twelve months, at properties those rules cover, and they say cause exists only on the listed grounds — which include demolition and conversion to a nonresidential use or a short-term rental, but not conversion to condominium, and a lease cannot contract around them. Until that is settled, treat a long-term tenant as needing the full statutory route and take advice before serving anything short.

Three more points.

- Colorado gives tenants no right of first refusal and no right to buy the unit on conversion; the right of first refusal in Colorado law belongs to the local government, for defined affordable multifamily properties of at least five units, and arises on a sale rather than a conversion.
- The conversion notification procedure is declared a matter of statewide concern, so a city or county may not adopt or enforce anything that conflicts with it — though local subdivision, building and licensing rules still apply.
- Colorado does not forbid converting rental housing to hotel, short-term rental or other transient use, or demolishing it; what it regulates is the eviction, which needs at least ninety days' written notice at the end of the term, with a description and timeline of the project and something concrete like a building permit or short-term rental licence application.

title: Criminal Activity: Colorado Already Writes the Term Into Your Lease
bodyText: You do not need a crime-free clause in Colorado, because the legislature has already put one in every lease. Colorado declares it an implied term of every lease of real property in the state that the tenant will not commit a substantial violation while in possession. That term is in your lease whether you write it or not, and it cannot be bargained away by leaving it out. What counts is narrower than "criminal activity" and is worth knowing precisely. A substantial violation is any act or series of acts by the tenant or any guest or invitee of the tenant that, taken together, either endangers a person on or near the property, or wilfully and substantially endangers the property of you, a co-tenant or anyone living on or near the property; or occurs on or near the property and is a violent or drug-related felony under the listed articles of the criminal code; or occurs on the leased premises or in the common areas, hallway, grounds, parking lot or other area in the same building or complex and is a criminal act under federal or state law or a local ordinance that both carries a potential sentence of a hundred and eighty days or more and has been declared a public nuisance under state law or a local ordinance based on a state statute. Note what that excludes: an ordinary misdemeanour with a short maximum, or a crime committed somewhere unconnected to the property, will not qualify. If it does qualify, the tenancy may be terminated at any time and the termination takes effect three days after service of a written notice to terminate, which must describe the property, give the exact date the tenancy ends and state the grounds, signed by you or your agent or attorney. There is no cure right. You carry the burden of proving the substantial violation on the balance of probabilities. Three limits must shape how you act. First, a tenant who did not know of and could not reasonably have known of or prevented a guest's or invitee's substantial violation has a defence if they immediately told a law enforcement officer. Second, you have no basis for possession where the tenant is a victim-survivor of unlawful sexual behaviour, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse that caused, contributed to or resulted in the alleged violation, documented as the eviction statute provides — though you may still proceed against the tenant who is responsible for it. Third, your lease must never contain a provision letting you terminate, impose a penalty on, or take any adverse action against a tenant for calling for police or other emergency assistance in a situation involving unlawful sexual behaviour, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse, and the agreement must not contain any waiver of the tenant's right to make those calls. A sweeping crime-free clause that counts police contact or arrests against a tenant walks straight into that bar. Finally, remember that for a tenant who has been in the property at least twelve months, at a property covered by Colorado's for-cause eviction rules, cause exists only on the grounds the statute lists, and a lease cannot add new ones. So your lease's job here is not to invent a ground but to keep your ordinary default and notice terms clean, and to document incidents carefully. Take advice before serving a three-day notice; these cases are fast and unforgiving.

title: Colorado's Cure Periods and Eviction Grounds
bodyText:
Colorado does not have one notice period; it has a grid, and using the wrong cell loses the case.

Start with the ground.

- For unpaid rent, you serve a demand in the alternative — pay the rent or give up possession — and the default residential period is ten days.
- For a breach of a material condition or covenant of the lease, the notice requires either compliance or possession, again ten days.
- For conduct that disturbs others or causes a nuisance interfering with the quiet enjoyment of other tenants or occupants of the same property, or of you or neighbours in an immediately adjacent property, or for negligently damaging the home, the notice must describe the specific conduct and require either that it stop or possession, again ten days.

Two shortcuts exist.

- For a nonresidential agreement or an employer-provided housing agreement, each of those periods is three days.
- For what Colorado calls an exempt residential agreement — a single-family home let by a landlord who owns five or fewer single-family rental homes and whose lease says the ten-day period does not apply — the period is five days. That shorter period depends entirely on the statement being in the lease, so if you qualify and want it, put it in before signing.

Then there are the no-cure routes.

- A substantial violation under Colorado's criminal-activity provision terminates the tenancy three days after written notice, with no chance to cure.
- Where you have already served a compliance notice for a particular covenant and the tenant breaches the same covenant again, you may terminate without giving another chance to comply — effective ten days after written notice for a residential tenancy, three days for a nonresidential or employer-provided one and five days for an exempt residential agreement.

Every notice has required contents.

- It must be in writing, specify the grounds including a specific description of the alleged violation or the no-fault ground, describe the premises, state the date and time possession must be delivered up, and be signed by you, your agent or your attorney.
- It must also tell the tenant that a tenant receiving supplemental security income, social security disability insurance or Colorado works cash assistance has a right to mediation before you file.
- It must be written in English, Spanish, or any other language you know or have reason to know is the tenant's primary language.
- If it demands unpaid rent it must now also tell the tenant that a tenant who has experienced unlawful sexual behaviour, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse that caused a missed payment may give you documentation and is entitled to a repayment plan of up to nine months.

Three limits.

- A lease may not waive the nonpayment notice requirement.
- A lease may not waive the victim-survivor protections, which take several breaches outside unlawful detention altogether where the conduct caused, contributed to or resulted in the breach and is documented as the statute allows.
- For a tenant who has been in the property at least twelve months, at a property covered by Colorado's for-cause rules, cause exists only on the listed grounds and a lease cannot add to them — so your lease should define breaches clearly but cannot manufacture a new ground.

Serving the wrong period, or a notice missing required content, is the most common and most expensive mistake here; take advice if you are unsure which cell you are in.

title: No Defective-Drywall Disclosure Duty in Colorado
