bodyText: Colorado has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant that a property contains, or may contain, defective or corrosive imported drywall, and no statute about drywall of any kind. The word does not appear in the Colorado Revised Statutes. Colorado's property-disclosure statutes all run to a buyer of real property rather than to a tenant, and they cover a closed list of subjects - special taxing districts, common interest community obligations, a former methamphetamine laboratory, the potable water source, transportation projects, oil and gas activity, future property taxes and elevated radon - with no entry for building materials. Colorado's construction-defect statutes give a claim against the builder, contractor or designer who did the work; they do not make a landlord disclose anything to a tenant. So this is left to you and to general law. Two things still bite even without a disclosure statute. First, you must deliver and keep the unit habitable, and defective drywall that produces corrosive gas, a sulfur smell, failing wiring or failing appliances would be a habitability problem you have to fix, not a disclosure you can paper over. Second, actively concealing a known serious defect, or answering a tenant's direct question falsely, can expose you to a misrepresentation or deceptive-trade-practice claim, which no amount of lease drafting cures. The cautious course is to disclose a known or suspected drywall problem in writing before signing, keep the inspection and remediation records, and put nothing in the lease that asks the tenant to accept the condition or waive a habitability right - a waiver of that kind is void in Colorado. Your city or county may require more than the state does; check local rules.

title: Why a Pre-Set Deduction Price List Backfires in Colorado
bodyText:
A lot of leases carry a price list - so much for a cleaning, so much per blind, so much per wall - and in Colorado that list is more likely to cost you money than to collect it. Colorado gives you no authority to pre-set a deduction figure, and it gives you four reasons not to.

- You may retain from the deposit only for unpaid rent, unpaid utility charges, another lawful charge the lease actually lists, or necessary repair work for damage beyond normal wear and tear that did not exist before the tenancy.
- Any lease provision assigning the tenant a charge for repairs, cleaning or other work due to normal wear and tear, or for a condition that preexisted the tenancy, is void as against public policy - so a flat cleaning charge that would apply whatever state the unit is in is void on its face, and void language in a lease is worse than no language.
- You carry the burden of proving your actual damages in court, and an amount you retain is presumed to unreasonably exceed your actual damages once it reaches 125 percent of them, which is exactly what a round-number price list produces when the real invoice comes in lower.
- Colorado's definition of normal wear and tear now covers damage and uncleanliness that comes from ordinary use, and only uncleanliness that leaves the unit substantially less clean than it was at move-in falls outside it.

The carpet and paint rules narrow you further: you cannot charge for replacing carpet throughout the unit, or repainting the whole interior, without substantial damage of that scale, and you may never treat carpet as substantially and irreparably damaged if it has not been replaced with new carpet in the ten years before the lease ended.

What works instead: list in the lease every category of charge you might ever need to recover, so the listing requirement is satisfied, then charge the actual cost of the actual work and keep the receipt, invoice, estimate or photograph that proves it. If a tenant asks in writing, you must hand that documentation over within fourteen days anyway. Request a walk-through inspection before move-out so damage is identified in writing while the tenant is still there. And remember the whole deposit section cannot be waived or modified against the tenant by any lease provision.

These rules changed on January 1, 2026; a price list copied from an older Colorado lease is now a liability.

Your city or county may add requirements; check local rules. Take advice before using any pre-set figure.

title: An Unclaimed Deposit Refund Belongs to the State, Not to You
bodyText: If you cannot get a deposit refund to a former tenant, the money does not become yours. Colorado's unclaimed property act names a security deposit expressly in the property it covers, and it makes you a statutory holder of that money for the tenant's account. There is no dormancy period written specially for deposits, so the catch-all applies: the refund is presumed abandoned at the earlier of three years after the tenant first had a right to demand it or three years after your obligation to pay arose - which for a deposit is the day your return deadline ran out. Before you report it you owe the tenant a notice. If you have an address in your records that your records do not show to be invalid and the amount is twenty-five dollars or more, you must mail that notice by first-class mail no more than one hundred eighty days and no less than sixty days before you file your report, or send it by email instead if the tenant consented to email from you and you have no evidence it bounced. The report itself is due before November 1 each year and covers the twelve months ending the previous July 1, and you pay or deliver the money to the state treasurer with it. Getting this wrong is expensive. Late reporting or delivery costs you interest at the statutory rate plus a civil penalty of two hundred dollars for every day you are late, up to five thousand dollars. Entering into any contract or arrangement for the purpose of evading the act, or wilfully not doing what the act requires, costs one thousand dollars a day up to twenty-five thousand dollars, plus twenty-five percent of the value of what you should have handed over - and a fraudulent report carries the same. A lease clause that forfeits an unclaimed deposit to you is exactly the kind of arrangement that invites the evasion penalty, and it is separately void because no lease provision may waive or modify the deposit statute to the tenant's disadvantage. Two Colorado timetables run alongside each other and you have to satisfy both. Under the deposit statute, if your refund payment comes back to you after you sent it to the tenant's last known address, you must hold it for at least one year and pay it out within fifteen calendar days of the tenant asking. Under the unclaimed property act the three-year clock then takes over. So the practical sequence is: send the refund on time, hold a returned payment for at least a year while you try to trace the tenant, send the statutory notice in the sixty-to-one-hundred-eighty-day window, and report and remit before November 1 of the year the three years run out. Keep the record of every step. Take advice if the sum is large or the tenancy ended in a dispute.

title: No Deposit Installment Right in Colorado - but You May Offer One
bodyText: Colorado gives a tenant no right to pay the security deposit in instalments, and sets no rules about how instalments would work if you offered them. Some states require a landlord to accept the deposit in two, three or six payments on the tenant's request; Colorado does not. You may require the whole deposit before occupancy. Nothing stops you offering instalments as a concession, and in a tight market many landlords do, so here is what to watch if you agree to it. The two-month deposit ceiling applies to the total you require, however it is paid, so instalments do not let you collect more. Do not treat an unpaid instalment as unpaid rent: Colorado bars a lease from characterising any amount other than the set monthly payment for occupancy as rent for which rent remedies, including eviction, are available, so a missed instalment is an ordinary contract debt you sue for, not a ground to evict or terminate. Do not attach a late fee to a missed instalment either, because Colorado forbids a charge related to the overdue payment of any amount that is not rent, and the late-fee statute only ever reached rent. And if you want to be able to recover an unpaid instalment out of the deposit itself, the lease has to list it: Colorado now lets you retain from the deposit only for unpaid rent, unpaid utility charges, another lawful charge the lease actually lists, or repair work for damage beyond normal wear and tear that did not preexist the tenancy. The cautious course is to write the instalment schedule and the total into the lease, state in plain words that the instalments are deposit and not rent, list the unpaid-instalment amount among the lawful charges recoverable from the deposit, and take no fee or interest for the privilege. Be consistent between applicants: who gets instalments and who does not is the kind of difference that invites a discrimination complaint. Your city or county may add requirements; check local rules, and take advice before building an instalment programme.

title: Taking Last Month's Rent Up Front Makes It a Deposit
bodyText:
Colorado's definition of a security deposit does not care what you call the money. It covers any advance or deposit of money, whatever its denomination, whose primary function is to secure performance of the rental agreement. So if you collect a sum at signing labelled last month's rent, and its real job is to give you a cushion in case the tenancy goes wrong, it is a security deposit in law, and everything that governs deposits governs it.

That matters in four ways.

- It counts against the two-month ceiling, so a deposit of two months' rent plus a last month's rent held back is over the line and the excess is not enforceable.
- You must return it, or account for it in writing with your exact reasons, within thirty days of the later of the lease ending and the tenant surrendering the property, or up to sixty days if your lease says so.
- You may retain from it only for unpaid rent, unpaid utility charges, another lawful charge your lease actually lists, or repair work for damage beyond normal wear and tear that did not preexist the tenancy.
- No lease provision can waive or modify any of that against the tenant.

Where the line falls is not spelled out in the statute. Rent genuinely paid in advance for an identified month, which you will apply to that month's rent whatever happens, is arguably payment rather than security - but Colorado has no provision and no test saying so, and the phrase last month's rent appears nowhere in the statutes. So the cautious course is to assume every penny you collect at signing beyond the rent for the first rental period is a security deposit: keep the running total at or under two months' rent, account for all of it at move-out, and do not take a separate last month's rent at all. If you want the comfort, raise the deposit within the cap instead.

Going the other way, nothing in Colorado law lets a tenant decide to skip the final month's rent and tell you to take it out of the deposit, and nothing stops your lease from saying they may not - which is worth saying, because a tenant who does it leaves you with no cushion for the damage you only find after they have gone. You can still apply the deposit to unpaid rent afterwards, in the written accounting.

Your city or county may add requirements; check local rules. Take advice before structuring any advance payment as something other than a deposit.

title: You Cannot Make the Deposit Depend on the Tenant's Move-Out Notice
bodyText:
Colorado requires no move-out notice and no forwarding address from a tenant before you must deal with the deposit, and you cannot create that requirement by putting it in the lease. Your clock starts at the later of two events - the lease terminating and the tenant surrendering the property with you accepting it - and runs thirty days, or up to sixty if your lease says so. Nothing in that depends on the tenant telling you anything. A lease provision that waives or modifies any part of the deposit statute to the tenant's disadvantage is void as against public policy, so a term saying the deposit is forfeited, or the clock paused, until the tenant supplies a forwarding address does nothing except make you look as though you were planning not to pay.

It is still worth asking for the notice and the address, because the statute protects you if you send to the wrong place: you are deemed to have complied by sending the statement, any documentation and any payment to the tenant's last known address, or to any email address for the tenant you have actual notice of. Having the address and the email in writing is how you prove where the last known address was.

If your payment comes back to you, hold it for at least a year and pay it out within fifteen calendar days of the tenant asking - and after three years an unclaimed refund goes to the state, not to you.

Two special cases.

- If a tenant vacates because you did not fix a gas hazard within seventy-two hours after written notice, the tenant does owe you a correct forwarding address, and your deadline collapses to seventy-two hours after they vacate, with a penalty of twice the deposit plus attorney fees if you miss it.
- If a tenant terminated because they are a victim of domestic violence, stalking, domestic abuse or unlawful sexual behaviour and gives you a new address, you must not disclose that address to anyone without their consent unless the law requires you to.

Finally, use the walk-through: either side may request one, and you must provide one at the tenant's request before the lease ends and after they have had a chance to move furniture out. A written, shared record of condition made while the tenant is standing there is worth more to you than any notice clause.

Your city or county may add requirements; check local rules.

title: Who May Do the Repairs, and the Agreement That Must Be Separate
bodyText: In Colorado the repairs are yours to make and yours to pay for, and you may not move that to the tenant in the lease. The warranty of habitability is deemed to be in every rental agreement, you are responsible for remedying a condition you have notice of at your own expense, and any agreement waiving or modifying any right, remedy, obligation or prohibition in the habitability part is void as contrary to public policy. You also may not charge the tenant a fee for a good, service or property necessary to comply with your own responsibilities, including your responsibility to provide a habitable living environment - and a lease fee that breaks that rule is a prohibited lease clause, void and unenforceable. There is exactly one route to making the tenant the repairer, and it is narrow. All of these must be true: the property is a single-family residence; you receive no subsidy from any governmental source for it; the agreement is entered into in good faith and set out in a writing that is separate from the rental agreement, signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration; and the tenant actually has the skills to do the work. Even then you may never agree that the tenant will do work that would endanger the tenant's health or safety. Where the tenant validly takes on a repair that relates to one of the statutory habitability characteristics, the tenant assumes that characteristic and its absence does not make the property uninhabitable - which is why the separate writing has to say precisely which tasks are covered. Put it in the lease instead and you have nothing: the statute requires a separate document, and a lease term that shifts a habitability duty is void. Gas work is not negotiable. You must hire a professional - a person licensed or certificated where a state, county or municipal government requires it, or, where no such authorisation is available or required, a qualified person carrying at least one hundred thousand dollars of public liability and property damage coverage - to remedy or repair a hazardous condition in gas piping, gas facilities, gas appliances or other gas equipment. Separately, if the tenant tells you in writing about a gas hazard found by the gas company's service personnel, you have seventy-two hours excluding weekends and legal holidays to get it repaired by a professional, and if you do not, the tenant may move out, the lease becomes void, and your deposit deadline collapses to seventy-two hours with a penalty of twice the deposit plus attorney fees if you miss it. One more thing to know about using a maintenance company. A tenant's written correspondence with your maintenance staff, or with a maintenance service you provide - including one provided by a third party - counts as notice to you of an uninhabitable condition, and your clock starts then. So whoever you designate, make sure their inbox is read daily and that what arrives there reaches you. Finally, since 2025 the attorney general or a county, city and county or municipality may ask a district court to appoint a receiver to operate a multifamily residential property where there is reasonable cause to believe the owner has a pattern of neglect - meaning disrepair that threatens tenants' health, safety or security, such as a vermin or rat infestation, filth or contamination, inadequate ventilation, illumination, sanitary, heating or life-safety facilities, inoperative fire suppression or warning equipment, or inoperative doors or window locks. That is the state designating a repairer for you, and it is the outcome to avoid. Your city or county may add requirements; check local rules, and take advice before signing any tenant-repair agreement.

title: Colorado's Own Accommodation Duty, and the Restoration Right You Do Not Have
bodyText:
Colorado has its own disability housing law, and it does not depend on federal law or federal guidance. Refusing a reasonable modification of the property that a person with a disability needs for full enjoyment of it, and refusing a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies, practices or services that a person with a disability may need for equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, are both unfair or discriminatory housing practices in their own right. So is discriminating on the basis of disability in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, in the services or facilities you provide with it, or in your advertising - and so is asking a prospective tenant about a disability at all. The statute reaches a disability of the applicant, of anyone who will live in the unit, and of anyone associated with them.

Colorado now defines a reasonable accommodation as an exception or adjustment to a rule, policy, practice or service that may be necessary for an individual with a disability to have equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing, and it says in terms that this includes public and common-use spaces - so a parking space, a mail area, a laundry room or a gate code is in scope, not just the inside of the unit.

Here is the trap. Federal law lets a landlord condition permission for a tenant-paid modification on the tenant restoring the interior to its previous condition where that is reasonable. Colorado's own statute contains no restoration proviso at all: it states the duty to permit reasonable modifications and stops. The phrase requiring an accommodation provision to be included in any lease, which some states have, appears nowhere in Colorado law either.

Two practical consequences.

- Do not copy a restoration clause out of a federal-style form lease and assume Colorado backs it up; it does not, and a clause that conditions a modification on something the statute does not allow you to require is itself a term or condition you may be answering for. Instead, when you agree to a modification, write a separate short agreement with the tenant, signed before work starts, saying who does the work, who pays, what the specification is, and what happens to the modification at the end - and treat the end-of-tenancy part as something you negotiated, not something you imposed.
- Remember too that you cannot charge any fee for a good, service or property necessary to comply with your own obligations, which is what an accommodation is.

Who to deal with and how: there is no prescribed form and no prescribed channel. A request counts however it arrives, including orally and including from someone acting for the tenant. Where the disability and the disability-related need are not obvious you may ask for reasonable documentation of both, and doing so is not itself discrimination - but you may not interrogate the nature or severity of the condition, and where the need is obvious you may not ask at all. Engage, in writing, promptly, and keep the record; an interactive process you can prove is your best protection, and for an assistance animal it is now a statutory condition of the presumption in the tenant's favour.

What it costs to get wrong: an aggrieved person may sue in state or federal district court within two years of the practice occurring or ending, without first filing an administrative charge, and the court may award actual and punitive damages, grant injunctions and affirmative relief, and in its discretion award the prevailing party attorney fees and costs. A second route also applies: a person with a disability who is subject to housing discrimination based on that disability may sue for a court order requiring compliance and either actual damages or a statutory fine of three thousand five hundred dollars for each plaintiff for each violation. A 2025 act rewrote that route and kept housing in it. The fair housing route carries no cap on actual and punitive damages.

Federal fair housing law and the Americans with Disabilities Act apply as well, on their own terms. Your city or county may add duties; check local rules. This is an area where getting it wrong is expensive and the law moved twice in two years, so take advice on any request you are inclined to refuse.

title: No Colorado Rule on Housing People Displaced by a Disaster
bodyText: Colorado has no statute about a tenant taking in people displaced by a wildfire, flood, storm or other disaster. It has no statutory guest limit, no limit on how long a guest may stay, no statutory definition of a guest, and no emergency-hosting right or duty either way. So the whole subject is left to your lease and to general contract law, and whatever your lease says is what governs - which is a reason to say something sensible rather than nothing. What Colorado does say matters more than the silence. First, who counts as a tenant is not up to you after the fact: in the habitability part of the law a tenant includes any member of the household and anyone who otherwise has your explicit or implicit permission to occupy the unit. If you know people have moved in and you say nothing for weeks, you may have given implicit permission and acquired tenants with full habitability rights. Second, the tenant is answerable for their guests: normal wear and tear excludes deterioration, damage or uncleanliness caused by negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse by the tenant, members of the household, or their invitees or guests, so guest damage is chargeable; and a substantial violation - broadly, endangering people or property, a violent or drug-related felony, or certain serious crimes on or near the premises - is a ground for possession whether committed by the tenant or by any guest or invitee. Third, occupancy numbers are a local matter: the fair housing statute expressly preserves reasonable local, state and federal restrictions on the maximum number of occupants, so your city or county may set a figure and you should check it rather than invent one. Be careful how you write a guest clause. A limit so tight that it effectively excludes households with children can run into familial status discrimination, which Colorado prohibits, and a clause that penalises a tenant for calling for peace-officer or emergency assistance in a domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behaviour or stalking situation is unlawful and cannot be waived. The cautious course: set a plain guest limit in nights per period rather than by relationship or family status, say that a longer stay needs your written consent and that you will not unreasonably refuse it, require the tenant to tell you who is staying and for how long, keep the tenant responsible for guests' conduct and damage, and handle a genuine disaster the way a reasonable landlord would - grant a time-limited written consent that names the people and the end date, so nobody becomes a tenant by accident and your insurance and your other tenants are not left guessing. If you expect to be asked, talk to your insurer first; a long unapproved occupancy can matter to coverage. Take advice before refusing a request that arises out of a declared disaster.

title: What a Declared Disaster Does, and Does Not, Do to a Colorado Tenancy
bodyText: A disaster does not end a Colorado tenancy by itself, and it does not stop the rent. Here is the shape of it. The tenancy survives. There is no Colorado statute that terminates a lease because a wildfire, flood or storm has made the property unusable, and none that suspends rent while it is unusable. What exists instead is a narrow landlord termination right that you only have if your lease gives it to you: where the property is damaged by a sudden environmental public health event, or by an action a governmental authority takes, and continued occupancy becomes impossible or unlawful, you may end the lease without further liability on either side - but only if you were not already in breach of the warranty of habitability before the event, only if repairing it into compliance would be impracticable, and only if you give at least thirty days' written notice, comply with all your habitability obligations through the termination date, give the tenant or their representative access to retrieve their belongings (or agree in writing to give access as soon as it is safe), return the whole security deposit on or before the termination date, and provide a prorated discount or refund for any rent paid for a period the unit was uninhabitable without you providing a comparable unit or hotel room. Miss one of those and you do not have the right. An environmental public health event means a disaster or environmental event, such as a wildfire, a flood or a release of toxic contaminants, that could create negative health and safety impacts or otherwise makes a property uninhabitable for tenants living nearby - so it reaches your building even when the fire was next door. Rent keeps running. A tenant you temporarily relocate still owes their rent for the relocation period and for the rest of the term. That protects you, and it is the reason the prorated-refund condition above exists as the counterweight. Your duties while it is unusable are substantial. Once you have notice of a condition that makes the property uninhabitable you must begin remedial action within seventy-two hours, or twenty-four where it materially interferes with the tenant's life, health or safety, and you must contact the tenant within twenty-four hours of notice - seventy-two if the property is inaccessible because of an environmental public health event - saying what you will do and when. If the tenant asks, you must provide a comparable unit or a hotel room, your choice, within twenty-four hours, at no cost to them. Remediation and cleanup after an environmental public health event must meet the applicable ANSI standards and all applicable building, fire, health and housing codes, and once a government entity, official, law enforcement officer or public safety officer says the unit is safe to re-enter you must let the tenant or their representative in to retrieve their property even if the building as a whole is still uninhabitable. When you have remediated, give the tenant documentation showing you met the standards. Submitting an insurance claim is not evidence that you remediated anything. Do not raise the rent. This is the one that catches people out. If the president declares a national emergency, or the governor declares a disaster emergency, and the declaration specifically declares a material decrease in residential housing units, then within the geographic area the declaration identifies, and for a year from the date of the initial disaster, a rent increase of more than the greater of last year's percentage increase or ten percent is rental price gouging and an unfair and unconscionable practice. For a unit that was not on the market just before the disaster, the comparison is to rent for similar dwellings in the designated area that were. The attorney general, the district attorney or the affected tenant can enforce it, and a tenant who wins is awarded statutory damages equal to their actual damages plus attorney fees and costs. Note how broadly disaster is defined - it now includes a market disruption as well as fire, flood, earthquake, wind, storm, epidemic, drought, infestation, explosion and civil disturbance. There is also a separate general price-gouging prohibition covering building materials, repair or reconstruction services and other necessities during a disaster period, which can reach what you bill a tenant for disaster repair work. Practical course: make sure your lease contains the termination right, because without it you do not have one; document the condition, your notice and every step you take from the first hour; get the tenant into alternative accommodation promptly if they ask, and keep the receipts; keep the rent where it was; and check your city or county rules, which may add duties the state does not. Take advice before terminating, because the conditions are cumulative and the consequences of getting one wrong are a breach of the warranty of habitability.

title: No Double-Letting Rule in Colorado - and Why That Is Worse, Not Better
bodyText: Colorado has no statute about letting the same unit, or the same room, to two tenants at once. There is no prohibition, no rent-abatement formula, no statutory notice and no statutory damages aimed at it, and Colorado does not even impose a statutory duty to deliver possession at the start of a tenancy - every possession provision in the code is about recovering possession, not handing it over. So the subject is governed by your lease and by general contract law: if you promise a start date and cannot deliver, you are in breach of your own agreement, and the tenant's damages are whatever they can prove - alternative accommodation, storage, moving costs twice over, time off work. Read your lease: if it contains a clause excusing you for a delayed start, it will be the only thing standing between you and those damages. Do not take the absence of a specific rule as comfort, because the real exposure sits elsewhere and it is large. If you have double-let and you resolve it by keeping one tenant out, you have excluded a tenant from a dwelling unit without resorting to court process, which is unlawful in Colorado unless the tenant consented or genuinely abandoned the unit. Changing the locks, not handing over keys, or cutting utilities to make the point all count. The tenant may sue in county or district court to stop you and to recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees, and on a violation the court must award statutory damages equal to their actual damages plus the higher of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, plus any other damages - and the court may order that possession be restored to them. That figure does not depend on your intentions and it is not capped. Note that in Colorado a tenant includes any household member and anyone with your explicit or implicit permission to occupy, so the person you treat as the loser of the double booking may be a tenant with those rights whether or not they ever signed. There is also no waiving your way out: a Colorado lease must not contain a waiver of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment, except that it may provide you are not responsible for a third party's violation of it beyond your reasonable control - and another tenant you yourself let in is not beyond your reasonable control. Nor may a lease waive the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, or a jury trial other than in a possession hearing. The practical course is prevention. Keep one authoritative record of which unit is committed to whom and from when, and reconcile it before every signature. Do not sign a second lease for a unit until the first prospective tenant has withdrawn in writing. Where a holdover or a late turnover means you may not be able to deliver on time, tell the incoming tenant in writing as soon as you know, offer them a dated choice to wait with rent abated for the delay or to walk away with everything they paid returned, and get their answer in writing. If it has already happened, resolve it by agreement and by paying for it, never by exclusion - and take advice immediately, because the exclusion route costs several times what the mistake does.

title: You Do Not Need a Drug-Free Addendum in Colorado - the Term Is Already Implied
bodyText: Colorado requires no drug-free or crime-free housing addendum, prescribes no wording for one, and does not regulate one. The words drug-free, crime-free and one-strike appear nowhere in its statutes in a housing sense. But that is not a gap, because Colorado has already written the term into your lease for you. It is declared to be an implied term of every lease of real property in this state that the tenant will not commit a substantial violation while in possession. You do not have to say it, and saying it adds nothing to your rights. A substantial violation means any act or series of acts by the tenant, or by any guest or invitee of the tenant, that taken together either endangers a person, or wilfully and substantially endangers the property of you, a co-tenant or anyone living on or near the premises, and occurs on or near the premises; or occurs on or near the premises and is a violent or drug-related felony under one of eight named articles of the criminal code; or occurs on the leased premises, or the common areas, hallway, grounds, parking lot or other area in the same building or complex, and is a criminal act under federal or state law or local ordinance that both carries a potential sentence of one hundred eighty days or more and has been declared a public nuisance under state law or a local ordinance based on a state statute. Note what that excludes. A drug offence that is not a felony under those articles, or conduct that is nowhere near the premises, is not a substantial violation however much you dislike it. Three limits you must build into any practice you adopt. First, you carry the burden of proving the substantial violation on the balance of probabilities, and it is a defence that the tenant did not know of, and could not reasonably have known of or prevented, a guest's or invitee's violation but immediately notified a law enforcement officer. Second, you have no basis for possession where the tenant is the victim of domestic violence or domestic abuse that caused or resulted in the alleged violation and that has been documented as the statute requires - though you may still proceed against the tenant who perpetrated it. Third, and this is the one a broadly drafted addendum breaks: your lease must not contain a provision authorising you to terminate, or to impose a penalty, because the tenant called for peace-officer or other emergency assistance in a situation involving domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behaviour or stalking, and the tenant cannot waive the right to call. An addendum that counts police contact against a tenant, or that treats any arrest or any police visit as a breach, is unlawful in Colorado. There is one more trap. Where the tenancy has run twelve months or more and the property is not exempt, Colorado requires cause to evict, and cause exists only as the statute describes it - so your lease cannot create a new ground for eviction by calling something a breach of a drug-free addendum. Below twelve months the cause requirement does not apply. On marijuana, the Colorado constitution is clear that nothing in the legalisation provision stops a person who occupies, owns or controls a property from prohibiting or otherwise regulating the possession, consumption, use, display, transfer, distribution, sale, transportation or growing of marijuana on or in that property - so a no-marijuana term is lawful, and is a different thing from a drug-free addendum. The practical course: rely on the implied statutory term rather than papering it, keep your rules about conduct and nuisance rather than about police contact or arrests, document incidents as they happen, and take advice before terminating on this ground, because the three-day notice route carries the burden of proof and the defences above. Your city or county may add requirements; check local rules.

title: The Deposit Clock After a Domestic-Violence Termination
bodyText: Colorado's domestic-violence termination rules were rewritten in 2025 and the deposit sits in the middle of them. Read this before you touch a deposit after a victim-survivor has ended a tenancy. The ordinary clock still applies. You must return the deposit, or account for it in writing with your exact reasons, within thirty days of the later of the lease terminating and the tenant surrendering the property with you accepting it, or up to sixty days if your lease says so. Colorado does not pause that clock until every occupant has handed over possession; the trigger is the termination or the surrender, whichever is last. The one thing that does suspend your obligation is money the victim-survivor owes you, and that is tightly conditioned. A victim-survivor who terminates and vacates is responsible for an amount not exceeding one month's rent - but only if you actually incurred economic damages as a direct result of the early termination, and only if you gave them documentation of those damages within thirty days after the agreement terminated. That amount is payable within ninety days after they vacate, and you are not obliged to refund the deposit until they have paid it. You and they may offset amounts owed each way against the one month's rent or the deposit, despite the general deposit statute. Three traps in that paragraph. First, if another tenant remains on the lease after the victim-survivor terminates, you must not collect the one month's rent from the victim-survivor at all. Second, you must give a written statement of your actual damages from the early termination within thirty days after the date they vacate, and if you do not, you forfeit the right to charge or collect any future rent following the termination - the whole entitlement, not just the late part. Note that the statute states one clock from termination of the agreement and another from the date of vacating; where those differ, work to the earlier of the two and you cannot be caught. Third, the statute still carries an older sentence saying the subsection applies only if you have experienced and documented damages equal to at least one month's rent, alongside the newer wording capping the claim at not more than one month's rent. The cautious reading, and the only one that is safe for you, is that you must document real economic damages and may claim no more than one month's rent regardless. What you may never charge. You must not deduct from the deposit, or otherwise charge a victim-survivor, for damage caused by the abuse they experienced; you may pursue that only from the responsible party. Separately, a victim-survivor who terminated and supplied the required documentation is not liable for damage to the unit caused by the responsible party or during the course of an incident, and anything you retain must comply with the one-month-rent rule. And where the victim-survivor and the responsible party are both on the lease, there is a presumption that the victim-survivor receives the full deposit, less only what you lawfully withhold under the deposit statute as assessed at the end of their tenancy. So the default is that the money goes to them, and you carry the burden of showing otherwise. Debt collection. You may not assign an alleged debt under these rules to a third-party debt collector unless you have complied with the damages and written-statement requirements and have given the victim-survivor at least ninety days' written notice of your intention to do so, sent by whatever method they asked you to use for correspondence or, failing that, their last known electronic contact details. And you may not assign it at all if they comply with your lawful collection notice before the ninety days expire. Getting it wrong is expensive. A tenant may sue to restrain further violations and recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees, and on a finding of violation the court shall award statutory damages equal to their actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, as well as any punitive damages. That is on top of the ordinary treble-damages exposure for wrongfully withholding a deposit. Practical course: diarise both thirty-day clocks the day the tenancy ends, send the written damages statement even if you intend to claim nothing, never charge the victim-survivor for the abuser's damage, release the deposit to the victim-survivor where both were on the lease unless you can document a lawful deduction, and keep their new address confidential. Take advice before claiming anything, and before sending any debt to collection.

title: Colorado Now Has a Lock-Change Right - and a Safety Duty on You
bodyText:
This changed in May 2025 and a lot of Colorado leases have not caught up. Once a tenant tells you they are a victim-survivor of unlawful sexual behaviour, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse and gives you one of the qualifying documents, four things are true at once.

- You may not stop them changing the locks, including electronic locks.
- You may not charge them a fee for it, take any adverse action against them for it, or retaliate in any way.
- You may not stop them taking other reasonable safety precautions either - the statute names window bars, cameras and other non-permanent modifications.
- You must take all steps reasonably necessary to ensure the safety of the unit in response to their safety concerns, which is an affirmative duty on you, not just a prohibition.

Any provision in your lease that prohibits a tenant from changing a lock as a safety precaution, or from taking other reasonable safety precautions, is null and void and unenforceable. So a standard alterations clause, or a no-lock-changes clause, simply does not apply in this situation - and leaving it in your lease unqualified is worse than useless, because it tells the tenant something that is not true. Changing the locks, or taking those precautions, is also expressly not a material violation of the lease and not a substantial violation, so it cannot be a ground for eviction.

What you do get. If the tenant changes a lock, they must make all reasonable efforts to give you a copy of the key, or the electronic code or other information needed to open an electronic lock, as soon as reasonably practicable and no later than fourteen days after the change. There is one exception: if you, your property manager or the owner is the person alleged to be responsible, they give the key or code instead to another person with authority to manage the property whom they consider safe, and that person must agree not to share it with you. Do not treat a delay in getting the key as a licence to re-enter or re-key; your access rights are unchanged and the penalty for getting this wrong is large.

What it costs. A tenant may sue to restrain further violations and to recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees, and if the court finds a violation it shall award statutory damages equal to their actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, as well as any punitive damages.

Two related points.

- Colorado has no general lock or re-key duty outside this provision - nothing requires you to re-key between tenancies, for example - but working locks on all exterior doors, and locks or security devices on windows designed to be opened, maintained in good working order, are a statutory habitability characteristic, and the lack of them makes the unit uninhabitable.
- The state crime-victim compensation fund may pay a victim for rekeying locks; that is the fund paying the victim, not an obligation on you, so do not read it as one.

Practical course: take the no-lock-change language out of your Colorado lease or qualify it, respond in writing to a safety concern with what you will actually do and when, keep the fourteen-day key arrangement in writing, and keep the fact of victimisation and any new address confidential - you must not disclose either to anyone, including a co-tenant, without the tenant's express written consent unless a court order requires it.

Take advice before refusing any safety request.

title: The Colorado Protection-Order Citations Your Forms Should Use
bodyText: If your Colorado lease, addendum or policy cites a protection-order statute, check the citation, because the provisions have moved and some of the old numbers are now empty shells marked repealed. Two separate moves have happened. The first was in 2013. The civil protection order provisions used to sit in one long section, and that section was repealed with effect from July 1, 2013 and its contents redistributed. The foreign protection order section was repealed at the same time and moved. So a form citing the old single civil-protection-order section, or the old foreign-protection-order section, is citing a repealed provision. What those subjects live in now, in Colorado's article 14 of title 13: a legislative declaration; definitions, which is where you find domestic abuse, domestic violence and sexual violence defined; emergency protection orders; the procedure for a temporary civil protection order; general provisions relating to civil protection orders; the firearm prohibition that attaches to one; the procedure for a permanent civil protection order; enforcement and peace-officer duties; modification and termination; fees and costs; foreign protection orders; and the transfer of wireless telephone service in domestic abuse cases. Article 14.5 of title 13 is a different thing - extreme risk protection orders, the firearm-surrender regime - and should not be cited as though it were the ordinary civil protection order article. There is also a criminal mandatory protection order in the criminal code, which is a third, distinct instrument. The second move was in 2025, and it matters more to you, because it is inside the landlord-tenant statute. The list of documents a tenant may give you to establish victim-survivor status was rewritten, and with it the protection-order wording. A qualifying order is now a valid civil, criminal or emergency protection order or restraining order issued under article 14 or article 14.5 of title 13, or under the criminal mandatory-protection-order section. Note what that does: it brings extreme risk protection orders and criminal protection orders expressly inside the list, where the older wording just said a valid protection order. Two further citation points worth getting right. The definitions used in the landlord-tenant provisions no longer stand alone: domestic violence is now defined as the conduct described in the criminal-code domestic-violence definition or any conduct described in the civil protection order article's intimate-partner-violence definition, and unlawful sexual behavior as the offences listed in the sex-offender-registration definition or any conduct described in the civil protection order article's sexual-violence definition. So the same tenancy provision now reaches across three titles. And the sex-offence list those definitions point to is amended nearly every session, so treat it as a moving list rather than a fixed one. Practical course: do not reproduce statutory text or numbers in a lease at all if you can avoid it - say that the tenant may provide the documentation Colorado law allows, and keep the detail in a separate addendum or policy you can update. If your forms do carry citations, check them each year, and never reject a tenant's document because it does not match a number in an old form. Take advice if you are unsure whether a document a tenant gives you qualifies; wrongly refusing one is expensive.

title: What Documentation You May Ask For - and What You May Not
bodyText:
Colorado replaced this list in May 2025 and the old version is still circulating in landlord forms, so read the new one carefully. Four documents qualify, and the tenant needs only one of them.

- A self-attestation affidavit, which is the tenant's own signed statement that they are a victim-survivor and that the incident is the cause of, or contributed to, the ending of the tenancy; it must name the party allegedly responsible if the tenant knows the name and considers it safe to give.
- A letter signed by a qualified third party - the statute names an employee, agent or volunteer of a victim-survivor service provider, an attorney, a social worker, a medical professional, a faith leader or a mental health provider from whom the tenant has sought assistance, and that list is not exhaustive - stating that the third party believes the incident occurred and is the grounds for ending the tenancy.
- A police report from the prior 120 days stating that the tenant reported the conduct.
- A valid civil, criminal or emergency protection order or restraining order.

Note four changes from the older rule, each of which will bite a landlord working from an out-of-date form.

- The police-report window is 120 days, not 60.
- There is now a self-attestation route, so a tenant with no report, no order and no professional letter still qualifies.
- The old split, under which a stalking victim could not use a medical professional's statement, is gone; the same four-item list covers unlawful sexual behaviour, stalking, domestic violence and domestic abuse alike.
- The notice itself may come from a qualified third party rather than the tenant.

The statute says in terms that additional or other documentation is not required to qualify the tenant. So do not ask for a second document, do not ask for a police case number, do not ask for medical records, and do not ask the tenant to describe what happened.

You have exactly two rights here.

- If the tenant wants to exercise a right that depends on the documentation but has not produced it yet, you may make a written request, and they must then provide it within seven days.
- If what they give you contains conflicting information, you may require a letter signed by a qualified third party instead.

That is the whole of your entitlement to question it.

Confidentiality is strict and it was tightened in 2025. Once a tenant, or a qualified third party acting for them, tells you the tenant is a victim-survivor, you must not disclose that information to any person - including a co-tenant - except with the tenant's express written consent or if a court order requires you to. The same applies to any new address they give you after terminating.

There is one place you must disclose: if the tenant gives you written or actual notice of their status and consents to you sharing it with the court, you must disclose it to the court in any civil action on the complaint, with the return of service filed with the court, or whenever you become aware of their status.

You also must not ask a rental applicant about victim-survivor status, consider it, or require them to disclose it - that bar applies at application stage, before anyone is a tenant.

Getting any of this wrong is costly: a tenant may sue to restrain further violations and recover damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees, and on a finding of violation the court shall award statutory damages equal to their actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, as well as any punitive damages.

Practical course: accept any one of the four documents at face value, date-stamp it, store it where no co-tenant or on-site staff member can see it, acknowledge it in writing, and move straight to the consequences - the termination and money rules, the lock-change right and the deposit rules. Do not reproduce the four-item list verbatim in a lease you will not update; point to Colorado law and keep the detail in an addendum.

Take advice before refusing a document.

title: Reselling Electricity Can Make You a Regulated Utility in Colorado
bodyText:
This is the one that surprises Colorado landlords. Some states exclude a landlord who resells electricity or gas to tenants on a metered basis from utility regulation. Colorado does not. Its public utility law declares every other supplier of electric energy to be affected with a public interest and to be a public utility subject to the Public Utilities Commission, whether the energy is supplied to the public or only to the supplier's own members, and the list of things the public utility law does not apply to has no entry for a residential landlord - it covers irrigation systems, constitutional municipal-utility exemptions, hotels and motels reselling intrastate toll services, pay-telephone resellers and cellular communications, and nothing else.

There is a route out, but you have to ask for it.

If you buy gas or electric service from a regulated utility in order to deliver it to end users whose combined usage is measured by a master meter or other composite measurement device, you are a master meter operator, and the commission may exempt you from rate regulation - on application or on its own motion - only if four conditions are all met:
- You charge the end users nothing beyond the actual cost the serving utility bills you, including no construction, maintenance, financing, administration, metering or billing costs for the distribution system you own.
- If you bill separately, the sum of the bills does not exceed what the utility billed you.
- If you bill separately, you pass on to the end users any refunds, rebates, rate reductions or similar adjustments you receive.
- You meet any other condition the commission imposes.

Note how tight the first condition is - it is a no-markup rule that goes further than the landlord-tenant fee rules do.

On passing refunds through, you must notify current end users, either by first-class mail with a certificate of mailing or in a regular monthly or more frequent written communication, tell them they may claim the adjustment within ninety days, and if more than one hundred dollars is left unclaimed after that, contribute the unclaimed amount to the low-income energy and water assistance fund. The commission also makes rules under this section, which are not covered here. So before you master-meter and resell electricity, find out whether you need a commission exemption.

The landlord-tenant side has its own limits, which apply whatever the commission says.

- You may not charge the tenant anything for utilities above what the utility provider charged for service to their unit, except the one narrow markup the lease may set - either 2 percent of the amount you were billed or a flat ten dollars a month, never both - and except under the allocated-billing safe harbour.
- You may not charge for common-area maintenance or for anything you did not actually provide, you may not charge above the total price of what you did provide, and an administrative charge may not increase by more than 2 percent over a lease term of a year or less. A fee that breaks any of those is a prohibited lease clause, void and unenforceable.
- Utility charges are not rent, so you cannot evict for them.

And there is a deadline worth diarising: for residential premises built under permits applied for on or after July 1, 2027, gas, electric and water service delivered to the premises must be metered either directly by the utility provider or by a submeter - so master-metering new construction stops being an option.

If your costs are shared out by a formula rather than measured by a meter, that is a ratio utility billing system and a different set of conditions applies, including a requirement to disclose the allocation method clearly and conspicuously in the lease or an addendum.

Practical course: work out whether you are metering or allocating, because the rules differ; keep the underlying utility bills and submeter data and give them to a tenant who asks; pick one administrative charge or none and never both; and take advice on the Public Utilities Commission question before you build or buy a master-metered building.

Your city or county may add requirements; check local rules.

title: No Emergency Contact Rule in Colorado
bodyText:
Colorado has no statute about emergency contacts in an ordinary residential tenancy, in either direction. Nothing requires a tenant to name an emergency contact, and nothing requires you to publish an emergency telephone number, staff a 24-hour line or answer the phone outside business hours.

The one emergency-contact duty in the Colorado statutes applies only to mobile home parks: a park landlord must set up and keep an emergency contact number, post it in the park common areas and put it in each rental agreement and each revision of the park rules, and a resident who uses that number in time to report a water, sewer, utility or common-area problem is treated as having given the landlord notice of it. That rule does not reach a site-built house, condominium or apartment. So the point is left to your lease and to general contract law.

Two things still bite.

- Your lease must state your name and address, or your authorized agent's, and you must tell tenants within one business day if that changes - so there is always a place a tenant can reach you, even without an emergency number.
- A habitability complaint only starts your repair clock when it reaches you in writing at the place the lease names, so make that address or electronic address easy to find and keep it monitored; an unread inbox does not stop the clock once notice has been delivered there.

If you ask tenants for an emergency contact, ask for it as an optional lease term, use it only in a real emergency, and do not share it: a tenant who is a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, stalking or unlawful sexual behavior has a statutory confidentiality right that you can breach by passing information to a co-tenant or anyone else without express written consent.

Your city or county may require more than the state does; check local rules.

title: Property Taken by Eminent Domain: No Colorado Lease Rule
bodyText:
Colorado has no statute that says what happens to a residential lease when the property is taken by eminent domain. Nothing ends the lease, nothing abates or apportions the rent, and nothing divides the condemnation award between you and your tenant. Colorado values the property as a whole, on an undivided basis, and your tenant is joined in the case as one of the persons interested in it, so the split between your interest and the tenant's is left to your lease and to general law. If your lease is silent, you and your tenant are arguing from first principles at the worst possible moment, so put a condemnation section in the lease.

There is one trap. A clause that lets you end the tenancy because part of the property has been taken is not safe in Colorado.

Once a tenant has been in the property twelve months or more, and the property is not exempt from the for-cause rules, you may only end the tenancy on one of the grounds the statute lists, and that list does not include a taking or a condemnation. The list of no-fault grounds is closed too: demolition or conversion, substantial repairs or renovations, you or a family member moving in, withdrawing a single-family home, townhome, duplex, triplex or condominium unit from the market to sell it, a tenant refusing reasonable new lease terms, and a history of late rent. No rental agreement provision can waive those requirements, so a condemnation clause that purports to give you a termination right does not get you one.

Where the whole property is taken and the condemnor takes possession, that is different: nobody can give the tenant possession any more, and the tenant's right to possess simply ends, which is why the optional clause is limited to that case.

If a partial taking leaves the property genuinely unfit to live in, you are in habitability territory, not termination territory: deal with it as a repair and alternate-housing problem, consider whether the demolition or substantial-renovation no-fault ground with its ninety days of notice actually fits, and take advice before serving anything.

The good news is that your displaced tenant is not left to you for compensation. The condemnor, which includes the state, a political subdivision and any person with condemnation power, must pay a displaced person the actual reasonable cost of moving and the direct loss of personal property, and must pay a residential tenant who lawfully occupied the dwelling for at least ninety days before negotiations started a replacement-housing payment of up to five thousand two hundred fifty dollars to cover the rent difference on a comparable replacement home for up to forty-two months, paid once the tenant leases a decent, safe and sanitary replacement within a year. Those payments go to the tenant, not through you, they are not income or resources for tax or public-assistance purposes, and the tenant has an appeal route if the agency refuses.

Point your tenant at the condemning agency's relocation officer early, and do not put anything in your lease that purports to assign those payments to you.

Your city or county may add requirements; check local rules.

title: No Employee Screening Mandate in Colorado - and Limits If You Screen
bodyText: Colorado does not require you to run a background check on anyone you hire to work at a rental property. There is no statute for onsite managers, leasing agents, maintenance technicians, cleaners or contractors, and no registry or clearance a rental employee has to hold. Colorado's mandatory criminal-history checks exist, but they all attach to particular regulated settings - child care, assisted living and other care facilities, schools and school coaches, corrections, peace-officer training, security guards, licensed occupations, driving instructors, firearms dealers - and residential property management is not one of them. So whether to screen is your call, and it is usually a good one for anyone who will hold keys, enter occupied units or handle money. But the moment you do screen, general Colorado employment law applies to you, and three rules catch landlords out. First, you may not say in a job advertisement or on an application form that a person with a criminal history may not apply, and you may not ask about criminal history, or require it to be disclosed, on the initial written or electronic application. You may obtain a publicly available criminal background report at any time, and you may ask about criminal history later in the process - at interview, for example. That rule applies to every private employer in Colorado regardless of size, it is enforced by the Department of Labor and Employment rather than by a lawsuit, and the penalties escalate from a warning to one thousand dollars to two thousand five hundred dollars. Second, you may not use a credit report for a hiring decision unless the credit information is substantially related to the job, which the statute defines narrowly around executive or management roles with fiduciary responsibility, access to personal or financial information, or authority to issue payments, collect debts or sign contracts - plus banks, financial institutions and positions where a report is required by law. A property manager who signs leases and handles rent receipts may well fit; a maintenance technician almost certainly does not. If you do rely on credit information to turn someone down, you must tell them that and tell them which information you relied on. Third, if you give a reference about a former employee you have statutory immunity for what you say about their job history and performance, which falls away only if the information was false and you knew or should have known it was false, and you must send the person a copy of a written reference if they ask. Do not maintain or circulate a blacklist; that is a crime. FEDERAL: the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act separately governs disclosure, authorization and adverse-action notices when you use a third-party screening company. Your city or county may add requirements of its own; check local rules. None of this is a lease matter, so nothing about employee screening belongs in your tenants' lease.

title: When You Can Get a Tenant's Energy Data - and When You Need Consent
bodyText:
Colorado runs an energy benchmarking program for large buildings, and if one of your buildings is in it you have to report its energy use to the Colorado Energy Office every year. A building is covered if it has 50,000 square feet or more of gross floor area and is occupied by a single occupant or a group of tenants. Single-family homes, duplexes and triplexes are excluded outright, and so are unheated storage buildings, stand-alone parking garages and hangars, buildings more than half used for manufacturing or industrial purposes, and, since 2025, agricultural buildings, for which you can apply for a standing exemption. Most small landlords are therefore outside this entirely; a mid-size apartment building is not.

Where you are covered, you usually do not need your tenants' permission to get the data. Each qualifying utility publishes an aggregation threshold of four or fewer utility customer accounts, and if the building has at least that many accounts the utility must give you aggregated meter data, with names, addresses, phone numbers and e-mail addresses stripped out, on request and without any tenant consent. The utility has to supply it through a secure web portal or request form, within thirty days of a valid request, in a format your benchmarking tool can take, and at least annually until you revoke the request or sell the building - and it must do that whether or not you are named on the utility account.

You only need consent for a covered building that falls below the threshold, which in practice means a large building with one, two or three utility customers. For those, Colorado says in terms that the consent may be given in a lease provision, and that is the cleanest way to get it.

Three rules go with it.

- The consent lasts until the tenant revokes it, so you cannot make it permanent or irrevocable.
- You do not need it at all from a tenant who moves out without ever expressly refusing.
- **You cannot charge a tenant a fee for any of this:** Benchmarking is your obligation, and Colorado voids a lease provision that charges a tenant for something you need in order to meet your own obligations.

If a tenant simply refuses, you are not stuck. You can apply to the Colorado Energy Office for a waiver for that year, provided the building is below the threshold, you asked the tenant for permission at least thirty days before the report was due, you can prove you asked, and you submit a plan to include an energy-data sharing provision at the next lease renewal. You can also ask for more time where a utility or a tenant will not supply what you need despite a good-faith effort.

Two timing points changed in 2025.

- The annual report is now due November 1 rather than June 1, starting with 2025 data reported in 2026.
- Where you can show the office that you lack access to the data, the building's operator - which the statute defines to include a tenant who is named on the utility bill and has access to the data - must file the report instead of you.

Your city or county may impose stricter benchmarking or performance requirements than the state, and the statute says so expressly; check local rules.

title: You Must Give Benchmarking Data to Prospective Tenants of a Large Building
bodyText:
If a building is covered by Colorado's energy benchmarking law - 50,000 square feet or more of gross floor area, and not a single-family home, duplex, triplex or one of the other excluded building types - there is a disclosure duty that bites at the moment you advertise, not at signing. When you list the building, or any part of it, for sale or for lease, you must furnish an electronic copy of the benchmarking data you reported for the previous calendar year, or for the most recent twelve-month period of continuous occupancy, to three groups: prospective buyers or tenants, any licensed broker who asks about the property, and any major commercial real estate listing service the property is listed on. A listing service that receives it then has to publish at least the property's Energy Star score, where it has one, and its energy-use intensity.

Note what this does and does not mean.

- It is a duty owed to a prospective tenant of a covered building, so it attaches to the listing of an apartment in a large building just as it does to a commercial suite, and an electronic copy satisfies it.
- It is not a lease clause, and nothing requires you to put the data in the lease or to have the tenant acknowledge receiving it - though keeping a dated record that you sent it is sensible, because the statute gives you no safe harbour and the air quality control commission enforces this program with civil penalties.

If you sell the building, you must also hand the new owner the energy-use data, any tenant consent documentation you hold, and anything else needed to benchmark the building, and you must transfer the building's record in the benchmarking tool and your standing data request to the utility.

Your city or county may require more; check local rules.

title: Who Can Appear in Court for an LLC or Corporate Landlord in Colorado
bodyText: If you hold your rental through an LLC, a corporation, a partnership or any other entity, be careful about who walks into court. Colorado makes it a statutory wrong, not just a rule-of-court problem, for a person who is not a licensed attorney to commence, conduct or defend an action in any court of record in which that person is not personally a party, and a non-attorney who appears in a court of record for someone else is in contempt of both that court and the Colorado Supreme Court. Your entity is a different person from you in the law's eyes, so an owner or manager appearing for the entity is appearing for another person. There are two statutory exceptions, and they are narrow. The first is for a closely held entity, which the statute defines as an entity with no more than three owners. Such an entity may be represented before any court of record or any administrative agency by one of its officers, but only where the amount at issue does not exceed fifteen thousand dollars, excluding costs, interest and statutory penalties, and only where the officer gives the court evidence of authority to appear, at or before the hearing. A written resolution naming the officer is enough, and the court may rely on it. An officer of a corporation, a general partner, the person in whom management of an LLC is vested, and a member of a limited partnership association are each presumed to have authority once they show they hold that office. Exercising this option does not, by itself, make the appearing officer personally liable for what the entity did. The second exception is small claims court, where the rule is reversed: an entity must be represented by its own officer, member or full-time employee rather than by a lawyer, and there is a provision aimed squarely at rentals - in an action arising under part 1 of article 12 of title 38, which covers security deposit and property damage disputes, a property manager who received deposits or rents, or who signed the lease on the owner's behalf, is permitted to represent the owner. Small claims is capped at seven thousand five hundred dollars and, critically for landlords, it has no jurisdiction at all over forcible entry, forcible detainer or unlawful detainer, so you cannot take an eviction there. Evictions therefore go to county court, where the closely held entity rule and its fifteen-thousand-dollar ceiling are what you have to work with. One point the statutes do not settle: what the amount at issue is in a possession-only eviction, where you are asking for the unit back rather than for money. Nobody should assume that a claim for possession is worth nothing for this purpose. The cautious course is to treat the fifteen-thousand-dollar ceiling as applying whenever money is claimed at all, to keep any money claim in a possession case well under it if you intend to appear through an officer, to bring the signed authorising resolution to every hearing, and to instruct an attorney where the entity has four or more owners, where the sums are larger, or where the case is appealed. None of this belongs in your lease: it is court procedure, and the lease neither grants nor removes the right to appear.

title: Colorado's Hardship Delays Are Built Into the Writ, Not Asked For
bodyText: Colorado does not give a tenant a general right to ask the court to postpone an eviction because of hardship, and there is no statute headed hardship stay. What it does instead is build fixed delays into the writ of restitution, so plan your turnover dates around them. The court cannot issue a writ at all until forty-eight hours after judgment. The sheriff cannot execute a writ on a residential tenancy until at least ten days after judgment. And the writ is not executable for thirty days after judgment, and must say so on its face, in two situations: where the residential tenant receives supplemental security income, Title II social security disability insurance, or cash assistance through Colorado Works; and, since 2025, where the tenant has asserted the victim-survivor defence with the required documentation, in which case your own filing asking for the writ must identify the tenant as a victim-survivor and state that the writ is not executable for thirty days. Two carve-outs cut the thirty days back to the ordinary ten. The first is a judgment for possession for a substantial violation. The second is for a small landlord: five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five total rental units including those homes. Note that the small-landlord carve-out is written into the benefit-recipient limb and not into the 2025 victim-survivor limb, so do not assume it rescues you there. Writs are executed only in the daytime, between sunrise and sunset. Separately, if the tenant appeals, everything stops: taking the appeal stays all further proceedings. In a nonpayment case the appeal is only perfected if the tenant deposits the rent the judgment found due, and then keeps depositing rent as it falls due; if the tenant misses a deposit, you can move to have the judgment affirmed with costs. If you think you will suffer serious economic harm while the appeal runs, you can petition for an additional undertaking, but only after a hearing and only if you show a substantial likelihood of that harm and that the appeal bond will not protect you. And if either side asks to put the trial off by more than five days, the court may require a bond for the damage the delay causes. None of this is a lease matter. You cannot shorten any of these periods by agreement, and nothing in this library's lease asks a tenant to waive them: the lease does not carry eviction procedure. If the sums or the timing matter to you, take advice and get the writ moving promptly after judgment.

title: Colorado Hides the Eviction Case Unless and Until You Win Possession
bodyText: Colorado does not seal or expunge eviction records, because it does not need to: it suppresses them from the start. The moment you file an eviction action, every court record of it is a suppressed court record, which means it is visible only to the judge, court staff, the parties and their attorneys, authorised judicial staff, and anyone holding a court order granting access. The court may use the parties' names internally for administration, but it may not publish them online for any reason. The suppression lifts only when an order granting you possession is entered, and even then it does not lift automatically if the parties agree the record should stay suppressed - which is worth knowing, because agreeing to continued suppression costs you nothing once you have your judgment and can be a useful thing to trade in a settlement. Three categories of outsider can get in. An attorney who is not a party's attorney, or someone acting for that attorney, may access the record if they affirm in writing that a party gave permission, that they are looking only in order to advise or decide whether to appear for that party or to evaluate the case for mediation, and that they are not accessing it for commercial purposes. Since 2025, someone acting for the attorney general may access a suppressed record to investigate a violation of state law the attorney general can enforce. And since 2025, a tenant who is a victim-survivor may move or petition to suppress the record, or to keep it suppressed, including a record that predates the change; if the tenant supplies the statutory documentation and asserts that public access risks their safety or that of a household family member, the court must suppress or continue to suppress the related records, including a judgment for possession. What this means in practice is the opposite of what landlords in most states expect. You will not find a public docket of a pending eviction when you screen an applicant in Colorado, and you should not build your screening around one; a tenant with a dismissed or settled case will usually have nothing public at all. Equally, your own case is not public while it is running, so do not assume filing creates pressure through publicity. If you want the record public after you win, say nothing - it becomes public by default; it is agreement that keeps it suppressed. None of this is a lease matter: it is court records procedure, and nothing you put in a lease can make a suppressed record public or commit a tenant not to seek suppression.

title: You Cannot Name a Service Agent for Eviction Papers in a Colorado Lease
bodyText: Some states let a lease name a person who will accept eviction court papers for the tenant. Colorado does not, and a clause like that in a Colorado lease buys you nothing. The statute sets out how a notice to vacate or a demand for rent or compliance must be served, and the list is short: hand it to a known tenant occupying the property; leave it with a person, or a member of the tenant's family, older than fifteen who lives on the premises or is in charge of them; or, only after you have attempted personal service at least once on each of two separate days and found nobody there, post it in a conspicuous place on the premises.
