The summons and complaint are different again: personal service as in any civil action, with a copy of the complaint served alongside, or - after a qualified process server has made a diligent effort and failed - posting on the premises plus mailing a copy to the tenant at the premises by first-class mail no later than the next business day after you file. Personal service or posting must happen at least seven days before the appearance date, and the server must endorse the time and manner on the summons. There is one addition you must know about. If a tenant gives you written or actual notice that they are a victim-survivor of unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse, you must make all reasonable efforts to serve the notice personally on that tenant, and only if personal service fails after three attempts may you fall back on posting - and then you must also send the notice by certified mail or a commercial courier with a receipt or other proof of delivery. Three attempts and proof of delivery, not one posting. There is also a special route for a tenant enrolled in Colorado's address confidentiality program, which protects relocated victims and relocated protected health-care workers. Such a participant may be served at the substitute address the state designates, by registered mail or certified mail with return receipt requested, with any process, notice or demand the law requires or permits - and the state forwards it. Service is complete at whichever is earlier: the day the participant actually receives it, or five days after the date on a return receipt signed on their behalf. Note three things about that. It runs through the Department of Personnel, not through any Secretary of State. It is permissive, not the only or necessarily the required way to serve a participant. And where the law gives the participant a right to act within a prescribed period of ten days or less, five days are added when service is by mail - so your cure and answer clocks stretch. Finally, you cannot pass the cost of any of this to the tenant. Serving a statutory notice is your own compliance step, Colorado bars a fee for a good or service you need in order to meet your own obligations, and it separately voids any lease clause assigning a penalty to a party stemming from an eviction notice or action - a bar with no small-property or mobile-home exception. So leave service out of the lease altogether, and use the statutory methods.

title: What a Colorado Lease Can and Cannot Exculpate
bodyText: Colorado has no general statute about exculpatory clauses, hold-harmless clauses or limitation-of-liability clauses in a residential lease. The word exculpatory appears only a handful of times in the whole Colorado code, and never in landlord-tenant law; the only statutory exculpation rules are about trustees and custodians. That does not mean you have a free hand, because Colorado instead voids particular waivers one at a time, and between them they cover almost everything a landlord would want to exculpate. Your written rental agreement must not contain a waiver of the right to a jury trial, except that the parties may agree to waive a jury in a hearing to determine possession; a waiver of the ability to pursue, bring, join, litigate or support any joint, class or collective claim arising from or relating to the tenancy; a waiver of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing; a waiver of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment; or a waiver of the mandatory mediation some tenants are entitled to. Anything included in breach of that list is void and unenforceable. On top of that, any agreement waiving or modifying any right, remedy, obligation or prohibition in the habitability rules is void as contrary to public policy, and a rental agreement that waives or modifies a habitability right or remedy is unlawful, void and unenforceable - as is any provision that charges a tenant a cost, fee or penalty because the tenant exercised or tried to exercise a habitability right. The security deposit rules cannot be waived or modified for the tenant's benefit either, the for-cause eviction rules cannot be contracted around, and a tenant's right to call for police or emergency help can never be waived. There is exactly one exculpatory term the statute expressly lets you use: your written rental agreement may provide that you are not responsible for a violation of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment committed by a third party acting beyond your reasonable control. That is a useful clause if your tenants' complaints are often about neighbours or outsiders, and it is the only carve-out on the list. If you own an owner-occupied duplex or triplex, or an accessory dwelling unit where you live on the property or on the same lot, the whole waiver list other than the eviction-penalty and fee-shifting bars does not apply to you, which leaves you free to go further than other landlords - but take advice before you do, because general contract and tort law still applies. Whatever you draft, do not try to exculpate yourself from your own negligence or from habitability: that is the one place Colorado has closed off completely, and a void clause can taint the rest of your lease and hand the tenant a fee-shifting argument.

title: Tenant Indemnity Clauses: Lawful in Colorado, Not Offered Here
bodyText: A tenant indemnity clause - one where the tenant agrees to defend you and cover your losses if someone makes a claim because of something the tenant, their household or their guests did - is not prohibited by any Colorado statute. No provision in Colorado's landlord-tenant law addresses tenant indemnity at all, and the prohibited-clause list does not include it. This library still does not offer one, for three reasons. First, the useful part of it is already covered by narrower clauses that are easier to enforce: the tenant's duty not to damage the property, the tenant's responsibility for the acts of guests, and the requirement to carry renter's insurance. Second, an indemnity drafted broadly will overshoot into territory Colorado has closed. If it reaches a claim arising from a condition you were obliged to repair, it operates as a waiver or modification of the habitability rules, and that is void; if it reaches anything you must do anyway, a charge under it is a charge for a good or service necessary for you to meet your own obligations, which Colorado bars, and a lease provision imposing such a charge is itself prohibited. If it reaches repairs, cleaning or other work needed because of normal wear and tear, or any damage or defective condition that predates the tenancy, the clause is against public policy and void outright. Third, a defence-and-indemnity obligation is worth little against an individual tenant with no assets and no insurer who will accept the tender, while the drafting risk is real. If you still want one, keep it to claims arising from the acts or omissions of the tenant, the household and guests, carve out anything arising from your own acts, your own negligence and your statutory duties, never make it a route to recover wear and tear or preexisting conditions, and take advice first.

title: The Three-Day Substantial Violation Termination Is Already in Your Lease
bodyText: Colorado gives you a fast route out of a tenancy where the tenant, a guest or an invitee has done something serious, and you do not need a crime-free clause to use it: the statute declares it an implied term of every lease of real property in this state that the tenant will not commit a substantial violation while in possession. A substantial violation is any act or series of acts by the tenant or any guest or invitee of the tenant that, taken together, either endangers a person, or wilfully and substantially endangers the property of you, a co-tenant or anyone living on or near the premises, and occurs on or near the premises; or occurs on or near the premises and is a violent or drug-related felony under the listed articles of the criminal code; or occurs on the leased premises, the common areas, a hallway, the grounds, the parking lot or another area in the same building or complex and is a crime under federal or state law or a local ordinance that both carries a potential sentence of incarceration of 180 days or more and has been declared a public nuisance under state law or a local ordinance based on a state statute. If you have one, the tenancy may be terminated at any time, and the termination takes effect three days after you serve a written notice to terminate. The notice must describe the property, state the particular date the tenancy will terminate, and set out the grounds, and it must be signed by you or by your agent or attorney. Four limits matter as much as the remedy. You carry the burden of proving the substantial violation by a preponderance of the evidence, so document it and get the police report. It is a defence that the tenant did not know of, and could not reasonably have known of or prevented, a substantial violation by a guest or invitee, but immediately notified a law enforcement officer. You have no basis for possession at all where the tenant is a victim-survivor of unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse that caused, contributed to or resulted in the alleged violation and is documented as the statute requires - though nothing stops you proceeding against the person who is responsible for that abuse. And this is a ground, not a licence: a clause that penalises a tenant for calling the police or for seeking emergency help is void and can never be waived. Two practical points. Where the for-cause eviction rules apply to your tenancy, a substantial violation is one of the listed causes, so this route survives them - you cannot invent extra grounds in the lease, but you do not need to. And a judgment for possession for a substantial violation is carved out of the thirty-day delay that otherwise applies before a writ may be executed against a tenant on SSI, social security disability or Colorado Works, so the writ follows the ordinary ten-day rule. Everything beyond the notice is court procedure and the lease does not carry it: take advice before serving a three-day notice, because getting it wrong resets you to the ordinary grounds and timelines.

title: The Seventy-Two-Hour Deposit Rule After a Gas Hazard
bodyText: Colorado normally gives you thirty days to return a security deposit, and lets the lease specify longer, up to sixty days. There is one situation where that collapses to seventy-two hours, and it is the single most expensive deadline in Colorado's deposit law. It starts outside your control. If service personnel from a gas provider become aware of a hazardous condition in a gas appliance, piping or other gas equipment at a residential building, they must tell the customer of record in writing, stating whether the hazard is a fire hazard or a hazard to life, health, property or public welfare, and explaining the possible cause. If the resident is your tenant, the tenant must immediately tell you or your agent in writing. From your actual receipt of that written notice you have seventy-two hours, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, to have the condition repaired by a professional - meaning someone licensed or certified where state, county or municipal law requires it, or, where no such authorisation exists or none is available, someone otherwise qualified who carries at least one hundred thousand dollars of public liability and property damage coverage. Get the proof of repair; it is an affirmative defence in any action over the deposit. If you do not get the repair done in that window and the building remains hazardous, the tenant may choose to vacate. Once the tenant vacates, the lease is null and void, all future rights and obligations under it end, and the tenant may demand the immediate return of the deposit. You then have seventy-two hours from the tenant vacating to deliver the deposit, or the part the tenant is entitled to, plus any rent rebate for the period after the tenant left. If the seventy-second hour falls on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, you have until noon on the next day that is none of those. The tenant must give you a correct forwarding address, and you comply by mailing the statement and payment there. You may still withhold for nonpayment of rent, nonpayment of utility charges, or repair work or cleaning the tenant contracted for, and if you withhold anything you must send a written statement listing the exact reasons, with payment of the balance at the same time. Nothing may be retained for normal wear and tear. Miss it and the retention is deemed wilful and wrongful: the tenant gets twice the deposit plus reasonable attorney fees. Note two things that make this harsher than the ordinary rule. The statute says it applies notwithstanding the ordinary deposit penalty provision, so the seven-day written demand a tenant normally has to make before suing does not stand between you and that liability. And seventy-two hours is seventy-two hours - there is no good-faith safe harbour written into this section. Treat a written gas-hazard notice as the most urgent thing in your inbox, call a professional the same day, and have the deposit ready to send the moment the tenant hands back the keys.

title: No Absence Notice Law in Colorado - But Absence Matters for Abandonment
bodyText:
Colorado has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you they will be away, and no statute giving you a remedy if they do not. There is no seven-day rule, no fourteen-day rule, and no statutory damages for silence. If you want notice of an extended absence you have to put it in the lease, and the extended-absence clause does exactly that: the tenant tells you no later than the first day of an absence longer than seven consecutive days, and if the tenant wilfully fails to, you may recover the actual damages the failure causes.

Keep two things in mind if you use it.

- **The measure must stay actual damages.** Colorado prohibits a lease provision that fixes a fee, damages or penalty for a tenant's failure to give notice of nonrenewal, allowing only the actual losses the failure causes, and it would be reckless to assume a fixed sum fares better for a different kind of missed notice.
- **The clause gives you no right to enter:** Colorado gives a landlord no statutory entry right during an absence, so your ordinary entry clause and its notice requirements still govern, absence or no absence.

Where absence does carry legal weight in Colorado is abandonment. You may not remove or exclude a tenant without court process unless the unit has been abandoned, and the statute lists four things that can evidence abandonment: the return of keys, the substantial removal of the tenant's personal property, notice by the tenant, or the extended absence of the tenant while rent remains unpaid - and any of them must be such as would cause a reasonable person to believe the tenant had permanently surrendered possession.

Read that carefully, because it is a trap as much as a tool. Absence alone is not enough: rent must also be unpaid, and the overall picture must point to permanent surrender rather than a long holiday or a hospital stay. Get it wrong and you have an unlawful removal, which costs the tenant's actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, plus attorney fees and costs, and a court may put the tenant back in. A tenant who told you in advance they would be away for six weeks has given you evidence against abandonment, not for it - which is one more reason the absence-notice clause is worth having.

When in doubt, use the court process.

title: Colorado's Protected Classes Go Well Beyond Federal Law
bodyText: Colorado's fair housing law protects more people than federal law does, and if you screen or advertise to the federal list you will break Colorado law. The Colorado list is disability, race, creed, color, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, familial status, veteran or military status, religion, national origin and ancestry - and, separately, source of income. The classes federal law does not have are creed, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, veteran or military status, ancestry and source of income, so plan your process around the Colorado list. The prohibition is broad. You may not refuse to show, rent or lease housing, refuse to receive and pass on a bona fide offer, or otherwise make housing unavailable because of a protected class. You may not discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of the tenancy or in the facilities and services you provide with it. And you may not cause any written or oral inquiry or record to be made about an applicant's protected characteristics at all - which is stricter than most landlords expect, because it reaches your application form, your notes and your emails, not just your decision. There is one express exception to the inquiry rule: you may ask about military or veteran status where the purpose is to establish eligibility for veteran or military housing or a benefit. You may also still check credit, and that is not an unfair housing practice, provided you check the credit of every prospective tenant. You are not required to rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to the health or safety of others or would result in substantial physical damage to the property of others - but from 2026 the mere presence of an assistance animal is neither a direct threat nor presumed to cause substantial damage, and only documented, specific conduct of the animal counts. Advertising is separately prohibited: you may not make, print or publish, or have made, printed or published, any notice or advertisement about renting housing that indicates a preference, limitation, specification or discrimination based on a protected class, and there is a parallel ban for source of income. Nor may you tell someone a unit is unavailable when it is, for a discriminatory purpose, or try for profit to induce someone to rent by talking about who is moving into the neighbourhood. Three further points. Restrictive covenants limiting transfer, rental or lease on a protected ground are unlawful to include, to honour, or to try to honour - so a covenant in your title does not protect you. Retaliating against anyone who opposed a practice, filed a charge or took part in an investigation is itself an unfair housing practice, and so is helping, inciting or coercing anyone else to discriminate. And your broker or property manager is covered too, because the statute defines a person to include an owner, lessee, proprietor, manager, employee or agent - their conduct is your exposure. Religious and denominational organisations, and genuine private clubs not open to the public, have narrow carve-outs for non-commercial lodgings they own, and nothing in the law restricts housing designed for people with disabilities or overrides reasonable occupancy limits. Colorado's own constitutional equality clause only reaches the state and its political subdivisions and only concerns sex, so it adds nothing against a private landlord. Your city or county may add classes of its own; check local rules. Only one fair-housing statement is required in a Colorado lease, and it is the source-of-income one.

title: Colorado's Fair Housing Exemptions Cover Familial Status Only
bodyText: This is the point small Colorado landlords get wrong most often. Colorado does have the familiar owner-occupied and small-owner exemptions, but read the words that introduce them: with respect to familial status, nothing in this part applies to the following. The exemptions are limited to familial status. They do not excuse discrimination on race, creed, color, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, veteran or military status, religion, disability, national origin or ancestry. If you are an owner-occupant of a small building, you may lawfully decline to rent to a household with children - and nothing else on the list. The two familial-status exemptions are these. First, a single-family house sold or rented by a private individual owner who does not own more than three such houses at any one time; on a sale by an owner who does not live there and was not the most recent resident, the exemption covers only one sale in any twenty-four-month period, and the owner must hold no interest in, and have nothing reserved on their behalf from, more than three such houses. Second, rooms or units in a dwelling containing living quarters occupied or intended to be occupied by no more than four families living independently of each other, where the owner actually maintains and occupies one of those living quarters as their residence. Note that Colorado's owner-occupied exemption is a four-family one, not the two-family exemption some states use. Now the part that catches people. The single-family exemption applies only if the house is rented without using the sales or rental facilities or services of any real estate broker, agent or salesman or anyone in the business of selling or renting dwellings, or their employees or agents - and only if it is rented without the publication, posting or mailing of any advertisement or written notice that violates the section. So the advertising ban survives the exemption. You cannot advertise "no children" and rely on the exemption; the moment you publish a discriminatory notice you have lost it, and you have committed the separate advertising offence as well. You are also deemed to be in the business of selling or renting dwellings, and so outside the exemption, if in the preceding twelve months you took part as principal in three or more transactions involving the sale or rental of a dwelling or an interest in one. Three other limits sit beside these. The source-of-income duties have their own, different exemptions: the source-of-income prohibitions do not apply to a landlord with three or fewer units of housing for rent or lease, and a landlord who owns five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five total rental units is not required to accept federal housing choice vouchers for those homes. Housing for older persons is outside the familial status rules entirely, but only if it meets the statutory definition - a state or federal programme designed for older persons, or housing intended for and solely occupied by people aged sixty-two or over, or housing intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person aged fifty-five or over per unit, which additionally must publish and follow policies showing that intent, have at least eighty percent of occupied units occupied by someone fifty-five or over, and comply with the commission's verification rules. If you rely in good faith on the older-persons exemption you are not personally liable for monetary damages, but only if you had no actual knowledge the community was not or would not be eligible and the owner or operator has formally stated in writing that it complies. And religious or denominational organisations, and genuine private clubs not open to the public, have narrow carve-outs for non-commercial lodgings they own or operate. Nothing here overrides reasonable occupancy limits. Your city or county may have narrower exemptions or none; check local rules before relying on any of this.

title: A Fair Housing Charge in Colorado: Your Right to Elect Court
bodyText: If a fair housing charge lands on you in Colorado, the choice of forum is partly yours, and the deadline for making it is short. A charge has to be filed with the Colorado Civil Rights Commission within one year of the alleged unfair housing practice or it is barred. Within ten days of filing, or of identifying you as an additional respondent, the director must serve you with a notice identifying the alleged practice and advising you of your procedural rights and obligations, together with a copy of the charge. The director must start investigating within thirty days. If the director then finds probable cause, the commission issues a notice and complaint - and at that point you, as respondent, may elect to have the claims decided in a civil action in district court instead of an administrative hearing. The complainant and any aggrieved person on whose behalf the charge was filed have the same right. The election must be in writing within twenty days of receiving the notice and complaint, and the commission then notifies everyone else. If all parties agree to an administrative hearing, that is what happens; if any party elects court, the commission must authorise the attorney general to bring and maintain the civil action in state district court. Final administrative disposition is supposed to happen within a year of the charge, and if that is impractical the commission must write to you and the complainant explaining why. Separately, an aggrieved person can simply sue. A private civil action may be brought in state district court or federal district court within two years of the practice occurring or ending, or of a breach of a conciliation agreement, whichever is last, and the two years do not run while an administrative proceeding on the same complaint is pending. They do not need to have filed a charge first, and the status of any charge does not matter - with two exceptions: if the director or a local agency has obtained a conciliation agreement with the aggrieved person's consent, the only action available is to enforce that agreement; and once an administrative law judge has begun a hearing on the record on a commission complaint, a private action on the same practice cannot be started. The court may appoint an attorney for the aggrieved person on request. What is at stake: actual and punitive damages, permanent or temporary injunctions, restraining orders and affirmative action orders, and attorney fees and costs to the prevailing party at the court's discretion - so a win can still be expensive. Since 2025 there is a floor: where the court awards damages and finds you violated one of the source-of-income or rental-assistance paragraphs and the violation concerns discrimination based on a person's use of a housing subsidy, it must award the plaintiff at least five thousand dollars, and the calculation of actual damages must take account of what the tenant lost by forfeiting their subsidy. The attorney general can also sue, within eighteen months. Relief does not unwind a contract, sale, encumbrance or lease already completed with a bona fide purchaser, encumbrancer or tenant who had no actual notice of the charge or action. Practical course: diary the twenty-day election window the moment a notice and complaint arrives, keep every application, advertisement, note and message, and take advice immediately - the election is a strategic decision, not a formality.

title: Child Care in a Rental: Your Permission Is the Gate
bodyText: Colorado does not make you let a tenant run a family child care home in your rental. There is no statute requiring it, no statute setting the terms on which you must allow it, and no statutory right for a tenant to operate one over your objection. The decision is yours and it belongs in the lease. What Colorado does regulate is the other obstacle a home child care provider hits, which is the community association. A common interest community association may not prohibit the operation of a licensed family child care home, and a metropolitan district is subject to the same rule for the properties it governs. But read those provisions carefully, because they are not about you. They remove the association's veto, not yours. The companion provision on home-based businesses is explicit about it: what an association may not prohibit is a home-based business operated at a unit by the unit owner, or by a resident of the unit with the unit owner's permission. So if you own a condominium or a home in a covenanted community and your tenant wants to run a licensed child care home, the association cannot stop it - but only if you have agreed. Your permission is the gate. Four things to know if you are deciding whether to agree. The association keeps its ordinary rules on architectural control, parking, landscaping, noise and other matters that are not specific to running a business, and it must make reasonable accommodation for fencing requirements that apply to licensed family child care homes. The association may require the owner or operator to carry liability insurance at reasonable levels its board sets, covering personal injury, death and damage to personal and real property arising from any aspect of the operation, in the common elements, in the unit itself or in any other unit - and the association must be named as an additional insured, with that cover primary to the association's own. The association rule does not apply at all in a community that qualifies as housing for older persons under the federal Housing for Older Persons Act. And local zoning still applies: a licensed family child care home has to comply with local government zoning, which the state has recently moved to standardise but has not abolished, so your tenant should confirm the position with the city or county. If you do decide to allow it, do not simply stay silent. Put the permission in writing, require proof of the licence and of liability insurance naming you as an additional insured, require compliance with the association rules and with local zoning, and say what happens if the licence lapses. A general residential-use-only clause in your lease will otherwise read as a refusal, which may be exactly what you want - but make that a choice rather than an accident. Take advice before granting permission, because the insurance and liability questions are real.

title: No Colorado Rule on Hunting Rights in a Farm Lease - and the Trap in the Wildlife Code
bodyText:
Colorado has no statute saying whether a tenant of rented farmland may hunt or fish on it. There is no default rule granting the tenant a sporting right, and none reserving it to you. The point is left entirely to your lease, and if your lease is silent you are relying on general property law to sort out something the wildlife code has already made easy for your tenant.

Here is the trap. Colorado makes it unlawful to enter privately owned land to hunt, trap or fish without first obtaining permission from the owner or the person in possession of the land. The person in possession of leased farmland is your tenant. So on the face of the statute your tenant can give a hunting party permission to come on to your land, and those hunters have not committed the offence - because they got permission from a person in possession, which is exactly what the statute asks for. Nothing makes the tenant get your consent first.

If that matters to you, reserve the sporting rights in writing; the optional sporting-rights clause does it, including a bar on the tenant giving permission to anyone else.

Two related points.

- The landowner preference programme that allocates big-game licences is for owners, not tenants: eligibility turns on being an owner shown by a recorded deed of a parcel of agricultural land of at least one hundred sixty acres that meets the habitat conditions. But if you take a licence voucher under it, transferring the voucher must include permission to access and hunt the land for the whole season the licence covers, and that permission cannot discriminate among hunters or impose restrictions beyond the manner of access - so you are committing your tenant to season-long hunter access, and the lease should say so before your tenant discovers it.
- If you are renting agricultural land, or a hunting cabin, yurt or hut in an unincorporated area with no public water, heat or sewer, rented for recreational purposes, that tenancy is outside Colorado's warranty of habitability altogether. That is a significant difference from an ordinary residential rental, and it cuts both ways: you do not carry the habitability duties, and the tenant has none of the habitability remedies. The prohibited-clause rules and the deposit rules still apply to a residential rental agreement, so do not read the habitability exception as a general exemption.

County and municipal rules on discharging firearms, and state wildlife seasons and licensing, apply whatever your lease says; check local rules.

title: No Deposit-Alternative Fee in Colorado - the Definition Closes the Door
bodyText: Colorado has no statute authorising a fee in lieu of a security deposit, no insurance-backed deposit-replacement regime, no requirement that you offer such a product to every applicant, and no right for a tenant to switch out of one and into a deposit. Nor is anything pending: no Colorado statute directs a state agency to write regulations for deposit alternatives, so unlike some states there is no product waiting on rules. What Colorado has instead is a definition that closes the door. A security deposit means any advance or deposit of money, whatever you call it, whose primary function is to secure the performance of the rental agreement. So if you collect a monthly or one-off charge whose job is to stand in for a deposit, it is a deposit in law however the paperwork is labelled, and the whole deposit regime attaches: the two-months-rent ceiling, the thirty-day return clock, the closed list of things you may retain it for, the written statement of deductions, the documentation you must hand over on request, and the treble damages for wrongful retention. Calling it non-refundable does not help you. Any lease provision that waives or modifies the deposit rules for the tenant's benefit is void, so a clause saying the deposit-replacement fee is not returnable is unenforceable and you will still owe it back. Three more rules bite on any such fee. You may not charge a tenant for a good, service or property that is not actually provided, so a fee that buys the tenant nothing real is unlawful. You may not charge a fee that increases by more than two percent over the course of a rental agreement of a year or less, utilities aside. And you must disclose the total price - the maximum total of everything the tenant must pay or cannot reasonably avoid - as a single number, more prominently than any other pricing information, so a deposit-replacement fee cannot be hidden in the small print of an advertisement. There is one new wrinkle on the ceiling itself, and it is narrow. From January 1, 2027 the two-months-rent cap does not apply where you and the tenant have signed a post-closing occupancy agreement under a purchase contract in which you bought the residence from the tenant - the sale-leaseback rent-back. Outside that case the cap stands. If you want to lower the barrier to entry for applicants without taking a big deposit, the lawful routes in Colorado are to charge a smaller deposit, or to agree in writing to take the deposit in instalments, not to invent a non-refundable substitute. On the credit-reporting question: Colorado imposes no notice duty on a landlord before reporting a damage claim to a credit bureau or passing it to a collector, with one exception - a debt arising from a victim-survivor's early termination may not be assigned to a third-party debt collector unless you have complied with the damages-documentation and written-statement duties and have given the tenant at least ninety days' written notice of your intent to assign, and you may not assign it at all if the tenant complies within those ninety days. General debt-collection law otherwise applies. Take advice before offering any deposit-alternative product in Colorado.

title: Colorado Has No State Fire Code for Rentals - Your Local Code Becomes a Habitability Duty
bodyText: Colorado has no statewide fire code or building code for private residential rentals. The state does adopt a fire and building code through the Division of Fire Prevention and Control, but the enforcement provision names a closed list of buildings - public schools, junior college districts, health facilities and school district buildings - and a house, condominium or apartment you rent out is not on it. Fire and building codes that apply to your property are adopted by your county or your municipality, and enforced by them. Do not read that as freedom. Colorado turns your local code into a state obligation through the warranty of habitability, in two places. First, the list of characteristics a residential premises must have includes compliance with all applicable building, housing and health codes where the violation would constitute a condition that materially interferes with the life, health or safety of the tenant. Second, the list of conditions that make a premises uninhabitable includes any inaccessible fire exits or egress in accordance with applicable building, housing, fire and health codes, and any missing, damaged, improper or misaligned chimney or venting on a fuel-fired heating, ventilation or cooling system. So a blocked exit, a bedroom window that will not open, a padlocked fire escape or a disconnected flue is not merely a local code citation: it is a habitability breach, with the written-notice clock, the repair deadlines, the alternate-housing exposure and the tenant remedies that come with it - and none of that can be waived in the lease. Four state-level pieces are worth knowing. If your property is in the wildland-urban interface, the state wildfire resiliency code board sets minimum codes and standards, and the local governing body with code authority - your city or town, your fire protection district, a fire-providing improvement district, or the county for unincorporated land outside a district - must adopt a code that meets or exceeds them within three months of the board adopting them. Enforcement is local, but if your local body has no enforcement rules it can ask the division to inspect and enforce, and the division may charge you, the property owner, a reasonable fee for that. Second, counties and municipalities carry state-imposed duties about energy codes when they adopt or update codes, and since 2025 adopting the wildfire resiliency code does not by itself trigger those energy-code duties - useful context when your jurisdiction updates its rules. Third, since 2025 a county building code must carry accessibility standards at least as stringent as the International Building Code. Fourth, and most expensive for you, from 2026 a county enforcing its building code has a clear civil-penalty range: at least one hundred dollars and up to two thousand six hundred fifty dollars per violation, with a presumptive maximum of five hundred dollars for a first violation, higher where aggravating factors are present, and an unpaid penalty becomes a recorded lien on the property that the county treasurer collects like unpaid taxes with a ten percent collection charge on top. A code problem you leave alone can end up as a lien, so fix it and keep the paperwork. Separately from any code, Colorado imposes its own alarm duties on rental property by statute, including carbon monoxide alarms, and those are not local rules you can ignore. Practical course: find out which codes your city or county has adopted and in which edition, keep the inspection and permit records for any work, never obstruct an exit or a window to gain storage or security, service flues and vents annually, and treat any fire-safety complaint from a tenant as a habitability notice from the moment it arrives in writing. Your city or county may require more than anything described here; check local rules.

title: No Fire Sprinkler Duty in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado has no statute that requires fire sprinklers in a rental home, and no statute that makes you retrofit sprinklers into a building that does not have them. Sprinklers are not on the list of characteristics a rental must have to be habitable, so the absence of a sprinkler system is not by itself an uninhabitable condition and does not give a tenant a habitability remedy. Four things still reach you. First, your local building and fire code is where any sprinkler requirement will actually come from - a home-rule city or a county, or a fire protection district, may require sprinklers in new construction, in a conversion or change of use, or when you pull a permit for substantial work, and the state leaves that to them. Check with your local building department and fire district before you remodel, add a unit or convert a building, and never assume the state's silence means your city is silent. Second, habitability does reach fire safety by another route: a rental is treated as uninhabitable if it substantially lacks compliance with applicable building, housing and health codes where the violation would materially interfere with the tenant's life, health or safety, and a blocked or inaccessible fire exit or egress is presumed to interfere materially - so if your building does have sprinklers, standpipes, alarms, fire doors or marked exits because a code required them, letting them fall out of service or blocking an exit is a habitability problem even though installing them was never a state duty. Keep exits clear, keep anything the code made you install working, and keep the service records. Third, if you do install or service a fire suppression system, the person doing the work must be a sprinkler fitter registered with the state, who must also hold any local licence or permit and comply with local building codes - so use a registered contractor and keep the paperwork. Fourth, you cannot make the tenant pay for it. Fire safety work that a code requires of the building is your own obligation as landlord, and Colorado voids a lease provision that charges the tenant a fee for a good, service or property needed for you to comply with your own responsibilities, including your duty to provide a habitable home. Put the cost in the rent, not in a separate fire-safety or life-safety fee. One practical note: because the state imposes no sprinkler duty, nothing requires you to tell a tenant that the building has no sprinklers, but if your marketing or lease says the building is sprinklered, make sure it is.

title: Firearms in Colorado Rentals
bodyText:
Colorado has no landlord-tenant firearms law at all. The words firearm, handgun, gun and weapon do not appear anywhere in Colorado's property title, so no statute gives you the right to ban firearms in a rental and no statute makes a ban unenforceable. That leaves it to your lease and to general contract law, with four practical consequences.

- **Colorado has no parking-lot or vehicle-storage statute binding landlords.** Some states forbid a property owner or employer from stopping a person keeping a lawfully owned firearm in a locked private vehicle; Colorado's version of that rule restrains only cities, counties and cities and counties, not a private landlord, so you need not write that concession into your lease.
- **Do not assume the state's silence means your city is silent.** Since 2021 a Colorado local government may enact firearm rules that are more restrictive than state law - it simply cannot go less restrictive - so check your city or county code and, if your building is in one, your common-interest community's declaration.
- **The duties worth putting in a lease are the ones Colorado already imposes on the tenant.** Firearms must be responsibly and securely stored when not in use so that an unsupervised juvenile, or a resident of the premises who is not legally allowed to have a firearm, cannot get to them; failing to do that on premises the person owns or controls, knowing a juvenile can get to the firearm or that an ineligible resident lives there, is a crime. Firing a gun into a dwelling, another building or an occupied vehicle is a felony. Restating those gives you a lease ground if a tenant ignores them, and costs you nothing.
- **Be careful how far you go.** A clause banning lawful possession inside the home is untested ground in Colorado: nothing in the statutes forbids it, but the state constitution says the right of no person to keep and bear arms in defense of his home, person and property shall be called in question, and court decisions on a private lease ban are not covered here. The cautious course is to restrict discharge and require secure storage rather than ban possession, and to take advice before going further.

One more trap: never write a firearm or crime-free rule so that it penalises a tenant for calling the police. Colorado voids a lease provision that lets you terminate, fine or take any adverse action against a tenant because the tenant or a household member or guest called for police or emergency assistance in a domestic violence, domestic abuse, stalking or unlawful sexual behavior situation, and that right cannot be waived.

Last, firearms are not a habitability or deposit matter: you cannot charge a tenant a fee for a firearm rule, and a lawful charge has to be listed in the lease before you can take it out of the deposit at all.

title: No Flood Disclosure Duty in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado does not require you to tell a residential tenant anything about flood risk. There is no flood-zone disclosure, no flood-history disclosure, no duty to say whether the building has ever flooded, no duty to say whether you carry flood insurance and no duty to tell the tenant that their own belongings are not covered by your policy. Colorado's statutory property disclosures - special taxing districts, common interest community obligations, a methamphetamine laboratory, the potable water source, transportation projects, oil and gas activity, estimated future property taxes, a metropolitan district website and elevated radon - almost all run to a buyer rather than a tenant, and none of them is about flooding. The one disclosure Colorado does make a landlord give a tenant is the radon disclosure, which shows the legislature knows how to impose a rental disclosure and has not done it for flood. So the point is left to your lease and to general contract law, and three things follow. First, silence is only safe if it is actually silence. Colorado's consumer protection law makes it a deceptive trade practice to make a knowing or reckless false representation about the characteristics of property, and separately to fail to disclose material information you knew at the time of an advertisement or sale where that failure was intended to induce the consumer into the transaction - and there is a catch-all for any knowing or reckless unfair, unconscionable, deceptive, deliberately misleading, false or fraudulent act or practice. So saying nothing when nobody asks is one thing; saying the basement has never flooded when you know it has, or staying quiet about a flood you know of in order to get the lease signed, is another. If a tenant asks, answer honestly or say you do not know. Whether a residential tenancy is within these particular paragraphs is not spelled out in the statute and would be for a court. Second, disclosing voluntarily is usually the better course, and costs you nothing: a short written statement that the property is or may be in a mapped flood hazard area, that your insurance does not cover the tenant's possessions, and that renters' insurance is the tenant's own protection, heads off the argument later and supports a renters'-insurance requirement if your lease has one. Keep it factual and do not guarantee that the property will not flood. Third, what Colorado does regulate is what happens after a flood, not before the lease. A flood is an environmental public health event, which triggers a set of habitability duties: you must contact the tenant, remediate to the standards the statute names, document that you did, grant access so the tenant can retrieve belongings once a government official says the unit is safe to enter, and in some cases you may terminate the lease - with thirty days' written notice, the deposit returned and rent prorated. Separately, during a declared disaster Colorado caps what you may charge a new or existing tenant, so do not raise rents in the aftermath without checking that rule. Your city or county may require more than the state does, especially in a mapped flood area; check local rules.

title: What a Foreclosure Does to a Colorado Tenancy
bodyText: Colorado's foreclosure statutes treat your tenant as a player in the foreclosure, not as a bystander, and that cuts both ways. Start with notice. When a public trustee foreclosure begins, the mailing list the lender gives the public trustee has to include the occupant of the property, addressed simply to "occupant", and, where the lender wants the foreclosure to wipe out an unrecorded lease, the lessee as well - mailed to the lessee at the premises. So your tenant will usually learn of the foreclosure from the public trustee whether or not you tell them. Next, your tenant has real rights in the process. For the purposes of the foreclosure article a lessee counts as a lienor, without any lien amount, which means the tenant is entitled to the lienor notices and can file a notice of intent to redeem and redeem the property. Separately, a holder of a junior interest whose instrument was recorded before the notice of election and demand was recorded can file a notice of intent to cure your default - and a change taking effect on July 1, 2026 narrows the wording of that cure provision to a junior lienor as defined in the foreclosure definitions, which a lessee is deemed to be for the purposes of the article; if a tenant with a recorded lease wants to cure, take advice rather than assuming either way. Note the practical limit: an unrecorded residential lease gets the mailed notice but not the cure right, because the cure right requires a recorded instrument. Then the sale. When all redemption periods expire, title vests in the holder of the certificate of purchase free and clear of all liens and encumbrances junior to the lien that was foreclosed. A lease signed after the deed of trust is junior, so the sale can extinguish it - but not automatically, and two provisions cut the other way. If your tenant was in actual possession before the notice of election and demand or lis pendens was recorded, and was not made a party, served, or notified as the foreclosure statutes require, the tenant is an "omitted party" whose interest the sale does not simply wipe out: it can be terminated only through a civil action that affords the tenant the cure or redemption rights the tenant would otherwise have had, and if an interested person files a document affirming the tenant's interest, subject to the terms and conditions of the lease, written or oral, then the tenant's interest is not affected by the foreclosure at all. Separately, in a common interest community, a tenant whose tenancy began before the lis pendens and whose lease is unrecorded is a deemed alternate lienor, second in priority; an alternate lienor who redeems after a lessee has redeemed takes the property subject to the lease, and that section leaves untouched the rights of a tenant whose residential lease is recorded. What Colorado does not have is a general rule binding every purchaser at a foreclosure sale to your lease, a state-law 90-day notice to the tenant after the sale, a rule redirecting rent to the purchaser, or a rule keeping a foreclosure-related eviction off a tenant's record. During the foreclosure a court may appoint a receiver where the security is clearly inadequate or the premises are being damaged, and the receiver takes possession and applies the rents and profits; if nobody applies for a receiver and the owner abandons the premises, the lienholder may take possession until the sale with a receiver's duties, including as to the rents. After the sale and during redemption, letting the premises fall into disrepair, failing to keep them yielding an adequate income, or not paying taxes, interest or insurance is treated as waste. Four practical points. First, do not put a clause in your lease letting you end the tenancy because the property is foreclosed. For a tenancy the for-cause eviction rules cover - broadly, a tenant of at least twelve months in a property that is not owner-occupied small housing or otherwise exempt - cause exists only on the statutory grounds, and foreclosure is not one of them; a rental-agreement provision waiving those requirements is void. Second, if you are the buyer at a foreclosure sale and someone is living in the property, do not assume you can simply remove them. Whether the for-cause rules continue to protect an occupant whose leasehold the sale extinguished is not answered by the statutes and would be for a court; the cautious course is to treat the occupant as a tenant, serve proper written notice, and take advice before filing. Third, federal law may give the occupant more than Colorado does, and it is the usual source of a 90-day notice after a foreclosure. Fourth, if you tell your tenant about a foreclosure, tell them the truth; no statute requires the disclosure, but a false statement about it is a different matter. The eviction itself is court procedure.

title: Renting a Home Back to the Owner You Bought It From in Foreclosure
bodyText: If you buy a home from an owner whose mortgage is in default and then rent it back to them, Colorado's Foreclosure Protection Act governs the whole transaction, and your lease is part of what it regulates. You are an equity purchaser if you take title to a residence the owner occupies as a principal residence that is encumbered by a residential mortgage loan at least thirty days delinquent or in default, unless you are buying it as your own home or you fall within one of the listed exceptions. Buying at the public trustee's or sheriff's foreclosure sale is one of those exceptions, so this is about buying from the owner before the sale, not about bidding at it. Five things follow. First, your contract has to contain the entire agreement and must set out your name, business address and telephone number, the street address and full legal description of the home, a clear and conspicuous disclosure of any of the owner's obligations you are assuming, the total consideration, the terms of payment, the date and time possession transfers, the terms of any rental agreement or lease, the specifications of any option or right to repurchase including every deposit, down payment, price and fee, a notice of cancellation, and a specific statutory notice in at least nine-point bold type saying that until the cancellation right ends you cannot ask the owner to sign a deed or any other document. The lease terms are not an afterthought you paper later; they belong in that contract. Second, the owner has a cancellation right until midnight of the third business day after signing, or noon the day before the foreclosure sale, whichever comes first, and the contract must carry a conspicuous twelve-point bold statement of it with duplicate detachable cancellation forms. Until you have complied, the owner can still cancel. Until the cancellation period has fully elapsed you must not take or induce a conveyance, record the contract or any lease, transfer or encumber the property, or pay the owner anything. Third, if the arrangement is a sale with an option for the owner to buy the home back - the classic rent-to-repurchase deal - it is permitted only if all five statutory conditions are met: the contract complies with the contents rules; it gives the owner a non-waivable thirty-day right to cure any default, exercisable on at least three separate occasions; you fully assume or discharge the lien in foreclosure and any prior liens that will survive it, without breaching those liens' terms; you verify and can demonstrate that the owner has or will have a reasonable ability to make the lease payments and to repurchase within the option term, with a rebuttable presumption of ability where housing and other debt payments do not exceed sixty percent of monthly gross income; and the repurchase price is not unconscionable, where a price more than twenty-five percent above what you paid raises a rebuttable presumption that the contract is unconscionable. Fourth, you cannot contract out of any of it. A provision purporting to waive these rights or a jury trial, to pick another state's law or courts, to lay venue outside the county where the property is, or to impose costs or fees greater than your actual costs and fees, is void against public policy. And you must not make untrue or misleading statements about the home's value, the proceeds the owner would get from a foreclosure sale, any contract term, the owner's rights, or the nature of any document you ask them to sign. Fifth, this is specialised work with criminal penalties attached and a general unconscionability standard on top. If you are considering it, get a Colorado real estate lawyer to paper it. Nothing in this library's lease templates is designed for an equity-purchaser reconveyance, and a standard residential lease will not satisfy these rules.

title: No Duty to Disclose a Foreclosure to a Colorado Tenant
bodyText: Colorado does not make you tell a tenant, or someone applying to rent, that the property is in foreclosure, that you have missed mortgage payments, that a notice of election and demand or a lis pendens has been recorded, or that a sale date is set. Several states require exactly that notice before a lease is signed; Colorado does not. The disclosure duties Colorado does put on a landlord are a short list, and foreclosure is not on it: the radon disclosure, which has to be given in a separate document before the lease is signed; the two habitability statements your lease must carry; the source-of-income statement; and, from January 1, 2027, a notice in every rental application about the data you will look at when you screen an applicant and the factors you will weigh. Three things are worth knowing anyway. First, your tenant will probably find out without you. When a public trustee foreclosure starts, the lender's mailing list to the public trustee has to include the occupant of the property, addressed to "occupant", and the public trustee must mail notice to the lessee of a single-family residence or a multiple-unit residential dwelling. So the choice is usually between your tenant hearing it from you and your tenant hearing it from a government notice in the mail. Second, no duty to volunteer is not a licence to misstate. It is a deceptive trade practice in Colorado to make a knowing or reckless false representation about the characteristics of property, to fail to disclose material information you knew at the time of an advertisement or sale where that failure was intended to induce the person into the transaction, and there is a catch-all for any knowing or reckless unfair, unconscionable, deceptive or misleading act or practice. Saying nothing when nobody asks is not the same as answering "no" when a tenant asks whether the house is in foreclosure. Third, telling the tenant early is usually the better commercial choice: a tenant who learns of a foreclosure from a trustee's notice is a tenant who stops paying rent, and a tenant who knows the position may redeem or cure, which the foreclosure statutes expressly allow a lessee to do. If you do disclose, put it in writing, keep it factual, and do not promise an outcome you cannot control. Finally, a different rule applies if you are buying a home from an owner in default and renting it back to them - that transaction is heavily regulated and has its own contract-disclosure and cancellation requirements. Your city or county may add a disclosure the state does not require; check local rules.

title: No Foreign-Ownership Restriction in Colorado - and What You Must Not Ask
bodyText: Colorado has no alien land law and no foreign-adversary ownership restriction. Nothing in Colorado's statutes limits who may own, buy or rent residential property by citizenship, nationality, residence or foreign control; there is no registry to file, no approval to get, no carve-out that makes a twelve-month lease to a foreign person void, and no rule requiring a deed or lease to a non-citizen to recite that fact or to give the person's name and address. Colorado law says the opposite in terms: no individual is disqualified from taking as an heir, devisee, grantee, lessee, mortgagee, assignee or other transferee because that person is or has been an alien. So a lease to a tenant who is not a United States citizen, or to a company owned abroad, is as valid as any other lease and needs no special wording. That silence does not mean you are free to take immigration status into account, and this is where Colorado landlords get into trouble. Colorado's Immigrant Tenant Protection Act makes it unlawful for you to demand or ask for information or documents about a tenant's or an applicant's immigration or citizenship status, to threaten to disclose that status to anyone in order to get the tenant to leave or to coerce them in any way, to harass, intimidate or retaliate against a tenant for exercising rights under that Act, to disclose or threaten to disclose that status to any person, entity or immigration or law enforcement agency, to refuse to enter into a rental agreement or approve a subtenancy based wholly or partly on that status, or to bring a possession action on that basis. There is one narrow carve-out: a landlord who is also the tenant's employer may collect what a state or federal employment form requires. State fair housing law separately forbids discrimination in housing on grounds including national origin and ancestry. The practical consequences for your paperwork: screen every applicant on the same financial and rental-history criteria; do not ask for a passport, a permanent resident card, an alien registration card or a work authorization document as a condition of renting; do not put an immigration-status representation, a citizenship warranty or an immigration-reporting threat in your lease or your application; and if you need to verify identity, use the same identity documents you would accept from anyone. If an applicant has no Social Security number or no United States credit history, treat it as a thin-file problem and ask for the alternative proof of income or payment history you would accept from any thin-file applicant, not as an immigration question. On the sale side, federal law can still bite - a foreign seller's sale of United States real property carries federal withholding obligations and some transactions can be reviewed on national-security grounds - but that is federal, not Colorado, law. Your city or county may have its own rules; check local requirements.

title: No Right to Redeem or Reinstate a Forfeited Lease in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado has no statutory redemption period for a tenancy. Some states let a tenant whose lease has been forfeited pay everything owed and get the tenancy back, even after judgment. Colorado does not: there is no provision anywhere in its civil-procedure title giving a tenant a right to redeem, reinstate or restore a tenancy after a forfeiture, and the only redemption right in Colorado law that touches a lease at all is in the foreclosure statutes, where a tenant counts as a lienor and may redeem the property from a foreclosure sale - which is about the property, not about reviving a forfeited lease. What Colorado gives instead is a cure window before you can sue. A failure to pay rent on demand works a forfeiture of the agreement, and you do not have to demand the rent on the day it falls due; but before the holdover becomes an unlawful detention you must serve a written notice requiring, in the alternative, payment of the rent or possession of the premises. The notice period is ten days for an ordinary residential agreement, three days for a nonresidential or employer-provided housing agreement, and five days for an exempt residential agreement - which means a single-family home let by a landlord who owns five or fewer single-family rentals and whose agreement says in terms that the ten-day period does not apply. That last point is the one landlords miss: the shorter period is not automatic for a small landlord; the lease has to say so. The notice requirement cannot be contracted away, and your lease must not contain a waiver of it. Three further things. First, a tenant who pays within the notice period cures, and separately you have to keep accepting the full amount owed until judgment, so do not treat the forfeiture as final the moment the notice expires. Second, if the breach is something other than rent, the alternative-notice machinery is different and so are the periods, and a repeat of the same breach has its own rule. Third, if your tenant is a victim of domestic violence or domestic abuse and the alleged breach resulted from it, Colorado blocks the eviction ground altogether on documentation, and that protection also cannot be waived in your lease. Since there is no redemption statute, anything you want to offer a defaulting tenant - a payment plan, a reinstatement on terms, a withdrawal of the notice - is a matter of agreement, so put it in writing, say plainly whether the tenancy continues or a new one starts, and do not charge a fee for the privilege. The eviction procedure itself is court process and this lease library does not carry it.

title: Which Edition of a Code or Standard Actually Binds You in Colorado
bodyText: When a Colorado statute, a local ordinance or your own lease points at an outside code or standard, the question is always which edition it points at, and Colorado answers it three different ways. First, for local codes, the edition is frozen. A Colorado municipality adopts a building, fire, plumbing, housing, mechanical or electrical code by passing an ordinance that adopts the code by reference, and that ordinance names the edition. If the body that wrote the code later amends it, the amendment does not reach you automatically: the municipality has to adopt the amendment by reference through the same procedure it used for the original code, or pass an ordinance setting out the whole text of the amendment. So the current International Building Code is not your obligation; the edition your city adopted is. The adopted code and any code it incorporates in turn have to be kept on file for public inspection while the ordinance is in force, and the clerk must keep copies available for purchase at a moderate price, so you can find out which edition applies by asking. Two useful details: penalty clauses cannot be adopted by reference at all and must be set out in full in the adopting ordinance, and a certified published copy of an adopted code is prima facie evidence of its contents in any Colorado court. Second, the habitability statute uses a time-of-installation standard for equipment. A rental is uninhabitable if it substantially lacks functioning appliances, plumbing or gas facilities, heating facilities or electrical wiring and equipment that conformed to applicable law at the time of installation and that are maintained in good working order. Read that carefully, because it cuts both ways: you do not have to bring an older installation up to the current code, but you do have to keep it in good working order, and a condition that materially interferes with the tenant's life, health or safety is a breach whatever the age of the equipment. Separately, habitability requires compliance with all applicable building, housing and health codes where the violation would materially interfere with the tenant's life, health or safety - that limb tracks the codes as they apply, not as they stood when the building went up - and the cleanup standards after a wildfire, flood or toxic release are measured against the current American National Standards Institute standards or those of its successor organization and the applicable building, fire, health and housing codes. Third, your own lease. Do not write a lease that promises compliance with "the current" anything, and do not name a code edition unless you mean it. The safer drafting is to refer to applicable law and applicable local codes without naming an edition, so the lease does not become inaccurate the moment your city adopts a new code - and to keep the house rules in a separate document the lease refers to, rather than reciting them. If the lease does name a standard, say explicitly whether you mean that edition or that standard as amended, and remember that tightening a rule mid-term is not the same as having had it from the start. One practical caution: state law also pins some standards to a named edition while letting the local enforcement agency choose which edition its building code adopts, so for any accessibility or construction question check both the state provision and your local code rather than assuming they match. Your city or county may be ahead of or behind the state here; check local rules.

title: Renting a Furnished Home in Colorado
bodyText:
Colorado has no law about furnished rentals. Nothing requires an inventory, nothing caps a separate furniture deposit, nothing sets a standard for the condition or age of furniture you provide, and a furnished letting is not treated differently from an unfurnished one. Furniture is also outside the warranty of habitability: the habitability rules reach appliances, and an appliance in Colorado means only a refrigerator, range stove, oven, air conditioner or cooling device that you include with the property. A broken sofa is not a habitability problem; a broken refrigerator you supplied is.

Four Colorado rules decide what actually happens when the tenancy ends.

- **There is no separate furniture deposit.** Any advance of money whose main purpose is to secure performance of the rental agreement is a security deposit whatever you call it, so a furniture deposit or an inventory deposit counts against the statutory cap and has to be returned under the deposit rules on the same timetable as the rest.
- **You can only retain deposit money for four reasons:** Unpaid rent, unpaid utility charges, other lawful charges listed in the lease, and necessary repair work for damage or defective conditions that exceed normal wear and tear and did not preexist the tenancy. That third limb is the one that matters here. If you want to be able to recover the cost of a damaged or missing item of furniture out of the deposit, list that charge in the lease, because a lawful charge has to be listed in the lease to be recoverable from the deposit.
- **"normal wear and tear" is defined by statute and your lease cannot narrow it.** It now covers deterioration, damage or uncleanliness arising from the use the unit is intended for or reasonably and typically used for, without negligence, carelessness, accident or abuse - but it does not cover uncleanliness that leaves the place substantially less clean than it was when the lease began. And a provision in or relating to a rental agreement that assigns the tenant a fee or charge for repairs, cleaning or other necessary work due to normal wear and tear, or for any damage or defective condition that existed before the tenancy, is against public policy and void. So a blanket furniture-cleaning fee or a flat "refurnishing charge" is unenforceable, while a charge for a specific item the tenant actually broke is not.
- **Document the starting condition.** Photograph and list every item with its condition and have the tenant sign the inventory at move-in: it is your evidence that damage did not preexist the tenancy, which you must prove, and the tenant can require you to hand over the photographs, inspection forms or reports, receipts, invoices or estimates in your possession within fourteen days of a written request. Either party may ask for a walk-through inspection, and you must provide one at the tenant's request before the lease ends and after the tenant has had the chance to remove furniture.

Two practical notes: do not use the deposit for ordinary depreciation of furniture, because that is the clearest case of normal wear and tear; and in a furnished letting bed bugs are a sharper risk, since a pest inspector may inspect bedding and upholstered furniture and your bed bug duties apply regardless of who owns the mattress.

Keep receipts and dates for the furniture you supply, because the age of an item is the first thing a court will ask about.

title: Your Termination Notice Must State the Cause - Specifically
bodyText: In Colorado the notice does the work, and a notice that does not state the cause is not saved by stating it later in court. Every demand or notice you serve before an eviction has to be in writing, has to specify the grounds of your right to possession - including a specific description of the alleged violation, or of the no-fault ground you are relying on - has to describe the property, has to say the date and time by which the property must be given up, and has to be signed by you, your agent or your attorney. "Specific description" means the actual facts: not "lease violation", but what was done, when, and which term of the lease it breached. For a no-fault eviction the notice must set out both the legal and the factual basis, and the legal basis has to be one of the statutory no-fault grounds - demolition or conversion, substantial repairs or renovations, your own or a family member's move-in, withdrawal from the rental market to sell, the tenant's refusal to sign a new lease with reasonable terms, or a history of late rent. If you write a different ground, or no ground, there is no valid notice. Four more requirements sit on the same notice. First, it must include a statement that a residential tenant who receives supplemental security income, social security disability insurance, or cash assistance through the Colorado works program has a right to mediation before you file an eviction complaint. Second, if the notice includes a demand for unpaid rent, it must also state that a tenant who has experienced unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse that caused them to miss a rent payment may give you documentation of it and is entitled to a repayment plan of up to nine months. Third, it must be written in English, Spanish, or any other language you know or have reason to know is the tenant's primary language. Fourth, the notice period is set by statute and depends on the ground and on the kind of agreement - ten days for most residential breaches and for nonpayment, three days for a nonresidential or employer-provided housing agreement, five days for an exempt residential agreement, and ninety days for each of the no-fault grounds - and your lease cannot shorten the nonpayment notice or waive it. Where you are ending a periodic tenancy or declining to renew a fixed term, and the property is one the for-cause rules do not cover, the notice must describe the property and give the particular date the tenancy ends, be signed, and run for at least ninety-one days for a tenancy of a year or longer, twenty-eight days for six months or longer, twenty-one days for one month or longer, three days for a week or longer or a tenancy at will, and one day for less than a week. Practical advice: keep a notice template that has a blank for the specific facts and fill it in every time; serve one ground per notice rather than a list you cannot prove; date and keep a copy of everything; and never charge the tenant for preparing or serving a notice, because Colorado voids a clause assigning a penalty stemming from an eviction notice or action and bars a fee for anything you need in order to comply with your own obligations. The eviction procedure after the notice is court process and this lease library does not carry it.

title: You Cannot Pass Government Fees to a Colorado Tenant
bodyText: Colorado closed this door in 2026. You may not require a tenant to pay a fee, charge or amount related to the payment of property taxes, and you may not require a tenant to pay for any good, service or property that you need in order to meet your own responsibilities or obligations as landlord - which is what a rental registration fee, a rental licence fee, a periodic inspection fee, a certificate of occupancy fee or a permit fee is. You also may not charge a tenant for something you do not actually provide, for the maintenance of common areas, or anything above the total price of what you are charging for. A charge that breaks any of these rules cannot be saved by putting it in the lease: a lease provision requiring a tenant to pay a fee, charge or amount that violates the pricing statute is a prohibited clause, and a prohibited clause is void and unenforceable. Do not think of these as "government charges" that sit outside the price rules. The statute's definition of a government charge is a charge imposed on consumers - a tax or fee imposed on, paid to or passed on to a government by the consumer. A registration or licence fee assessed on you as the owner is not that; it is your cost of doing business. The practical consequence is simple: build those costs into the rent you set, and advertise and disclose the rent as a single total price, more prominently than any other pricing information. That is lawful, and it is the only lawful route. Three further traps. First, if a government charges a fee or fine because of something at the property, you still cannot charge the tenant for your own compliance failures, and a flat pass-through written into the lease is void even if the tenant caused the underlying condition - any recovery has to be framed as reimbursement of a specific amount the tenant actually caused, and it has to be a lawful charge listed in the lease before you can take it out of the deposit. Second, never charge anything tied to an eviction. Colorado voids a clause that assigns a penalty to a party stemming from an eviction notice or an eviction action, and that bar applies to every residential rental agreement in Colorado without exception - no carve-out for a duplex, a triplex, an owner-occupied property or a mobile home park. So a court filing fee, a process server fee, a sheriff's fee, a posting fee or an attorney cost recovered as a lease charge is void. Any fee-shifting clause you do use has to run to the prevailing party, and the court has to find that the party prevailed and that the fee is reasonable. Third, the penalties are real. A violation of the pricing statute is a deceptive, unfair and unconscionable act or practice. A tenant may send you a written demand; if you do not make full tender or stop charging within fourteen days, you are liable for actual damages plus interest at eighteen percent per annum compounded annually, and the tenant does not have to send a demand at all before suing. One lawful adjacent route exists and is narrow: where you are billed by a third party for a service, the lease may require the tenant to pay either a markup or fee of up to two percent of the billed amount or a markup or fee of up to ten dollars per month - but not both. That is a third-party service billing allowance, not a government fee pass-through. Your city or county may also regulate what you may charge; check local rules.

title: Passing a Government Fine to a Colorado Tenant
bodyText:
Colorado gives you one route and only one.
