Where a municipality serves you and your tenant with notice that a nuisance ordinance has been violated by the tenant on the property you rent them, you may deliver written notice to the tenant to abate the nuisance; if the tenant has not abated it within five days, you may enter the exterior area of the property and abate it yourself. And unless your lease says otherwise, the tenant is liable to you for your direct costs of abating the nuisance and for the amount of the fine imposed on you, running from the date the tenant received the municipality's notice. Read that date limit carefully: you cannot recover a fine imposed before the tenant got the municipality's notice. There is a matching limit on the municipality: an ordinance may make you liable as owner for a nuisance your tenant committed only if the municipality notified both you and the tenant of the nuisance before imposing a fine or other liability.

If abatement means removing a vehicle, you must use a towing carrier and have the vehicle stored under appropriate protection, and none of this limits the tenant's own remedies if you harm them or their other property.

Because the tenant's liability is a default that applies "unless the lease provides otherwise", the main risk in your lease is accidentally writing something narrower or different and losing the default. So either say nothing and rely on the statute, or restate it accurately.

Outside that municipal nuisance route, Colorado has no fine pass-through.

Nothing lets you charge a tenant for a code violation, a fire-code citation, a short-term-rental penalty, a trash or weed abatement assessment, a parking or towing citation against you, or any other governmental penalty, and several rules make a flat pass-through clause dangerous.

- You may not charge a tenant for a good, service or property you need in order to comply with your own responsibilities, so a fine for a condition you were obliged to fix is yours.
- You may not charge for the maintenance of common areas, so a common-area citation is yours.
- You may not charge above the total price of what you charge for, or for anything you did not actually provide, and a lease provision requiring a fee that violates the pricing statute is void.
- You may not assign any penalty stemming from an eviction notice or an eviction action, and that bar has no exception at all in Colorado.

Four more rules.

- Weed, brush and rubbish removal is assessed against the land itself as a lien with priority over other liens except general taxes and prior special assessments, so an unpaid assessment becomes your title problem, not the tenant's - deal with it quickly.
- **Any amount you do recover is not rent:** Do not call it rent, do not add a late fee or interest to it, and do not take it out of a rent payment.
- If you want to recover it from the security deposit, it has to be a lawful charge listed in the lease.
- Never charge a tenant for a nuisance, disturbance or police-response fine that arises from domestic violence, domestic abuse, stalking or unlawful sexual behavior against the tenant, or from a call for police or emergency help: Colorado voids a lease provision penalising those calls, the right cannot be waived, you must not charge a victim-survivor for damage caused by the abuse, and where the tenant documents the abuse, a disturbance the abuse caused or contributed to is not an unlawful detention on the nuisance ground. Which documents count for that ground is not settled: the police report and the protection or restraining order plainly fit it, while the self-attestation affidavit and the qualified third-party letter the statute also allows are worded for its other grounds. The cautious course, and the one to follow, is to accept any of the four.

Home-rule cities may do this differently, and local ordinances are where the fines come from; check your local code.

title: Lease Guarantors in Colorado - No Statute, Three Real Limits
bodyText:
Colorado has no lease-guaranty statute. Nothing requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, nothing says a guarantor is bound only for the original term, nothing addresses what happens on renewal, and nothing sets out how a guarantor is released. That makes the guaranty a pure contract question, and it makes the drafting your protection rather than the statute's. Three limits still apply.

- **The writing.** Colorado's statute of frauds makes every special promise to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another person void unless it is in writing and signed by the person being held to it, and the same applies to any agreement that by its terms will not be performed within a year. So a guaranty has to be a signed writing from the guarantor. Get the guarantor's own signature, on the lease or on a guaranty that identifies the lease, and give them a copy.
- **Renewals.** Because no statute answers it, whether a guaranty survives a renewal, an extension, a month-to-month continuation or a rent increase depends entirely on what the guaranty says - and the general law of suretyship is not friendly to a landlord who changes the deal and then relies on the old guaranty. Say in the guaranty whether it covers renewals, extensions and month-to-month continuation, and whether it covers rent changes made under the lease. If it does not, get a fresh guaranty when the lease renews, and get one whenever the rent or the term changes materially. State a maximum so the guarantor knows what they are signing and you have something enforceable rather than an open-ended promise a court may read narrowly. This covers the statutes and not court decisions, so treat the drafting as the whole of your protection.
- The guaranty can never be worth more than the tenant's own liability, and Colorado caps that liability in several places. If the tenant dies and the lease ends early, a clause requiring liquidated damages, rent accelerated beyond the end of that month or ten business days after the unit is vacated, repayment of concessions or move-in discounts, or any other early-termination fee is void - and a guarantor cannot be made to pay what the tenant does not owe. If a tenant terminates as a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, stalking or unlawful sexual behavior with the required documentation, your recovery is capped at one month's rent and only where you have incurred and documented economic damages - again, nothing more from the guarantor. And any fee that Colorado's pricing rules make unlawful against the tenant is not collectable from the guarantor either.

One trap that catches landlords out: money from a guarantor is still a security deposit. Colorado defines a security deposit as any advance or deposit of money, whatever it is called, whose primary function is to secure performance of the rental agreement, and that definition does not care who handed it over. So a guarantor deposit, a co-signer deposit or an extra payment taken because the applicant needed a guarantor is a security deposit: it counts toward the limit of two monthly rent payments, it has to be accounted for and returned under the deposit rules on the same timetable, and it cannot be kept except for the statutory causes. If you are unsure whether routing the money through a guarantor escapes the cap, assume it does not - the statute is drafted around the function of the money, not its source, and the penalty for wrongful retention is treble damages plus the tenant's fees and costs.

Finally, a guarantor is not a tenant: do not treat them as an occupant, do not give them a right to enter, and do not share the tenant's information with them beyond what the guaranty needs, particularly where the tenant has victim-survivor confidentiality rights.

title: Guests Have No Rights of Their Own in Colorado - and Four Things That Follow
bodyText:
Colorado gives a tenant's guest no statutory rights. There is no visitor access right, no rule that you must let guests in, no bar on restricting guests in your lease or house rules, and no state rule about overnight guests or how long one may stay. Where Colorado does mention guests, it is to make the tenant answerable for them, so the silence is mostly in your favour.

Four things follow.

- **Guest conduct is attributed to your tenant.** The implied term that a tenant will not commit a substantial violation covers acts by any guest or invitee of the tenant, and a condition that would otherwise breach the warranty of habitability is not a breach at all where it was substantially caused by the misconduct of the tenant, a household member, or a guest or invitee of the tenant, or someone under the tenant's direction or control. There are two limits on that: a tenant has a defence if they did not know of and could not reasonably have known of or prevented the guest's substantial violation but immediately notified a law enforcement officer; and conduct that is the result of domestic violence, domestic abuse, stalking or unlawful sexual behavior against your tenant is not the tenant's misconduct.
- **A guest who stays long enough stops being a guest.** Colorado's definition of tenant for the habitability rules reaches every member of the tenant's household and any person who has explicit or implicit permission from you to occupy the unit. So if you knowingly let someone live there, they are a tenant for those purposes whether or not they signed anything - which means your habitability duties run to them, and it also means you should decide deliberately, in writing, who may occupy and for how long, rather than letting it happen by acquiescence.
- **A guest does get the benefit of one protection.** Colorado's anti-retaliation rule protects a tenant who organizes or becomes a member of a tenants' association, and "organizing" is defined to mean any lawful concerted activity by a tenant or a tenant's guest or an invitee for mutual aid or for establishing, supporting or operating a tenants' association, or for exercising any other right or remedy provided by law. Retaliation includes raising rent, cutting services, terminating or refusing to renew, bringing or threatening a possession action, intimidating or harassing, and charging or seeking to collect any fee, cost or penalty - and a tenant need only show the protected activity was a motivating factor, with damages of the greater of three months' rent or three times actual damages, plus fees and costs. Whether that protection extends to a guest in their own right, or only shields the tenant whose guest took part, is not spelled out; the cautious course is to treat organizing activity by a guest exactly as you would the tenant's.
- **You may restrict guests but you may not charge for them.** A guest fee is a charge for something you do not actually provide, and a charge for the use of common areas is barred outright, so a guest fee or visitor-parking fee written into the lease is void. And never write a guest rule that penalises a call for police or emergency help: Colorado voids a lease provision that lets you terminate, fine or take adverse action against a tenant for calls for peace-officer or other emergency assistance in a domestic violence, domestic abuse, stalking or unlawful sexual behavior situation, and that right cannot be waived.

If you want guest limits, put them in house rules the lease refers to, state the limit in days rather than in a vague standard, and apply it consistently.

Your city or county may regulate occupancy; check local rules.

title: When a Defect Is "Material" in Colorado - and Why It Changes Your Deadline
bodyText: Colorado does not have one habitability standard; it has two, and which one applies decides how fast you must act and what the tenant can recover. The first limb is the statutory list: the property is uninhabitable if there is mould associated with dampness, or any other dampness condition that if unremedied would materially interfere with the tenant's health or safety; or if it substantially lacks any of the listed characteristics - working appliances you supplied, waterproofing and weather protection with unbroken windows and doors, plumbing or gas facilities, running water and enough hot water, working heat, electrical lighting and wiring, clean and pest-free common areas, extermination, enough exterior rubbish receptacles serviced often enough, sound floors, stairways, elevators and railings, working locks on exterior doors and on windows designed to open, compliance with building, housing and health codes where the violation would materially interfere with the tenant's life, health or safety, the post-disaster cleanup standards, methamphetamine remediation, the radon requirements and the cooling-device requirements; or if it is otherwise unfit for human habitation. Note the word "substantially": a minor shortfall in one of those characteristics is not the standard, and minor mould on surfaces that get damp as part of their proper use is expressly excluded. The second limb is a condition that materially interferes with the tenant's life, health or safety, whether or not it is on the list. That limb is where the shorter deadline lives. You must commence remedial action within twenty-four hours of having notice where the condition materially interferes with the tenant's life, health or safety, and within seventy-two hours where the premises is uninhabitable but not materially interfering. The presumption that you failed to act in a reasonable time bites after seven days for a materially interfering condition and after fourteen days for an ordinary uninhabitable condition. And if a court finds a breach, the fair rental value of the unit is rebuttably presumed to be zero for the whole period a materially interfering condition went unremedied, and fifty percent of the rent for the whole period where the condition did not materially interfere - so materiality is the difference between owing back half the rent and owing back all of it. There are two more materiality rules worth knowing. A deficiency in a common area does not make the unit uninhabitable unless it materially affects the tenant's use of their own unit. And a code violation only counts if the violation itself would materially interfere with the tenant's life, health or safety - so not every code ticket is a habitability breach. Finally, a short list of conditions is presumed to be materially interfering, and you can only rebut that by clear and convincing evidence; a court or jury can also find any condition or combination of conditions materially interfering even if it is not on any list. The practical rule for your operations is simple: do not spend time classifying. Treat every report of no heat in winter, no water or hot water, gas or electrical hazards, sewage or water intrusion, a broken exterior lock or window lock, blocked fire exits, infestation, chimney or venting faults, or a lift a disabled tenant depends on as a twenty-four-hour matter, contact the tenant within twenty-four hours whatever the condition, and write down when you were told and what you did. Your lease cannot lower any of this.

title: The One Way Habitability Can Be Shifted in Colorado - and It Is Not in the Lease
bodyText: You cannot write habitability out of a Colorado lease, and the statute says so twice. Any agreement waiving or modifying any right, remedy, obligation or prohibition in the habitability rules is void as contrary to public policy, except as the habitability rules themselves allow. And separately, a rental agreement or any other agreement between you and the tenant that waives or modifies a right or remedy in those rules is unlawful, void and unenforceable - including a provision that charges the tenant a cost, fee or penalty because the tenant exercised or tried to exercise one of those rights. So a clause making the tenant responsible for repairs, a clause requiring verbal rather than written notice, a clause cutting your response time, a clause requiring the tenant to claim on their own renter's insurance, a clause charging a call-out fee when the tenant reports a defect, and an "as is" or "tenant accepts the premises in their present condition" clause are all void in Colorado as far as they touch habitability - and the last one is doubly ineffective, because before you let the property you must ensure it is fit for human habitation and not in any of the uninhabitable conditions, and letting a property that is not compliant is itself a breach. There is exactly one exception, and it has five conditions you must meet. For a single-family residence for which you receive no governmental subsidy, you and the tenant may agree that the tenant will perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodelling needed to comply with the warranty of habitability, but only if the agreement is entered into in good faith; it is set out in a writing separate from the rental agreement; that writing is signed by both of you; it is supported by adequate consideration; and the tenant has the requisite skills to do the work. Read that second condition carefully, because it is where landlords go wrong: the agreement cannot be a clause in the lease or an addendum that forms part of it - it has to be a separate signed writing. Two more limits. Where what the tenant takes on is one of the listed habitability characteristics, the tenant assumes the obligation for that characteristic and its absence no longer makes the property uninhabitable - which is the point of the exercise - but you may never agree that the tenant will do work whose performance would endanger the tenant's health or safety, and any such agreement is barred outright. In practice the exception is worth using only for a genuinely skilled tenant in a single-family home at a real rent reduction, documented separately, with the specific tasks listed. There are a few other things the statute does let you decide, which are permissions rather than waivers: you may restrict a portable cooling device on the four statutory grounds if you disclose the restriction in writing and give the required information about cooled common spaces or nearby community cooling spaces; you may provide in the lease that you are not responsible for a third party's breach of quiet enjoyment beyond your reasonable control; and where a third party outside your control caused a condition and you took reasonable, necessary and timely steps but cannot fix it, the tenant's only remedy is to terminate. Also, where a public housing authority or other provider receives federal financial assistance directly from the federal government, no provision of the habitability rules in direct conflict with federal law or regulation is enforceable against that provider. None of that lets you lower the standard generally. Treat habitability as a floor set by statute, keep repair obligations in your own hands, and get advice before using the single-family exception.

title: The Habitability Presumptions That Decide Your Case
bodyText: Colorado builds presumptions into its habitability rules, and they decide most disputes before any evidence about the repair itself is heard. Know all four. First, a presumption that you did not act fast enough. If the tenant shows the property was uninhabitable or materially interfering and that you had notice, it is rebuttably presumed that you failed to commence remedial action, failed to continue it, or failed to complete it within a reasonable time, if either you did not contact the tenant within the required time after notice, or the condition still existed fourteen calendar days after you received notice of an uninhabitable condition, or seven calendar days after notice of a condition that materially interferes with the tenant's life, health or safety. You can rebut it, but only by proving on the balance of probabilities one of three things: that you started and continued remedial action but could not finish because of circumstances outside your reasonable control; that the work needed entry and the tenant unreasonably refused you entry; or that the tenant's conduct unreasonably delayed or prevented you. Even then, you must keep making reasonable efforts, including prompt correspondence and good-faith cooperation with the tenant and, where needed, with maintenance staff, contractors or a government official. If the tenant refuses entry, the clocks are tolled until the date the tenant proposes or another date they accept. Outside those three rebuttals, the tenant carries the burden of proving a breach. Second, a presumption that certain conditions are serious. Twelve conditions are rebuttably presumed to interfere materially with the tenant's life, health or safety: no waterproofing or weather protection so the weather gets in; any hazardous gas condition; inadequate running water or hot water, other than temporary disruptions for necessary work or ones you could not reasonably prevent; no working heat from October through April; any hazardous electrical condition; loss of electricity caused by your failure to maintain the system; no working locks or security devices on exterior doors and openable exterior windows; no working plumbing or sewage disposal, or any condition letting sewage, water or moisture in other than through properly working systems; infestation by rodents, vermin, pests or insects; inaccessible fire exits or egress under the applicable codes; a missing, damaged, improper or misaligned chimney or venting on a fuel-fired heating, ventilation or cooling system; and an inoperable lift where the tenant has a disability preventing stair use or relies on the lift and there is no other working lift. To rebut any of those you need clear and convincing evidence - a higher standard than the balance of probabilities - and even where you succeed, a court or jury may still find that any condition, or combination of conditions, materially interferes. Third, a presumption about the money. If a court or jury finds a breach, the fair rental value of the unit is rebuttably presumed to have been zero dollars for the whole period a materially interfering condition went unremedied, and fifty percent of the lease rent for the whole period where the condition did not materially interfere. That is the single most expensive presumption in the statute, and it applies to the entire period, not to the days after a complaint. Fourth, one presumption in your favour: if you replace a malfunctioning appliance with a new one that is not identical, it is rebuttably presumed that choosing a different appliance was not retaliatory, so long as the replacement provides substantially the same features. What all this means operationally: contact the tenant within twenty-four hours every time, start work immediately, and keep records - you must keep all written notices, correspondence and documentation about any uninhabitable condition and any remedial action for the whole tenancy and at least three years after, and give the tenant any of it within ten calendar days of a request. Those records are how you rebut a presumption; without them you will not.

title: Your Lease Does Not Promise Habitability - It Carries Two Required Statements
bodyText: Colorado does not make you write a promise of habitability into the lease, because the promise is already there. The warranty of habitability is deemed part of every rental agreement by statute, from the day occupancy begins and for as long as the tenant lawfully occupies the home, whether or not a word of it appears in your document. Nothing in the lease can waive it or cut it down, so adding your own habitability language gains you nothing and a badly worded version can only hurt you. What Colorado does require is two separate statements inside the rental agreement itself, both in at least twelve-point bold-faced type, and both in force since January 1, 2025. The first tells the tenant that every tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing under Colorado's warranty of habitability and that the law forbids you to retaliate in any way for reporting unsafe conditions, requesting repairs, or seeking to enjoy that right. The second must appear in both English and Spanish, and must give an address where the tenant can mail or hand-deliver written notice of an uninhabitable condition together with an email address or an accessible online tenant portal where the tenant can deliver that notice. If you run an online tenant portal, the same English-and-Spanish contact information must also be posted conspicuously inside the portal. Leaving either statement out is a violation of the habitability rules, and the attorney general can pursue a civil penalty for each tenant affected, so treat both as mandatory lease content rather than optional boilerplate. The habitability rules are declared a matter of statewide concern and a conflicting local ordinance is unenforceable, but a city or county may still add duties that do not conflict, so check local rules.

title: The One Way a Habitability Duty Can Be Shifted - and It Is Not in the Lease
bodyText: In Colorado you cannot waive, reduce or reshape a habitability duty by agreement. Any agreement that waives or modifies a right, remedy, obligation or prohibition in the habitability rules is void as against public policy, and a lease or side agreement that waives or modifies one of those rights is unlawful, void and unenforceable - including any provision that charges the tenant a cost, fee or penalty for exercising or trying to exercise a habitability right. There is exactly one route the statute leaves open, and it is deliberately narrow. For a single-family residence where you receive no governmental subsidy, you and the tenant may agree that the tenant will perform specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling needed to meet the habitability standard, but only if four things are true: the agreement is made in good faith, it is in a writing separate from the rental agreement, it is signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration, and the tenant actually has the skills to do the work. Put it in the lease and it does not qualify. Where that agreement covers one of the listed habitability characteristics, the tenant takes on that characteristic and its absence no longer makes the home uninhabitable, which is the whole point of the exception. Even then you may never agree that the tenant will do work that would endanger the tenant's health or safety. Nothing in the tenant's own cleanliness and care duties lets you modify your habitability obligations either. Colorado gives you no option to let the tenant accept named defects in exchange for a stated rent reduction, and no separate heat-level agreement document of the kind some states allow, so do not import one. If you want to use the single-family exception, have the separate agreement drafted and reviewed before the tenancy starts.

title: Contaminated Land: What Colorado Makes You Put in the Lease
bodyText:
Colorado has no general duty to tell a prospective tenant that a property is or was contaminated. What it does have is narrower and easy to miss.

Where a cleanup leaves residual contamination that is safe for some uses but not all, or leaves an engineered feature that has to be monitored, maintained or operated, the state requires a recorded environmental covenant or a recorded notice of environmental use restrictions over the land. Every one of those instruments must itself require the owner to incorporate it, in full or by reference, into any lease or other instrument granting a right to use the affected property. So if your property carries one, your lease has to carry it too, and failing to incorporate it is a breach of the recorded instrument rather than of the lease. The restriction binds your tenant as a person using the land whether or not you mention it, which is precisely why you should mention it: a tenant who paves over a protective cap or digs where digging is forbidden has exposed you to a state enforcement order, an attorney general suit or an injunction, and your lease is your only route to control that.

The Department of Public Health and Environment keeps a registry of every environmental covenant and notice of environmental use restrictions, so you can check the land before you let it, and the covenant or notice is recorded in the county records.

Colorado has no brownfield-status disclosure of the kind some states require in an instrument of conveyance. The only other contamination disclosure in Colorado's statutes is about methamphetamine laboratories, and it runs from a seller to a buyer of residential real property, not from a landlord to a tenant; for a rental the point arrives through habitability instead, because a premises used as a methamphetamine laboratory is uninhabitable until it is remediated to the state board of health standards.

A city or county may add duties of its own; check local rules.

title: No Duty to Hand Over Health-District Rental Rules
bodyText: Colorado puts no duty on you to give a tenant a copy of a health district's or county public health agency's rental regulations, on request or otherwise, and no general duty to refer a tenant to a health agency. One narrow referral duty does exist and it is easy to miss: if you obtain a bed bug inspection and the inspector finds no bed bugs in the unit or any adjoining unit, the written notice you must give the tenant within two business days has to tell the tenant that they may contact the local health department if they remain concerned. Nothing stops a tenant contacting any agency about bed bugs at any time. What Colorado does give the local agency is power of its own, used against you directly rather than through the lease. A county or district board of health examines and abates nuisances, sources of filth and causes of sickness, may order the owner or occupant to remove one at their own expense within twenty-four hours, may do the work itself and recover the cost from the owner or occupant, and may assess the cost against the property; refusing entry can be met with a court warrant. Willfully failing to remove such a condition within forty-eight hours of an agency order is a class 2 misdemeanour and leaves you liable for the authority's removal expenses as well. Because the state is silent on the disclosure point, this is left to your lease and to general contract law. Two practical consequences. First, do not promise in the lease to supply rules you do not hold; if you want to give a tenant local health rules, give them the agency's contact details instead, and say the rules are the agency's and may change. Second, a lease clause requiring the tenant to comply with applicable health, housing and building codes is worth having, because the agency's orders can reach the occupant as well as you. Keeping common areas and the areas under your control clean, sanitary and free of accumulated debris, filth, rubbish and garbage is your own habitability duty whatever the local agency does, so you cannot charge the tenant a fee for that work. A local public health agency or a home-rule city may have rental rules of its own; check with the agency directly.

title: Heat Is Your Duty, and October to April Is the Dangerous Window
bodyText:
In Colorado a home is uninhabitable if it substantially lacks functioning heating facilities that met the law when they were installed and are kept in good working order. That duty is yours, the repair is at your expense, and you cannot charge the tenant a fee for a good or service you need in order to meet it.

From October through April the stakes rise: the absence of functioning heating facilities and equipment fixtures in those months is presumed by statute to materially interfere with the tenant's life, health and safety, which shortens your response clock from seventy-two hours to twenty-four and can oblige you to put the tenant in a comparable unit or a hotel at your cost on request. You can only rebut that presumption by clear and convincing evidence.

A missing, damaged, improper or misaligned chimney or vent on a fuel-fired heating system carries the same presumption, so treat venting faults as emergencies. Hazardous conditions of gas piping, gas facilities, gas appliances or other gas equipment also carry it, and Colorado requires you to hire a professional for that work rather than doing it yourself.

You may not shift the heating duty to the tenant in the lease; the only route Colorado leaves open is a separate signed written agreement, outside the lease and supported by consideration, on a single-family premises for which you receive no governmental subsidy, where the tenant has the skills and the work would not endanger them. Making the tenant responsible for paying the gas or electricity that runs the heat is a different thing and is permitted, but it does not move the duty to keep the heating facilities working.

Never cut the heat off: willfully causing the termination of heat is unlawful exclusion, and the tenant recovers actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars.

Colorado sets no minimum indoor temperature, so if you want a temperature floor you have to put one in the lease.

One piece of equipment law that surprises landlords: the state boiler inspection regime exempts boilers in private residences and in apartment houses of fewer than six family units, which means a boiler in an apartment house of six or more units is inside it unless the city runs a comparable inspection code of its own. Domestic-type water heaters are exempt whatever the building.

A city or county may require more; check local rules.

title: Renting in an HOA or Condominium: the Costs Stay With You
bodyText:
If your rental is in a homeowners or condominium association, Colorado leaves almost everything about renting to the association's declaration and bylaws, and almost everything about the money to you. Read the declaration before you let the property.

Condominium bylaws are expressly allowed to contain restrictions and requirements about leasing a unit, including rights of first refusal and other restraints on transferring it, and no Colorado statute limits how far those restrictions may go, caps what the association may charge to approve a lease, or requires the association to accept your tenant. Nor does Colorado give an association any right to demand rent from your tenant when you fall behind on assessments; the one route the statute provides is a court-appointed receiver in an action to collect assessments or foreclose the lien, and a receiver collects from you, not under your lease. There is no statutory association-held tenant deposit in Colorado.

On home child care the answer is the other way round and worth knowing: an association may not prohibit the operation of a licensed family child care home, and may not prohibit a home-based business run at a unit by the owner or by a resident with the owner's permission. Those protections run against the association, not against you - it is your permission that unlocks them - and the association keeps its reasonable rules on architectural control, parking, landscaping and noise, may insist on liability insurance naming itself as an additional insured for a family child care home, and the child care protection does not apply in a community qualifying as housing for older persons.

Now the money, which is where landlords get caught.

- From January 1, 2026 you may not require a tenant to pay a fee, charge or amount for the maintenance of common areas, and the habitability rules define common areas to include the grounds, areas and facilities held out for the use of tenants generally. Association dues are mostly exactly that, so a line item passing your HOA dues or a common-area assessment to the tenant is unlawful and the lease provision creating it is void.
- You also may not charge the tenant for anything you need in order to meet your own obligations, which covers getting the association's approval to lease and keeping the unit in compliance with the declaration, nor more than the total price of what you are charging for, nor for anything you do not actually provide.
- Where the association bills you for a service, you may pass through the billed amount and add either a markup or fee of up to two percent of what you were billed or one of up to ten dollars a month, but not both.
- **You may not call any of it rent:** Only the set monthly payment for occupancy can be rent for which eviction and the other rent remedies are available.

Whether you may pass on an association fine that your tenant's own conduct caused is genuinely unsettled, because the bar is written in terms of a fee for a good, service or property and a fine is none of those, while the catch-all forbids any charge that violates the pricing section. The cautious course is not to write a fine pass-through into the lease at all: require the tenant to comply with the association's rules, treat a breach as a lease breach with the ordinary notice and cure remedies, and recover a real loss as damages rather than as a fee.

Take advice before you try anything more aggressive.

title: Holding Deposits: No Colorado Rule, and a Definition That May Swallow Yours
bodyText: Colorado has no statute about a holding deposit. Nothing in the statutes names one, permits one, caps one, says when you must return it, or gives the applicant a doubling remedy if you back out. A pre-lease holding deposit is left to your written agreement with the applicant and to general contract law. That sounds like freedom, and it is the trap. Colorado defines a security deposit as any advance or deposit of money, whatever you call it, whose primary function is to secure the performance of a rental agreement for a residential premises. Money you take to hold a unit is plainly an advance of money, and once the applicant signs, its function is to secure the tenancy. The statute does not say whether a deposit taken before any rental agreement exists is inside the definition, so you cannot be sure which side of the line yours falls on. Draft so that it does not matter. Put the arrangement in writing before you take a cent, and in it: say exactly what the money is for; say whether it is refundable and in what circumstances; say that it will be credited in full to the security deposit or the first month's rent when the lease is signed; and keep it, together with any other advance, within two monthly rent payments, which is the ceiling on the deposit you may require. Then handle the return on the statutory deposit timetable, which is the cautious reading, rather than whenever you get around to it. Keep the holding deposit separate from the application fee, which has its own rules: you may charge only your actual or average processing cost, the same amount to everyone applying for the same unit or any unit you are offering at the same time, nothing at all if the applicant gives you a portable tenant screening report, and you must give a receipt, a disclosure or itemisation of the expenses, and a refund of any unused part within about twenty days. One more duty bites whatever you call the money: from January 1, 2026 you must not misrepresent the nature and purpose of any amount a person may pay, including whether it is refundable, and you must disclose that clearly and conspicuously before the person agrees to pay. An applicant who paid an unlawful amount can demand it back, and if you refuse within fourteen days you face actual damages plus eighteen percent interest a year compounded annually. The safest practice is simple: take the application fee at your real cost, do not take holding money at all, and if you must, take it under a short written agreement that credits it to the lease.

title: No Statutory Holdover Rate - So "the Maximum Allowed by Law" Gets You Nothing
bodyText:
Colorado has no statutory holdover rate. There is no doubled or trebled rent for a tenant who stays past the end of the term, no per-diem multiplier, no separate figure for subsidised units, and no cap on a holdover rate you set yourself.

That has a consequence landlords miss: a lease clause entitling you to holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law entitles you to nothing extra in Colorado, because applicable law permits no particular amount. If you want a holdover figure you have to write the figure.

Because the measure is left to the lease, four limits matter.

- **The amount must look like compensation, not punishment:** Colorado's general contract law will not enforce a liquidated sum set so far above your real loss that it operates as a penalty, so keep the figure within sight of the daily rental value and your actual re-letting loss.
- **A holdover charge is not rent.** Colorado forbids a lease from characterising any amount other than the set monthly payment for occupancy as rent for which the rent remedies, including eviction, are available, so you cannot bring a nonpayment eviction over unpaid holdover charges; you recover them as damages.
- **Do not tie the charge to an eviction.** A clause assigning a penalty to a party stemming from an eviction notice or an eviction action is void, so the trigger must be the days the tenant stays after the term ends, never the notice you serve or the case you file.
- You cannot charge a late fee or interest on an unpaid holdover charge, because Colorado bars any charge related to the overdue payment of a fee, charge or amount that is not rent.

Remember too that for a tenancy of twelve months or more at a property the for-cause rules cover, the term simply ending is not by itself a ground for possession, so a holdover clause is not a substitute for the notice those rules require. If the tenant keeps paying and you keep accepting, you are likely in a month-to-month tenancy on the old terms, which may be what you want.

Take advice before relying on a high holdover figure.

title: A Tenant's Home Business: Protected Against the HOA, Not Against You
bodyText:
Colorado does protect a home business, but read who it is protected against. A community association may not prohibit the operation of a home-based business at a unit by the unit owner, or by a resident of the unit with the unit owner's permission, and may not prohibit a licensed family child care home. A home-based business for this purpose means one whose main office is at the unit, or whose operations primarily occur there. Notice how the protection is built: for a tenant it switches on only with the owner's permission, which means it binds the association and leaves the decision with you. Nothing in Colorado law makes a home business a permitted use of a rented home against the landlord's wishes, and nothing stops your lease restricting or banning business use of the property.

If you do give permission, the association keeps real powers: it may adopt and enforce reasonable rules on architectural control, parking, landscaping, noise and nuisance, those rules and the local noise and nuisance ordinances still apply, it may require a family child care home to carry liability insurance at levels its board sets with the association named as an additional insured, and the child care protection does not apply at all in a community that qualifies as housing for older persons.

Three practical points.

- Colorado's Cottage Foods Act lets a producer use a home kitchen to make a limited range of non-hazardous foods that do not need refrigeration and sell them directly to end consumers in Colorado without a licence or inspection, subject to a food safety course, labelling and a revenue limit, so this is the home business most likely to turn up in a rental; the Act gives the producer no right against you, and both the revenue measure and other details change on January 1, 2027.
- Child care licensing is not covered here, so confirm licensing requirements separately before relying on anything about a family child care home.
- Local zoning is where home occupation permits, customer traffic and signage limits actually live; tell the tenant to get their own permits and check the local rules.

If you are willing to allow a home business, say so in writing with conditions rather than leaving it to be argued about later.

title: Homestead and Exemption Waivers Do Nothing in a Colorado Lease
bodyText: Leave homestead and exemption waivers out of your Colorado lease. They are a form imported from other states, and here they buy you nothing while making your lease look oppressive. Colorado's homestead exemption protects a homestead from execution and attachment, but it protects it only while the property is occupied as a home by the owner or the owner's family, and the exemption belongs to the owner. Your tenant is not the owner of the rented home, so the tenant has no homestead right in it to give up, and a clause purporting to waive one is empty. Where Colorado does allow a homestead waiver, it works only through an instrument that conveys or encumbers the property: the exemption may be released by a signed writing from the person who could convey the property, and a waiver or release of the homestead written into a mortgage, deed of trust or other lien instrument is construed only as a subordination of the homestead to that lien, not as a general surrender of it. A lease is neither a conveyance nor a lien, so none of that machinery is available to you. The separate collection exemptions, which protect a judgment debtor's wearing apparel, household goods, tools of trade, vehicles, health aids, retirement funds and a modest bank balance from levy and sale, are not made waivable by contract anywhere in Colorado's statutes; the only consensual route the statutes recognise is a consensual lien granted with the owner's consent, which is a security interest rather than a lease term. Whether a court would enforce a contractual waiver that the legislature never authorised is a question only case law could answer, so the cautious course is clear: do not include one. Two things worth knowing in the other direction. A tenant's security deposit held by you is itself exempt from garnishment by the tenant's creditors, so do not pay a deposit over to a garnishing creditor without legal advice. And if you obtain a money judgment against a former tenant, these exemptions are what will limit your collection, which is a reason to price and document your risk at the start of the tenancy rather than relying on collection at the end.

title: No Health or Care-Facility Early Exit in Colorado - So Your Lease Decides
bodyText: Colorado gives a tenant no statutory right to end a lease early because of illness, infirmity, incapacity, or a move into a nursing home, an assisted living residence or any other care facility. A statewide search of the Colorado Revised Statutes found no such provision, no notice period for it, and no cap on what you may recover if it happens. Nor is there anything for a family member, a guardian or a conservator to invoke on the tenant's behalf. So the point is left entirely to your lease and to general contract law, which means the tenant stays liable for the rent for the rest of the term unless your lease says otherwise or you agree to let them go. In practice you will face the request, often from an adult child, and often with little notice. Decide the policy before it arrives and write it into the lease rather than improvising, because an ad hoc deal made under pressure is where disputes start. If you want to allow an early exit, the lease is where the notice period, the documentation you want and the amount the tenant pays belong, and the library's early termination clause is the place to put them. Keep two limits in view when you set that amount. You cannot characterise an early-exit charge as rent for which eviction and the other rent remedies are available, so it is recoverable as damages and not through a possession case. And a charge set far above your real loss risks being treated as an unenforceable penalty, a question only a court could settle. Four statutory early exits do exist and none of them is about health in general: the tenant may end the lease without liability or penalty for an unremedied breach of the warranty of habitability, or for the same condition recurring within six months; the tenant may end it without liability if a condition that materially interferes with life, health or safety cannot be fixed within sixty consecutive days of a hotel stay you are paying for; you may end it, if the lease allows, where a sudden environmental public health event or a government action makes occupancy impossible or unlawful, on thirty days notice and on the statutory conditions; and a tenant who is a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking may end it on providing the statutory documentation. If a tenant dies during the lease, separate rules apply and are set out elsewhere in this library. One last point: where the tenant has a disability, an early-exit request may also arrive as a request for a reasonable accommodation under fair housing law rather than as a contractual request, which is a different analysis with different consequences. Take advice before refusing one.

title: Talk-First Clauses Are Fine; Mediation Waivers and Cost Clauses Are Not
bodyText:
Colorado has no statute about pre-suit informal dispute resolution clauses, so a clause asking both sides to describe a dispute in writing and meet to try to settle it before suing is lawful. Keep it non-binding and make sure it says, in terms, that it does not delay or limit any notice, deadline or remedy the law provides, including a possession action or emergency relief. That sentence is not decoration. Colorado makes unlawful, void and unenforceable any provision of a lease or other agreement that waives or modifies a habitability right or remedy, and a talk-first requirement that actually stopped a tenant going to court, or delayed a repair claim or a restraining order, would be exactly that.

Two specific traps sit next to this clause.

- Colorado requires mediation before you file an eviction against a residential tenant who receives supplemental security income, social security disability insurance or Colorado works cash assistance, unless one of the statutory exceptions applies, including the exception for a landlord with five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five rental units in total. A tenant can give up that mediation voluntarily, but the waiver must never be in the lease or in any other agreement with you. Put it there and you have a void provision and, worse, a missing affirmative defence waiting to get your eviction dismissed without prejudice.
- You may not include a clause letting you recoup the costs of that mandatory mediation; such a clause is void. You pay only your own share, and the mediation must be free to the tenant.

Arbitration is a different animal and no binding arbitration clause is offered here for Colorado. If you are considering one, know that from 2026 a predispute arbitration agreement and a predispute joint-action waiver are not valid or enforceable, at the request of the person alleging the conduct, in a sexual harassment or sexual misconduct dispute, and that the court rather than the arbitrator decides that question; and that a lease must not waive the right to bring or join a joint, class or collective claim at all.

Take advice before putting any binding dispute clause in a Colorado residential lease.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code or Condemnation Orders - But They Start Your Clock
bodyText: Colorado does not require you to tell an applicant or a tenant about an outstanding building inspection order, code-violation notice or condemnation order on the property. In Colorado the word condemnation in the statutes means eminent domain; condemning a building as unfit is a local code function. So on disclosure the state is silent and the point is left to your lease and to general contract law, which in practice means you should still think hard before letting a unit with an open order against it, and should answer a direct question honestly rather than evasively. Silence on disclosure is not silence on consequences, and this is where landlords get hurt. A written notice from a governmental entity about a condition is, by statute, notice to you of that condition for habitability purposes, whether or not you pass it on. From the moment it lands your clock runs: twenty-four hours to start remedial action where the condition materially interferes with the tenant's life, health or safety, seventy-two hours otherwise, plus the duty to contact the tenant within twenty-four hours with your plan and an estimate of timing. Compliance with applicable building, housing and health codes is itself part of the habitability standard where a violation would materially interfere with the tenant's life, health or safety, and before you let a unit at all you must ensure it is fit for human habitation and not in any of the uninhabitable conditions the statute lists. Letting a unit that is not in compliance is itself a breach of the warranty of habitability, and the tenant may use any of the statutory remedies. There is also a rebuttable presumption that you failed to act within a reasonable time if the condition is still there fourteen days after you had notice, or seven days where it materially interferes with life, health or safety. Keep every government notice, your correspondence and your repair records: you are required to keep them for the whole tenancy and three years after, and to give the tenant any of them within ten days of a request. The practical rule is simple. An open order is a habitability problem, not a disclosure problem. Fix it, document it, and if it cannot be fixed before the tenancy starts, do not start the tenancy. A city or county may impose its own disclosure or placarding duty; check local rules.

title: What Happens If You Inspect Without Giving Notice
bodyText:
Colorado has no general statute telling you how much notice to give before entering a rented home, so there is no general statutory penalty for entering without notice either. Your notice obligation therefore comes from your own lease, from the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment, which your lease may not waive, and from the law of trespass; and because the obligation is contractual, the consequence of breaking it is a contract and tort problem rather than a statutory fine.

That is not a reason to be casual, because the two places Colorado does impose a notice duty are the two most common reasons to go in.

- If you, a qualified inspector or a pest control agent must enter to inspect for or treat bed bugs, you must give the tenant reasonable written or electronic notice at least forty-eight hours beforehand, and a landlord who fails to comply with the bed bug rules is liable to the tenant for the tenant's actual damages. Two useful details: your lease may set a different minimum notice time for that entry, and the tenant may waive the notice. On the other side, a tenant who has been given notice must not unreasonably deny access, and you can go to court for injunctive relief and an order granting access, with any such order served on the tenant at least twenty-four hours before you enter.
- If you need to get in to start or continue work on an uninhabitable condition, you must give at least twenty-four hours advance written notice, state the date and time and a reasonable estimate of how long you will need, and the tenant may reasonably refuse that slot and propose another, in which case your statutory repair clock is paused until the agreed time. You do not need advance notice where the condition materially and imminently threatens life, health or safety, or poses an active and ongoing threat of substantial and material damage to the property.

Get this wrong and the exposure is real: the tenant may sue under the habitability rules, with costs, attorney fees and in some cases punitive damages available, and the attorney general may pursue a civil penalty of up to twenty thousand dollars for each violation, counted separately for each tenant. Keep the notice in writing, keep a copy, and never use an inspection as a pretext; charging a tenant a cost, fee or penalty because they exercised a habitability right is void, and retaliating against a tenant for complaining carries damages of up to three months rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees.

A city or county may set its own entry rules; check local rules.

title: No Key-Control Mandate in Colorado - But Watch What You Charge for Keys
bodyText: Colorado does not require you to run a key-control policy, keep a master-key log, restrict who holds passkeys, or screen or background-check the employees and contractors who hold keys, and it imposes no extra duties on larger complexes. A statewide search of the Colorado Revised Statutes found nothing on the point. So this is left to your own practice and to your lease, and the cautious course is to run a key policy anyway: issue keys against a signed receipt, keep a list of who holds a master key, collect keys when staff leave, and screen anyone who will have access, because an incident involving a staff member with a key is a negligence problem for you whatever the statute says. Colorado does regulate two things closely, and both catch landlords out. First, the locks themselves are your duty. A home is uninhabitable if it substantially lacks working locks on all exterior doors and locks or security devices on windows designed to be opened, and the absence of working locks or security devices on exterior doors and openable windows is presumed to materially interfere with the tenant's life, health and safety. Repairing or replacing them is at your expense, and from January 1, 2026 you may not charge the tenant a fee for a good, service or property necessary to comply with your own obligations, including the duty to provide a habitable home. That means no lock fee, no security-device fee, and no re-keying charge for getting the unit ready for the next tenant: turnover re-keying is your cost, and a lease provision assigning a cleaning or repair charge for ordinary turnover work is void anyway. Second, where you may charge, the ceiling is tight. A charge for replacing a key the tenant lost, or for re-keying at the tenant's request, must be for something you actually provide and must not exceed the total price of what you are charging for. If a locksmith bills you, you may pass on the billed amount, and you may add either a markup or fee of up to two percent of what you were billed or one of up to ten dollars a month, but never both. You cannot characterise the charge as rent for which eviction is available, and you cannot add a late fee or interest to it because it is not rent. One safety rule overrides your key policy entirely. A tenant who gives you notice of being a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking, with the statutory documentation, may change the locks, including electronic locks, and take other reasonable safety precautions, and you must not prevent it, impose fees for it, take adverse action or retaliate; a lease term forbidding it is null, void and unenforceable, and you must take all steps reasonably necessary to make the unit safe in response to the tenant's safety concerns. The tenant must make all reasonable efforts to give you a copy of the key or the electronic code as soon as reasonably practicable and no later than fourteen days after the change, unless you or your manager is the person alleged to be responsible, in which case the key goes to another person with authority to manage the property whom the tenant considers safe. Finally, never remove a lock, door or window to pressure a tenant: that is unlawful exclusion, and the tenant recovers actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars. A city or county may require more; check local rules.

title: Colorado Does Not Fine You for a Prohibited Clause - Three Other Things Happen Instead
bodyText: Colorado attaches no penalty to knowingly putting a prohibited term in a residential lease. The statute that lists the forbidden terms says only that any provision included in violation of it is void and unenforceable. There is no per-clause fine, no multiple of the rent, no statutory damages figure and no offence of knowing use, and a statewide search of the Colorado Revised Statutes found no such provision anywhere. Do not read that as permission. Three consequences do follow, and together they are worse than a fixed fine. First, the clause simply does not work when you need it, and you will usually discover that in the middle of a dispute, after you have relied on it. Second, from January 1, 2026 the attorney general may independently bring civil and criminal actions to enforce the prohibited-lease-clause part of the statute, along with the domestic violence protections and the bed bug rules, and in doing so may seek any of the penalties or enforcement mechanisms available anywhere in the landlord and tenant article, including penalties available to aggrieved tenants. That is a wide power, and it is new. Third, the particular prohibited clause decides what else you face. A clause that waives or modifies a habitability right or remedy, or that charges the tenant a cost, fee or penalty for exercising one, is unlawful, void and unenforceable, and a violation of the habitability rules exposes you to the tenant's remedies, including costs, attorney fees and punitive damages, and to an attorney general civil penalty of up to twenty thousand dollars for each violation, counted separately for each tenant. A clause requiring a fee that breaks the pricing rules is itself a prohibited clause, and charging it is a deceptive, unfair and unconscionable act or practice; a tenant who demands the money back and is refused for fourteen days can recover actual damages plus eighteen percent interest a year compounded annually. A clause assigning a charge for repairs, cleaning or other work due to normal wear and tear, or for damage that existed before the tenancy, is void as against public policy, and wrongly keeping deposit money carries treble damages plus fees and costs. The practical point is that there is no cheap fixed price for a bad clause here. Have the lease reviewed against the prohibited list before you use it, and fix a clause you find rather than leaving it in on the theory that the worst case is it will be ignored.

title: What a Tenant Can Do If You Breach - and How Fast It Escalates
bodyText: Colorado gives a tenant a broad menu of remedies for a breach of the warranty of habitability, and the tenant may use more than one. Know the whole list, because the cheapest outcome for you is almost always to fix the condition on time. The tenant may end the lease with no liability or financial penalty, on ten to sixty days written notice stating the unremedied conditions, the intent to leave and the termination date, which must be at least ten days out; if you fix the problem before that date you may agree in writing to call the termination off. The same right arises if the same condition comes back within six months of being fixed, on at least ten days notice given within thirty days of the recurrence. The tenant may repair and deduct: with at least ten days advance written notice, or forty-eight hours where the tenant reasonably believes the condition materially interferes with life, health or safety, the tenant may hire a licensed or otherwise qualified professional who is not a relative and whose estimate is reasonably consistent with industry standards, and deduct the cost from one or more rent payments on giving you a receipt. A broken or malfunctioning appliance may be replaced on three days notice with one of comparable quality and features, and the cost deducted. Only one notice is needed to deduct across several rent periods. If the tenant deducts without substantially complying, you may pursue any legal remedy, and a court that finds the tenant deducted in bad faith must award you double the amount unlawfully deducted. The tenant may sue, or counterclaim, for actual damages including the reduction in fair rental value, plus court costs, reasonable attorney fees, punitive damages and any other damages the court orders. The tenant may obtain an injunction or specific performance, which can extend to relief for other similarly situated tenants, to orders making you stop particular practices, and to orders making you adopt policies to prevent repeats, with the court keeping the case open to police compliance; and if the tenant moves out, you may not re-let the unit until it complies. The tenant may get an immediate temporary restraining order without notice to you, with no bond and no need to prove irreparable injury. And the tenant may raise the breach as an affirmative defence to your possession or rent claim, without a bond, without having spent anything and without having used any other remedy. That defence is where the numbers get painful. Fair rental value is rebuttably presumed to be zero for any period a condition materially interfered with life, health or safety, and fifty percent of the rent for any period of another uninhabitable condition. If the tenant proves the defence you are denied possession, the tenant is the prevailing party, the court orders the repair and a rent reduction, orders you to refund the difference between the reduced value and what was paid, awards actual damages, costs and attorney fees, and nets everything off against the rent you claim. On a documentation request the court orders disclosure at least ninety-six hours before trial, and if you fail to produce your records the trial is continued and repeated failure can bring sanctions. Two narrow defences are yours: that the tenant's own conduct made the repair impracticable, by refusing or unreasonably denying entry or otherwise unreasonably delaying you; and that a third party outside your control caused the condition and you took reasonable, necessary and timely steps, in which case the tenant's only remedy is to terminate. A fee-shifting clause only pays you if it runs to the prevailing party, and even then a court may award you fees under the habitability rules only if it finds the tenant filed a frivolous claim or counterclaim. Finally, you cannot contract out of any of this: a lease or side agreement that waives or modifies a habitability right or remedy, or that charges the tenant a cost, fee or penalty for exercising one, is unlawful, void and unenforceable.

title: Colorado Does Not Require You to Carry Landlord Insurance
bodyText: Colorado has no statute requiring a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, no minimum coverage amount, no requirement to name the tenant or anyone else as an insured, and no duty to tell the tenant whether you carry insurance at all. Nothing in the state code makes insurance a condition of renting out a dwelling unit. That makes insurance a business decision rather than a compliance one, and the cautious course is still to carry it: you are responsible by statute for the condition of the unit, your tenant and the tenant's guests are on the property for the whole term, and the statutory damages Colorado attaches to a landlord's wrongful act run into five figures on a single unit. Two practical points. A home-rule city or county may require insurance as part of a local rental licence or registration scheme, so check your local rules before relying on the absence of a state rule. And do not bill your own insurance premium to the tenant as a separate monthly fee: since January 1, 2026 Colorado bars a fee for a good or service you do not actually provide to the tenant, bars a fee above the price of what you do provide, and bars a fee that rises by more than two percent over a lease of a year or less. Whether a premium pass-through survives those limits has not been decided by any court, so build the cost into the rent instead, where it is plainly lawful. Requiring the tenant to carry renters' insurance is a different question and is not prohibited; the only place Colorado's tenancy statutes mention tenant insurance is the electric-vehicle-charging provision, which lets you insist on a certificate of insurance naming you as an additional insured before the tenant installs a charging system.

title: Colorado's Landlord Lien on a Tenant's Belongings
bodyText: Colorado gives you a statutory landlord lien, and it is narrower and slower than most landlords expect. If you rent furnished or unfurnished rooms or apartments for your tenants' housekeeping purposes, or trailer space as the keeper of a trailer court, you have a lien on the tenant's personal property then on or in the rental premises for unpaid board, lodging or rent plus the reasonable cost of enforcing the lien, but expressly not attorney fees. The lien reaches household furniture, goods, appliances and other personal property of the tenant and the tenant's household that is on the premises, and it does not reach pet animals, small kitchen appliances, cooking utensils, beds, bedding, necessary wearing apparel, personal or business records and documents, or personal effects. Those exclusions are the practical heart of the rule: in an ordinary rented home very little of what is actually there is subject to the lien. You cannot liquidate it yourself. If the charges are unpaid thirty days after they fall due you may file a lien foreclosure action in the county or district court, and if you do not commence that action within sixty days the lien terminates, although the parties may agree to extend that by up to thirty more days. Only after you hold a judgment may you sell, and then only after ten days of notice of the time and place with a description of the property, one newspaper publication or three posted notices, and delivery or mailing of the notice to the owner, at a public auction between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. for cash. Your recoverable cost of keeping the property until the sale is capped at ninety dollars. If you sell or dispose of the property without substantially complying with the statute, the tenant recovers the value of the property, never less than one hundred dollars, plus reasonable attorney fees. There is one shortcut: no court action is required if the property is abandoned, which the statute presumes when the owner has not contacted you for at least thirty days and you genuinely know of no evidence that they mean to keep it; even then you must give fifteen days of notice of the proposed manner and date of disposal by registered or certified mail with a return receipt signed by the addressee only, publish the notice if it comes back unclaimed, and keep the proof for a year. Two traps. Asserting the lien while the tenant is still living there is allowed, in that you or your agent may enter at a reasonable time and peaceably take control of covered property, but an assertion that substantially interferes with the tenant's right to reasonably occupy and enjoy the premises is unlawful, forfeits the lien altogether and gives the tenant a damages action; and locking the tenant out or cutting services to secure the property is a far more expensive mistake, because the unlawful-removal statute carries the tenant's actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars. The lien is also not a substitute for suing, since it does not take away your right to sue for the charges or for whatever is still owed after a sale. Two points of genuine doubt, with the cautious course. The statute speaks of renting rooms or apartments, so whether it reaches a whole detached single-family house let to one household is unsettled; assume it may not, and plan on an ordinary money claim instead. And Colorado's general exemptions from execution and garnishment are written for writs rather than for this kind of possessory lien, so the exclusion list in the lien statute itself is what you can rely on. This library does not offer a landlord lien clause: the lien is yours by statute whether or not the lease mentions it, and a lease term is far more likely to overreach, by claiming excluded items, adding the attorney fees the statute withholds, or purporting to let you sell without a judgment, than to add anything you do not already have. If you want one anyway, claim no more than the statute gives and take advice first. Mobile home parks are governed separately and this guidance does not cover them.

title: No Statewide Landlord Registration in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado does not register or license residential landlords. There is no statewide rental registry, no state rental licence, no requirement to file your ownership with the county assessor before letting a property, and no requirement that an out-of-state individual owner appoint an in-state agent or broker. An out-of-state company is different: if it transacts business here it must file a statement of foreign entity authority with the Secretary of State and keep a Colorado registered agent, and until it files it may not sue to collect its debts, including rent (C.R.S. §§ 7-90-701, 7-90-801, 7-90-802). Anyone renting under a name other than their true name needs a statement of trade name on file before suing to collect a debt (C.R.S. §§ 7-71-101, 7-71-102) (see "Out-of-State Landlords: Companies Must Register an Agent, and Name Yourself in the Lease"). The only statewide registry in Colorado's landlord-tenant law covers mobile home parks, whose owners must register each park with the state annually, give the state a long list of park and ownership details including the legal owner behind a limited liability company, and face a delinquency fee of up to five thousand dollars for missing the deadline; nothing like that applies to a site-built rental. What Colorado does require is much simpler and still catches landlords out: the written rental agreement must state the name and address of the landlord or the landlord's authorised agent, and if that identity changes the new landlord or agent has one business day to give each tenant written or electronic notice or to post the new identity conspicuously on the premises. Treat that as your registration obligation and keep it current, because a sale, a change of management company or a transfer into a new entity starts the one-business-day clock. The one real exposure is local. Colorado expressly gives municipalities the power to license, regulate and tax any lawful occupation or business place and gives counties the power to license short-term rentals and set the fees and terms, so a home-rule city or a county may well require you to register a rental, hold a licence, pass an inspection or name a local contact. Check your city and county rules before you let a property, and do not read the absence of a state rule as permission. If you also let the property for stays of under thirty days, local short-term-rental licensing is a separate regime and you should check that too.

title: What You Can Recover When a Colorado Tenancy Ends Badly
bodyText: In Colorado you do not have to choose between getting the property back and getting your money. In the same eviction action, once the tenant has been personally served, the court enters judgment for possession and then finds the rent due at the time of trial, the damages you have suffered up to trial from the unlawful detention, and the damages up to trial from injury to the property, and enters judgment for those amounts with costs. Two limits shape that. Everything is measured to the date of trial, so future rent for the rest of the term is not part of an eviction judgment; and the whole judgment has to fit the court's jurisdictional limit, which in county court is twenty-five thousand dollars in total for rent, detention damages and property damage, exclusive of costs and fees. If the monthly rental value is above twenty-five thousand dollars, or a verified answer puts your allegations in issue in certain of the statutory grounds, the county court must send the case to the district court. Attorney fees are the trap. The prevailing party in an eviction is entitled to damages, reasonable attorney fees and costs, except that a residential landlord or tenant who wins gets no attorney fees at all unless the rental agreement itself contains a provision for either party to obtain them. So a Colorado lease with no fee provision means you pay your own lawyer even when you win, and a lease with a one-sided fee provision is a prohibited clause. The clause has to run to the prevailing party, and the court must still find that the party prevailed and the fee is reasonable. If all you want is money, you have other routes: a plain claim for unpaid rent can go to small claims court up to seven thousand five hundred dollars, or to county court up to twenty-five thousand, or to district court above that. But small claims cannot hear an eviction, so a combined possession-and-money claim has to start in county court. Keep in mind too that the tenant can stop a nonpayment eviction by paying everything lawfully due under the notice, plus any rent still owed under the lease or an eviction-stage repayment plan, at any time until the judge enters judgment for possession, and that right cannot be waived by any written agreement. Finally, Colorado has no statute letting you accelerate the remaining rent and no statute requiring you to re-let to cut your losses; both are left to general contract law, so an acceleration clause is risky and the cautious course is to sue for rent as it falls due and to re-let promptly. Separate statutory limits override anything your lease says in two situations: a tenancy ending because the tenant died, and a tenancy a documented victim-survivor of domestic violence, stalking or unlawful sexual behaviour ends early.

title: The Hard Ceiling on a Colorado Late Fee
bodyText: Colorado sets a single hard ceiling on a residential late fee: the greater of fifty dollars or five percent of the past-due rent payment. That is a maximum, not a suggested figure, and it is the number to check your lease against before you enter an amount. Three limits travel with it. You cannot charge anything until the rent payment is at least seven calendar days late, counted in calendar days and not business days. You cannot charge more than one late fee for the same late payment unless the fees added together still fit under the ceiling. And you cannot charge interest on a late fee, or take a late fee out of a rent payment the tenant makes. The ceiling only applies to late rent. Since January 1, 2026 Colorado separately bars any charge connected to the overdue payment of a fee, charge or amount that is not rent, so you cannot put a late fee on an unpaid utility bill, pet fee, parking charge or any other non-rent item at all, at any amount. The consequence of overshooting is not just that you cannot collect the excess: a lease provision that does not comply is void and unenforceable, which means a lease stating a fee above the ceiling gives you no late fee at all rather than the maximum one. The figure in your lease should be your own amount and should be chosen to stay under the ceiling at the lowest rent the lease could ever carry, because five percent of a reduced or prorated rent is a smaller number than five percent of a full month.
