The rest of the late-fee regime, including the disclosure requirement, the one-hundred-and-eighty-day notice deadline, the subsidy-portion rule and the penalties, is covered in the related guidance.

title: Law Enforcement and Your Colorado Lease
bodyText: Colorado does not make you a partner of the police and does not let your lease make the tenant one. No statute requires a landlord, as a landlord, to cooperate with or hand information to law enforcement, no statute requires the tenant to do so, and there is no Colorado crime-free housing addendum law of the kind some states have. But two general duties bind you as they bind everyone. Colorado makes it the duty of every person who has reasonable grounds to believe a crime has been committed to report it promptly to law enforcement, and a good-faith report is immune from civil liability; the statute sets no penalty (C.R.S. § 18-8-115). And if you or your staff find a tenant dead and the cause is unknown, or the death may be unnatural, accidental, from drugs or another cause the coroner must look into, you must report it immediately to the police or the coroner, and the body must not be moved before the coroner arrives unless that is needed to identify the person, protect the property, preserve evidence or protect life, health or safety (C.R.S. § 30-10-606(1.2)). What Colorado does have are limits that cut against a cooperation clause, and two of them are absolute. First, your rental agreement must not contain a provision letting you terminate the tenancy, impose a penalty or take any adverse action against a tenant because the tenant called for peace-officer or other emergency assistance in a situation involving domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behaviour or stalking, and no agreement may contain a waiver of the tenant's right to call for police or emergency help. That bar does not depend on the clause mentioning domestic violence: a general rule penalising repeated police calls, excessive emergency service, nuisance complaints or disturbances can breach it in practice, and the exposure is the tenant's actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, with attorney fees. Second, you must not demand, request or collect information about a tenant's immigration or citizenship status, and must not disclose or threaten to disclose it to any person, entity, or immigration or law enforcement agency, unless the law or a court order requires it. So a lease term promising to share tenant information with the authorities on request is not something you should sign up to. Third, if a tenant tells you they are a victim-survivor of stalking, unlawful sexual behaviour, domestic violence or domestic abuse, you must not pass that on to anyone, including a co-tenant, without the tenant's express written consent or a court order, although if the tenant consents to your sharing it with the court you must disclose it to the court in a civil action. The one place Colorado's law points the other way is a tenant protection, not a landlord tool: where a guest or invitee commits a substantial violation, the tenant has a defence to eviction if they did not know of it and could not reasonably have known of or prevented it but immediately notified a law enforcement officer. The practical course is to leave law enforcement out of your lease entirely. You can still call the police about criminal conduct on your property, respond to a lawful subpoena or court order, and rely on Colorado's implied statutory term that the tenant will not commit a substantial violation while in possession. A city or county may add its own nuisance or crime-free requirements, so check local rules.

title: No Colorado Lead-Safe Certificate for a Rental
bodyText: Colorado does not issue a lead-safe certificate for a dwelling, does not require one before you let a property built before 1978, and has nothing for you to attach to a lease. The word lead-safe appears in Colorado's statutes only as a statement of state policy: the legislature chose the goal of lead-safe housing rather than lead-free housing, meaning housing where no significant lead-based paint hazard is present rather than housing stripped of all lead paint. The certification Colorado does operate is of people and firms, not of buildings. The state certifies those who inspect, assess the risk of, plan, design, supervise or carry out lead-based paint abatement in pre-1978 housing and in facilities regularly used by young children, and by statute those training and certification requirements may not be more stringent than the federal programme. Enforcement of the abatement standards, though not the certification requirements, can be delegated to local health or building departments. What that means in practice. If lead paint in your rental needs abatement, use a certified abatement contractor and keep their certification, the scope of work and the clearance testing in your file: that paperwork is your evidence, and there is no state certificate that substitutes for it. If a certified assessor reports that your property has no significant lead-based paint hazard, that report is useful to you, but it is not a state certificate and no statute gives it any legal effect in a tenancy. Do not represent a unit as lead-safe or lead-free in a listing or a lease unless you can prove it, because a false statement about the characteristics of a property is a deceptive trade practice in Colorado quite apart from lead law. FEDERAL: the pre-1978 lead disclosure and the EPA-approved pamphlet are federal requirements that apply in Colorado and are not state law; see the library's federal lead row. A home-rule city or county may add its own requirements, so check local rules.

title: Colorado Adds No Lead Notices of Its Own
bodyText:
Beyond the federal disclosure, Colorado adds nothing. There is no Colorado lead disclosure form, no state lead pamphlet, no state registry of lead-tested properties, no notice to tenants when lead work is done in the building, and nothing a Colorado lease has to carry or have attached to it about lead. Neither title of the statutes that governs landlords and tenants mentions lead at all.

Colorado's lead law lives in its public health title and does two things: it funds a state programme that gathers information, screens children and produces educational materials aimed at health-care providers, child care providers, schools, parents, the real estate industry and owners of rental properties; and it certifies the people and firms who inspect, assess and abate lead-based paint.

There is one state-required piece of lead paperwork for a dwelling, and it is not yours as landlord and not part of the lease: anyone who performs a renovation of pre-1978 housing for compensation must give a lead hazard information pamphlet to both the owner and the occupant before starting, and that requirement is itself suspended if the federal funding behind it is withdrawn. So if you hire a contractor to renovate an older unit while a tenant is in it, expect the contractor to hand the pamphlet to you and to the tenant, and keep a record that it happened.

Two other lead rules exist nearby but are not yours.

- Drinking water must be tested for lead by child care centers, family child care homes and eligible schools, and the duty falls on the operator, not on the owner of the building, so if you rent to someone running a licensed child care home you may be asked to cooperate with sampling or remediation rather than to carry out the testing yourself; a child care licence condition may require more, so check.
- There is a rural grant programme for asbestos and lead paint abatement that pays local governments, not landlords, and it expires in mid-2027.

FEDERAL: the pre-1978 lead disclosure, the EPA pamphlet and the renovation rules are federal and apply in Colorado whatever the state does; do not treat Colorado's silence as relief from them.

title: What a Colorado Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Colorado prescribes a short, closed list of things a written residential rental agreement must contain, and a missing item is a missing disclosure rather than an untidy lease. Four are mandatory for every lease. The agreement must state the name and address of the person who is the landlord or the landlord's authorised agent. It must carry a statement that Colorado law prohibits source-of-income discrimination and requires a non-exempt landlord to accept any lawful and verifiable source of money, including government or private assistance; a landlord with five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five rental units in total is exempt from that one. And since January 1, 2025 it must carry two statements in at least twelve-point bold-faced type: one saying every tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing under the warranty of habitability and that retaliation for reporting unsafe conditions, requesting repairs or seeking that right is prohibited; and one, in English and Spanish, giving an address where the tenant can mail or deliver written notice of an uninhabitable condition together with an email address or an accessible online tenant portal for the same purpose. Three more are conditional on what you charge. If you want a late fee at all it must be disclosed in the rental agreement, so a lease silent on late fees gives you none. From January 1, 2026, a lawful charge is only recoverable out of the security deposit if it is actually listed in the lease, which makes an itemised list of your charges a money issue and not housekeeping. And from March 26, 2026, if you allocate utility costs among tenants by a ratio billing system, the method of allocation must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously in the rental agreement or an addendum to it. Two Colorado disclosures are deliberately not lease content, and putting them in the lease does not discharge them. Radon must be disclosed before signing, in writing, in a separate document that the tenant signs to acknowledge receipt, with the prescribed warning statement, everything you know about radon testing and mitigation, and the state brochure. Bed bugs are disclosed on request, not as a standing clause: you must not offer a unit you know or reasonably suspect has bed bugs, and on request from a prospective tenant you must say whether the unit had bed bugs in the previous eight months, and on request from a tenant or prospective tenant give the last date it was inspected and found free of them. There is one more written disclosure that does not have to be in the lease but is easiest to put there: if you restrict portable cooling devices, you must disclose the restriction in writing and tell the tenant whether you will run a cooled common space during an extreme heat event, or where nearby community cooling spaces are. Colorado has no blank-space or completeness statute, but fill or strike every placeholder before anyone signs, because an unfilled habitability-notice address is a missing required statement. Mobile home park agreements have their own content rules and are not covered here, and a city or county may require more.

title: Colorado Does Not Require Initialed Lease Clauses
bodyText: Colorado requires no initials anywhere in a residential lease. No statute makes a clause unenforceable because the tenant did not initial it, none requires a separate signature line beside a particular term, and none requires a tenant to sign an acknowledgment of any lease provision. The legislature plainly knows how to require this when it wants to: a foreclosure consulting contract in Colorado has to be dated, personally signed with every page initialed by each home owner, and notarised in the home owner's presence. It chose none of that for leases. The one signed acknowledgment Colorado does require of a residential tenant is not a lease clause at all. The radon disclosure must be given before the lease is signed, in writing, in a document separate from the lease that the tenant signs to acknowledge receipt. That signature is a compliance step, so capture it on its own document and keep it; initialing a radon paragraph inside the lease does not discharge the duty. What this means for your lease. Initials are evidence, not compliance. There is no legal penalty for leaving them out and no legal benefit from putting them in, but a tenant initial beside an unusual or expensive term, or beside a required bold-faced statement, is cheap proof that the term was read, and that proof is worth having if a dispute ever reaches a judge. If you use initials, be consistent, because a lease with some clauses initialed and others blank invites the argument that the blank ones were never agreed. The two things Colorado does insist on are that the lease be signed by both of you and that you give the tenant a copy of the signed agreement no later than the seventh day after the tenant signs, electronically unless the tenant asks for paper. Electronic signature is fine: for the habitability provisions, writing means any record conveying information in a retainable or visually displayable form, including electronic and digital records, though that definition does not extend to the written notices and demands used in an eviction, which should be handled on paper.

title: Recording a Colorado Lease Is Optional
bodyText: Colorado never requires you to record a residential lease. There is no lease registry, no filing fee you must pay, no deadline, and no consequence in the tenancy for leaving a lease unrecorded. Recording is simply available: a lease is an agreement affecting title to real property, so it may be recorded with the county clerk and recorder for the county where the property sits. What recording buys you is priority against strangers, not anything against your tenant. Colorado is a race-notice state: an unrecorded instrument is not valid against someone who acquires rights in the property and records first, unless that person had notice of it before acquiring those rights. Between you and your tenant the lease is fully effective whether or not it is recorded. The practical upshot for a residential landlord is that recording is almost never worth it. A one-year lease will be over before any priority contest matters, recording puts the rent, the parties' names and the whole document into a public index, and it creates a record you may later have to release. The cases where it is worth thinking about are a long lease, a lease with an option to purchase or a right of first refusal, or a tenant who has spent real money on the property and wants the term protected against a future buyer or lender; in those cases take advice first, and consider recording a short memorandum of lease rather than the lease itself so the commercial terms stay private. If your property happens to be Torrens-registered land, a historical system Colorado closed to new applications in 2018 and wound down by recording the old certificates in the ordinary records, a lease of three years or more was required to be registered with the registrar of titles; if a title search turns up a certificate of title rather than ordinary recorded deeds, ask a title company about it rather than assuming the ordinary rules apply. One warning either way: do not record anything you know to be groundless or materially false about title, because Colorado makes that a damages claim with attorney fees on top.

title: How Long a Colorado Lease May Run
bodyText: Colorado puts no ceiling on how long a residential lease may run. There is no maximum term, no renewal cap and no registration or approval triggered by length. The only term limits in Colorado's statutes bind public landlords such as school districts, counties, municipalities and special districts leasing out their own property, and they have nothing to do with a private rental. What Colorado does impose is a writing requirement at the one-year line, and it is strict. A lease for a term of more than one year must be in writing and subscribed by the party granting the lease, and a contract to lease for longer than one year is void unless the contract, or a note or memorandum of it expressing the consideration, is in writing and subscribed by that party. A lease for a term of one year or less can be oral and is still a valid interest in land. So the practical rule is simple: anything over twelve months must be a signed writing, and the signature that matters is the landlord's, because the statute requires the subscription of the party by whom the lease is to be made. Get the tenant's signature too, since Colorado separately requires you to give the tenant a copy signed by both of you within seven days. An authorised agent may sign for you, but the agent's authority must itself be in writing. Three length-related points worth knowing. Colorado has no spousal-consent requirement for leasing: it is not a community-property state, and no statute makes a spouse's signature necessary. The one exception sits in the homestead rules, which require both spouses of a married owner to execute a conveyance or encumbrance of homesteaded property; a homestead only exists where the property is occupied as a home by the owner or the owner's family, so an ordinary rental is not homesteaded, but if you are letting out a home you or your family still occupy, or letting part of one, the cautious course is to have both spouses sign. Second, a tenancy of twelve months or more pulls the tenant into Colorado's cause-required eviction regime, which does not apply during the first twelve months of a tenancy, so a thirteen-month lease is a materially different legal animal from an eleven-month one. Third, from January 1, 2026 the tenant's right to void the lease and vacate for a radon-disclosure failure does not apply to a lease of one year or less. Length is therefore a real legal choice, not just a commercial one.

title: No Parity Rule Between Colorado Lease Types
bodyText: Colorado has no lease-type parity statute. Nothing forbids you from offering a month-to-month tenant terms less favourable than a fixed-term tenant gets, nothing caps the premium you may charge for month-to-month flexibility, and nothing requires the two kinds of tenancy to carry the same rules, deposit or fees. Charging more for a month-to-month arrangement than for a twelve-month lease on the same unit is lawful in Colorado as a matter of state law. Four state rules still apply whatever the tenancy type, and they are where landlords actually get caught. You may not raise rent more than once in any twelve-month period of consecutive occupancy by the tenant, and that limit applies regardless of whether there is a written agreement, how long the tenancy has run, and whether the tenancy is fixed-term, month-to-month or for an indefinite term. Where there is no written agreement at all, a rent increase needs at least sixty days of written notice, and you may not serve a notice to terminate that kind of tenancy with the primary purpose of raising the rent in a way that sidesteps the notice rule. Once a tenant has been in the premises twelve months, the cause-required eviction regime applies and you may not increase rent in a discriminatory, retaliatory or unconscionable manner to get around it. And the notice you must give to end or not renew a tenancy depends on how long the tenancy has run, not on which label the lease carries. So treat lease type as a commercial choice that is free in principle but constrained in practice: price the two options as you like at the start, then remember that a mid-tenancy move from one type to the other does not reset the once-a-year increase clock, and that a sudden increase aimed at a tenant who has complained is a different problem entirely. A city or county may regulate more, though Colorado forbids local governments from controlling rents on private residential property, subject to that statute's own exceptions.

title: Colorado Sets No Minimum Type Size for a Lease
bodyText: Colorado does not set a minimum type size for a lease. No statute says how small the body text may be, and Colorado has nothing like the rule some states have making an unreadably printed contract inadmissible in evidence. Small print will not void your lease by itself. Colorado does prescribe type size for three specific pieces of text, and those are hard requirements rather than style preferences. The statement that every tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing under the warranty of habitability and that retaliation is prohibited must appear in the rental agreement in at least twelve-point bold-faced type. The statement giving an address and an email address or online portal for written notice of an uninhabitable condition must appear in the rental agreement in at least twelve-point bold-faced type and in both English and Spanish. And the radon warning, which belongs on its own separate document rather than in the lease, must be in bold-faced type that is clearly legible and in substantially the prescribed form. Getting the size wrong on any of those is a defective disclosure, not a formatting quibble. Practical guidance. Set the whole lease in a size you would be content to read aloud to a judge, keep the two bold-faced statements visibly larger and bolder than the surrounding text so a measurement argument never arises, and if you shrink text to fit a page, shrink anything other than the statutory statements. Remember that the twelve-point floor is a floor: nothing stops you from using a larger size, and nothing is gained by hugging the minimum. If you deliver the lease electronically, make sure the required statements remain at the prescribed size and in bold in whatever the tenant actually receives, because a PDF that reflows or a portal that strips formatting can turn a compliant lease into a non-compliant one.

title: How Long You Have to Sue a Colorado Tenant
bodyText: Colorado gives a landlord an unusually generous window for rent and a much shorter one for everything else, so the label you put on a claim matters. Unpaid rent has its own six-year limb: all actions for arrears of rent must be brought within six years after the cause of action accrues. The same six years covers an action to recover a liquidated debt or an unliquidated but determinable amount of money due to you, which is how most lease money claims are framed. Any other contract action on the lease is three years unless it falls in that six-year limb. A claim in tort, including damage to the property that you sue on as negligence rather than as a breach of the lease, is two years. Accrual decides when the clock starts. A debt, obligation, money owed or performance accrues on the date it becomes due, so each month of unpaid rent starts its own six-year period on its own due date rather than all of them starting when the tenancy ends. A claim for injury to property accrues when both the injury and its cause are known, or should have been known with reasonable diligence, which for move-out damage is usually when you inspect. Partial payments are the question landlords ask most, and Colorado's answer is split. A tenant's acknowledgment or promise to pay does not revive a time-barred claim unless it is in writing and signed by the tenant. But the statute expressly says it does not alter the effect of a payment of principal or interest, which leaves the effect of a part payment to the general law rather than settling it. Do not build a collection strategy on the idea that a small payment resets the clock: treat the six years as running from each due date, and get any payment arrangement in writing and signed. Two more practical points. If you sue a tenant and the tenant counterclaims on something arising out of the same transaction, that counterclaim has to be brought within one year after you serve your complaint, which is a reason to serve promptly and completely rather than drip-feeding claims. And do not try to shorten these periods by a lease clause: Colorado voids a lease provision that waives or modifies the security deposit and related protections for the tenant's benefit, the enforceability of a contractual shortening is untested here, and nothing is gained because the statutory periods already run in your favour on rent. Deposit disputes work the other way round, since the tenant's treble-damages claim depends on their own written demand and notice before suit.

title: Liquidated Damages in a Colorado Lease
bodyText: Colorado has no statute that generally permits or forbids a liquidated damages clause in a residential lease. Whether a fixed sum stated in advance is an enforceable estimate of loss or an unenforceable penalty is decided by the courts under general contract principles, and this library cannot settle it for you. What Colorado does have are four specific rules that beat anything your lease says, and between them they remove most of the situations where landlords reach for a liquidated damages clause. If the lease ends early because the tenant died, a clause requiring liquidated damages is void and unenforceable, as is a clause accelerating rent beyond the end of that month or ten business days after the unit is vacated, a clause clawing back concessions or move-in discounts, and a clause imposing any other fee, damages or penalty for the early termination. If the tenant fails to give the notice of nonrenewal your lease requires, you may recover only your actual losses from that failure, not a fixed sum. A lease provision assigning a fee or charge to the tenant for repairs, cleaning or other necessary work due to normal wear and tear, or for damage or a defective condition that existed before the tenancy, is against public policy and void; the clause fails, not just the charge. And on the security deposit, you must prove your actual damages, an amount you keep is presumed to exceed them unreasonably once it reaches one hundred and twenty-five percent of them, and a court may find a smaller amount unreasonable too. There is also a bar on any clause assigning a penalty stemming from an eviction notice or action, and from 2026 a bar on any fee, charge or amount that breaks Colorado's landlord pricing rules. The practical conclusion is to price your losses rather than stipulate them. Charge the tenant what the breach actually costs you, document it with invoices and estimates, and keep the figures in your file, because you will carry the burden of proving actual damages if the deposit is in dispute. If you do want a stipulated sum for something the statutes leave open, make it a genuine pre-estimate of loss that you can justify, keep it well under anything that looks punitive, and take advice first. A clause that reads as a penalty risks being struck out altogether and leaving you with nothing.

title: You Cannot Lock Out a Colorado Tenant for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Colorado gives you no lockout right for unpaid rent, and no way to buy one in the lease. There is no opt-in self-help lockout, no advance-notice-and-key-access procedure of the kind a few states allow, and nothing a tenant can agree to that creates one. It is unlawful to remove or exclude a tenant from a dwelling unit without resorting to court process, and unlawful removal or exclusion expressly includes willfully cutting off utilities and willfully removing doors, windows or locks for any reason other than repair or maintenance. A separate rule makes it unlawful to remove or exclude a tenant, or even to start a court process to do so, because the tenant has not paid late fees. The exposure is what makes this the most expensive mistake in Colorado landlording: the tenant must be awarded their actual damages plus the higher of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, together with any other damages, attorney fees and costs, and the court may order possession restored to the tenant. On a unit renting for a modest amount, one afternoon of changed locks can cost five figures and put the tenant back in the property. Two things are not lockouts and are worth distinguishing. If the unit has genuinely been abandoned, court process is not required, but abandonment has to be evidenced by the return of keys, the substantial removal of the tenant's property, notice from the tenant, or an extended absence while rent goes unpaid, and the evidence has to be enough to make a reasonable person believe the tenant permanently gave up possession; a tenant who is simply behind on rent and still living there has not abandoned anything. And a mutually agreed handover is lawful, which means a written agreement made at the time the tenant actually leaves, not a clause signed at the start of the tenancy. Write nothing into the lease that penalises the tenant because a notice was served or a case was filed, because Colorado voids that kind of clause outright with no exemption for small or owner-occupied properties. Remember too that a tenant can stop a nonpayment eviction by paying everything lawfully due at any point until the judge enters judgment for possession, and that right cannot be waived by any written agreement. The lawful route is the only route: serve the correct demand, file, get a judgment, and let an officer execute the writ.

title: The One Way Colorado Lets You Shift Repair Duties to the Tenant
bodyText:
Colorado lets you move repair and maintenance work that habitability law would otherwise make your job onto the tenant in one situation only, and the conditions are strict.

- The home must be a single-family residence and you must receive no subsidy from any governmental source for it.
- The agreement must be made in good faith, must be set out in a writing that is separate from the lease itself, must be signed by both of you, and must be supported by adequate consideration - so a paragraph inside the lease, or an addendum with nothing given in return, does not work.
- The tenant must actually have the skills to do the work.
- You may never shift work that would endanger the tenant's health or safety, whatever the tenant is willing to agree to.

Where the agreement is valid and covers one of the conditions on the state's minimum-standards list, the tenant takes on that condition and its absence no longer makes the home uninhabitable, which is the whole value of the arrangement to you.

Outside that route there is no way to shift a habitability duty. The warranty of habitability is implied in every rental agreement, you must remedy and repair to a habitable standard at your own expense, and any agreement that waives or modifies a habitability right or obligation is void. So you cannot make the tenant responsible for the common areas, for the exterior rubbish receptacles, for extermination or for anything else on the minimum-standards list by writing it into the lease, and since January 1, 2026 you cannot charge the tenant a fee for a good or service you need in order to meet your own obligations either.

Ordinary tenant housekeeping duties are a different thing and are perfectly enforceable in the lease: keeping the unit clean and sanitary, taking the tenant's own rubbish out, using the fixtures and appliances reasonably, mowing, watering and clearing snow.

Two further points worth knowing.

- If the condition was substantially caused by the tenant, a household member, a guest or someone under the tenant's control, it is not a breach of the warranty at all, so you do not need a duty-shift agreement in order to deal with tenant-caused damage - though that exception does not apply where the condition is the result of domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking against the tenant.
- Because the agreement has to sit outside the lease, take advice on its wording before you use one; a defective agreement leaves you with the full habitability duty and the tenant with a statutory claim.

Mobile home parks are governed by a separate part of the statute and are not covered here, and a city or county may add duties of its own, so check your local rules.

title: No Energy-Conservation Charge in Colorado - and What You May Bill Instead
bodyText: Some states let a landlord recover the cost of an energy-efficiency improvement from tenants through a monthly conservation charge, on condition that each new tenant is told about it before signing, and give the tenant a rent deduction if the notice is missed. Colorado has nothing of the kind. There is no conservation charge, no conservation surcharge, no efficiency fee, no notice duty attached to one and no rent-deduction remedy anywhere in the state statutes. That is not a gap you can fill by agreement, because Colorado's fee rules run the other way. Since January 1, 2026 you may not charge a tenant a fee related to utilities above what the utility provider charged for service to that tenant's unit, you may not charge for the maintenance of common areas, you may not charge above the price of what you actually supply, and you may not charge for anything you need in order to meet your own obligations. A charge designed to recover your capital spending on insulation, windows, a heat pump or a more efficient boiler is a charge for your own asset, and billing it as a separate monthly line is very likely void. There are three lawful routes instead. First, build the cost into the rent: the rent itself is not a fee and is not capped by the fee rules. Second, if you buy gas or electricity on a master meter and pass it through to tenants, you may not add anything at all to what the utility billed you - no construction, maintenance, financing, administration, metering or billing cost - the total you bill all tenants may not exceed the utility's bill, and you must pass on any refund, rebate or rate reduction and tell your tenants about it in writing so they can claim it within ninety days. Operating a master meter also normally requires an exemption from the Public Utilities Commission, so do not start one without checking. Third, you may allocate utility costs among tenants of the same premises by a ratio billing system, but only with no markup or administrative fee, with common-area and shared-facility usage left out of what you allocate, with the aggregate not exceeding the utility's bill for the whole property, and with the allocation method disclosed clearly and conspicuously in the lease or an addendum. For buildings whose permits are applied for on or after July 1, 2027, gas, electricity and water have to be metered directly or by submeter, so plan new construction around direct metering rather than allocation. A home-rule city or county may have its own utility-billing or benchmarking rules, so check locally.

title: Methamphetamine Contamination: No Tenant Disclosure Duty, But Hard Rules You Must Follow
bodyText: Colorado does not require you to tell a tenant or an applicant that the property was once used as a methamphetamine laboratory. The written disclosure the state does require runs from a seller to a buyer, so it bites when you sell the rental, not when you let it - and Colorado publishes a free public online database of residential properties that have been used as meth labs, which an applicant can check for themselves, so assume prospective tenants may find out anyway. What the state does impose on you is much harder than a disclosure. Once a peace officer notifies you that chemicals, equipment or supplies of an illegal drug laboratory are on the property, or the laboratory is otherwise discovered and you have notice, you must bring the property up to the state board of health clean-up standards, or demolish it; if you demolish, the local authority may make you fence it off. Until the structure is certified you must not let anyone in who is not trained or certified to handle contaminated property - that includes tenants, applicants, cleaners and your own contractors. An unremediated unit is also uninhabitable as a matter of law, so you are in breach of the warranty of habitability while it stays that way, and remediation is at your expense. Breaking the board rules carries an administrative penalty of up to fifteen thousand dollars a day per violation until the violation is corrected. Local governments may declare an unremediated lab a public health nuisance, may require the property to meet clean-up standards before anyone occupies it, may notify the public and may charge inspection and testing fees, so check your city or county rules as well. Two things work in your favour. Once a contractor and a consultant issue you certificates of compliance, you are immune from health-based civil claims by any current or future owner, tenant, occupant or neighbour arising from the laboratory, you no longer have to disclose the former use to a buyer, and the property drops off the public database five years after the later certificate. And Colorado's self-help eviction ban - which is otherwise absolute and carries severe statutory damages - expressly does not reach a removal or exclusion that is consistent with the drug-laboratory cleanup rules, so clearing a contaminated unit under those rules is the one situation in which you may exclude a tenant without going to court. Do that only on documented advice, because getting it wrong puts you back inside the self-help penalty. Personal property in a contaminated structure has its own rule: the owner of the personal property has ten days from discovery to remove or clean it, after which you may dispose of it during the clean-up without liability to that owner, provided you secure the property and debris so nobody is exposed to the chemicals. This is an area where a mistake is both a health risk and a large penalty, so take advice early.

title: No Military Airfield Zone Disclosure in Colorado
bodyText: Several states make a landlord tell the tenant, before signing, that the property sits in a military airfield noise zone or accident-potential zone, and give the tenant a window of thirty days or so to walk away if the disclosure was not made. Colorado has nothing of the kind. There is no military-zone disclosure, no map or distance test that triggers one, no prescribed wording and no termination right attached to one, whether the property is next to Fort Carson, Peterson, Schriever, Buckley, the Air Force Academy, Pueblo Chemical Depot or the Greeley Air National Guard station. The state handles military airfields through land-use planning rather than through leases: a county or city whose boundaries come within two miles of a military installation larger than five hundred acres has to send proposed zoning changes and comprehensive-plan or land-development amendments to the installation commander, who may comment on whether they fit the airfield safety and noise standards of the federal air installation compatible use zone, and the local government has to consider those comments. That duty runs between governments; none of it reaches you or your tenant. Practical consequences. You are not obliged to volunteer anything about aircraft noise, overflight or crash risk, and Colorado's consumer-protection nondisclosure provision carries an intent-to-induce qualifier, so silence alone is unlikely to be a deceptive practice. But a tenant who signs, then finds jets overhead at six in the morning, is a tenant who leaves, disputes rent or complains - and if you answer a direct question about noise inaccurately you are on much weaker ground than if you had said nothing. So the cautious and commercially sensible course is to describe the aircraft noise plainly in the listing or at the viewing, keep a note that you did, and answer questions straight. Do not promise that noise will stay within any particular level, since you do not control it. If the local zoning for your property carries airfield-related conditions, those come from your city or county, not from the state, so check locally. If the property is inside a published noise or accident-potential contour and you are drafting a noise acknowledgment, take advice on the wording.

title: Minors, Eighteen-Year-Olds and Who Can Actually Be Your Tenant
bodyText: In Colorado full age is eighteen. A person who has turned eighteen can enter a lease and is bound by it to the full extent as any other adult, can manage their own property, and can sue and be sued without a guardian or anyone acting for them. So you can rent to an eighteen-year-old, hold them to the lease and name them in an eviction exactly as you would a forty-year-old; a parent is not needed, and the lease is not a family expense of the parents by operation of that statute, which matters if you were counting on the parents. If you want a parent on the hook, make them a co-tenant or a guarantor in their own right. Below eighteen the position is different and Colorado's statutes do not help you. The state has no statute that gives a person under eighteen the capacity to lease a home, and a minor under eighteen who has no legal guardian is classed as a person under disability for litigation purposes. What that means in practice is that a lease signed only by a person under eighteen is not something you should rely on: the general law of minors' contracts, which Colorado has not modified by statute for leases, leaves such a contract vulnerable, and you may find you cannot enforce the rent obligation you thought you had. The cautious course is simple. Put at least one adult on the lease as a tenant, and list any under-eighteen household member as a permitted occupant rather than as a tenant. Nothing in Colorado's eviction statute limits who may be named as a defendant by age, and there is no minor-tenant filing bar, so the statute does not stop you suing a minor - but how a minor party must be represented in a Colorado civil action is set by the court rules rather than by statute, so if you ever face an occupant under eighteen with no adult on the lease, get advice before filing rather than after. Do not turn any of this into a policy of refusing households with children: whom you rent to is constrained by fair housing law, and an age rule applied to the household rather than to the person signing is a different and much riskier thing.

title: Colorado Has No Mold Disclosure - It Has a Mold Repair Clock Instead
bodyText: Colorado does not make you disclose mold, past mold, mold remediation or mold risk to a tenant or an applicant. There is no mold disclosure form, no mold information booklet to hand over, no mold clause the lease must contain, no statutory mold standard and no testing threshold anywhere in the state statutes. What Colorado does instead is far more demanding, and it is where your attention belongs. Mold associated with dampness makes a home uninhabitable as a matter of law, and so does any other condition making the place damp which, left alone, would materially interfere with the tenant's health or safety - with a narrow exception for minor mold on surfaces that collect moisture as part of their normal use, such as a shower surround. Once you have written notice of mold or dampness you are on a clock. Within seventy-two hours you must install a containment, stop the active water sources feeding the mold and put in a high-efficiency particulate air filtration device to cut the tenant's exposure. Then, within a reasonable time, you must keep the containment up throughout the work, set up any additional protections workers and occupants need, eliminate or limit the moisture sources and dry everything affected, decontaminate or remove the damaged materials, check by post-remediation testing whether the remediation actually worked, and reassemble the place so the damp does not simply come back. If the condition interferes with the tenant's life, health or safety you must also provide, on request, a comparable unit or a hotel room at your expense. All of this is at your cost, you cannot push it onto the tenant's renter's insurance, and you cannot charge a fee for it. Because disclosure is not required, the sensible practice is the opposite of a disclosure form: document the condition of the unit at move-in, keep your repair and remediation records - you must keep habitability records for the whole tenancy and three years afterwards, and produce them to the tenant on request within ten days - and never put anything in the lease that tells the tenant to report problems verbally, because that wording gives up your right to written notice and starts your clock on a phone call. A city or county may have its own indoor-air or mold rules, so check locally.

title: Your Tenant's Unpaid Water Bill Becomes a Lien on Your Property
bodyText: This is one of the places where Colorado gives a landlord no protection at all, so plan around it rather than hoping. If water, sewer or sanitation service is supplied by a special district - which covers most suburban Front Range property, including metropolitan districts and water and sanitation districts - then every unpaid fee, rate, toll, penalty or charge is a perpetual lien on and against the property served until it is paid, and the district can foreclose it the way a contractor forecloses a mechanics' lien. If the service comes from a city or town sewerage system, or from a county water or sewerage system, the unpaid charges are certified to the county commissioners, become a lien on the real property served and are then collected as though they were part of the taxes. Nothing in any of those statutes cares who used the water or whose name was on the account. There is no affidavit you can file to say you do not live there, no exemption for a bill run up by a tenant, and no clause you can put in a lease that stops the lien attaching - a lease binds your tenant, not the utility. One related trap: if the city abates a nuisance such as weeds, brush or rubbish at your property, that assessment is also a lien, and it ranks ahead of every other lien except general taxes and prior special assessments. What to do about it. The safest arrangement is to keep water and sewer in your own name and recover the cost through the rent, or through a utility allowance, so that you always know the bill is paid; remember that if you bill utilities through you cannot add anything above what the provider charged for service to that unit. If the tenant is to be the utility customer, make the lease require proof that the account is open in the tenant's name and proof of payment on request, check the account yourself before you return the deposit, and treat an unpaid utility bill as a deposit deduction only if the lease actually lists utility charges as a tenant obligation - Colorado now limits deposit retention to nonpayment of rent, nonpayment of utility charges, nonpayment of other lawful charges listed in the lease, and repair of damage beyond normal wear and tear. On a sale or refinance, ask the district or the city for a payoff or a certificate of no outstanding charges rather than relying on the tenant's word. A home-rule city may have its own billing, deposit and shut-off rules, so check locally.

title: The Written Demand You Must Serve Before an Eviction for Unpaid Rent
bodyText:
Before you can start an eviction for unpaid rent in Colorado you must serve a written demand that gives the tenant the alternative of paying the rent or giving up the property.

- For a residential tenancy the period is ten days.
- It drops to five days if your lease is an exempt residential agreement, which means a single-family home let by a landlord who owns five or fewer single-family rental homes and whose lease actually tells the tenant that the ten-day period does not apply - if the lease does not say so, you get ten days, not five.
- It is three days for a nonresidential letting or an employer-provided housing agreement.

You cannot shorten any of this by agreement: the statute says in terms that no such agreement may contain a tenant waiver of the notice requirement.

The demand has to be in writing, state the grounds for your right to possession with a specific description of the alleged violation, describe the premises, state the date and time by which the property must be given up, and be signed by you, your agent or your attorney.

It must also carry two statements, and be in the right language.

- That a residential tenant who receives supplemental security income, social security disability insurance or Colorado works cash assistance has a right to mediation before you file.
- Where you are demanding unpaid rent, that a tenant who has experienced unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse that caused the missed payment may give you documentation and is entitled to a repayment plan of up to nine months.
- Also, the demand must be written in English, in Spanish, or in any other language you know or have reason to know is the tenant's primary language.

If a tenant does give you that documentation, you must offer a repayment plan within three business days of serving the demand or of receiving the documentation, whichever is later, you may not charge any fee, interest or penalty connected with the plan, and failing to offer one is a defence to your eviction.

Two further points that catch landlords out.

- Only the monthly payment for occupancy is rent you can demand on this track: late fees and other charges are not rent, and a demand that lumps them in is defective.
- This notice is court procedure, so it does not belong in your lease - the one thing the lease can do is carry the exempt-residential-agreement statement if you qualify.

A defective demand usually means starting again, so have your form checked.

title: In Colorado You Cannot Make a Deposit Nonrefundable
bodyText: Some states let you keep part of a deposit as nonrefundable so long as you say so in the lease, and require a particular notice when you do. Colorado has no such notice rule, because it does not let you do the thing the notice would describe. Colorado defines a security deposit as any advance or deposit of money, whatever you call it, whose main function is to secure performance of the lease. So a move-in fee, a cleaning deposit, a redecorating fee, an administrative fee charged at signing, a key or remote deposit, a holding deposit applied to the tenancy - if its real function is to secure the tenant's performance, it is a security deposit, it is subject to the deposit rules, and calling it nonrefundable in the lease does not change that. From January 1, 2026 a provision in or relating to a lease that waives or modifies any part of the deposit statutes for the tenant's benefit is against public policy and void, and so is any provision assigning the tenant a fee or charge for repairs, cleaning or other necessary work due to normal wear and tear, or for damage or a defective condition that existed before the tenancy began. A pet deposit has its own rule and the statute says in terms that it must be refundable; it is also capped. Where does that leave money you genuinely want to keep? Three lawful routes. Charge it as rent: the monthly payment for occupancy is not a deposit and not a fee, and pet rent is expressly allowed up to its own cap. Charge a rental application fee before the tenancy, but understand that Colorado treats any nonrefundable fee collected before the tenancy begins as an application fee, which means it must be limited to your actual or average cost of processing the application, must be the same amount for every applicant for that unit or any unit you are offering at the same time, cannot be charged at all if the applicant gives you a portable tenant screening report, and has to come with a disclosure or itemisation and a receipt. Or charge for a real optional service the tenant actually receives, priced at no more than it costs you - never for something you are obliged to provide anyway and never for common-area maintenance. Practical consequences: do not use the words nonrefundable deposit anywhere in your lease, do not list a nonrefundable cleaning or redecorating charge, keep every refundable sum in one clearly labelled security deposit, and remember that you may only retain from it for unpaid rent, unpaid utility charges, unpaid other lawful charges that the lease actually lists, and repair of damage beyond normal wear and tear that did not pre-exist the tenancy.

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice to Give in Colorado
bodyText: A handful of states require the notice that part of a deposit is nonrefundable to be given on its own piece of paper, signed separately from the lease, before any money changes hands. Colorado imposes no such requirement, and the reason is worth understanding rather than filing away: Colorado does not allow a nonrefundable deposit at all, so there is nothing for a separate notice to be about. Money whose main function is to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit whatever you call it and however the lease describes it, a pet deposit must be refundable, and from January 1, 2026 a lease provision that waives or modifies the deposit rules for the tenant's benefit is void. So do not look for a separate nonrefundable-deposit form to hand over, and do not create one: a signed acknowledgment that a sum is nonrefundable adds nothing, because the tenant cannot agree away the deposit rules, and a document of that kind is evidence that you tried. Colorado does use the separate-document device in two places you should know about, so that you do not confuse them with this one. If you want a tenant of a single-family home to take on repairs the habitability rules would otherwise leave to you, that agreement must be in a writing separate from the lease, signed, supported by its own consideration. And the radon disclosure cannot live inside the lease either. Both of those are covered by their own entries.

title: Out-of-State Landlords: Companies Must Register an Agent, and Name Yourself in the Lease
bodyText: If you live outside Colorado, or own through an out-of-state company, Colorado does not make you, as an individual, appoint a resident agent for your rental property or register as a nonresident owner, and nothing in its landlord-tenant law bars you from suing a tenant until something is filed. Two general business filings can, though. An out-of-state company that transacts business in Colorado must file a statement of foreign entity authority with the Secretary of State naming a Colorado registered agent; until it does it may not sue to collect its debts, such as unpaid rent, a court may stay its case, and it faces a civil penalty of up to five thousand dollars (C.R.S. §§ 7-90-701, 7-90-801, 7-90-802, 7-90-803). Owning property "without more" is not transacting business, but whether renting it out is more is a case-law question, so file before you need to sue. And if you rent under any name other than your own true name, a statement of trade name must be on file before you can sue to collect a debt from a tenant you dealt with under that name (C.R.S. §§ 7-71-101, 7-71-102). Being out of state also does not keep you out of a Colorado court: owning real property here submits you to its courts for claims arising from it, and you can be served outside the state (C.R.S. §§ 13-1-124(1)(c), 13-1-125). It also does not require your tenant or anyone else to withhold Colorado income tax from the rent; the only withholding Colorado applies to out-of-state owners of real property arises when the property is sold, not while it is let. So the special nonresident machinery that some states operate simply does not exist here. What does exist applies to every landlord in the state and is easy to get wrong when you manage from a distance. Your lease must state the name and address of the landlord or of the landlord's authorized agent, and if that identity or address changes you have to tell the tenant within one business day. A post-office box or a management company address is fine as long as it is a real address at which you can be reached and it is the address of the person actually authorised to act. Get this right for practical reasons as well as legal ones: the address you put in the lease is where the tenant will send the written notice of an uninhabitable condition that starts your repair clock, and a stale or unmonitored address does not stop that clock running. Your lease must also carry the two habitability statements Colorado requires, including an address where the tenant can mail or personally deliver written notice and an email address or online portal for the same purpose. Three practical points for a distant owner. Make sure someone in Colorado can actually attend the property within twenty-four hours, because the habitability timetable assumes it. If you own through a company, keep its foreign-entity filing and registered agent current (see above). If you are deciding whether to form a Colorado entity or how to handle tax on the rent, take advice.

title: Never Charge the Tenant for Serving a Notice
bodyText: Do not charge a tenant anything for preparing, posting, serving or delivering a notice - not a notice-service fee, not a posting fee, not a three-day-notice charge, not a courier or process-server cost, and not an administrative fee for the paperwork. Colorado forbids a rental agreement from containing a clause that assigns a penalty to a party stemming from an eviction notice or an eviction action arising from a breach of the agreement, and a provision that breaks that rule is void and unenforceable. There is no exemption for a small landlord, for an owner-occupied duplex or triplex, for an accessory dwelling unit or for a mobile home park: the carve-outs elsewhere in that section do not reach this prohibition, so it applies to every residential rental agreement in the state. A second rule reaches the same charge from the other direction. Since January 1, 2026 you may not require a tenant to pay a fee for a good or service that is necessary for you to comply with your own responsibilities or obligations - and serving the statutory demand is your compliance step, taken so that you can bring your own case. A fee that breaks that rule is itself a prohibited lease clause. So the charge fails twice over, and the attempt leaves you worse off than if you had never made it: the clause is void, the tenant may have a consumer claim with interest on top of actual damages, and the attorney general has been able to enforce the prohibited-clause rules directly since January 1, 2026. What you can recover is narrower and comes from the court, not the lease. The prevailing party in an eviction action is entitled to damages and costs of suit, and may recover reasonable attorney fees only if the lease contains a provision allowing either party to obtain them - so a fee clause has to run both ways, and a one-way fee-shifting clause is itself a prohibited term. Unpaid rent remains recoverable as rent. Everything else you spend getting to court is your own cost of doing business; price it into the rent rather than into a fee.

title: You Cannot Shorten or Waive Colorado's Notice Periods by Agreement
bodyText: In some states a lease can shorten the notice to quit, or have the tenant give it up altogether. Colorado does not work that way, and a clause that tries is worse than useless because it will not save the eviction it was written for. For unpaid rent the statute says in terms that no agreement may contain a tenant waiver of the notice requirement, so a clause reciting that the tenant waives the ten-day demand, or that one day is enough, is simply void and you will still have to serve the full demand. For a tenancy that Colorado's for-cause eviction rules cover - broadly, a tenant who has been in the property twelve months or more, outside the exempt property types - any provision of a lease or other agreement purporting to authorise or effect a waiver or modification of those rules is void and unenforceable, and that includes their notice requirements. For an ordinary termination or non-renewal the periods are fixed by the length of the tenancy: at least ninety-one days for a tenancy of a year or longer, twenty-eight days for six months or longer but under a year, twenty-one days for a month or longer but under six months, three days for a week or longer but under a month or a tenancy at will, and one day for less than a week. Those periods are the statute's, not the parties', and nothing in the section lets a lease reduce them. The only statutory excuse from giving notice runs the tenant's way, not yours: a tenant with a fixed-term tenancy that by agreement ends on a set date does not have to give written notice. You still do. So do not draft a clause that says no notice is required at the end of the fixed term, because the statute does not give you that, and a clause stating it will mislead your own staff into a defective termination. Three related non-waivables, since they come up in the same drafting conversation. A lease may not contain a waiver of the domestic-violence protections in the eviction statute, may not waive the tenant's right to call for police or emergency assistance, and may not contain a waiver of the pre-filing mediation right. There is one lawful way to get a shorter nonpayment period, and it is the statute's own: if the property is a single-family home and you own five or fewer single-family rental homes, a statement in the lease that the ten-day period does not apply gives you five days instead. That is not a waiver, it is the statute's alternative measure.

title: The Extra Statements Your Colorado Notice Must Carry
bodyText: Colorado has added content requirements to notices over the last few years, and a notice that is missing them is defective even if the period and the grounds are right. Beyond the basics - in writing, grounds with a specific description of the alleged violation or the no-fault ground, a description of the premises, the date and time by which possession must be delivered, and your signature or your agent's - every demand or notice must state that a residential tenant receiving supplemental security income, social security disability insurance or Colorado works cash assistance has a right to mediation before you file. Where the notice demands unpaid rent it must also state that a tenant who has experienced unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse that caused the missed payment may give you documentation and is entitled to repay over a period of up to nine months. And the notice must be written in English, in Spanish, or in any other language you know or have reason to know is the tenant's primary language - so if you have been corresponding with the tenant in another language, that is the language of the notice. For a no-fault eviction there is more - but only where Colorado's cause-required rules apply at all, which they do not in a tenancy's first twelve months, nor to a short-term rental, nor to an owner- or master-tenant-occupied single-family home, duplex or triplex, nor to a mobile home space, nor under an employer-provided housing agreement. You must allow at least ninety days, during which the tenant stays in possession on the existing lease terms; the written notice must give the vacate date; and for a demolition or conversion it must describe the project with a timeline and show material evidence that it will go ahead, such as a copy of the building permit or the application. For substantial repairs or renovations the notice must give an expected completion date and a general description of the work, and you must then get on with the work without unreasonable delay. Every no-fault notice must state the legal and factual basis for the eviction, and the legal basis must be one the statute lists. There is also a service point that is easy to miss: if a tenant has told you, in writing or otherwise, that they are a victim-survivor of unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse, you must make all reasonable efforts to serve personally, and only after three failed attempts may you post and then also send the notice by certified mail or a commercial courier with proof of delivery. Finally, the question landlords ask once the notice is out: can you start work on the unit, shut off a service or take out an appliance while the tenant is still there? No. Your habitability duty runs for the whole period the tenant lawfully occupies, decreasing services is itself prohibited retaliation with damages of three months' rent or three times actual damages, and willfully cutting off utilities or removing doors, windows or locks is an unlawful exclusion with its own heavy statutory damages. Serving the notice and then making the place hard to live in is the single most expensive mistake available to a Colorado landlord. These are procedural duties, not lease terms, so none of this belongs in your lease.

title: Municipal Nuisance Fines: The Statutory Default Runs Your Way - Don't Contract It Away
bodyText: This is one of the rare places where Colorado's default rule favours the landlord, and the way to keep it is to leave it alone. If a city serves you and your tenant with notice that the tenant has committed a violation of a nuisance ordinance on property you rent out, you have the right to give the tenant written notice to abate the nuisance; if the tenant does not abate it within five days of delivery, you may enter the exterior area of the property and abate it yourself. Your lease may still give you broader entry rights than that, and the statute says so. If the abatement means removing a vehicle, you may only do it by hiring a towing carrier to take the vehicle to a lot for storage under appropriate protection - do not move or dispose of it yourself. Then comes the part that matters: unless the lease provides otherwise, the tenant is liable to you for your direct costs of abating the nuisance and for the amount of the fine imposed on you from the date the tenant received the city's notice. That liability arises from the statute, not from your lease, so you do not need a clause to get it - and a clause that allocates nuisance costs or municipal fines differently, or that says nothing about costs while purporting to deal comprehensively with fines and charges, is how landlords accidentally lose it. Before you add any clause about fines, abatement costs or charges for tenant conduct, check that it does not read as providing otherwise. Two protections on the city's side. A municipal ordinance may impose liability on you for a nuisance your tenant committed only if the municipality notifies both you and the tenant before imposing a fine or other liability, so if a fine arrives with no notice to the tenant, say so. And where the city itself abates weeds, brush or rubbish, the cost is assessed against the land as a lien that outranks everything except general taxes and prior special assessments, so deal with the notice rather than waiting. Finally, three limits on using tenant conduct against the tenant. A nuisance or disturbance that interferes with quiet enjoyment is a ground for eviction, but it needs a ten-day written notice describing the specific conduct, and a tenant's lawful exercise of a legal right is not a disturbance. A tenant who is being blamed for a disturbance that is the result of domestic violence or abuse against them has a statutory defence. And you must never write - or enforce - anything that penalises a tenant for calling the police or for emergency assistance in a situation involving domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking, which is a trap in exactly this kind of clause. Local nuisance ordinances vary and are not covered here, so read the city's notice carefully.

title: Where Colorado Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Colorado regulates residential leases heavily, but a short list of points is left to what your lease actually says - and in each of them the right exists only if the lease claims it. These are worth going through deliberately, because silence costs you the benefit. The security deposit return period is one month by default, and your lease may specify a longer period of up to sixty days; no longer. What you may keep from the deposit is now a closed list, and one item on it is unpaid other lawful charges listed in the lease - so a charge you never listed is a charge you cannot deduct. Attorney fees in an eviction are not recoverable by a residential landlord at all unless the lease contains a provision for either party to obtain them, and that provision has to run both ways, because a one-way fee-shifting clause is a prohibited term. If the property is damaged by a sudden environmental public health event, or a government action makes continued occupancy impossible or unlawful, you may terminate without further liability only if the lease permits termination and you meet the statute's other conditions, including thirty days' written notice, access for the tenant's belongings, return of the deposit and a refund of rent for the uninhabitable period. If the property is a single-family home and you own five or fewer single-family rental homes, a statement in the lease that the ten-day nonpayment notice period does not apply gives you a five-day period instead. If you allocate utility costs between tenants of the same property by a ratio billing system, the allocation method has to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously in the lease or an addendum, and the other conditions met, or the allocation is unlawful. Your lease can also give you entry rights broader than the bare statutory right to enter the exterior to abate a nuisance, and the nuisance statute says so expressly. Two more: a tenant has no right to install an energy-efficiency measure on leased property except with the permission of the lessor, and from January 1, 2027 you may impose reasonable restrictions on a tenant's portable solar generation device, including requiring prior notice and restrictions about fire or electrical overload, damage and location - but not an unreasonable prohibition, which would be void. Three cautions. A term the statute lets you have is still subject to the prohibited-clause list and the fee rules, so check it there before you use it. Where the statute requires something to be in a writing separate from the lease - a single-family tenant repair agreement, the radon disclosure - putting it in the lease does not work. And the statute never lets you reduce a notice period, waive a habitability or deposit protection, or waive the tenant's right to call for emergency assistance, whatever the tenant signs.

title: No Ordnance or Demolition Disclosure in Colorado - But the Meter Rules Do Bind You
bodyText: Three disclosures travel together in other states, and Colorado has only the third. There is no duty to tell a tenant that the property is near a former military ordnance location, and no ordnance registry or map to consult; the word appears once in the entire Colorado code, and it is about the state's custody of its own military equipment. There is also no duty to disclose a planned demolition before the lease is signed - no notice that you have applied for a demolition permit, that one has been issued, or that you intend to pull the building down at the end of the term. Demolition matters at the other end of the tenancy instead, and the rules there are strict: if you plan to demolish, convert to a non-residential use or convert to a short-term rental, that is a no-fault eviction ground for a tenancy the for-cause rules cover, and it needs at least ninety days, during which the tenant stays on the existing lease terms, plus a written notice giving the vacate date, describing the project with a timeline and showing material evidence that it will go ahead, such as the building permit or the application. So a landlord planning a demolition does not have a disclosure problem, but does have a notice-period problem - plan the ninety days into your programme. The metering limb is the one that binds you, and it is a genuine lease requirement. If you allocate utility costs among tenants of the same property by a ratio billing system rather than metering each unit, you must disclose the allocation method clearly and conspicuously in the lease or in an addendum to it, and the allocation itself is lawful only if the total billed to all tenants does not exceed the utility's bill for the whole property, you add no markup, surcharge or administrative fee, and common-area and shared-facility utility costs are left out of what you allocate. For property built under permits applied for on or after July 1, 2027, gas, electricity and water have to be metered either directly by the utility or by a submeter, so new construction should be designed for metering rather than allocation. If you buy on a master meter and resell, the master-meter rules add their own conditions and normally require a Public Utilities Commission exemption. The state's own metering mandate, by contrast, binds water suppliers rather than landlords, and allows a single meter for a customer that is not a detached single-family residence - so do not assume your building is individually metered just because the law requires metering. Finally, remember what Colorado does require you to disclose, since the list is specific rather than general: radon, bed bugs on request, the two habitability statements, your identity and address, the utility allocation method, and any restriction you impose on portable cooling devices.

title: Facilities You Provide Become Facilities You Must Maintain
bodyText:
Colorado does not hand you a list of facilities you must install in a rental home. The law works the other way round: whatever you provide or promise becomes part of what you must keep working. An appliance counts as yours to maintain only if it is part of a written agreement with the tenant or you actually provided it, so an appliance you never supplied is not your problem - but a refrigerator, range stove, oven, air conditioner or cooling device you did supply must have conformed to the law when it was installed and must be kept in good working order.

Shared facilities work the same way. The grounds, areas and facilities held out for tenants generally, or whose use you promise to a particular tenant, are common areas, and they are part of the residential premises: they must be kept reasonably clean, sanitary and free of accumulated debris, filth, rubbish and garbage, with proper extermination when there is an infestation. Floors, stairways, elevators and railings must be kept in good repair, and there must be enough exterior receptacles for garbage, waste and rubbish, in good repair and emptied often enough to contain it. A fault in a common area only makes the unit itself legally uninhabitable if it materially affects the tenant's use of the unit, but it is still a breach of your maintenance duties and the tenant can still sue on it.

Three practical consequences.

- Say in the lease exactly which facilities come with the unit and which are shared, because it is the promise of use that pulls a facility into your duties - an amenity you never promised is not one you have to keep.
- Do not charge a separate fee for maintaining common areas, and do not charge for anything you are obliged to do anyway: since January 1, 2026 both of those charges are void in Colorado, and a lease provision imposing one is a prohibited clause.
- If you take away an amenity you promised, you are withdrawing something the tenant is paying for; close it only for repair, safety or legal compliance, keep the closure as short as you can, and tell tenants in writing why and for how long.

Your city or county may add its own requirements for shared facilities, so check local rules.

title: Taking the Property Back for Yourself or Your Family
bodyText: Colorado gives you a route to recover a rental home for yourself or a family member, but it is a statutory route with conditions, not something you create in the lease. Once the tenant has been in the property twelve months, Colorado's for-cause eviction rules apply unless your property is exempt, and from that point you may recover the home for your own use as a residence, or for a family member's, only at the end of the lease term and only if all of this is true: you serve proper written notice at least ninety days before the date the tenant must leave (forty-five days if you or your spouse are on active military duty), and the tenant may stay on the existing lease terms during that period; no substantially equivalent unit in the same building is vacant and available to house you or the family member; you or the family member actually move in within three months after the tenant leaves, which can be extended for a reasonable time where you or the family member has a disability and the home needs changes; and you do not list the home as a long-term or short-term rental for at least ninety days after the date the tenant had to leave. The notice must state the legal and factual basis you are relying on. Two traps. You cannot use this to end a lease early: Colorado's no-fault grounds operate at the end of the term, and a lease clause that purports to let you terminate mid-term for your own occupancy is unenforceable against a tenant the for-cause rules cover, because cause exists only as the statute describes it and the rules cannot be waived by agreement. And during the first twelve months of a tenancy, or where the property is exempt - a short-term rental, an owner- or master-tenant-occupied single-family home with or without an accessory unit, duplex or triplex that is not a four-or-more-unit property, a mobile home space, or employer-provided housing - the for-cause rules do not apply at all, and ending a fixed term early then depends entirely on what your lease says. Reserving that right in the lease is lawful for those exempt tenancies, and a silent lease gives you nothing; this library does not currently offer the clause, because the same words would be void for a covered tenancy, so if you want it, have a lawyer draft it for your particular property. Whichever route you use, the eviction itself still has to go through the court.

title: You Must Hand Every Tenant the Parking Rules in Writing
bodyText:
Colorado changed this in 2025 and most landlords have not caught up. If you have tenants, you must issue each tenant a written document containing the applicable parking regulations, and you must do it before you adopt or change those regulations, or before the person agrees to become a tenant. A rule buried in the middle of the lease is not what the statute asks for: it asks for a written document containing the parking regulations, handed to the tenant before they commit. The cautious course is a separate parking-rules sheet or addendum, delivered before signing, with the tenant signing a copy to acknowledge receipt, and a fresh sheet delivered before any change takes effect. Keep the signed copies - they are your only proof.

The duty sits inside Colorado's rules on booting, so it bites hardest if a vehicle on your property is ever immobilized. A vehicle immobilization company may not boot a vehicle on private property normally used for parking unless the parking regulations, and a warning that a vehicle parked in breach of them may be immobilized at the owner's expense, were given to the driver on entering and parking - and for a property with tenants, the way you give that notice is the written document to each tenant.
