From January 1, 2026 you must also have posted signs that meet nine specific requirements, including a minimum size of two square feet, lettering at least an inch high, the name and phone number of the boot company, text in English and Spanish, and placement at every entrance and inside the parking area.

Other limits worth knowing:
- The company cannot boot without documented, non-automated permission for that individual vehicle given in the previous twenty-four hours, and it cannot take that permission from you if you would earn income from the booting.
- It cannot patrol your property looking for violations.
- It must normally give twenty-four hours' written notice on the windshield first, though not for a repeat offender, a fire lane, a disabled space, a blocked driveway, a resident's own assigned or rented space, or a residents-only lot - but visitor spaces do need the notice.
- It cannot boot because a plate check shows expired registration unless a peace officer ordered it.
- It cannot boot a resident's inoperable car parked in that resident's own space or driveway.

A breach by the company is a deceptive trade practice the Attorney General or a district attorney can act on.

Charging the tenant for parking is a separate question governed by Colorado's fee rules, and towing is governed by its own statute, not this one.

Your city or county may add requirements, so check local rules.

title: Entry for Routine Services Is Yours to Set - With Two Exceptions
bodyText:
Colorado has no general statute telling a landlord how much notice to give before entering a rented home, and no rule that lets you in without notice for regularly scheduled services such as filter changes, smoke-alarm checks, lawn work or routine pest treatment. That means routine-service entry is whatever your lease says it is, so a lease that says nothing leaves you arguing about it. Set it out: the services, how often, the hours, how much notice and how you will give it.

Two statutory limits bound what you write.

- If the visit is in reality work to fix a condition that makes the home uninhabitable, part 5 takes over: you must give written notice at least twenty-four hours before entering, state the date, time and how long you expect to be there, and the tenant may reasonably refuse that slot and propose another, in which case the clock on your repair duty is paused. You may enter without advance notice only where the condition imminently threatens someone's life, health or safety or is actively causing substantial damage. Your lease cannot shorten any of that, because an agreement that waives or modifies a part 5 right or duty is void.
- **Bed bugs have their own rule:** Forty-eight hours of written or electronic notice before entering to inspect or treat - and this is the one place Colorado expressly lets the lease set a different minimum time, so if you want a shorter or longer period for bed-bug visits, say so in the lease. The tenant must not unreasonably deny access once notice is given, and may waive the notice.

Practical advice: give written notice even where the law does not require it, keep a log of what you sent and when, and never use a routine-service visit as cover for an inspection you would otherwise need the tenant to agree to.

A home-rule city or county may impose its own entry-notice rule, so check local requirements.

title: Who Must Warn Tenants Before Pesticides Are Applied
bodyText: Colorado has no statute that makes a landlord warn tenants generally before pest control is carried out. The notice duties sit on the licensed applicator you hire. Colorado keeps a state registry of pesticide-sensitive people who have given medical proof, and before a commercial, registered limited commercial or registered public applicator makes a structural pesticide application to a multiunit dwelling, it must take reasonable actions to give advance notice of the date and approximate time to any registered person living in that building. The same advance-notice duty applies before a turf or ornamental application where a registered person has listed the property as a residence, workplace or school, lives on an abutting property, or lives in a multiunit dwelling abutting the common area being treated - and for turf, ornamental or aquatic applications the applicator must also post warning signs at the entry points at the time of treatment. That is the applicator's job, not yours, and you cannot contract out of it. Two things are your job. Bed bugs are governed separately: you must give the tenant reasonable written or electronic notice at least forty-eight hours before anyone enters to inspect for or treat bed bugs, and the lease may set a different minimum time if you want one. And infestation is a habitability matter: appropriate extermination in response to rodents, vermin, pests or insects, throughout the property and in the common areas, is one of the characteristics the law requires, so a pest problem you do not deal with can make the home legally uninhabitable. Watch the licensing line if you do your own spraying. Applying pesticides in the course of running your rental business, on property you own or lease, makes you a limited commercial applicator. You need no business licence for that, but you must register with the Department of Agriculture if you apply restricted-use pesticides, and the owner or a designee must have been trained in the core elements of pesticide use before applying a listed general-use pesticide. Once you are a registered applicator the registry notice duties above are yours too. Local rules cut both ways here: a city or county cannot impose stricter notification requirements on commercial applicators, but it keeps the power to impose notification requirements on property owners, so check your local code. The cautious course either way is to tell every affected tenant in writing, well before treatment, what will be applied and when.

title: No Pet-and-Eviction Fact Sheet to Hand Out in Colorado
bodyText: Some states make a landlord who knows the tenant has a dog or cat give out an official state fact sheet about what happens to pets if the tenant is evicted. Colorado does not. Nothing in the state code requires you to deliver a fact sheet, brochure or pamphlet about pets and eviction, and no state agency publishes one for this purpose; the only informational document Colorado makes a landlord give a residential tenant is the radon brochure that goes with the radon disclosure. So there is nothing to hand over and nothing to acknowledge in the lease on this subject. That does not mean pets and eviction are unregulated. Colorado caps what you may take as a pet deposit and what you may charge as pet rent, treats a service or assistance animal as not a pet at all, and - unusually - does impose duties about a tenant's animals after a writ of restitution has been executed, which is the one place where pets and eviction genuinely meet in Colorado law. Those are covered by their own entries in this library. What this absence leaves to you is the lease: say clearly which animals are allowed, how many, what the tenant must do about damage, noise and waste, and that the tenant remains responsible for removing the animal and its belongings at the end of the tenancy. Keep any pet charge inside the statutory caps, and do not describe a pet charge as rent for eviction purposes unless it is the statutory pet rent. A home-rule city or county could add its own requirement, so check local rules if you want certainty.

title: No Plain-Language Test for a Colorado Lease - But Two Formatting Rules That Bite
bodyText: Colorado has no plain-language or readability law for residential leases. There is no reading-level score your lease must meet, no requirement that it be divided and captioned by section, no requirement that it be written in short sentences or everyday words, and no dollar threshold above which a different standard applies. There is also no consumer-contract statute that reaches a lease: the phrase does not appear in the Colorado code at all. The nearest consumer-protection provision requires a seller to hand the customer a written order, contract or receipt in readable, clear and unambiguous language, but it applies at the time of an installment sale of goods or services, which a residential lease is not, so do not treat it as a lease standard in either direction. One real exception: if you rent space or homes in a mobile home park, a genuine plain-language duty does apply to you, along with an obligation to provide notices in English and Spanish and, on request, in one further language and read aloud. That regime is specific to mobile home parks and does not reach ordinary site-built rentals. What does apply to every Colorado lease is formatting, not readability, and it is prescriptive. Every rental agreement must carry a statement, in at least twelve-point bold-faced type, that the tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing under the warranty of habitability and that retaliation for reporting unsafe conditions, requesting repairs or asserting that right is prohibited. Every rental agreement must also carry, in English and Spanish and in at least twelve-point bold-faced type, an address where the tenant can mail or hand-deliver written notice of an uninhabitable condition and an email address or online tenant portal for the same purpose. The lease must state the name and address of the landlord or authorized agent, and unless you are a small landlord it must carry the source-of-income non-discrimination statement. The tenant must get a signed copy within seven days. Practical advice: readable drafting is still worth doing, because an ambiguous term is read against the party that wrote it and because Colorado voids a long list of lease provisions outright, but spend your compliance effort on the statements the statute actually prescribes.

title: No Consumer-Restrictions Statement Required in a Colorado Lease
bodyText: A few states run their residential leases through a consumer-contract plain-language law: the lease has to pass a readability test, and it has to carry a statement near the front listing every term that restricts the tenant or waives a tenant right, with an optional route to have the wording preapproved by the attorney general and a dollar ceiling above which the law does not apply. Colorado has none of that. There is no consumer-contract statute in the Colorado code, no statement of consumer restrictions, no readability standard, no preapproval procedure and no dollar threshold. You do not need to list your lease's restrictive terms anywhere, and no state official reviews lease wording in advance. Two consequences worth acting on. First, the absence cuts the other way on enforceability: because Colorado will not police your drafting in advance, it polices it afterwards, and a long list of lease provisions is simply void if it appears - a penalty tied to an eviction notice or action, a one-way attorney-fee clause, a jury-trial waiver outside a possession hearing, a class-action waiver, a waiver of good faith and fair dealing or of quiet enjoyment, a waiver of mandatory mediation, a non-renewal-notice penalty beyond actual losses, calling a non-rent charge rent, a third-party billing markup beyond the statutory allowance, and any fee that breaches Colorado's fee statute. Second, the statements Colorado does require are specific and prescribed: the habitability and anti-retaliation statement in twelve-point bold-faced type, the bilingual notice-address statement, the landlord identity statement, and the source-of-income statement unless you are exempt. Those are your front-of-lease obligations, and they are the ones to get right. Nothing stops you from adding a plain-English summary of the lease for your tenants, and it is good practice, but make clear that the lease itself governs so the summary cannot be read as varying it.

title: No Right of Political Access to Your Property - But Watch Tenant Organizing
bodyText: Colorado gives no one a statutory right to come onto your rental property to campaign. No provision of the state code lets a candidate, a campaign worker, a petition circulator, a political organization or a canvasser enter a building, knock on tenants' doors or use a common area, and there is no state rule requiring you to allow political literature to be distributed or political signs to be displayed. So access by outsiders for political purposes is yours to control through your house rules, and a trespass rule that applies even-handedly to all non-residents is lawful. Three qualifications matter. First, your tenant's own activity is different and is protected: Colorado forbids retaliation against a tenant for organizing or becoming a member of a tenants' association or similar organization, and the statutory meaning of organizing is wide - any lawful concerted activity by a tenant or a tenant's guest or invitee for mutual aid, or for establishing, supporting or operating a tenants' association, or for exercising any other right the law gives. Prohibited retaliation includes raising rent, cutting services, terminating or refusing to renew, bringing or threatening a possession action, intimidating or harassing the tenant, and charging the tenant any fee, cost or penalty - and the damages are at least three months' rent or three times actual damages, plus fees. A house rule that bans tenants from meeting, leafleting their neighbours or inviting a tenant-organiser in is therefore dangerous, and a rule aimed at outsiders should be written so it plainly does not catch the tenants themselves or their invited guests. Second, if the property is in a homeowners or condominium association, the association cannot prohibit the display of a sign by the owner or occupant of a unit inside the unit boundaries or in a window, and cannot regulate window or yard signs by subject matter or content, though it may make content-neutral rules on number, placement and size and may ban commercial messages. That provision binds the association, not you as landlord, so your lease may still restrict signs - but if you are also bound by association rules, do not assume a sign ban is enforceable there. Third, mobile home parks have their own assembly rules and their own anti-retaliation provision, which this entry does not cover. Federal and constitutional free-speech law is not addressed here, and a home-rule city or county could add a local rule, so check local requirements before enforcing a blanket ban.

title: Pools: the State Rules Stop at the Property Line of a Resident-Only Pool
bodyText: Colorado has a swimming-area statute, and the first thing to know is that it probably does not apply to you. It expressly does not apply to a swimming pool constructed in connection with or appurtenant to a single-family dwelling, a condominium or an apartment house where the pool is used solely by the people living there and their guests. So a pool at your rental property, open only to your residents and their guests, is outside the state part altogether: there is no state-imposed fence or barrier requirement, no lifeguard requirement, no requirement to post safety rules, no requirement to give the tenant a pool-safety notice at signing, and nothing to submit to the state health department. If your pool is open to anyone else - sold as a membership, let to the public, or shared with a facility that charges for use - the state part does apply, and then you are in a different world: plans for construction, extension, enlargement, remodeling or modification must go to the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment for review, the water must be kept clean and continuously filtered and disinfected and clear enough to see the bottom, and the pool must carry at least one twelve-foot reaching pole and at least one fifteen-inch life ring with seventy-five feet of line, kept conspicuously available, with full illumination whenever night swimming is allowed. The department also has rule-making power over swimming areas, so check the current health-department rules rather than relying on the statute alone. Do not read the absence of a state rule as an absence of risk. Cities, towns and cities and counties may regulate swimming areas by ordinance and may be stricter than the state, and in practice the local building code is where pool fencing, gate latches and barrier heights live - so check your local code before you build, alter or fence a pool. The pool is a common area, which means keeping it clean, sanitary and free of debris is part of your habitability duty, and a code violation that materially interferes with life, health or safety is itself a habitability breach. Two money points: you cannot charge a tenant a fee for the maintenance of common areas, so do not bill pool upkeep as a separate charge, and a charge for pool access is at best doubtful for the same reason - build it into the rent. Finally, nothing stops you from making house rules for the pool, requiring adult supervision of children, banning glass and setting hours; that is the sensible route, and it is the one Colorado leaves to you.

title: You Cannot Stop a Tenant Cooling the Unit - Four Narrow Exceptions
bodyText:
Since May 2024 a Colorado landlord may not prohibit or restrict a tenant from installing or using a portable cooling device, and that bar applies to the lease as well as to anything else you agree with the tenant. A portable cooling device means an air conditioner or evaporative cooler, including one mounted in a window or designed to sit on the floor; it does not include a permanent cooling device whose installation requires permanent alteration of the unit, so a through-wall or split system is a different question.

There are only four grounds on which you may restrict installation or use:
- The installation or use would violate a building code or state or federal law.
- It would violate the manufacturer's written safety guidelines for installing or using the device.
- It would damage the premises or make them uninhabitable.
- It would need more amperage than the building, the unit or the circuit can carry.

Nothing else counts - not appearance, not the look of a window unit from the street, not a general no-alterations rule.

If you do restrict on one of those grounds, three duties follow.

- You must disclose the restriction in writing to the tenant or prospective tenant.
- You must tell them whether you intend to operate one or more cooled common spaces at the property that will be available to tenants during an extreme heat event.
- If you do not intend to operate such a space, you must give information about community cooling spaces near the property that the tenant can use during an extreme heat event - public spaces such as recreation centers, community centers and public libraries that stay at or below eighty degrees Fahrenheit - unless there are none known within ten miles.

Where you restrict on the amperage ground at a property with multiple units, you must prioritize a tenant who asks in order to accommodate a disability over other tenants' requests, and none of this cuts down your separate duty to allow reasonable modifications and accommodations for a person with a disability.

Two consequences to keep in view.

- Failing to comply with the cooling-device rules is itself one of the characteristics whose absence makes a residential premises uninhabitable, which puts it inside the warranty of habitability with its twenty-four and seventy-two hour response clocks and its remedies.
- If you supply a cooling device yourself, it becomes an appliance you must keep in good working order.

Put the disclosure in the lease if you restrict, keep the written manufacturer guidance or the electrical assessment you relied on, and record any disability-related prioritisation you make.

title: Tenant Solar: Your Consent Governs Now, Reasonable Restrictions From 2027
bodyText:
This answer changes on January 1, 2027, and you need both halves of it.

Today, a tenant has no statutory right to install solar on your property. Colorado voids a covenant, restriction or condition in a deed, contract, security instrument or other instrument affecting the transfer or sale of, or any interest in, real property that effectively prohibits or restricts installing or using a renewable energy generation device - a solar energy device, a qualifying wind-electric generator, a geothermal energy device or a heat pump system - but the same statute, and the parallel energy-efficiency-measure statute, both say they confer no right to place such a device on property that is owned by another person or that is leased, except with the permission of the lessor. So until 2027 your written consent is the whole of it, and a clause requiring your prior written consent before a tenant attaches anything to the building holds.

From January 1, 2027 that changes for one specific class of device. A portable-scale solar generation device means a single photovoltaic system per address, plus associated equipment, designed or commissioned to supply no more than 1,920 watts to the grid and labeled and listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory - the balcony or patio plug-in panel. From that date no person may directly or indirectly unreasonably prohibit the installation, use or operation of such a device, and a covenant or restriction that explicitly or indirectly unreasonably prohibits or restricts one is unenforceable and void as a matter of public policy. A lease term is a covenant or restriction, so plan on your blanket solar ban being unenforceable against a plug-in device from 2027, even though the older statutes still say a tenant needs your permission; that tension has not been resolved by any court, and the cautious course is to stop relying on a flat ban and switch to conditions.

The statute expressly leaves you those conditions: a real property owner may require reasonable restrictions on the installation, use or operation of a device, including requiring prior notice of installation and restrictions aimed at preventing fire or electrical overload of the existing electrical system, preventing damage or harm to people or property, and controlling where the device goes.

Other limits that help you:
- The device must include a feature preventing it from energizing the grid during an outage.
- A tenant must not connect more than one device to a single wall outlet per address.
- Installation must comply with fire code requirements and applicable local building codes pertaining to health and safety.
- From 2027 a device of more than 391 watts cannot lawfully be sold, leased or rented in Colorado unless it is UL labeled and listed.

A device of 391 watts or less is exempt from the state photovoltaic installation requirements and from building safety or product listing provisions that would require altering the building's wiring, so do not demand an electrician's permit for one of those. Note also that the utility cannot make the tenant get its approval or pay it a fee for the device, so do not tell a tenant to clear it with the utility first.

Anything larger or permanently attached - roof mounts, facade mounts, anything needing wiring work - is outside the 2027 rule and still needs your consent.

Put your conditions in the lease now, get the notice requirement in writing, and take advice before agreeing to a permanent installation. Local rules may also apply.

title: Which Colorado Duties Depend on How Many Units You Own
bodyText: Several Colorado landlord duties turn on the size of your portfolio or the type of your property, and the tests are not interchangeable. Read the recurring small-landlord test carefully, because it has two limbs and both must be satisfied: you must own five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five total rental units including those single-family homes. A landlord with four single-family houses and a four-unit apartment building fails the second limb and is not a small landlord for these purposes, even though the first limb is met. That test switches three things. The lease need not carry the source-of-income non-discrimination statement, although the underlying duty not to discriminate is a separate question and the exemption does not simply switch it off. You are not required to accept federal housing choice vouchers for those single-family homes - and note that a different and smaller threshold sits alongside it: the source-of-income prohibitions on refusing to rent, discriminating in the terms of a tenancy, advertising a limitation, misrepresenting availability and blockbusting do not apply at all to a landlord with three or fewer units of housing for rent or lease, so three-or-fewer and five-or-fewer do different work and you need to know which one you are relying on. And you are not required to go through mandatory mediation before filing an eviction against a tenant who receives supplemental security income, social security disability insurance or Colorado works cash assistance. A fourth, narrower test applies to the shortened notice periods: a lease of a single-family home by a landlord who owns five or fewer single-family rental homes is an exempt residential agreement, which carries five-day rather than ten-day notice periods, but only if the lease itself gives notice that the ten-day period does not apply. Note the difference - that one has no second limb about total units, and it does nothing unless your lease says so. Then come the property-type thresholds, which depend on the building rather than the portfolio. If you live at the property, an owner-occupied single-family home with or without an accessory dwelling unit, a duplex or a triplex is outside Colorado's for-cause eviction rules, provided it is not a multifamily property of four or more units; the same kinds of owner-occupied properties are also exempt from several of the prohibited-lease-clause rules, which means you may lawfully include terms other landlords may not. Fair housing design-and-construction duties attach to covered multifamily dwellings, meaning buildings of four or more units with an elevator and the ground-floor units of other buildings of four or more units. Boilers in apartment houses of fewer than six family units are exempt from the state boiler inspection article. And state energy benchmarking reaches only larger commercial and multifamily buildings, not single-family homes, duplexes or triplexes. Practical advice: write down which tests you pass, keep the count current as you buy and sell, and re-check every time your portfolio changes, because the duty switches on the day you cross the line, not at renewal. A city or county may set its own thresholds for licensing or registration, so check local rules too.

title: No Possession Bond or Confessed Judgment in Colorado
bodyText: A few states let a landlord post a bond and obtain possession quickly, or let the lease include a confession of judgment so that the tenant agrees in advance that judgment may be entered for possession at the end of the term. Colorado has neither. The phrase does not appear in the state code, no statute authorises a bond that shortens or substitutes for the ordinary process, and no statute lets a lease pre-authorise a judgment against the tenant. Getting possession from a tenant who will not leave means going to court, and nothing you put in the lease changes that: Colorado makes self-help removal unlawful with severe statutory penalties, so you cannot change the locks, remove doors or windows, cut off utilities or put the tenant's possessions out. There is one express statutory bar close to this subject, and it applies only to mobile home parks: a park rental agreement must not authorise a third person to confess judgment on a claim arising from the agreement or from the mobile home park statutes, and such a provision is against public policy, unenforceable and void. For ordinary site-built rentals the code contains no comparable prohibition, which is not a licence to use one - a confessed-judgment clause in a residential lease has no statutory footing in Colorado, would be read against you as the drafter, and would sit badly beside the rules that void a long list of lease terms and that allow a jury-trial waiver only for a hearing to determine possession. Treat the clause as unavailable rather than merely untested. What is worth having in the lease instead is the ordinary machinery: a clear statement of the term and the surrender date, the holdover consequences the law does allow, a notice provision, and an attorney-fee clause that runs to the prevailing party, which is the only form Colorado permits. Bonds do exist in Colorado eviction practice, but they are court-stage devices - a bond on appeal, for example - and they belong to the court process rather than to the lease. A home-rule city or county could add local requirements, so check local rules.

title: No Duty to Test a Private Well or Share Results With Tenants
bodyText: If the rental home draws its water from a private well, Colorado imposes no statutory duty on you to test the water, to test it at any interval, to use a certified laboratory, or to give a tenant the results, a summary or a warning. The state minimum general sanitary standards for water and the department's powers over them apply to public water systems, which means a system with at least fifteen service connections or one that regularly serves at least twenty-five people - a single rental house, or a handful of them, on a private well is not that. The one potable-water disclosure Colorado does prescribe runs the other way: a seller of residential real property must disclose on the listing contract, the contract of sale or the seller's property disclosure whether the source is a well, a water provider or something else, and must include a copy of the current well permit if one is available. That duty is owed to a buyer, not to a tenant, so it does not transfer to your lease. Do not read the silence as a licence. Water that is not safe or not running is squarely a habitability problem: running water at all times, and hot water in the amount the tenant needs for cleanliness and health, furnished to the proper fixtures and connected to an approved sewage disposal system, is one of the characteristics the law requires, and compliance with applicable health codes is another. An unsafe well is also exactly the sort of condition that materially interferes with life, health and safety, which triggers the twenty-four-hour response clock rather than the seventy-two-hour one. The sensible course, which costs little: test the well before the tenancy and then annually for coliform bacteria and nitrate, keep the laboratory reports, give the tenant a copy with the lease and after each later test, tell the tenant in writing not to tamper with the wellhead or the treatment equipment, and fix a problem promptly and at your own expense - you cannot charge a tenant a fee for something you are obliged to do anyway. If you supply treatment equipment, it becomes equipment you must keep in working order. Note two things outside the lease: the well itself is permitted under Colorado water law, which is a separate regime, and the state has a lead-testing programme for schools and child care centers whose duty falls on the facility rather than on the building owner. A home-rule city or county, or a county health department, may require testing on a sale, a transfer or a new well, so check local rules.

title: What Colorado Law Already Forbids Your Tenant to Do
bodyText:
Colorado writes the tenant's basic duties into statute, so they apply whether or not your lease repeats them - though repeating them is still worth doing, because it makes the duty something the tenant has signed and gives you a lease violation to point to.

Every tenant has a duty to use the part of the premises within their control in a reasonably clean and safe manner, and the statute says a tenant fails that duty by substantially failing to do any of six things:
- Comply with the obligations building, health and housing codes impose on tenants where those materially affect health and safety.
- Keep the dwelling unit reasonably clean, safe and sanitary so far as the condition of the unit allows.
- Dispose of ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste in a clean, safe, sanitary and lawful way.
- Use the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, elevator and other facilities and appliances reasonably.
- Behave, and require the people in the premises under their control to behave, so as not to disturb the neighbours' peaceful enjoyment of their own homes.
- Promptly tell you if the home is uninhabitable or if a condition could make it so if it is not fixed.

Separately, a tenant must not knowingly, intentionally, deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly let anyone under their control do so - note that negligence is enough, which is broader than most lease wording.

Three practical points.

- The duty to tell you about problems promptly is the tenant's duty that most helps you, so make the reporting route obvious in the lease and remind tenants of it.
- Unreasonably refusing you entry to carry out repair work gives you a defence if the tenant later complains about the delay, and for bed bugs the statute expressly says the tenant must not unreasonably deny access once you have given notice - but the tenant may reasonably refuse a particular time and propose another, so keep records of what you offered.
- **There are two things this statute cannot do for you:** It cannot be used to push a habitability duty onto the tenant, because nothing in it authorises modifying your obligations, and it cannot be enforced against a tenant who is a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, stalking or unlawful sexual behavior where the conduct complained of was caused by or contributed to by the abuse - and you may never penalise or take adverse action against a tenant for calling the police or emergency services in such a situation, whatever your house rules say.

title: No Written-Promise Rule - So Put Pre-Move-In Repairs in the Lease Yourself
bodyText: Some states make a landlord reduce every promise to clean, repair or improve the unit to writing, with a completion date, and deliver it before the lease is signed. Colorado has no such rule. Nothing in the state code requires a pre-lease promise to be written, dated or delivered in advance, and no state form exists for it. That cuts both ways, and the exposure is yours. An oral promise made while showing a unit is still a promise, and your tenant will say you made it; with nothing in writing it becomes one person's word against another's. Meanwhile, three Colorado rules mean the promise often does not matter, because the duty exists anyway. Before you let the property you must ensure it is fit for human habitation and not in any of the uninhabitable conditions the statute lists; leasing a unit that is uninhabitable at the inception of occupancy is itself a breach of the warranty of habitability; and nothing in a lease can waive or modify those duties. So a promise to fix a broken heater or an infestation adds nothing to what you already owe, and failing to do it exposes you to the habitability remedies, not just to a contract claim. What is worth doing. Write down the work you have agreed to do, exactly what it covers and the date it will be finished, and attach it to the lease or make it a numbered section - the library's existing condition and entire agreement clauses are where that belongs. Keep the entire agreement clause, because it is your main protection against a tenant relying on something said at a showing, and never let your staff promise work you have not written down. If the agreement runs the other way - the tenant is to do specified repairs or maintenance - Colorado has one narrow route and strict conditions: only for a single-family residence for which you receive no governmental subsidy, only in a writing separate from the lease, signed by both and supported by adequate consideration, only where the tenant actually has the requisite skills, and never where the work would endanger the tenant's health or safety. Anything looser will not hold. Finally, be careful what you say rather than write: a false representation about the characteristics or uses of the property can be a deceptive trade practice under Colorado consumer law, which carries its own remedies, and that risk does not depend on the promise being in the lease.

title: Colorado Requires No Chemical-Exposure Warning in a Rental
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warning does not apply in Colorado, and no Colorado statute requires you to post or give a tenant a warning that the building or anything in it contains chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. You do not need a chemical warning sign, a lease warning paragraph or a warning in your advertising. Colorado instead regulates particular hazards, and those are the ones to get right: radon must be disclosed to a residential tenant in a separate written document, and federal law requires the lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978. Methamphetamine contamination has a Colorado disclosure rule, but it runs to a buyer of the property rather than to a tenant, so it does not give you a lease duty. If you actually know of a chemical or contamination problem in the unit, say so in writing before the tenant signs and fix it: a known hazard can make the unit uninhabitable whatever the disclosure rules say, and silence about a defect you know of can be argued as a deceptive trade practice. A city or county may require more, so check local rules.

title: Property Tax and Your Colorado Rental
bodyText: Colorado does not make you tell a tenant how much of the rent goes to property tax. There is no annual statement, no statement on a rent change, and nothing the lease has to carry. Colorado's rule runs the other way: from January 1, 2026 you may not require a tenant to pay any fee, charge or amount related to the payment of property taxes. So do not add a "property tax", "tax recovery" or "tax pass-through" line to the rent or to a charges schedule. If your taxes go up and you want more rent, raise the rent itself at the next lawful increase, within the rent-increase rules, rather than billing the tax as a separate item. Two property-tax points that do affect you. First, if you advertise a furnished home for rent, the county assessor may ask you (not more than twice a year) for a list of the addresses you advertise, and you must provide it; an agent who advertises for you must give the assessor a list by owner and address. Second, furniture and other personal property you supply in a rental is generally taxable personal property once the home is rented furnished, where the same items in your own home would be exempt, so expect a personal property schedule from the assessor and list the items on it. A city or county may add its own requirements, so check local rules.

title: Colorado Bans the Question, Not Just the Decision
bodyText: In Colorado it is an unfair housing practice to make, or cause to be made, any written or oral inquiry about an applicant's disability, race, creed, color, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, familial status, veteran or military status, religion, national origin or ancestry - and to keep a record of it. That is a separate wrong from refusing to rent, so you can break this rule even if you rent to the person. Go through your application form, your online listing questions, your screening script and your notes and take out anything that asks about or records those traits, including questions about where someone is from, their accent or first language, their church, whether they are married or have children, pregnancy, or the nature or severity of a disability. Do not keep a file note recording any of it either. Four things you may still do. You may ask about military or veteran status when the point is to work out whether the person qualifies for veteran or military housing or a veteran or military benefit. You may run a credit check, provided you run one on every prospective tenant. You may ask a residential tenant whether they receive supplemental security income, social security disability insurance or Colorado Works cash assistance, because you need that answer for the mandatory-mediation rule. And from August 12, 2026 you do not discriminate merely by asking for reasonable documentation supporting a claimed disability or disability-related need for an assistance animal, or by running a good-faith interactive process, unless the disability or the need is obvious. Ask every applicant the same neutral questions - who will live in the home, income, rental history, references - and write your reasons down in those terms. Separately, never ask about immigration or citizenship status. A city or county may add requirements, so check local rules, and take advice before relying on any exemption.

title: Unlawful Use of the Property Does Not Void a Colorado Lease
bodyText:
No Colorado statute makes a lease void, or ends it automatically, because the tenant uses the home for an unlawful purpose such as drug dealing, gambling or prostitution. The lease stays in force until you end it, so your right to act comes from the lease terms and from the eviction statutes, not from any automatic forfeiture.

What Colorado does instead is turn the property itself into a class 1 public nuisance when it is used for prostitution or human trafficking, as gambling premises, for making, growing, selling or storing a controlled substance, for theft, for drug paraphernalia, for child sexual exploitation, or in the commission of any felony. That exposes the building and its contents to a district attorney's abatement action, closure and a lien for costs, and the owner carries that risk even though the tenant is the wrongdoer, which is why acting promptly matters. The statute itself assumes you will evict: the owner need not be made a party to the nuisance action until the tenant or occupant is evicted.

Your tenant is also already bound without a clause - Colorado makes it an implied term of every lease that the tenant will not commit a substantial violation while in possession.

Three things not to do.

- Do not change the locks, cut utilities or put the tenant out yourself; the only exception Colorado allows for removal without court process is a removal consistent with the state cleanup rules for an illegal drug laboratory, and getting that wrong costs you the tenant's actual damages plus the greater of three months' rent or five thousand dollars.
- Do not write a clause penalising the tenant for calling the police or emergency services, which Colorado voids.
- If the tenancy has run twelve months or more and the property is not exempt, remember that cause for eviction is only what the statute lists, so a lease cannot invent a new ground.

Take advice before acting on suspected criminal use, and report it to law enforcement.

title: No Recycling Notice Duty in Colorado - But You Must Supply Trash Receptacles
bodyText: Colorado does not require you to tell tenants where or how to recycle, to hand out a recycling notice, or to provide recycling containers or collection at a rental. What Colorado does require is trash capacity: a home is treated as uninhabitable if it substantially lacks an adequate number of appropriate exterior receptacles for garbage, waste and rubbish, in good repair and on a service schedule frequent enough to contain and properly dispose of it all. That is a habitability characteristic, so it is your duty, it cannot be waived or shifted to the tenant by the lease, and you cannot charge a separate fee for meeting it. Common areas you control must also be kept reasonably clean and free of accumulated debris, filth, rubbish and garbage. The tenant's side is already covered by statute: every tenant has a duty to dispose of ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste from the unit in a clean, safe, sanitary and legally compliant manner. What to do: say in the lease who arranges and pays for waste collection, where the bins are, and when they are serviced; make sure the number of bins and the pickup frequency actually match the number of units; and, if recycling is available, tell tenants about it as a courtesy rather than as a legal notice. Many Colorado cities and counties do regulate residential recycling and waste collection, including at apartment buildings, so check your local rules - that is where any recycling obligation will come from.

title: No Tenant Display Right in Colorado - Keep Any Display Rule Content-Neutral
bodyText: Colorado gives a tenant no statutory right to display religious or cultural items at a rental - no doorpost item right, no altar or shrine right, no flag or holiday decoration right - and it places no limit on a landlord's display rules. The one Colorado rule of that kind is aimed at homeowner and condominium associations, not at you: an association may not prohibit the display of a religious item or symbol on the entry door or entry door frame of a unit, unless the item threatens public health or safety, stops the door opening or closing, breaks a law or ordinance, is obscene or illegal, or covers more than thirty-six square inches in total. If your rental sits in a common interest community, the association cannot ban your tenant's door item on those terms, and the association must give notice if the item has to come down while it works on the door. That rule does not bind you, so your display rules come from the lease. Two limits that do bind you. Religion, creed, national origin and ancestry are protected classes in Colorado, and discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a tenancy on those grounds is an unfair housing practice - so a rule that allows some displays but not those of a particular faith or culture, or that is enforced that way, is a real risk, and so is any advertisement that signals it. And you cannot charge the tenant for repairs or cleaning due to normal wear and tear: small nail or adhesive marks from a door or wall item are likely to be normal wear and tear, so do not write a fixed charge for them into the lease. A content-neutral rule is lawful if you want one: write it about size, placement, fire safety, blocking exits and damage to doors and walls, keep it off the subject matter of the display, apply it to every tenant the same way, and consider allowing a small door or door-frame item that causes no damage. Take advice before refusing a display request, and check local rules.

title: Rent Concessions in Colorado - Write Them as a Credit, Never as a Clawback
bodyText:
No Colorado statute regulates rent concessions, so a free month, a move-in credit or a period of reduced rent is whatever the lease says it is. Write it down in the lease using the Rent Concession clause, with the amount and the exact rental periods it covers, so there is no later argument about what the rent really is.

Three Colorado rules shape how you word it.

- Put the full Monthly Rent in the lease and describe the concession as a credit against named months, rather than writing a low rent that later goes up. Colorado lets you raise rent only once in any twelve-month period of a tenant's continuous occupancy, whatever kind of tenancy it is, and in an agreement of a year or less it bars any fee, charge or amount that rises by more than two percent during the term. Whether a concession simply expiring counts as a rent increase or a rising amount is not settled by the statutes, so the safe drafting is the credit form: the rent never changes, the credit just runs out.
- **Do not write a clawback.** If a tenant dies and the lease ends early, a clause making anyone repay or refund a concession or move-in discount is void, along with any other early-termination fee, damages or penalty; and if a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, stalking or unlawful sexual behaviour ends the lease with the required documentation, the most you can ever recover is one month's rent, only if you have documented your actual economic loss on time. A clawback clause that cuts across those is unenforceable and makes your lease look punitive.
- **Advertise honestly:** Colorado now requires the total price to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously as a single number, more prominently than any other pricing information, so a headline "net effective rent" that only works because of a concession is a real exposure. Say the actual monthly rent, then describe the concession.

If you want the concession to depend on the tenant staying, take advice before drafting it; a forfeiture written as liquidated damages is the kind of term Colorado voids.

title: Rent Control Is Banned in Colorado - But Three Other Limits Apply
bodyText: Colorado has no rent control and no rent stabilization, and no Colorado city or county may enact one: the legislature has declared rent control on private residential housing a matter of statewide concern and barred any county or municipal ordinance or resolution that would control rent on private residential property or a private residential housing unit. Two things are not rent control for that purpose - a voluntary agreement between the local government and a permit applicant or owner to limit rent or provide affordable housing, and a deed restriction limiting rent placed on the title under such a voluntary agreement. A local government cannot refuse your development permit just because you decline to enter one of those agreements. That still leaves three real limits on what you can charge. First, you may raise the rent only once in any twelve-month period of a tenant's continuous occupancy, whatever kind of tenancy it is, and notice rules apply. Second, during a declared disaster that specifically declares a material decrease in residential housing units, charging more than the greater of last year's increase percentage or ten percent above the pre-disaster rent for that home is rental price gouging - an unfair and unconscionable practice the attorney general, a district attorney or the tenant can act on, with the tenant's actual damages, fees and costs. The disaster period runs for a year from the initial disaster. Third, a subsidised tenancy follows its programme's rent rules. Note the direction of travel on local power: the rent-control ban does not stop a city or county licensing, registering, inspecting or taxing rental businesses, and since 2025 a municipality or county may bring its own civil action to enforce most of Colorado's landlord-tenant statutes, including the habitability, prohibited-lease-clause and bed-bug parts. So check local rules; they can add duties even though they cannot cap your rent.

title: Colorado Does Not Ban Demanding Rent for a Bad Unit - It Makes the Rent Worth Nothing
bodyText: Colorado has no rule forbidding you to ask for or collect rent while a home is substandard or has been cited, and no rule making a code violation an automatic defence. What Colorado does is worse for you if the condition is serious. A breach of the warranty of habitability is an affirmative defence both to your action for possession and to your action to collect rent, and the tenant does not have to post a bond, spend any money first, or use any other remedy to raise it. The tenant only has to show the breach happened within sixty days before, or at any time during, the period you say the rent is owed, or that it started earlier and continued into that period; and the condition need not still exist at trial. If the tenant proves it, the court denies you possession, orders the repair, and reduces the fair rental value - which is rebuttably presumed to be zero for any period a condition materially interfered with the tenant's life, health or safety, and fifty percent of the lease rent for any period it did not. You can also be ordered to repay the difference between that reduced value and the rent the tenant actually paid, plus the tenant's damages, costs and attorney fees. And if a court orders injunctive relief or specific performance and the tenant moves out, you may not rent the home again until it complies with the warranty of habitability. So the practical rule is: do not rely on being allowed to demand the rent. Fix the condition, document what you did and when, keep the records the habitability rules require, and reduce the rent in writing for any period the home was not fit. Never put a clause in the lease that waives or modifies any of these habitability rights, or that charges the tenant a cost, fee or penalty for using them - that is void. A city or county may have its own rules about renting a cited unit, so check locally.

title: Raising Rent During the Term in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado does not forbid a written lease from scheduling a rent change during a fixed term, and the sixty-day notice rule applies only where there is no written agreement at all. But one limit is absolute: you may not increase rent more than once in any twelve-month period of a tenant's consecutive occupancy, and that applies whether or not there is a written agreement, however long the tenancy, and whether it is a fixed term, month to month or indefinite. So a schedule can raise the rent at most once a year, and a lease that steps the rent up twice in a year is unenforceable as to the second step no matter what the tenant signed. Three further cautions. In an agreement of one year or less, no fee, charge or amount you require may rise by more than two percent over the course of the agreement, except utility costs - so keep stepped charges out of a short lease. Colorado has no safe harbour for an increase written into the lease: increasing rent is itself on the statutory list of prohibited retaliation, the tenant only has to show that a protected complaint, a tenants' association, or using a habitability remedy was a motivating factor, and the damages are the greater of three months' rent or three times actual damages plus fees. For a tenancy the for-cause rules cover, a rent increase must also not be discriminatory, retaliatory or unconscionable to get around those rules. And during a declared disaster that specifically declares a material decrease in housing units, a raise above the greater of last year's increase percentage or ten percent is rental price gouging. One important point about this library's own Colorado lease: the Notice of Rent Increase clause promises the tenant that rent will not increase during the fixed Term. If you want a scheduled increase during the term, you cannot use that clause as written - pick one approach, say it once, and take advice before drafting a stepped or index-linked rent.

title: Splitting the Rent Into Installments in Colorado
bodyText:
Colorado says nothing at all about paying rent in installments. No statute lets you do it, stops you, or decides whether a scheduled installment counts as a partial payment, so it is purely a matter of the lease. If you want to take the monthly rent in two or more payments - say half on the first and half on the fifteenth - use the Rent Installments clause, state each amount and the day it is due, and say in the lease that payments made on that schedule are not partial payments of rent.

The one thing to get right is the late fee. In Colorado you cannot charge a late fee unless a rent payment is at least seven calendar days late; the fee cannot exceed the greater of fifty dollars or five percent of the past-due rent payment; it must be disclosed in the lease; and you cannot charge it more than once for each late payment unless the total still fits inside that cap. Splitting the month into two payments creates two payments that can each be late, so tie the late charge to the rental period, not to each installment, or you risk charging twice for one month and making the whole provision void and unenforceable.

Three more Colorado points.

- You cannot charge for processing a payment unless a payment method that costs the tenant nothing is reasonably available, so a twice-monthly schedule must not double a processing charge.
- You cannot charge anything for the overdue payment of something that is not rent, so never attach a late charge to a non-rent item in the schedule.
- Anything non-refundable you collect before the tenancy starts counts as a rental application fee and is capped accordingly, so do not turn move-in money into a pre-tenancy fee by spreading it out.

Finally, state the length of the lease separately from the payment schedule, so a twice-a-month schedule is never read as a half-month tenancy.

Paying a security deposit in installments is a separate question with its own rules.

title: Colorado Does Not Make a Tenant Pay Rent Into Court to Defend
bodyText: Colorado has no rent-escrow procedure and no rule requiring a tenant to pay rent into court, or into a court registry, before raising a defence or a counterclaim in a possession case. In particular, a tenant raising a habitability defence does not have to post a bond to assert or perfect it, does not have to have spent any money on the problem, and does not have to have used any other habitability remedy first. The lease cannot add such a requirement, because a lease provision that waives or modifies a habitability right or remedy is void. Where rent does go into court, it is after the hearing rather than before. If the tenant proves a habitability defence, the court denies you possession and makes that conditional on the tenant paying any rent still owed to you or into the court registry within thirty days after the court works out the amount. If the tenant raises the defence in a nonpayment case and loses, the court gives the tenant fourteen days to pay you or the court what is owed, and dismisses your nonpayment claim with prejudice if the tenant pays - unless the court finds the defence was brought frivolously or to delay. On appeal from a county court judgment in a nonpayment case, the tenant must deposit the rent found due when filing, or the appeal is not perfected, and must keep depositing rent as it falls due; if the tenant stops, the court must affirm your judgment with costs on your motion. Separately, if either side asks for a trial delay of more than five days, the court may require a bond from either party for damages caused by the delay. There is no mandatory counterclaim rule: the tenant's written answer must set out every defence then available, but a counterclaim is governed by the ordinary civil rules. Practically: expect conditions and a counterclaim to be raised at trial, keep your rent ledger and repair records ready, and do not rely on holding the tenant's money as leverage. Eviction court procedure doesn't belong in the lease; see your legal tracker and take advice.

title: Whoever Acts as the Landlord Owes the Habitability Duty in Colorado
bodyText: Some states have a rule saying that whoever collects the rent keeps the landlord's repair duties, whatever a lease, assignment, deed, mortgage or deed of trust says. Colorado has no such provision - and it does not need one, because of how it defines the landlord. In Colorado the landlord for habitability purposes is the owner, manager, lessor, sublessor, successor in interest, or agent of the owner of the premises. So the duty follows the role, not the paperwork: a property manager, a master tenant who sublets, an agent who collects the rent, and anyone who takes the property as successor in interest all answer as landlord. On top of that, any agreement waiving or modifying any right, remedy, obligation or prohibition in Colorado's habitability rules is void as contrary to public policy, and a lease provision that waives or modifies one, or charges the tenant a cost, fee or penalty for using one, is unlawful, void and unenforceable. So you cannot split the rent from the repair duty by contract, and you cannot buy or inherit the rent stream free of it. Practical points. If a manager or master tenant collects the rent, make the management or master-lease agreement put the repair obligations and the record-keeping squarely on whoever will actually do them - that allocation binds the two of you, but it does not reduce what the tenant can require of you. Tell the tenant in the lease exactly where to send a habitability notice, because written notice to the right address is what starts your deadlines. And if you sell or transfer the property, tell tenants about the change in your identity or agent, because the duty and the deposit travel with the premises. Assigning the rents to a lender does not move the duty either; Colorado has no assignment-of-rents statute, and a lender or receiver that takes over collection is acting as owner or agent.

title: Colorado Does Not Require Rent Receipts - Give Them Anyway
bodyText: No Colorado statute requires you to give a tenant a receipt for rent, even for rent paid in cash. There is no cash-receipt duty, no rule making a missing receipt a defence to a nonpayment case, and no rule presuming that earlier months were paid because you gave a receipt for a later month. That means the records are yours to keep and the risk of not keeping them is yours too. If a tenant says they paid and you say they did not, you will be proving a negative out of your own ledger, and for a nonpayment case you have to prove the amount owed. So the cautious practice, especially for cash: give a dated written or electronic receipt for every payment, showing who paid, the amount, the period it covers, how it was paid and the balance left, and keep a copy for at least six years, because an action for arrears of rent can be brought within six years in Colorado. Three related Colorado duties you do have. You must give the tenant a signed copy of the rental agreement within seven days. If you withhold anything from the security deposit, you must send the written statement of the exact reasons within the statutory period, and on the tenant's written request give the documentation you hold - photographs, inspection forms or reports, receipts, invoices or estimates - within fourteen days. And a late fee cannot be charged at all unless you gave written notice of it within one hundred eighty days after the rent was due, which is another reason to put every charge in writing when it arises. If you accept rent by electronic transfer or through a portal, remember that a cost-free payment method has to be reasonably available to the tenant before you charge anything for processing a payment.

title: Colorado Has No Rent-Reporting Rule - the Pilot Programme Expired
bodyText: Colorado does not require you to offer positive rent reporting, does not bar you from reporting on-time or late rent, does not require a tenant's election in the lease, and does not require you to notify the tenant before you report a rent debt to a credit bureau. Colorado did have a rent-reporting-for-credit pilot run through the Colorado Housing and Finance Authority, but that section was repealed with effect from September 1, 2024, and nothing in the 2025 or 2026 sessions revived it, so there is no state programme to join or offer. Colorado's own credit-reporting statute regulates the credit bureaus rather than the people who send them information, so your obligations as a furnisher come from federal law, not from Colorado. Cautious course: report only amounts genuinely owed and not in real dispute; tell the tenant in writing before you or a collection agency report a debt, and give an address for disputes; correct errors promptly; and if you do report rent payments, say so in the lease so the tenant knows. Do not use reporting, or the threat of it, as leverage over a tenant who has complained about conditions, asked for a repair, called for emergency assistance or exercised any other legal right - Colorado treats that kind of pressure as retaliation, and the statutory list of prohibited retaliation includes taking any action that intimidates, threatens, harasses or discriminates against a tenant, as well as charging or seeking to collect any fee, cost or penalty. Remember too that a late fee is not rent in Colorado and cannot be collected as rent, so do not report a late fee as unpaid rent.

title: Taxes on Rent in Colorado
bodyText: There is no Colorado sales tax on ordinary residential rent. The state sales tax reaches the entire amount charged for rooms or accommodations, but only where the room is in a hotel, apartment hotel, lodging house, motor hotel, guesthouse, guest ranch, trailer coach, mobile home, auto camp or trailer court or park - not an ordinary house or apartment let to a resident. On top of that, a natural person who is a permanent resident of one of those places and who has a written agreement for occupancy of at least thirty consecutive days during the calendar year or the preceding year is exempt from the state sales tax, and since January 1, 2021 that exemption also applies to a local sales or use tax that piggybacks on the state tax unless the local government expressly taxed it when it adopted or amended its ordinance. Note the practical point in that exemption: it turns on a written agreement, so put the term in writing. Short-term letting is different. Counties may levy a lodging tax on the purchase price charged for rooms or accommodations, and since July 1, 2025 the county ceiling is six percent rather than two, with the tax not applying inside a municipality that levies its own lodging tax. Local marketing districts and municipalities impose their own lodging taxes too, and many Colorado jurisdictions license and tax short-term rentals. Whether a whole-house short-term rental falls within the state's accommodation list is not settled by the statute's words, so if you let a property for stays of under thirty days, check with the Colorado Department of Revenue and your city or county before you decide you owe nothing, and register and collect if in doubt. Two things you must not do. Do not require a tenant to pay any fee, charge or amount related to the payment of property taxes. And if you do have to collect a lodging or sales tax, it must be built into the single total price you advertise, not added on afterwards, and it cannot be labelled or collected as "rent".

title: Rental Inspections in Colorado Are a Local Matter
bodyText: Colorado has no statewide rental-inspection programme, no statewide rental licence or registration, and no state certificate you have to post or renew. Nothing in Colorado law makes your rental subject to a periodic government inspection. That does not mean inspections never happen - it means they come from your city or county. Counties may adopt and enforce a building code through a county building inspector, counties and municipalities have broad police powers, and a municipality may license, regulate and tax any lawful occupation or business place, which is where local landlord licensing, rental registration and periodic inspection schemes come from. Since 2025 a municipality or county may also bring its own civil action to enforce most of Colorado's landlord-tenant statutes, so local enforcement now has real teeth. Code compliance matters to you directly: a home is treated as uninhabitable if it substantially lacks compliance with applicable building, housing and health codes where the violation would materially interfere with the tenant's life, health or safety. Colorado does not say whether your lease can authorise a housing inspector to enter, and no statute requires a tenant to let one in without the tenant's consent or a court order, so do not rely on a lease clause to deliver a government inspector into an occupied home. What to do: find out whether your city or county has a rental licence, registration or inspection programme and comply with it; keep your own inspection and repair records, which the habitability rules expect you to maintain; and where you need access yourself, use the entry terms in the lease and give the tenant proper notice. If an inspector asks for access to an occupied unit, arrange it with the tenant rather than asserting a right over them, and ask the authority to serve its own notice or get its own order if the tenant refuses.

title: No Colorado Renter's-Insurance Statute - What You May and May Not Do
bodyText:
Colorado has no statute on renter's insurance. Nothing requires a tenant to carry it, nothing requires you to tell the tenant in writing that your own policy will not cover their belongings, and nothing sets up a force-placement scheme that lets you buy a policy and bill the tenant for it. So whether the tenant must insure is purely a matter of your lease.

Three Colorado rules do bite once you write such a clause.

- You may not require the tenant to claim on their own policy for a repair cost the habitability rules make yours, and you may not file a claim against the tenant's policy at all without the tenant's express written permission given when the claim goes in - so the clause must not treat the tenant's policy as a repair fund.
- If you buy insurance yourself because the tenant did not, anything you charge the tenant is a fee and runs into Colorado's 2026 fee rules: you cannot charge more than the actual total price of what you bought, you cannot add an administrative or processing markup on top of it, and you cannot call it rent or evict for it. The safe course is to make proof of coverage a lease condition the tenant must satisfy, not a cost you advance and mark up.
- A liability-insurance requirement is expressly treated as a reasonable condition for keeping a pet in affordable housing financed by the state division of housing, which is good evidence the requirement itself is lawful, but it says nothing about charging for one.

Keep the minimum coverage figure modest and your own, set a clear deadline for proof, and give the tenant the carrier choice.

A city or county may add duties of its own, so check local rules.

title: No Right to End a Colorado Lease Because a Repair Costs Too Much
bodyText: Colorado does not let you decide a repair is not worth the money and end the tenancy instead. There is no cost threshold, no economic-feasibility test and no uneconomical-repair termination right anywhere in Colorado's landlord-tenant law, and the habitability duty is yours at your own expense for as long as the tenant lawfully occupies the unit. Three narrower reliefs do exist, and none of them turns on cost. If a sudden environmental public health event or an action by a government authority makes continued occupancy impossible or unlawful, you may terminate - but only if your lease says you may, only if you were not already in breach, only if repairing into compliance would be impracticable because of that event, and only on at least thirty days' written notice, with access for the tenant to retrieve their property, the full deposit returned by the termination date and a prorated rent refund for the uninhabitable period. If a condition you are fixing cannot be remedied within sixty consecutive days for reasons outside your reasonable control, you can stop paying for the tenant's hotel after sixty days, provided you give written notice saying so and return the full deposit, and the tenant may then end the lease with no penalty. And where a third party you do not direct or control caused the condition and you have taken reasonable, necessary and timely steps but cannot fix it, the tenant's only remedy is to terminate. Practical upshot: budget for the repair, use the thirty-day route only on the statutory facts, and never put a clause in the lease letting yourself cancel because a quote came back high - a provision that waives or modifies a part 5 right or remedy is void, and so is a clause charging the tenant a fee or penalty for exercising one.

title: No Rent Escrow in Colorado, So No Escrow Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states let a tenant pay rent into an escrow account or a court registry while repairs are outstanding, and then let a small landlord escape that remedy by putting an exemption notice in the lease. Colorado has neither half of that. A Colorado tenant's remedies for a habitability breach are the ones the statute lists: end the lease on ten to sixty days' written notice, end it if the same condition comes back within six months, hire a professional and deduct the cost from rent after giving you notice and a chance to fix it, replace a broken appliance and deduct that, sue or counterclaim for damages, seek an injunction or a restraining order, and raise the breach as a defence to an eviction. None of those involves escrow, and there is nothing for an exemption notice to switch off. Nor is there a small-landlord carve-out from the repair rules themselves: the habitability rules reach every residential tenancy however the arrangement is labelled, subject only to a fixed list of arrangements that are outside them altogether, and none of those is a size or unit-count test. So do not copy an out-of-state clause saying the property is exempt from a repair-escrow or rent-withholding statute - it buys you nothing in Colorado and a provision that waives or modifies a habitability right or remedy is void anyway. Two things are worth knowing instead. There is one narrow written-agreement route: for a single-family rental where you receive no government subsidy, you and the tenant may agree, in a signed writing separate from the lease and supported by real consideration, that the tenant will do specified repairs - but only if the tenant actually has the skills, and never where the work would endanger the tenant's health or safety. And Colorado does have one genuine exemption notice that has to appear in the lease, though it has nothing to do with repairs: a landlord who owns five or fewer single-family rental homes gets a five-day rather than ten-day notice period for unpaid rent only if the lease itself says the ten-day period does not apply. A city or county may add duties of its own, so check local rules.

title: Everything a Colorado Lease Has to Say or Hand Over
bodyText: Colorado does not prescribe a lease form, and no state form has to be the first page, but it does prescribe particular statements and documents. In the lease itself: the name and address of the landlord or the authorized agent; a statement that source-of-income discrimination is prohibited and that a non-exempt landlord must accept any lawful and verifiable source of money, which you may skip only if you have five or fewer single-family rentals and no more than five rental units in total; a statement in at least twelve-point bold-faced type that every tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing under the warranty of habitability and that retaliation for reporting unsafe conditions is prohibited; and a second statement, also twelve-point bold-faced and in both English and Spanish, giving a mailing or delivery address plus an email address or online portal where the tenant can send written notice of an uninhabitable condition. If you use a tenant portal, the same English-and-Spanish notice has to be posted conspicuously inside the portal too. If you want to charge a late fee, the lease has to disclose it; if you allocate utilities among tenants by a ratio billing system, the lease or an addendum has to disclose the allocation method clearly and conspicuously. Separately from the lease, before signing you must hand the tenant a radon document the tenant signs - the statutory warning in bold-faced type in substantially the statutory form, everything you know about the property's radon levels, and the state radon brochure - and the radon document cannot live inside the lease. You must give the tenant a copy of the signed agreement within seven days of their signature, on paper if they ask for paper. Bed-bug history must be disclosed if the tenant asks before signing. Federal law, not Colorado law, supplies the lead-based-paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing. Three traps. Nothing turns a Colorado lease into a sale just because you add a purchase option, but the radon and seller-disclosure statutes for buyers are separate from the tenant ones, so do not substitute one for the other. The source-of-income exemption is about the statement, not the duty. And a city or county may require more, so check local rules.

title: Listing Fees in a Colorado Lease, and the Ten Fees You May Never Charge
bodyText:
Colorado does not order you to put a master fee list in the lease, but from 2026 three rules make one close to essential.

- Before a tenant agrees to pay anything that is not part of the advertised total price, you have to disclose it clearly and conspicuously, including whether it is refundable, exactly what it is for, and who gets the money.
- You can only keep deposit money for an other lawful charge if that charge is actually listed in the lease, so an unlisted charge cannot come out of the deposit.

Third, ten categories of fee are flatly barred, and a lease provision imposing a barred fee is void:
- Anything above what the utility provider charged for service to the unit, except the narrow third-party allowance.
- Any fee that rises by more than two percent over a lease of a year or less, utilities excepted.
- Anything tied to property taxes.
- Anything for processing rent or other payments unless a genuinely cost-free way to pay is reasonably available to the tenant.
- Any charge for the late payment of something that is not rent.
- Anything for a good, service or property you need in order to meet your own obligations, including providing a habitable home.
- Anything above the total price of what you are charging for.
- Anything for something you do not actually provide.
- Anything for maintaining common areas.
- Anything that otherwise breaks the section.

Breaking it is a deceptive, unfair and unconscionable act: a tenant can send you a fourteen-day written demand, and if you do not pay up you are liable for actual damages plus eighteen percent a year compounded annually, with no pre-suit requirement before they simply sue.

Four more limits worth knowing.

- A late fee needs rent to be at least seven calendar days late, is capped at the greater of fifty dollars or five percent of the past-due rent, must be in the lease, may be charged only once per late payment, carries no interest, and cannot be the basis of an eviction.
- No amount other than the set monthly payment for occupancy may be called rent, so you cannot use rent remedies to collect a fee.
- Any nonrefundable fee you collect before the tenancy starts counts as a rental application fee, which is limited to your actual or average screening cost - so a nonrefundable move-in, administrative or holding fee is caught.
- Pet deposits and pet rent have their own caps.

Keep your fee list short, honest and itemised, name the recipient of each pass-through, hand over the third-party bill, and never charge for your own compliance.

title: No Colorado Tenant Rights Guide to Hand Over
bodyText: Colorado publishes no official tenant rights-and-responsibilities guide that you have to give a tenant before signing or at renewal, and there is no signed acknowledgment to collect for one.
