What Colorado does instead is put the rights statements inside the lease: a twelve-point bold-faced statement that the tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing and that retaliation for reporting unsafe conditions is prohibited, a second twelve-point bold-faced statement in English and Spanish giving the address, email or portal for notices of an uninhabitable condition, and a statement that source-of-income discrimination is prohibited. There is exactly one state-published document you must hand over: the department of public health and environment's radon brochure, which goes into the separate radon disclosure document the tenant signs before signing the lease, along with the statutory radon warning and everything you know about the property's radon levels. Mobile home parks are different - the state division produces a rights-and-responsibilities notice for posting in a park under the Mobile Home Park Act's dispute resolution programme - and this guidance does not cover them. Two practical points. Because no guide is prescribed, there is no safe-harbour document you can hand over in place of getting the in-lease statements right, so check those statements word for word and type size. And a city or county may publish and require its own tenant handbook, so check local rules before you decide you have nothing to give.

title: House Rules in Colorado - No Statute, But Five Limits and One Trap
bodyText:
Colorado has no house-rules statute for ordinary rentals. There is no list of tests a rule has to pass, no requirement that rules be reasonable or applied evenly, and no statutory power to change rules in the middle of a fixed term. That cuts both ways: your rules bind the tenant only as a matter of contract, so attach them to the lease, have the tenant sign them, and get written agreement to any mid-term change rather than announcing one.

Five limits bind the content of a rule even though nothing governs rules as such.

- A rule must not penalise a tenant, or let you take any adverse action against a tenant, for calling the police or other emergency services in a situation involving domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking, and that right cannot be waived in any agreement.
- A rule must not waive or modify any habitability right or remedy, and must not charge the tenant a fee or penalty for exercising one.
- A rule must not impose a fee that Colorado's fee rules bar, and must not charge for normal wear and tear or for anything that was already wrong when the tenancy began.
- A rule must not block a tenant from installing an electric vehicle charging system on the statutory terms, and from 2027 a rule that unreasonably prohibits or restricts a portable-scale solar generation device is void as against public policy.
- A flat ban on assistance animals is presumed discriminatory, so pet rules need an accommodation carve-out.

Now the trap. If your rules say the tenant may give you notice of an uninhabitable condition verbally, you have waived your right to receive that notice in writing - and written notice is what starts your repair clock and what you will want to prove. Keep every notice route in your rules in writing.

One more thing worth knowing: if a municipality fines you for a nuisance your tenant caused, the tenant is liable to you for your abatement costs and for the fine from the date the tenant got the municipality's notice - unless your lease or rules provide otherwise. So do not write a rule that allocates nuisance costs or municipal fines differently, or you will have given that away.

Mobile home parks have their own rules regime under the Mobile Home Park Act and this guidance does not cover them.

title: No Sanitary-Code Variance to Give a Colorado Tenant
bodyText: Some states let a landlord hold a variance from the state sanitary or housing code and then require the variance to be handed to the tenant and attached to the rental agreement. Colorado has nothing of the kind. Colorado's housing standard is the warranty of habitability, which lists the conditions that make a unit uninhabitable and gives you no route to be excused from any of them: there is no variance, waiver or hardship exemption, and an agreement waiving or modifying a habitability right or obligation is void as contrary to public policy. So you have no variance document to disclose, and you should not sign anything that purports to be one. Two Colorado variance powers do exist near this subject, and neither reaches a tenancy. The state health department may grant exemptions and variances from the minimum general sanitary standards for public water systems, which runs to the water supplier. And a local board of health may grant a variance from the on-site wastewater treatment system rules, which runs to whoever applies for it, usually the owner or installer at the time of construction - that is a construction approval, not a standing excuse from habitability, and holding one does not let you provide a unit that is uninhabitable. Practical course: if a local health or building authority has issued you any order, notice or approval about the property, keep it with your records and treat the habitability rules as applying in full anyway. A city, county or local board of health may have its own variance procedure and its own notification rules, so check local rules; this guidance looks only at state statute.

title: Colorado Has No Seasonal Tenancy - Only Two Duration Carve-Outs
bodyText: Colorado has no seasonal-tenancy category. There is no shortened notice period for a summer or ski-season let, no special deposit rule, no exemption from habitability because the term is short, and the word "seasonal" does not appear in Colorado's landlord-tenant law at all. What Colorado has instead is two carve-outs keyed to duration and use. A short-term rental property is outside the for-cause eviction rules: that means a dwelling let for less than thirty consecutive days for money and for temporary, recreational, business or transient purposes, and also a dwelling let for less than six months to the person who just sold it to you. And transient occupancy in a hotel or motel lasting less than thirty days is outside the warranty of habitability altogether. Nothing else switches off. If you let a house or apartment for a season, you still owe the full warranty of habitability, you still have to carry the prescribed lease statements, the deposit rules and the thirty-day return deadline still apply, the fee rules still apply, the prohibited lease terms still apply, and you still have to give proper notice to end the tenancy. In practice the for-cause rules were never going to reach a seasonal let anyway, because they only begin to apply once a tenant has been a tenant of the premises for at least twelve months. Two further points. The for-cause rules do include a no-fault ground for converting a premises to a short-term rental, with limits on relisting it afterwards, so a change of use is a separate question from a short term. And counties and municipalities may license, regulate and tax short-term rentals, so check local rules before you let by the week - the state carve-outs say nothing about whether your city allows the use at all.

title: Colorado Does Not Tell You Where to Keep the Deposit - But Three Rules Still Bite
bodyText: Colorado has no deposit-holding rule for an ordinary residential rental. You do not have to put the deposit in escrow or a trust account, you do not have to keep it separate from your own money, you do not have to post a bond instead, you do not have to tell the tenant which bank holds it, and there is no unit-count threshold that switches any of that on. The one Colorado trust-account duty - deposit each security deposit into a separate trust account, do not commingle it, and you may keep the interest as your fee for administering it - applies to a mobile home park, not to a house or apartment. Three rules do bind you even so. If your interest in the unit ends, whether by sale, assignment, death, appointment of a receiver or anything else, then within sixty days whoever is holding the deposit must either transfer it to your successor and notify the tenant by mail of the transfer and the transferee's name and address, or return it to the tenant; doing that relieves the holder of further liability, and the transferee then has all the rights and obligations of a landlord holding a deposit. If you send the refund and the payment comes back to you, you have to hold it for at least a year. And the refund goes by mail to the tenant's last known address, or by secured electronic transfer if the tenant consents. Practical course: even though nothing requires it, keeping deposits in a dedicated account is the cheapest way to prove you still hold the money and to meet the thirty-day return deadline, and Colorado banking law expressly allows an account whose stated purpose is holding a tenant's security deposit. Do not treat the deposit as income, and never spend it on the landlord side of the ledger before the tenancy ends.

title: No Interest Is Owed on a Colorado Security Deposit
bodyText: Colorado does not require you to pay the tenant interest on a security deposit. There is no statutory rate, no accrual date, no second-anniversary trigger, no annual payment duty, no administration fee to deduct and no bond alternative to any of that - the subject simply is not addressed for ordinary residential rentals. So you keep whatever the money earns, and nothing has to be said about interest in the lease. Two things to watch. If you do promise interest in the lease, you have made a contract and you will owe it, so do not copy an out-of-state interest clause into a Colorado lease unless you mean it. And interest cuts the other way when you get the refund wrong: if a court finds you wrongfully withheld a deposit you face treble the amount wrongfully withheld plus the tenant's costs and reasonable attorney fees, and a fee that breaks Colorado's pricing rules carries eighteen percent a year compounded annually on top of actual damages. Mobile home parks are different - a park owner must hold each deposit in a separate trust account and may keep the interest as compensation for administering it - and this guidance does not cover them.

title: What Happens to the Deposit When You Sell or Stop Owning the Property
bodyText: Colorado does deal with this, and it binds whoever is actually holding the money - you, your agent or your executor. When your interest in the dwelling unit ends, by sale, assignment, death, appointment of a receiver or any other way, the holder has a choice of exactly two things, and must do one of them within sixty days. Either transfer the deposit, or what is left of it after lawful deductions, to your successor in interest and notify the tenant by mail of the transfer and of the transferee's name and address; or return the deposit, or the remainder after lawful deductions, to the tenant. Do one of those properly and the holder is relieved of further liability. Nothing else discharges you: a closing statement crediting the buyer, or a line in the purchase contract saying the buyer assumes the deposits, does not by itself satisfy the notification duty to the tenant. On the buying side, once you receive transferred deposit funds you are deemed to have all the rights and obligations of a landlord holding a deposit, so you inherit the return deadline, the limits on what you may retain and the penalty exposure - get a written accounting of each deposit, the move-in condition records, and any documentation the seller holds before you close, because the tenant can demand that documentation from you afterwards. Note the deadline change: before 2026 the statute said a reasonable time, and from January 1, 2026 it is sixty days. Separately, if your identity or your authorized agent changes you must notify each tenant or post the change within one business day, which is a different duty with a much shorter clock. Mobile home park deposits are held in a trust account under the Mobile Home Park Act and this guidance does not cover them.

title: No Deposit-Standards Posting Rule in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado does not regulate how you arrive at a deposit figure. There is no requirement to use consistent criteria, no requirement to publish or post your deposit standards, no requirement to hand a prospective tenant a schedule before signing if you charge different tenants different amounts, and no unit-count threshold that turns any of that on. The amount is your decision, subject to one hard limit: you may not require a deposit that exceeds two months' rent under the rental agreement, and from 2027 a narrow exception lets that cap fall away for a post-closing occupancy agreement where you bought the home from the person now renting it. Contrast the application fee, which Colorado does standardise: that fee must be no more than your actual or average processing cost, must be the same amount for everyone applying for the same unit or for any unit you are offering at the same time, must come with a disclosure of anticipated expenses or an itemisation of actual ones, must come with a receipt, and cannot be charged at all if the applicant gives you a portable tenant screening report. Two cautions. Charging different deposits to different applicants is not regulated as such, but it is still exposed to fair housing law if the difference tracks a protected characteristic or a lawful source of income, so write down your reason and apply it the same way every time. And whatever you charge, label it accurately: any nonrefundable amount you collect before the tenancy starts is treated as a rental application fee and inherits that cost limit, so a nonrefundable move-in or administrative charge dressed up as a deposit is a problem. Mobile home park deposits are capped at one month's rent under the Mobile Home Park Act and this guidance does not cover them.

title: Locks Colorado Requires, and the Devices It Does Not
bodyText: Colorado's security-device duty comes from the habitability rules, and it is short: every exterior door must have a lock, every window designed to be opened must have a lock or a security device, and all of it must be maintained in good working order. Lacking working locks or security devices on exterior doors that allow entry, or on openable exterior windows, also raises a rebuttable presumption that the unit is uninhabitable, which puts you on the clock to start fixing it within seventy-two hours of notice, or twenty-four hours if the condition materially interferes with the tenant's life, health or safety. Beyond that, Colorado specifies nothing. There is no deadbolt or keyless-bolt specification, no peephole or door-viewer requirement for any construction date or unit count, no sliding-door or window-latch rule, and no duty to rekey or change locks between tenancies. You may of course rekey at turnover as a matter of practice, and the lease can make the tenant pay the cost of rekeying if keys are not returned or a replacement is needed. One statutory lock-change right does exist and it runs the other way: a tenant who gives you notice of being a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, unlawful sexual behavior or stalking with the required documentation may change the locks, including electronic locks, and take other reasonable safety precautions, and you must not prevent that, impose fees for it, take adverse action over it or retaliate; a lease term prohibiting it is void, you must take all steps reasonably necessary to make the unit safe in response to the tenant's safety concerns, and the tenant has to make all reasonable efforts to give you a key or code within fourteen days. Finally, never deal with a dispute by removing hardware: willfully removing doors, windows or locks, other than as required for repair or maintenance, is unlawful removal or exclusion of the tenant with severe penalties. Local building codes may require more, so check local rules.

title: No Work Cards for Staff in Colorado Senior Housing
bodyText: Colorado requires no work card, work permit, sheriff's registration or state clearance for people who work in housing for older persons or in any other residential rental property. The phrase does not exist in Colorado law, and there is no background-check duty imposed on you as a landlord before you put someone on site. The only Colorado licensing question for rental staff is real estate broker licensing, and it turns on who employs the person and what they do. Renting or leasing property for someone else for compensation falls inside the definition of a real estate broker, so a third-party management company and its people generally need to be licensed. But a regularly salaried employee of the owner of an apartment building or complex who acts as the on-site manager of that building or complex is exempt, and so is a regularly salaried employee of an owner of condominium units acting as on-site manager, in each case only for the customary duties of an on-site manager done for that employer. So an in-house, salaried, on-site manager needs no licence; a contractor paid a commission to lease your units is in different territory, and so is an on-site manager who starts doing work beyond the customary on-site role or works for someone other than the owner. Three practical points. Colorado does separately regulate housing for older persons as an exemption from familial-status discrimination, which is about who you may rent to, not who you may employ. If you run assisted living rather than a rental, that is a licensed health facility with its own staffing rules and this guidance does not reach it. And a city or county may license rental operators or managers, so check local rules. If you are unsure whether a role needs a broker licence, take advice before hiring.

title: Denying a Service Animal Is a Criminal Offense in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado has a separate service-animal statute that sits outside the fair housing act, and it names housing expressly, so you do not have to ask whether a rental building is a place of public accommodation. A qualified individual with a disability has the right to be accompanied by a service animal individually trained for that individual, with no extra charge for the animal, in any place of employment, housing or public accommodation, and a trainer or a person with a disability accompanied by an animal in training has the same right. That means your pet restrictions, pet deposits, pet rent, breed and weight limits and no-pets rules give way, and you may not charge anything extra for the animal. Denying it is a crime. It is unlawful to withhold, deny or deprive those rights or attempt to, to threaten to interfere with them, or to punish someone for exercising them, and doing so is a petty offense; interfering with, injuring or harming a service animal, or setting another dog on one, is a class 2 misdemeanor. On top of that the person whose rights were affected can sue you for a court order, attorney fees and costs and either actual damages plus damages for noneconomic loss or a statutory fine of five thousand dollars for each violation, and someone who wilfully or wantonly harms a service animal owes the owner treble actual damages. Two balancing points in your favour. The person who has control or custody of the animal is liable for damage the animal causes to persons, premises or facilities, including housing, and remains subject to the dangerous-dog law, so a service animal is not a licence to cause harm. And a broader category, the assistance animal, which includes emotional support animals, is handled as a reasonable accommodation under the discrimination rules rather than by this criminal provision - though a blanket ban on assistance animals is presumed discriminatory, so do not write one. Ask only for reasonable documentation, keep the request and your answer in writing, decide promptly, and never charge a fee or deposit for the animal. Federal fair housing law applies alongside all of this and is not restated here. Take advice before refusing any animal request.

title: Colorado's Animal-Misrepresentation Offenses Do Reach Housing
bodyText: Colorado has two offenses for faking an animal's status, and the one aimed at housing says so in terms. A person commits intentional misrepresentation of entitlement to an assistance animal if they intentionally misrepresent an animal in their possession as an assistance animal in order to get a right or privilege that state or federal law gives a person with a disability as a reasonable accommodation in housing, they were previously given a written or verbal warning that doing so is illegal, and they know either that the animal is not an assistance animal for them or that they do not have a disability. The second offense covers misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or a service animal in training to obtain the service-animal rights, which include housing, on the same prior-warning and knowledge elements. Three things make these far less useful to you than they sound. The prior warning is an element, not a formality, so nothing is an offense until a warning has been given - if you are going to rely on this at all, give a plain written warning early and keep a copy. The penalties are tiny: the assistance-animal offense is a civil infraction and the service-animal offense a petty offense, and both carry twenty-five dollars for a first offense, fifty to two hundred for a second and one hundred to five hundred for a third or later. And a written finding by a physician, a licensed mental health professional or a nurse that the person has a disability and a disability-related need for the animal is a complete affirmative defense to the assistance-animal offense, while the absence of such a finding proves nothing. Practical course: treat these as background, not as a tool. Do not accuse a tenant or applicant, do not demand proof beyond reasonable documentation, and do not refuse an animal because you suspect misrepresentation - denying a genuine service animal is itself a criminal offense in Colorado with far heavier consequences, and a blanket ban on assistance animals is presumed discriminatory. Federal fair housing law governs what you may ask, and is not restated here. Take advice before refusing any animal request.

title: Servicemember Tenants: Colorado Stays Evictions but Gives No Lease-Termination Right
bodyText: Colorado has its own servicemember statute, and it is narrower than people expect. It protects a tenant who is called to Colorado state military service, or to state defense force active duty, for more than thirty days by order of the governor to enforce the law, keep the peace, protect citizens or protect property. If that tenant gives you written notice within thirty days of being called up, and the unit is occupied mainly as a home by the tenant, the tenant's spouse or a dependent, then an eviction, a distress action or a requirement to deposit accrued rent cannot go forward against them while the service lasts and for thirty days afterwards. A court can also stay any civil case involving them for the same period, and must stay it on their application unless the court thinks their ability to pay the agreed rent, or to prosecute or defend, is not materially affected. A court can still let the case proceed if it finds no substantive prejudice from the service. The tenant has to put a copy of their orders and an adjutant general certificate before the court, and may be asked to recertify every thirty days. What Colorado does not give is a right to end the lease. There is no state early-termination right for a servicemember, no state notice form, no rent ceiling that triggers a stay and no deadline for deciding a servicemember's application. The tenant's termination right is federal, so treat a termination request as a federal question and do not rely on state law to refuse it. Rent still accrues during a stay; the stay delays the remedy, not the debt. Keep any call-up notice, orders and certificate with the file, and take advice before filing against a tenant you know is on state orders.

title: Veteran or Military Status Is a Protected Class in Colorado Housing
bodyText: Colorado treats veteran or military status as a protected characteristic in housing, alongside disability, race, creed, color, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, familial status, religion, national origin and ancestry. That means you must not refuse to show, rent or lease to someone, make a home unavailable, or treat them differently in the terms, conditions or privileges of the tenancy, because they are a member or veteran of the United States Armed Forces, the Armed Forces Reserve or the National Guard. The protection does not cover someone dishonorably discharged. Colorado goes one step further than most people expect: it also bans the inquiry and the record, so a written or oral question about military or veteran status, or a note of it in your file, is itself an unfair housing practice. The one exception is an inquiry whose purpose is to work out eligibility for veteran or military housing or a veteran or military housing benefit, so ask only when that is genuinely why you are asking and record why. A restrictive covenant limiting the transfer, rental or lease of housing on that basis is covered too. Keep the question off your application form and out of your showing script, train anyone who answers the phone for you, and remember a city or county may require more.

title: A Landlord on Active Military Duty Gets 45 Days Instead of 90
bodyText: If you are an individual on active military duty with the United States military forces, or the spouse of someone who is, Colorado shortens one of its longest notice periods for you. Where a landlord takes back a home for the landlord's own use and occupancy, or for a family member, the ordinary written notice of that no-fault eviction is at least ninety days before the tenant must leave. For a landlord on active military duty, or that landlord's spouse, the period is at least forty-five days. Everything else about the ground still applies: you or your family member must move in within three months after the tenant leaves, no substantially equivalent unit may be vacant and available in the same building, you must not list the home for long-term or short-term rental for at least ninety days after the vacate date, and the tenant stays in possession on the existing lease terms during the notice period. This shortened notice only matters where the for-cause rules apply at all, which is a tenancy of at least twelve months in a property the statute covers; outside those rules the ordinary termination-notice periods govern. Serve the notice properly and keep proof of your duty status with the file.

title: No Sex-Offender Disclosure Duty in Colorado - the Registry Is Public Instead
bodyText: Colorado does not make you tell an applicant or a tenant that a registered sex offender lives at, in or near the property, and it does not give you a notice form or a lease statement to use. It handles the problem the other way round, by making the registry information available to the public. A local law enforcement agency must release registration information about an adult registrant to anyone living in its jurisdiction, and may post some of it on its website; the Colorado Bureau of Investigation will give any person a list of registrants on proper identification, and posts certain offenders, including sexually violent predators, on a website linked from the state home page. Information about people who are on the registry only because of a juvenile adjudication is kept back, and you can only get it by affirming in writing that you will not publish it, will not use it for financial gain and will not use it to harass or distress anyone, and by describing your need; a false statement to get that record is a misdemeanour carrying a fine of up to a thousand dollars per violation. So the practical course is this: point applicants and tenants to the public registry rather than answering the question yourself, because a volunteered answer that turns out to be wrong or out of date is a risk you did not have to take, and the statute itself says the information is not meant to be used to punish people. Say nothing in the lease about it. If you do choose to answer, answer only from the public record and date your answer. A city or county may require more, so check local rules, and take advice before refusing or ending a tenancy on this ground.

title: Registration Offences Escape Colorado's Five-Year Screening Limit
bodyText: Colorado's one rule connecting sex-offender registration to renting is a screening permission, and it is worth knowing precisely. If you use criminal history as a criterion on an application, you must not consider an arrest record from any time, or any conviction older than five years before the date of the application. Four categories escape that five-year limit, and one of them is any offence that required the applicant to register as a sex offender. For those, you may consider the conviction record or deferred judgment however old it is. The other three are unlawful distribution, manufacture, dispensing or sale of methamphetamine, unlawful possession of materials to make methamphetamine or amphetamine, and any offence in part 1 or part 6 of article 3 of title 18, which is the homicide and sexual-assault range. This is a permission, not a requirement: nothing obliges you to screen for criminal history at all, and if you do not use criminal history as a criterion the limit never bites. Apply whatever criteria you use to every applicant the same way, keep them written down, and remember the separate rules on rental and credit history, income and portable screening reports.

title: Colorado Sets No Residency Limit on Registered Offenders - and No Duty on You
bodyText: Colorado has no state law telling a registered sex offender where they may or may not live. There is no distance rule measured from a school, park or day care, no limit on how many registrants may share a dwelling, and no offence of knowingly renting a home to one. There is also nothing requiring you to find out, to refuse, to evict or to put a statement in the lease, and no safe harbour you earn by including one. Two things do exist and are worth separating from the rest. Where an offender lives can be restricted by a court as a condition of probation, by the parole board as a condition of parole, or by a community-corrections placement, and an adult offender supervised from another state commits a felony by residing here without the interstate compact administrator's permission. Those bind the person, not you, and they can mean that a particular applicant is not free to live at your property even though you are free to rent to them. The other is screening: if you use criminal history as a criterion, Colorado lets you look at a registration offence however old it is. Because the state is silent on occupancy, what your lease says is what governs, under ordinary contract law: your occupancy clause, your guest and additional-occupant rules and your screening criteria do the work. Apply them to every applicant the same way, and do not write a registrant-specific clause, because a term aimed at a class of people invites a discrimination argument you do not need. Home-rule cities and counties in Colorado do impose residency restrictions of their own, so check local rules for the property's address before you rely on any of this.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice, and No Font or First-Page Rules Beyond Twelve-Point Bold
bodyText: Colorado asks for no special notice because a rental is a single-family home. There is no statement you must put in the lease about who may occupy a single-family residence, no occupancy presumption to disclose and no acknowledgment form. Colorado also has no rule about where in the lease a disclosure must appear, and none that measures a disclosure against the size of the surrounding text. What it does have is three absolute typographic minimums, and those you must meet. Every rental agreement must carry a statement in at least twelve-point bold-faced type that every tenant is entitled to safe and healthy housing and that retaliation for reporting unsafe conditions is prohibited, and a second statement, in English and Spanish and also in at least twelve-point bold-faced type, giving the address and the e-mail address or online portal for notice of an uninhabitable condition. The radon warning must be in bold-faced type that is clearly legible, in substantially the statutory form, and it has to sit in a separate document the tenant signs, not in the lease. If you must give the portable-screening-report advisement, that is twelve-point bold-faced type as well. One place that does ask about single-family homes is worth knowing: if you want the tenant to take on specified repairs in a single-family residence where you receive no government subsidy, that agreement has to be in writing separate from the lease, signed and supported by consideration, and only where the tenant has the skills and the work would not endanger them. Because Colorado sets no placement rule, put the required statements where a reader will actually see them; first page or immediately above the signature block is the sensible choice.

title: No Shoreline or Water-Access Disclosure in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado is landlocked and its statutes say nothing about shoreline, beach or waterfront access in a lease. There is no notice you owe a tenant about a boundary at the water's edge, about public access across the property to a lake, reservoir or stream, about who owns the bed or the bank, or about erosion or flooding at the shore. The only water-source disclosure in Colorado's property title is owed by a seller to a buyer, not by a landlord to a tenant. So if your property fronts a reservoir, a lake, a river or a ditch, what the tenant may and may not do there is governed by your lease and by general law, not by a disclosure statute. Three practical consequences. First, say in the lease whether the tenant may use any water frontage, dock, bank or beach at all, and on what terms, because silence invites an argument that use was permitted. Second, if the water is not yours to give, say so: Colorado water rights, ditch easements, and public or association access rights can run across or alongside your land, and a tenant who assumes otherwise can create a trespass or a liability problem for you. Third, if there is a natural swimming area or a pool on the property, separate safety rules apply and they are not a disclosure rule. A city or county may require more, and if the property is in a floodplain or a special district there may be other duties; check them. Take advice before promising a tenant any water access you have not confirmed you hold.

title: Shorter Notice for Showings: Colorado Has No Statutory Notice to Waive
bodyText:
Colorado does not set a general notice period before you enter a let home, so there is nothing for a tenant to waive when you want to show the place to prospective tenants or buyers. The notice is whatever your lease says it is, and the lease may set a shorter notice for showings near the end of the tenancy than for other entries. Colorado also has no rule requiring a waiver of entry notice to be signed in a document separate from the lease, so the showings term can sit in the lease itself.

Three statutory notices do exist and none of them is about showings.

- If you enter to carry out habitability repair work you must give at least twenty-four hours written notice, say the date and time and a reasonable estimate of how long you will need, and the tenant may reasonably refuse that slot and propose another; the tenant may also let you in on less than twenty-four hours notice.
- If you, an inspector or a pest-control agent enter to inspect for or treat bed bugs, the notice is at least forty-eight hours written or electronic unless your lease sets a different minimum, and the tenant may waive it.
- If the property is a space in a mobile home park, separate rules apply and the notice is seventy-two hours.

Keep the showings notice real rather than none, and keep it inside stated daytime hours: Colorado makes a lease waiver of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment void, and a term that let you in at any hour with no notice at all would invite that argument.

Give the notice in the way the lease provides, keep a record of it, and do not use a showing as a way around the repair-entry notice.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection in Colorado - and One Rule That Helps You
bodyText: Colorado has passed nothing to protect a tenant whose pay stops in a government shutdown. There is no delayed rent due date, no bar on a late fee, no eviction moratorium and no repayment-plan right keyed to a federal or state shutdown or furlough, and no lapse-in-appropriations trigger anywhere in the statutes. So the rent is due when the lease says it is due, and your ordinary remedies are unchanged. One provision does mention a shutdown, and it runs your way: where you rent to a tenant with housing assistance and the first payment from the housing authority is late because of processing delays or a government shutdown, Colorado's source-of-income rules expressly leave you free to exercise any right and pursue any remedy available under law. That is a permission, not an instruction, and it does not override the rest of Colorado law: your late fee still cannot be charged until rent is at least seven days late and still cannot be charged on the part of the rent a subsidy provider owes, your notice periods are unchanged, and the for-cause eviction rules still apply to a covered tenancy of twelve months or more. Practically, a shutdown is a business decision rather than a legal one. If you choose to give a tenant extra time, do it in a dated written agreement that says exactly what is deferred and when it is payable, so the deferral does not become an argument that you waived the due date for good. Do not label a deferral charge as rent. And check local rules: a city or county may act in a way the state has not.

title: Colorado Does Not Limit Renting Out a Single-Family Home
bodyText: No Colorado statute stops you letting a house in a single-family zone, caps how many homes on a street may be rented, or makes your right to let conditional on living on the lot yourself. Colorado has in fact moved the other way. A local government may not limit how many people live together in a single dwelling based on their family relationship; it may set occupancy limits only on demonstrated health and safety standards, such as building, fire or state water-quality standards, or on affordable-housing programme guidelines. And in the larger municipalities and census places covered by the accessory-dwelling-unit rules, the jurisdiction must allow one accessory dwelling unit alongside a single-unit detached dwelling and must not require either that unit or the other dwelling on the lot to be owner-occupied. There are two exceptions to that: the jurisdiction may ask the owner to show they live on the parcel when the application is to build or convert the accessory unit, and when the application is for a short-term rental licence or permit. Separately, local governments cannot control your rents on private residential property. None of this means local rules are irrelevant. Zoning, licensing, short-term-rental permits, rental-licence and inspection programmes and nuisance ordinances are all live in Colorado, home-rule cities and counties use them, and the state rules above only cut back particular kinds of restriction in particular places. Check the zoning and any rental-licence or short-term-rental rules for the property's address before you advertise, and remember that a homeowners association declaration can restrict leasing even where the city cannot.

title: No Colorado Smart-Lock Statute - but Four Rules Still Govern What You Install
bodyText: Colorado has passed nothing like Washington's smart-access law. No statute tells you whether you may fit a smart lock or an app-based entry system, what data you may collect from it, whether you must offer a physical key as an alternative, how long you may keep entry logs, or what notice you owe before switching a tenant over. So the question is governed by your lease and by four rules that already exist. First, locks are a habitability item: working locks on all exterior doors, and locks or security devices on windows designed to be opened, must be maintained in good working order, and the lack of them is a condition that breaches the warranty of habitability. A smart lock that fails, loses power or depends on the tenant's phone or your network still has to leave the tenant able to secure and enter the home. Second, you may not willfully remove doors, windows or locks except as repair or maintenance requires, and doing so is an unlawful removal or exclusion carrying a serious penalty; remotely disabling a tenant's credential is the modern version of that and should never be used over a rent dispute. Third, a tenant who is a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, stalking or unlawful sexual behavior and who gives you the statutory documentation may change the locks, expressly including electronic locks, and you must not prevent it, charge for it or retaliate; any lease term forbidding it is void. The tenant must make all reasonable efforts to give you a key, the electronic code or other access information within fourteen days. Fourth, a charge is a charge: a fee for the app, the fob or the smart-lock hardware runs straight into Colorado's fee rules, including the bars on charging for something you must provide anyway, for something not actually provided, and for the maintenance of common areas. Write the lease terms you need: who holds credentials, that the tenant must not disable or remove the device, that lost-credential replacement is handled like a lost key, and that you will give the tenant a working means of entry if the system fails. Say in writing what the system records and who sees it, because Colorado's silence is not a licence and a tenant has a non-waivable implied covenant of quiet enjoyment. Entry notice is unchanged: holding a credential is not permission to enter. Take advice before using entry logs for anything other than security.

title: Smoke Drifting Between Units: No Colorado Statute, and a Waiver You Mostly Cannot Have
bodyText:
Colorado has no law about tobacco or cannabis smoke moving from one apartment into another, and no law saying whether a tenant can agree in advance to put up with it.

Four things do govern the subject.

- The Clean Indoor Air Act bans smoking, including the use of an electronic smoking device, in the enclosed common areas of multiple-unit residential buildings - restrooms, lobbies, hallways and the like - and the ban is not limited to places where your staff work. It also covers the common areas of retirement facilities, publicly owned housing and nursing homes, but not a resident's own quarters. Post signs and enforce it in your hallways; you can be on the wrong side of this one without any tenant complaining.
- Private homes and private residences are outside the Act, so the Act does not tell you whether a tenant may smoke inside the unit; that is your lease's job.
- **You may make a non-smoking building by choice:** The owner or manager of a place the Act exempts may post signs prohibiting smoking, and once posted the place counts as one where smoking is prohibited under the Act. So a no-smoking policy backed by posted signs borrows the statute's own enforcement.
- **A waiver will not save you.** Colorado makes a lease waiver of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment void, so a clause by which the tenant accepts smoke drift generally is unenforceable. The only disclaimer the statute allows is for a violation committed by a third party acting beyond your reasonable control, which will not cover smoke you could have stopped - for example by enforcing your own no-smoking rule against the neighbour.

The practical course: decide whether the building is smoke-free, say so in every lease and in the house rules, cover cannabis expressly because a property owner may regulate marijuana on the property, post the signs, and treat a drift complaint as a rule-enforcement problem rather than something to disclaim.

A local ordinance may be stricter than the state Act and cannot be less strict, so check local rules.

title: Tenants on SSI, SSDI or Colorado Works: Mediation Before You File
bodyText: Colorado does not give a tenant a continuance or a right to have the case reinstated because a benefit or voucher payment arrived late. What it gives instead is a mediation precondition, and missing it can cost you the case. If a residential tenant receives supplemental security income, Title II social security disability insurance or cash assistance through Colorado Works, that tenant has a right to mediation before you file an eviction complaint. Three things follow. Your written demand or notice must itself say that such a tenant has that right. Your complaint must carry a signed affidavit saying either that the tenant receives one of those benefits and mediation happened and was unsuccessful, or that mediation did not happen for one of the stated reasons - the tenant did not disclose, or declined to disclose in writing in response to your written inquiry, that they receive one of them; or they do not receive one; or you are a 501(c)(3) that offers mediation anyway; or you are a landlord with five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five rental units in total. And if the tenant does receive one of those benefits, the writ of restitution must say it is not executable for thirty days after judgment, and the officer must not execute it until then, instead of the usual ten days; that longer delay does not apply to a judgment for a substantial violation or to the five-or-fewer landlord. Failure to comply with the mediation requirements is an affirmative defence, and if you cannot show you met them the court must dismiss without prejudice, so you start again. Mediation is run by a trained neutral third party at no cost to the tenant, you pay only your own share, each side may bring a lawyer, and the office of dispute resolution must schedule it no later than fourteen calendar days after you ask for it. Two practical points. You may ask a tenant in writing whether they receive one of these benefits, and asking for the purpose of complying with the complaint requirements is not an unfair housing practice - so send a written inquiry and keep it. And although a tenant may voluntarily waive the mediation right, the waiver must not be in the lease or in any other agreement with you, so do not put one there: the lease term would be void. None of this is lease content, and the lease does not carry it.

title: No Special-District Statement Belongs in a Colorado Lease
bodyText: Colorado has a great many special districts, including the metropolitan districts that fund new subdivisions, and it has real disclosure rules about them - but every one of those rules is owed by a seller to a buyer, or by the district to the county, and none is owed by a landlord to a tenant. There is no statement you must put in a lease, no acknowledgment for the tenant to sign and no bold-type notice. A contract for the purchase and sale of residential real property must carry a bold-faced special-taxing-district disclosure, and an owner selling residential property inside a metropolitan district must give the purchaser estimated district property taxes and a written statement about the district's powers; those are sale documents. The district itself has to record a public disclosure document and a boundary map with the county clerk and recorder, and must publish an annual notice to electors, so the information your tenant might want is already public and you can simply point them to the district office, the district's website, the county clerk and recorder or the division of local government. Two things are worth knowing. First, a tenant who is registered to vote and lives in the district is an eligible elector in that district's elections, so district representation is not something the lease has to give them. Second, district service charges can reach you: unpaid fees, rates, tolls, penalties or charges of a special district are a perpetual lien on the property served until paid, so if your tenant pays the district directly for water or sewer and stops paying, the lien attaches to your property rather than following the tenant. That is a reason to track those accounts, and it is also why a lease term that makes the tenant responsible for a district utility account should require proof of payment. Nothing stops you telling a tenant voluntarily that the property sits in a district; if you do, keep it accurate and dated.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure in Colorado - and No State Sprinkler Mandate for Rentals
bodyText: Colorado does not make you tell a tenant whether the building has a fire-sprinkler system, whether it does not, or what would happen if it failed. There is no statutory notice, no lease statement and no acknowledgment form. The state also imposes no sprinkler requirement of its own on an existing rental: whether sprinklers are required is a building and fire code question, and in Colorado those codes are adopted and enforced locally, so the answer comes from the city or county and from the permits for the building, not from a statute. The only state sprinkler statute regulates the trade, by requiring sprinkler fitters to be registered. Two consequences for you. First, if you say anything about sprinklers, say it accurately: a wrong or stale statement about a safety system is the kind of representation about the characteristics of a property that Colorado's consumer-protection law reaches, and silence is treated differently from a false statement. Second, a sprinkler system that exists is part of the premises you must maintain. Colorado's warranty of habitability requires compliance with all applicable building, housing and health codes where a violation would create a condition that materially interferes with life, health or safety, so a disabled or unmaintained sprinkler system in a building whose code requires one is a habitability problem rather than a disclosure problem. Compare carbon monoxide alarms, which Colorado does regulate for rentals by statute, including replacing a missing or non-operational alarm before a new tenancy and giving the tenant the batteries. Keep service and inspection records for any system the building has, do not let a tenant obstruct or tamper with sprinkler heads, and check the local fire code and your certificate of occupancy before telling a tenant the building is or is not sprinklered.

title: Colorado's One-Year Rule: Which Leases Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Colorado's threshold is one year, and it is a validity rule rather than a recording rule. A contract for leasing land for longer than one year is void unless the contract, or a note or memorandum of it that expresses the consideration, is in writing and signed by the party who is to grant the lease - that is, you as landlord. So a lease of exactly one year or less can be oral and still be enforceable, while an eighteen-month or two-year oral lease is not. Two refinements matter in practice. The signature the statute insists on is the landlord's, so a written lease you have not signed is the weak case, not one the tenant has not signed; get both signatures anyway, and note that an agent may sign for you only if the agent's authority is itself in writing. And the writing must express the consideration, so state the rent. Assignment and surrender are caught by a separate rule: no interest in land other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year may be created, granted, assigned, surrendered or declared except by a writing signed by the party doing it. That means a surrender of a longer lease, or an assignment of it, should be documented in writing and signed, and an informal handover of keys is not a safe surrender. A separate general provision makes any agreement void unless written and signed by the party charged if by its terms it is not to be performed within one year of being made, which catches a lease agreed now to start later even when the term itself is short. Recording is optional in Colorado for ordinary land, with one closed-class exception noted below: any instrument affecting title may be recorded, and Colorado is a race-notice state, so an unrecorded lease is good between you and your tenant and against anyone with notice of it, but not against someone who acquires rights and records first without notice. If a long lease matters commercially, record it or record a short memorandum of it. Finally, a separate statute requires you to give the tenant a signed copy of a written rental agreement within seven days, and that is a duty even where the one-year rule would not have required a writing at all. Put every residential tenancy in writing regardless of length; the one-year rule is a floor, not advice. One exception, narrow but real: if your land is registered under Colorado's old Torrens system - a closed class, since no new applications have been accepted since 1 January 2018 - a lease of more than three years must be registered, and until it is, it binds only you and your tenant and not the land itself. If you do not know whether your land is registered, a title search will tell you.

title: Every Colorado Figure That Is Capped - One Place to Check
bodyText: Colorado caps more landlord figures than most states, and the caps sit in several different statutes. Money you hold: the security deposit must not exceed two monthly rent payments, a pet deposit must not exceed three hundred dollars and must be refundable, and pet rent must not exceed thirty-five dollars a month or one and one-half percent of the monthly rent a month, whichever is greater. From January 1, 2026 you must return the deposit within thirty days, and although your lease may specify a longer period it may not exceed sixty days. Money you charge: a late fee cannot be imposed until rent is at least seven calendar days late, is capped at the greater of fifty dollars or five percent of the past-due rent, can be charged only once for each late payment, carries no interest, cannot be charged on the portion of the rent a subsidy provider owes, and cannot be charged at all unless you gave written notice within one hundred eighty days of the due date. An application fee must be no more than your actual or average cost of processing the application, must be the same for every applicant for the same unit or for any unit you offer at the same time, and cannot be charged at all if the applicant gives you a portable tenant screening report. Where a third party bills you for a service you pass through, you may add either a markup or fee of up to two percent of the billed amount or up to ten dollars a month, but not both. No fee may increase by more than two percent over the course of a rental agreement of one year or less, utilities excepted. What you may require: you cannot require an applicant to have an annual income of more than two hundred percent of the annual rent, you cannot look at a conviction older than five years except for four named categories, and you cannot look at rental or credit history older than seven years. Timing: you may raise the rent only once in any twelve-month period of consecutive occupancy, whatever the lease says and whatever kind of tenancy it is. Early termination by a victim-survivor who gives you the statutory documentation: you may recover no more than one month's rent, only if you actually incurred economic damages as a direct result and documented them to the tenant in time. And during a declared disaster period in a designated area, a rent increase of more than the greater of last year's increase or ten percent is price gouging. Two rules about how to use this list. State your own figure in the lease, not the cap - a lease that recites the maximum hands the tenant the ceiling and gives you nothing. And a provision that breaks one of these caps is usually not merely unenforceable as to the excess: the late-fee and deposit statutes make the offending provision void, and a fee that violates the pricing statute is a prohibited lease term. Mobile home parks have their own regime and are not covered here.

title: The Six Ways a Colorado Tenant Can End the Lease Early
bodyText:
Colorado gives a tenant six statutory routes out of a lease, and none of them can be written out of the lease.

- **An unremedied habitability breach:** If the condition that caused the breach is still unrepaired, the tenant may terminate with no liability or financial penalty by giving you ten to sixty days written notice naming the condition, stating the intent to terminate and vacate, and giving a termination date at least ten days out. If you start or finish the repair before that date, the two of you may agree in writing to cancel the termination and carry on under the existing lease - so a prompt repair plus a written rescission is your remedy.
- **Recurrence:** If the same condition comes back within six months of being fixed, the tenant may terminate by giving you at least ten days written notice within thirty days of the recurrence, with the same written-rescission escape.
- A condition caused by a third party you do not direct or control, where you have taken reasonable, necessary and timely steps but cannot fix it: there the tenant's only remedy is termination on the first route.
- **Retaliation:** If you increase rent, decrease services, terminate or refuse to renew without the tenant's written consent, or take the other listed steps because the tenant complained in good faith, joined a tenants' association or exercised a habitability remedy, the tenant may terminate and also recover the greater of three months rent or treble actual damages plus fees.
- A tenant who is a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, stalking or unlawful sexual behavior may terminate on notice with any one of the four kinds of statutory documentation, and what you may recover is capped and conditional.
- **Radon:** If you failed to give the radon disclosure, or failed to make a reasonable effort to mitigate within one hundred eighty days of being told a measurement professional found four picocuries per liter or more, the tenant may void the lease and vacate - though from January 1, 2026 that route does not apply to a lease of one year or less.

Two more points.

- You get one statutory termination route of your own, and only if your lease provides for it: where a sudden environmental public health event or government action makes continued occupancy impossible or unlawful, you may terminate on the statutory conditions, including thirty days written notice and returning the deposit by the termination date - but only if the lease says you may, so that clause has to be in the lease before you need it.
- Colorado gives no termination right for a landlord's misrepresentation, and no military termination right; the servicemember route is federal.

title: No Radiator-Cover Duty or Rider in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado has nothing like New York's radiator-cover rule. There is no duty to fit covers on steam or hot-water radiators, no duty triggered by a tenant with a young child or a vulnerable household member asking for one, no scald-protection standard for a dwelling, and no mandatory lease rider or annual notice on the subject. The word radiator appears once in the whole of Colorado's statutes, in the boiler-pressure rules, and those bind boiler owners and inspectors rather than landlords - and boilers in a private residence, or in an apartment house of fewer than six family units, are exempt from that article altogether. Heating reaches your lease by a different road. Functioning heating facilities that conformed to applicable law when installed and are maintained in good working order are a required characteristic of a habitable dwelling, and the lack of functioning heating facilities and equipment fixtures maintained in good working order from October through April is itself a condition that breaches the warranty of habitability. So a radiator that leaks, bangs, will not shut off or scalds because it is broken is a habitability problem you must fix; a radiator that is simply hot is not something Colorado requires you to cover. The practical course if a tenant asks: treat it as a reasonable request rather than a legal demand. A cover you fit voluntarily becomes part of the premises you maintain, so fit something fitted for the purpose rather than improvised, do not block the heat output or the air flow, and record what you did. Where the request comes from a tenant with a disability, handle it as a reasonable-modification or reasonable-accommodation question under Colorado's fair-housing provisions rather than under any radiator rule. And check the local building and fire code and any association rules, because the state's silence does not make the subject unregulated everywhere.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Illness at the Property: Colorado Says You Need Not Disclose
bodyText: Colorado is one of the states that answers this question directly, and the answer is in your favour. Facts or suspicions about circumstances that happened at a property and that could psychologically impact or stigmatize it are declared by statute not to be material facts that must be disclosed in a real estate transaction. The statute names two kinds of fact in particular: that an occupant is, or was at any time suspected of being, infected with HIV or diagnosed with AIDS, or has any other disease that medical evidence shows is highly unlikely to be transmitted by living in a dwelling; and that the property was the site of a homicide, another felony, or a suicide. Read the protection carefully, because it is narrower than it first looks. The no-cause-of-action sentence runs only to a real estate broker or salesperson, so if you let your own property without a broker you are relying on the first sentence — that these are not material facts — rather than on an express immunity. The cautious course is simple: say nothing about a death, a crime or a former occupant's health, do not volunteer it, and do not answer a direct question with something untrue. Silence is protected; a false statement about the condition or history of the property is a different matter and can be a deceptive trade practice. Two things the statute does not let you do. You may not use a person's HIV status, AIDS diagnosis or any other disability as a reason to refuse to rent, to charge more, or to impose different terms — disability is a protected class in Colorado and under federal fair housing law, and an inquiry into it is itself unlawful. And the statute does not cover everything a tenant might find alarming: methamphetamine contamination, lead-based paint and radon have their own disclosure regimes that still apply, and no Colorado statute requires or forbids telling a prospective tenant about a registered sex offender nearby. A city or county may add its own disclosure rules, so check local requirements.

title: Stove and Refrigerator: You Need Not Provide One, But Naming One Creates a Duty
bodyText:
Colorado does not make you supply a stove, an oven or a refrigerator. The habitability statute says in terms that nothing in it requires you to provide an appliance. What it does say is that the appliance rules bite to the extent an appliance is part of a written agreement between you and the tenant, or is otherwise actually provided to the tenant at the start of or during the tenancy. So the decision is yours, but it is made once and it is made by what you write and what you leave in the unit.

The statutory list of appliances is a refrigerator, a range stove, an oven, an air conditioner, a permanent cooling device and a portable cooling device. Where you provide one, or your lease says you will, it must have conformed to the law in force when it was installed and must be maintained in good working order. A unit that substantially lacks functioning appliances is deemed uninhabitable, which puts you on the habitability clock: you must start remedial action within seventy-two hours of notice, or within twenty-four hours if the failure materially interferes with the tenant's life, health or safety, and keep going until it is fixed. A broken refrigerator in July, or the only cooking appliance in the home, can easily cross that line.

The repair is at your expense and you may not charge the tenant a fee for it, because no fee may be charged for a good or service you need in order to meet your own obligations, and since January 1, 2026 a lease provision assigning the tenant a charge for repairs or cleaning due to normal wear and tear is void outright.

There is a particular remedy to know about here. If an appliance you provided is broken or malfunctioning, the tenant may give you three days' advance written notice and then buy a replacement of comparable quality with substantially the same features, deduct the cost from one or more rent payments, and give you the receipt. That is less notice than for any other repair-and-deduct, so an unanswered appliance message can turn into a deduction from next month's rent very quickly.

The practical advice is this.

- Decide deliberately whether you are providing a stove and a refrigerator.
- If you are not, say so clearly in the lease and do not leave an old one behind, because an appliance actually provided is covered whatever the lease says.
- If you are, list it, note its condition at move-in, and answer appliance reports the same day.

Mobile home parks are governed by a separate part of the statute and are not covered here, and a city or county may require more, so check your local rules.

title: Letting to Students in Colorado: No Special Rules, But Four Things Change
bodyText: Colorado has no student-housing statute. Nothing in the state's landlord-tenant law turns on whether your tenant is a student, and nothing gives you a shorter notice period, a different deposit rule, a group-liability rule or an academic-year exception. A private house, apartment or room let to students is an ordinary residential tenancy and every rule in this library applies to it, including the habitability duties, the deposit rules, the fee rules and the notice periods. Four things are worth knowing. First, the habitability part of the statute does not reach two kinds of student accommodation: residence at a public or private institution where the residence is incidental to the provision of education, and occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in the part of a building operated for that organization. So a college-run residence hall and a fraternity or sorority house operated by the organization sit outside those rules, while a private landlord's house down the street does not, however the arrangement is labelled. If you are a private owner letting to students, assume you are fully covered. Second, the for-cause eviction rules only begin to apply once a tenant has been a tenant of the premises for at least twelve months, so a nine- or ten-month academic-year lease will usually never become a for-cause tenancy — but a tenant who renews into a second year will cross that line mid-tenancy. Third, your city or county cannot cap the number of people who may live together in a dwelling based on how they are related to each other; local occupancy limits may now rest only on demonstrated health and safety standards such as building, fire or wastewater standards, or on affordable-housing programme guidelines. That removed the old unrelated-persons caps that used to decide how many students could share a house. You may still set your own occupancy limit in the lease, but set it on bedrooms and the property's capacity, not on family relationships, because familial status is a protected class. Fourth, everything people usually think of as a student-housing rule is left to your lease: joint and several liability, per-bedroom leases, parental guarantees, summer subletting, early-departure terms and furniture. Draft those terms carefully and consistently with the rest of the lease, because no statute will fill a gap for you, and screen any charge against Colorado's fee rules before you add it. A city or county may require a rental licence or add other duties, so check local rules, and take advice before using a guarantee or a joint-liability term you have not used before.

title: Stalling a Voucher Inspection Is Now a Fair Housing Violation in Colorado
bodyText:
No Colorado statute mentions a housing-authority inspection by name, so people often assume there is nothing to break. That changed on May 29, 2025. It is now an unfair housing practice, unlawful and prohibited, for a landlord to fail to make reasonable efforts to respond in good time to requests for the information and documents a rental assistance application needs, and to fail to cooperate in good faith with a tenant who is applying for rental assistance — including by refusing to provide documents required by a state agency, a local agency or any other administering entity to support the tenant's application. Scheduling a required inspection, signing the agency's forms and handing over the paperwork are exactly what that cooperation duty is about, so running the clock down until the tenant loses the subsidy is the behaviour the provision targets.

Two things make this sharper than the rest of Colorado's source-of-income rules.

- **The small-landlord exemptions do not cover it.** The exemption that switches off the source-of-income provisions for a landlord with three or fewer rental units is written to cover a specific list of paragraphs, and this cooperation duty is not on that list, so it reaches you however few units you own. The separate relief for an owner of five or fewer single-family homes is about not having to accept a housing choice voucher at all; it does not license stalling once you have a tenant who is applying.
- **The money is fixed at the bottom.** Where a court awards damages for a subsidy-related violation of this provision, it must award the tenant at least five thousand dollars, and in working out actual damages the court must take account of what the tenant lost by forfeiting the subsidy. Commission penalties of up to ten thousand dollars for a first violation, and more for repeat violations, sit on top of that.

What to do in practice.

- **Treat an agency request like a legal deadline:** Answer it, keep a dated record of what you sent and when, and give the agency a direct contact.
- Let the inspector in and fix what the inspection finds, because repairs to meet a habitability standard are yours to make and yours to pay for, and you may not charge the tenant a fee for a good or service you need in order to meet your own obligations.
- If you need the tenant's cooperation for access, Colorado has no general statutory entry-notice period for an ordinary residential tenancy, so your own entry clause is what governs — make sure it covers entry by a government inspector and give the tenant proper written notice under it. The only statutory entry-notice period Colorado sets is forty-eight hours for a bed-bug inspection or treatment, and even that applies only to bed bugs and can be varied by the rental agreement.

Finally, the inspection standards themselves are federal and are not restated here; take advice if an agency tells you the unit has failed and you disagree.

title: Colorado Can Put a Receiver In Charge of a Neglected Rental Building
bodyText: Since 2025 Colorado has had a receivership remedy aimed squarely at neglected rental housing, and it is the most serious consequence in the state's landlord-tenant law. The attorney general may apply to the district court for the appointment of a receiver to operate a multifamily residential property where the attorney general has reasonable cause to believe someone has engaged in, or is engaging in, a pattern of neglect in connection with it. So may a county, a city and county, or a municipality. A pattern of neglect means evidence that a person has kept the property in a state of disrepair that threatens the health, safety or security of the tenants or the public, and the statute lists what counts: a vermin or rat infestation; filth or contamination; inadequate ventilation, illumination, sanitary, heating or life-safety facilities; inoperative fire suppression or warning equipment; inoperative doors or window locks; and any other condition that is a hazard to tenants, occupants or the public. Understand what being put into receivership actually means for you. The hearing can come as little as three business days after service, and the application takes precedence over any other civil or criminal case in that court. A receiver who is financially and legally independent of you is appointed, must file a remediation plan within thirty days and must report to the court every thirty days. The receiver collects the rent — applying it first to utilities and services, then to the cost of putting the violations right, and only then to the ordinary running of the building, the mortgage and the receiver's own fees — and may enter contracts, borrow money and secure the borrowing by granting liens on your building. It may not raise rents, fees or costs above the levels charged when it was appointed, and it may not bring an eviction for rent that went unpaid before the receivership began. Receivership does not wipe anything out for you: it does not relieve you of civil or criminal liability or of any duty, and it does not suspend your obligations for taxes, operating and maintenance expenses, mortgages, liens or repairs. Tenants keep their own habitability remedies for anything that happened before the receiver arrived, and keep their counterclaims and defences in any possession case the receiver brings. Getting out takes work. Nobody may even apply to end the receivership until ninety days after it began, and the court may only end it on a finding that doing so is in the public interest and in the tenants' best interest, and that you have shown you will finish the remaining work on the court's timetable, paid or deposited the money the receiver needs, agreed to assume every obligation including the debts and liens the receiver incurred, paid the receiver's costs, and posted a bond of up to fifty percent of the building's fair market value — forfeited if you breach again. The court can reappoint the receiver if you do not comply, and can appoint a monitor over your management after the receivership ends. Two practical points. The statute does not define "multifamily residential property", so do not assume a small building is outside it; the safe assumption is that any property with more than one dwelling unit could be reached. And this sits on top of, not instead of, local enforcement: a home rule municipality keeps its full power to pass ordinances and safeguard residents, and your city or county may have its own repair-order, condemnation and licensing machinery. One thing that does run in your favour on the local side: where a municipality serves you and your tenant with notice of a nuisance-ordinance violation the tenant committed, and the tenant does not abate it within five days of your written notice, the tenant is liable to you for your direct abatement costs and for the fine imposed on you from the date the tenant got the municipality's notice — but only unless the lease provides otherwise, so do not write a lease term that allocates abatement costs or municipal fines away from the tenant and accidentally give that up. The best protection is the obvious one: answer habitability notices on time, keep the records the statute requires, and never let a building drift into the condition this section describes. Take advice immediately if an agency or the attorney general contacts you about conditions.

title: You Cannot Pass a Property Tax Increase to a Colorado Tenant
bodyText: A tax escalation clause — the kind that makes the tenant pay a share of any increase in the property taxes over a base year — does not work in Colorado and should not be in your lease. From January 1, 2026 you may not require a tenant to pay any fee, charge or amount related to the payment of property taxes, and a lease provision that charges a fee breaking that rule is one of the terms a Colorado residential rental agreement may not contain, so it is void and unenforceable whatever the tenant signed. Calling it a tax recovery, a tax pass-through, an assessment share or a reimbursement makes no difference; the prohibition is written around what the money is for. An insurance escalation clause is a different provision but we do not offer one either, and the cautious course is not to use one. Nothing names insurance in the prohibition, but a premium on your own policy is not a good, service or property actually provided to the tenant, you may not charge above the total price of a good or service you do charge for, and in a rental agreement of one year or less no fee may increase by more than two percent over the course of the agreement apart from the cost of utilities supplied to the unit. Add to that the requirement that the total price be disclosed as a single number more prominently than any other pricing information, which an open-ended escalator defeats, and an insurance escalator is a poor risk for very little gain. The lawful way to deal with rising taxes and premiums is to charge more rent. Build your expected costs into the rent figure itself, and when they rise, raise the rent at the next lawful opportunity. Two limits govern that. You may not increase rent more than once in any twelve-month period of the tenant's consecutive occupancy, and that applies whether or not there is a written agreement, however long the tenancy, and whether the tenancy is fixed, month to month or for an indefinite term. And you must give the notice the law and your lease require before an increase takes effect. A written lease may schedule a rent step during the term, but only one step in any twelve months. The penalty side is worth knowing before you keep an old escalation clause in a template. A landlord who charges an amount the fee statute prohibits engages in a deceptive, unfair and unconscionable act or practice; a tenant may send a written demand and, if you do not put it right within fourteen days, may recover the amounts charged plus actual damages with interest at eighteen percent a year compounded annually, and the attorney general may enforce the prohibited-clause rules independently. Your city or county may have rules of its own about charges, so check local requirements, and take advice before using any variable charge in a Colorado residential lease.

title: A Broadband Provider Can Require Access to Your Multiunit Building
bodyText: Since August 2024 Colorado has given licensed broadband internet service providers a right of access to residential multiunit buildings, and the rules are detailed enough that you need to know them before you answer a provider's letter.
