A multiunit building means a residential multidwelling building or a mobile home park; a commercial or non-residential building is not one. A provider that has a valid request for service from a tenant may access your property and install the broadband facilities needed to serve the building if it gives you sixty days of prior written notice of its intent, by certified mail with return receipt requested and a copy by email, and offers you an access agreement containing the long list of terms the statute prescribes. The deadline is the part that catches owners out: if you do not respond within sixty days, after the provider has made at least two attempts to notify you, that silence is deemed to be authorisation for access. If you are unresponsive or refuse to engage about the look of the building, the provider installs according to its own reasonable assessment of your building's aesthetics. So answer the letter. You keep real rights. You may impose conditions reasonably necessary to protect the safety, security, appearance and condition of the property and the safety and convenience of other people; you may put reasonable limits on when the provider may come; and you may require reasonable, non-discriminatory compensation for the access. You are entitled to just and reasonable compensation, and the statute lists the five factors the parties must consider in setting it, including how much of your property the equipment physically occupies, the long-term damage it may cause, interference with normal use and enjoyment, the monthly cost of utilities to run it, and the effect on the value of the property. You may refuse access outright for nine listed reasons, including that the provider will not comply with your reasonable conditions, is not licensed and authorised, cannot verify that a tenant actually requested service, that physical limitations prevent installation in existing space, that the work would significantly harm historically or architecturally significant elements, that it would cause environmental harm such as disturbing asbestos or lead paint, that it would significantly impair existing providers, that it would cause undue damage or impair essential services to tenants, or that the compensation dispute is unresolved after mediation. Disputes with the provider have to go to mediation before anyone sues, and a party that skips mediation pays the alternative dispute resolution costs. Several terms the access agreement must contain are there to protect you: the provider installs at its sole expense and owns the facilities, must get each tenant's consent before entering that tenant's home, must keep insurance, must repair damage, must remove the facility and repair the damage within ninety days of the agreement ending, must not interfere with other services, must keep to a described and limited area with exterior infrastructure at or below grade in incorporated areas, and must have a fixed and not perpetual term. Billing is strictly between the provider and the tenant: you take on no liability for service charges, you do not collect for the provider, and you have no obligation to hand over information about tenants. Where a unit is individually owned and owner-occupied, including a condominium, the provider needs that unit owner's approval before serving it, and a tenant's request from a condominium unit is only valid with the owner's prior written consent. One prohibition runs against you directly, and it is the one most likely to be broken by accident: you must not discriminate in rental charges or otherwise against any tenant or lessee who requests or receives broadband internet service under these rules. So no higher rent, no worse unit, no lost amenity and no retaliation for a tenant who signs up with a provider you did not want in the building. Mobile home parks are inside this regime rather than outside it: a provider may install to serve a mobile home in a park under the same part, and a park owner gets all the owner rights it gives. Two gaps to know about. Colorado has no statute at all about cable television access, satellite dishes or antennas in a rental; the broadband part covers broadband internet service, and nothing else. FEDERAL: a federal communications commission rule limits what a landlord may do about a tenant's own antenna or satellite dish in an area under the tenant's exclusive use and control; that is a federal regulation rather than Colorado law, it is not restated here, and you should take advice before refusing a tenant's dish. Finally, your city or county may regulate installations.

title: Tenancy at Will in Colorado: Three Days, and a Trap
bodyText: Colorado's statutes mention a tenancy at will three times and never say what one is. There is no statutory definition, so whether a particular arrangement is a tenancy at will, a periodic tenancy or something else is a question of common law on the facts. What the statutes do give you is the notice period and the eviction ground. The notice to terminate a tenancy at will is at least three days of written notice, which is the same period as for a tenancy of a week or longer but less than a month. The notice must describe the property and give the particular date the tenancy will end, and must be signed by the party giving it or by that party's agent or attorney. Both landlord and tenant use the same section. Then comes the trap. The three-day route only exists for some properties. The notice-to-terminate section is written for a landlord of nonresidential real property, or of a residential premises that falls inside one of the listed exemptions from Colorado's for-cause eviction rules, or for a tenant of any property at all. A tenant can therefore always end a tenancy at will on three days of notice, but a landlord of ordinary covered residential property cannot use that section to end one. The same limitation is built into the eviction grounds: holding over after a tenancy at will or at sufferance has been terminated is a ground for possession only for nonresidential property or for a residential premises inside those same exemptions, and for a covered residential tenancy cause exists only as the for-cause statute describes. So for a covered residential tenancy, calling the arrangement a tenancy at will gets you nothing: you still need cause or a qualifying no-fault ground, with its own longer notice. The exemptions that matter most here are the ones that put a property outside the for-cause rules altogether: a short-term rental; an owner-occupied or master-tenant-occupied single-family home with or without an accessory dwelling unit, a duplex or a triplex that is not a multifamily property of four or more units; a premises let under an employer-provided housing agreement; a tenant who has not been a tenant of the premises for at least twelve months; and a tenant not known to you to be a tenant. The twelve-month limb is the one that moves: a tenancy that starts outside the for-cause rules comes inside them once the tenant has been there a year. Practical advice. Do not create a tenancy at will on purpose. If you want flexibility, use a written month-to-month tenancy, which gives you a known notice period and a document to point at, and understand that in a covered residential tenancy you still need cause. If you have let someone stay without any agreement at all — a former tenant's guest, an occupant after a sale, someone you allowed in with no term and no rent — take advice before serving anything, because which notice applies turns on how a court characterises the arrangement, and serving the wrong notice usually means starting again.

title: If Your Tenant Files for Bankruptcy, Colorado Law Says Almost Nothing
bodyText: Colorado has no statute about what happens to a tenancy when the tenant goes bankrupt. There is no state provision on whether the lease survives, whether you may terminate, what happens to the deposit, how arrears rank, or what you must do when you hear about a filing. A search of every title of the Colorado Revised Statutes turns up only three mentions near a tenancy, and none of them answers the question: bankruptcy status is one of the items a portable tenant screening report has to be current about; Colorado has denied its residents the federal bankruptcy exemptions and limits them to the exemptions its own statutes give; and filing a bankruptcy petition does not sever a joint tenancy in real property. That means the answers come from federal bankruptcy law, which is outside this library, and from your lease. FEDERAL: the federal Bankruptcy Code governs the automatic stay, what happens to a residential lease in the estate, the treatment of a term making bankruptcy itself a default, and the ranking of your claim; none of it is Colorado law, none of it is read or restated here, and you should take advice from a lawyer as soon as you learn of a filing rather than acting on your lease. What Colorado law does still do, and what it means for you. Stop and get advice before serving any notice or filing anything. Colorado's own rules do not pause for a bankruptcy, but acting while a federal stay is in place is the kind of mistake that costs far more than the arrears. Do not rely on a lease term that makes a bankruptcy filing a default or a ground for termination. Nothing in Colorado forbids such a term, but for a tenancy covered by the for-cause eviction rules cause exists only as the statute lists it, and a lease cannot add a new ground; and federal law has its own view of a term triggered by the filing itself. On the deposit side, Colorado allows you to retain reasonable amounts only for unpaid rent, unpaid utility charges, other lawful charges listed in the lease, and necessary repair work for damage beyond normal wear and tear that did not pre-exist the tenancy, so a bankruptcy does not widen what you may keep, and your right to keep anything may itself be caught by the federal case. Colorado gives you six years to sue for arrears of rent, which is longer than many landlords expect, so a claim does not evaporate quickly. And note Colorado's statutory landlord lien over the tenant's household goods on the premises, which has its own exclusions and which federal bankruptcy law may affect; do not act on it without advice. The practical sequence is simple: record what you are owed and what condition the property is in, keep every notice and ledger, stop all collection and eviction activity, tell your lawyer, and let the federal case set the pace.

title: Tenant Data: Colorado's Duties Fall on You Even as a Small Landlord
bodyText: Colorado has no statute that simply says a landlord must keep tenant information confidential, and nothing that sets out when you may share it and with whose consent. What it has instead is a consumer-protection data regime that catches you because of what you hold, not because you are a landlord, and most landlords do not realise they are inside it. The regime applies to a covered entity, which means any person who maintains, owns or licenses personal identifying information in the course of their business, vocation or occupation. A rental application with a social security number, a driver's licence number, a bank account number or a pass code puts you squarely inside that definition. There is no small-business exemption and no unit threshold. Three duties follow. First, you must have a written policy for the destruction or proper disposal of paper and electronic documents containing personal identifying information, and the policy has to require that when the documents are no longer needed you destroy them, or arrange their destruction, by shredding, erasing or otherwise making the information unreadable or indecipherable. A drawer of old applications with no written policy is a breach of this on its own. Second, you must implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of the information and to the nature and size of your business and its operations, and if you hand the data to a third-party service provider — a screening company, a property manager, a payment processor — you must either provide the security protection yourself or require that provider to maintain reasonable security procedures too. Third, if there is a security breach of computerised data that includes personal information about a Colorado resident, you must promptly and in good faith investigate, and unless the investigation shows misuse has not occurred and is not reasonably likely to occur, you must notify the affected Colorado residents as quickly as possible and in any event within thirty days of determining that a breach occurred. If the breach is reasonably believed to have affected five hundred Colorado residents or more, the attorney general must be notified within the same thirty days. A waiver of these notification rights or responsibilities is void as against public policy, so do not put one in your lease. Two more rules to keep in view. You must not publicly post or display an individual's social security number, print it on a card needed to access your services, require it to be sent over an insecure and unencrypted internet connection, require it to log in to a website without a second authentication factor, or print it on materials mailed to the individual outside the application and account exceptions the statute allows. And from January 1, 2027 you must comply with the court rules on protecting and redacting personal identifying information in eviction filings and must redact it from any supporting document you file that may become publicly accessible; where a court actually requires the information you may submit it confidentially under judicial department procedures. For that duty the statute defines personal identifying information as a social security number, birth date, driver's licence number, state identification number, bank account number, credit card number and debit card number. Colorado's broader privacy act is a different animal and will not usually reach you: it applies to a controller that does business in Colorado and either handles the personal data of a hundred thousand consumers in a calendar year, or makes money from selling personal data and handles the data of twenty-five thousand. But watch the biometric limb, which applies to a controller that controls or processes any amount of biometric identifiers or biometric data at all, however small. If you install fingerprint or face-recognition entry, you may be inside that act for that data even as a small landlord. Finally, two confidentiality duties that are specific rather than general: where a tenant tells you they are a victim-survivor of domestic violence, stalking, unlawful sexual behavior or domestic abuse, you owe a separate statutory confidentiality duty that now reaches disclosure even to a co-tenant and requires the tenant's express written consent; and a real estate broker working for you owes confidentiality to the tenant as well as to you. Keep the written policy, keep the data in as few places as possible, destroy what you no longer need, and take advice before responding to any third party who asks you about a tenant.

title: Flags and Signs: No Tenant Right in Colorado, But Keep Your Rule Content-Neutral
bodyText:
Colorado gives your tenant no statutory right to fly a flag, put up a yard or window sign, hang a banner or display anything else at a rental, and it puts no statutory limit on the display rules you set. No state statute requires a landlord to permit a display, and none forbids a landlord from restricting one. So this is yours to decide in the lease and your house rules.

The display rights Colorado does create are aimed at homeowner and condominium associations, not at landlords, and two of them matter to you if your rental sits in a common interest community.

- An association may not prohibit the display of a flag on a unit owner's property, in a window of the unit or on a balcony adjoining the unit, may not regulate flags by subject matter, message or content apart from commercial messages, and may not prohibit installing a flag or flagpole — though it may set reasonable content-neutral rules on number, location and size.
- An association may not prohibit the display of a sign by the owner or occupant of a unit on property within the unit's boundaries or in a window of the unit, again without regard to subject matter, message or content apart from commercial messages, subject to reasonable content-neutral rules on number, placement or size. The word "occupant" in the sign provision is the one to notice: it reaches your tenant directly, so in a common interest community your tenant's window or yard sign is protected against the association even though it is not protected against you.

Two cautions before you write a strict rule.

- **A blanket ban on signs and notices can collide with Colorado's retaliation statute.** A landlord must not increase rent, decrease services, terminate or refuse to renew, bring or threaten a possession action, intimidate, threaten, discriminate against, harass or retaliate against a tenant, or charge any fee, cost or penalty, in response to the tenant organising or becoming a member of a tenants' association, and the statutory meaning of organising is wide. Enforcing a display rule against a notice about a tenants' meeting is the shape of claim that produces damages of up to three months of rent or three times actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees, and lets the tenant end the lease. Carve tenant-organising material out of your rule.
- **Keep the rule content-neutral in form and in enforcement:** Say how many items, how big, and where, and apply it the same way to every tenant and every message. A rule enforced only against displays you dislike invites both a retaliation claim and a discrimination claim.

Related points: Colorado gives a tenant no religious or cultural display right either, and the association rule about a religious item on an entry door has its own limits; and nobody has a right of political access to your property.

Mobile home parks are different and are not covered here, and a city or county may regulate signs, so check local rules.

title: Housing an Employee: Three Exemptions and One Trap
bodyText: If you house someone who works for you, Colorado treats the arrangement differently from an ordinary tenancy, and the differences cut both ways. Three things move in your favour, but each has a precise trigger and none of them is automatic just because your tenant happens to be an employee. First, Colorado's warranty of habitability does not apply to occupancy by an employee or independent contractor whose right to occupy is conditional on performing services for an employer or contractor. Read that carefully: the exemption turns on the right to occupy being conditional on the work, not on the occupant being an employee. If you let a flat to someone who also works for you, and the letting would continue whether or not the job did, the habitability rules apply in full. Second, Colorado's for-cause eviction rules do not apply to a residential premises leased to a tenant under an employer-provided housing agreement, which the statute defines as a residential tenancy agreement between an employee and an employer where the employer or an affiliate of the employer acts as landlord. So you do not need cause or a qualifying no-fault ground for that tenancy. Third, where a tenant holds over contrary to a material condition or covenant of the agreement, the usual ten days of written notice to comply or quit is reduced to three days for an employer-provided housing agreement. The trap is that these are three different definitions, and a given arrangement can sit inside one and outside another. Write the arrangement down. State in the document that the right to occupy is conditional on the employment or the contract, name the employer and the employee, say what happens to the occupancy when the work ends and by when the unit must be given up, and keep the housing document separate from the employment contract so that neither accidentally rewrites the other. An undocumented arrangement is the one most likely to be characterised as an ordinary tenancy with the full habitability duties and the full notice periods. Agricultural employers have duties nobody else has, and they are easy to breach by accident. An employer must not interfere with an agricultural worker's reasonable access to visitors at the worker's employer-provided housing at any time the worker is there. Nobody other than the worker may prohibit, bar or interfere with access to or exit from an agricultural worker's residence, whether by erecting or maintaining a physical barrier, by force or the threat of force, or by any order or notice given in any manner. So a gate, a sign-in rule or a no-visitors notice at worker housing is squarely within that prohibition. An employer must also post notice of agricultural workers' rights conspicuously on the premises, including in the worker's employer-provided housing, wherever notices to employees are customarily posted, and electronically where that is how the employer usually communicates. And an agricultural employer that provides both housing and transportation must provide transportation at least one day a week to a place where workers can get basic necessities, do financial transactions and meet key service providers, reduced to one day every three weeks for range workers on the open range, and not required at all for a worker who has their own vehicle and may park it on the employer's property. Since May 2025 the separate right of access to key service providers has been narrowed: it now runs to locations other than the employer's property, while access through remote channels including telehealth appointments may not be interfered with on the employer's property. The visitor-access right at the worker's housing was not narrowed. Finally, nothing here changes the fee rules, the deposit rules or the anti-retaliation rules, which apply to an employee tenancy like any other, and rent that is deducted from wages brings Colorado's wage-payment rules into play, which are outside this library. Take advice before you write an employee-housing arrangement, and check local rules.

title: No Colorado Duty on a Tenant to Pass On Legal Papers, So Your Lease Must Say It
bodyText: Colorado has no statute making a tenant tell you about a lawsuit, a foreclosure, a tax sale, a code-enforcement action or anything else aimed at the property, and no statute making a tenant hand you the papers. Some states do; Colorado does not. It also has no attornment statute, so there is no state rule voiding a tenant's recognition of a stranger as the new landlord and no state rule confirming one. Both points are left entirely to your lease and to general contract law. That matters more in Colorado than you might expect, because of how the foreclosure notice works. The mailing list the foreclosing party gives the public trustee or sheriff has to include the occupant of the property, addressed simply to "occupant" at the property address, and for a public trustee sale a lessee with an unrecorded possessory interest at the premises, where the lender wants the foreclosure to end that possessory interest. Notice goes by regular mail and is complete on mailing. So if you do not live at the property, your tenant may be the first and only person at the address to learn that something is happening, and nothing obliges them to tell you. Put the duty in the lease. Colorado's clause for this is already in the library and it does the work: it requires the tenant to give you a copy of anything about the property that arrives at the premises from a court, a sheriff, a public trustee, a lender or lienholder, a government agency, an association or a utility, within a short fixed period, by a stated method, and it makes clear the tenant need not act on the document and takes on no liability for it. Three drafting points. Keep the duty to forwarding and notifying only; a clause that made the tenant liable for the proceeding, or that charged the tenant a fee or penalty for not forwarding, would run into Colorado's prohibited-lease-term rules and its fee rules. Do not ask the tenant to forward personal papers unconnected with the property. And give a real address or portal for the copies to go to, and read what arrives, because the clause is worthless if nobody opens the email. Finally, nothing in Colorado requires you to tell the tenant about a proceeding either, but telling them yourself before an "occupant" letter does is usually the better course: a tenant who learns from a stranger that the building is being foreclosed is a tenant who stops paying and starts looking.

title: You May Run a Tenant Portal, But You May Not Make It the Only Way In
bodyText: Colorado is comfortable with online tenant portals. Its habitability rules actually assume one may exist: every rental agreement must state an address where the tenant can mail or personally deliver written notice of an uninhabitable condition, and an email address or accessible online tenant portal or platform where the tenant can deliver such notice. If you do provide a portal, you must post in a conspicuous place in it a statement, in English and Spanish, giving that mailing address and the email address or portal. Note the structure: the mailing or personal-delivery address is required in every case, so the portal is an addition to it and never a replacement for it. What you may not do is make the portal compulsory. Colorado's electronic transactions act applies only to transactions between parties each of which has agreed to conduct transactions by electronic means, and whether they agreed is determined from the context and surrounding circumstances including their conduct. More importantly, a party who agrees to conduct a transaction electronically may refuse to conduct other transactions electronically, and that right may not be waived by agreement. So a lease term saying that all payments, notices and signatures must go through your portal, or that the tenant waives any right to deal with you on paper, is unenforceable to that extent. The act also says in terms that it does not require any record or signature to be created, sent, received or stored electronically. Three practical limits follow. First, keep a paper and in-person route open for everything, and say so in the lease. Second, do not charge for using it. From January 1, 2026 you may not require a tenant to pay a fee, charge or amount related to the processing of rent or other payments if a means of payment that is cost-free to the tenant is not reasonably accessible to the tenant, so a portal with a card or convenience fee needs a genuinely free alternative that the tenant can actually use. Third, do not assume a portal message counts as statutory service. The habitability part's definition of "written" does include electronic and digital records, but it expressly does not apply to the written notice or demand requirements in Colorado's eviction article, so a demand for rent or a notice to quit still has to be served the way that article requires. Two more things worth knowing about portals. A tenant's written correspondence through a maintenance service or portal you provide can constitute notice to you of an uninhabitable condition, which starts your repair clock — so the portal has to be monitored every day, not when you get round to it. And if a receiver is ever appointed over the building, the statute contemplates the receiver communicating with tenants through the property's online tenant portal, so treat it as a channel that outlives your own use of it. Finally, think about the data. Running a portal makes you the holder of tenant personal identifying information, which brings Colorado's written-disposal-policy, reasonable-security and breach-notification duties into play.

title: The Records You Must Keep, and What a Tenant Can Demand
bodyText: Colorado has no general rent-ledger duty. Nothing requires you to give a tenant a running statement of account, an annual summary, or a ledger on demand. What it does have are three specific record duties, and the first one is strict enough that most landlords are in breach of it without knowing. Habitability records. You must maintain accurate and complete records of all the written notices and correspondence about uninhabitable conditions and all documentation relevant to any uninhabitable condition or to remedial action taken to remedy or repair one. You must keep them for the whole period the tenant occupies the unit and for at least three years afterwards. And on the tenant's request you must give the tenant any record, notice, correspondence or other documentation related to a condition or remedial action within ten calendar days. That covers the maintenance emails, the texts, the portal messages, the contractor invoices, the photographs and the inspection notes. Build the habit of filing them as they happen, because reconstructing three years of maintenance correspondence after a demand is not realistic, and the records are exactly what a court will order you to produce if the tenant raises habitability as a defence — repeated failure to produce them can be good cause for sanctions against you. Payment receipts. When a tenant pays in person with cash or a money order you must give a receipt at the same time, showing the amount paid and the date. For any other payment, if the tenant asks you must provide a receipt within seven days showing the amount, the recipient and the date, unless you already have a procedure that gives the tenant a record of the payment with the same three items. You may give an electronic receipt unless the tenant asks for paper, in which case paper it is; a receipt may be part of a billing statement. So a portal that issues a dated payment confirmation naming the payee satisfies this without more. Deposit documentation. Where you have not provided the required written statement within fourteen days of a tenant's written request, you must provide the documentation in your possession or control that is relevant to the retention of the deposit, including photographs, inspection forms or reports, receipts, invoices or estimates. That duty, and the rest of the deposit regime, started on January 1, 2026. Two further points. From January 1, 2027 you must comply with the court rules protecting and redacting personal identifying information in eviction filings and must redact it from any supporting document you file that may become publicly accessible, so the way you keep records should let you produce a redacted version. And holding tenant records makes you a covered entity under Colorado's data rules: you need a written disposal policy, reasonable security, and breach notification within thirty days. One Colorado record duty points outward rather than to the tenant: on the county assessor's request, and no more than twice a year, an owner or agent who advertises furnished residential property for rent must give the assessor a list of those properties by address. Mobile home parks have their own, heavier record regime and are not covered here. Local rules may add more.

title: A Tenant Repair Agreement Must Be a Separate Document, Not a Lease Clause
bodyText: Colorado allows a tenant repair agreement, but it is deliberately hard to make one and it can never live in the lease. Four conditions all have to be satisfied. The property must be a single-family residence premises. You must receive no subsidy from any governmental source for it. The agreement must be made in good faith and set out in a writing that is separate from the rental agreement, signed by both of you, and supported by adequate consideration — so a paragraph in the lease does not work, an addendum attached to the lease is risky, and an agreement with nothing given in return does not work either. And the tenant must actually have the skills to do the work. Even with all four satisfied, you may never agree that the tenant will do work that would endanger the tenant's health or safety. The payoff, where the agreement is valid, is real: to the extent the tenant's performance relates to one of the statutory habitability characteristics, the tenant takes on that characteristic and its absence no longer makes the property uninhabitable. That is why the separate writing has to list the specific tasks rather than gesture at maintenance generally. Because the statute requires a document outside the lease, this library does not offer a tenant repair clause for Colorado. Other states' leases often carry one, and copying such a clause into a Colorado lease would be worse than useless: it would not meet the separate-writing requirement, and a lease term that shifts a habitability duty is void as contrary to public policy. Ordinary housekeeping and yard duties are a different matter and are perfectly enforceable in the lease — keeping the unit clean and sanitary, taking out the tenant's own rubbish, using fixtures and appliances reasonably, mowing, watering and clearing snow — because none of them is a habitability duty of yours. Keep the line clear between those and anything on the statutory minimum-standards list. Take advice on the wording before you use a separate tenant repair agreement; a defective agreement leaves you with the whole habitability duty and the tenant with a statutory claim. Mobile home parks are governed by a separate part of the statute and are not covered here.

title: Repair and Deduct: How a Colorado Tenant Can Spend Your Money
bodyText: Of all the remedies Colorado gives a tenant for a failure to repair, the one to plan around is repair and deduct, because it lets the tenant spend your money without a court order. The tenant may deduct from one or more rent payments the cost of repairing or remedying a condition that breaches the warranty of habitability if five things are true: the tenant gave you at least ten days of advance written notice of an intent to hire a licensed or otherwise qualified professional, reduced to forty-eight hours where the tenant has a good faith belief that the condition materially interferes with the tenant's life, health or safety; you then failed to sufficiently remedy or repair it in that period, or failed to provide a comparable dwelling unit or hotel room where the statute requires one; the professional is not a relative of the tenant and gives an estimate reasonably consistent with industry standards; the tenant actually hired that professional; and the tenant gives you a receipt, invoice or proof of payment within a reasonable time after the work, or within thirty days of your asking. There is a faster version for appliances. Where an appliance you provided is broken or malfunctioning, the tenant may, instead of repairing it, replace it and deduct the cost on three days of advance written notice, if the replacement is of comparable quality with substantially the same features and the tenant gives you the paperwork. Three days is the shortest clock in the whole scheme. A tenant deducting over two or more rental periods only has to give you one notice. Your protection is narrow: if a court finds the tenant purposely deducted in bad faith, it must award you double the amount unlawfully deducted, and you may pursue any other legal remedy where the tenant has not substantially complied. That is a remedy after the event, not a way to stop a deduction. Everything else on the menu is covered elsewhere in this library, but keep the shape in mind: the tenant can end the lease with no liability or financial penalty on ten to sixty days of written notice, or on ten days if the same condition recurs within six months of being fixed; can sue or counterclaim for actual damages including the reduction in fair rental value, plus costs, attorney fees, punitive damages and anything else the court orders; can obtain injunctive relief or specific performance, with the court keeping jurisdiction to police compliance and with relief available to similarly situated tenants; can get an immediate temporary restraining order without notice to you and without posting security or proving irreparable injury; and can raise the breach as an affirmative defence to a possession or rent claim without posting a bond, without having spent anything and without having used any other remedy first. Two numbers make delay expensive. If a court or jury finds a breach, the fair rental value of the unit is rebuttably presumed to be zero dollars for the whole period an unremedied condition materially interfered with the tenant's life, health or safety, and fifty percent of the rent where it did not. And if injunctive relief is ordered and the tenant moves out, you may not re-rent the unit until it complies with the warranty. The one thing you must not do is try to manage any of this through the lease. A rental agreement or other agreement that waives or modifies a right or remedy in the habitability part is unlawful, void and unenforceable, and that expressly includes any provision charging the tenant a cost, fee or penalty because the tenant exercised or tried to exercise one of these remedies. You also cannot require a process the statute does not: a notice is valid if it substantially complies, and using one remedy does not stop the tenant using another or any remedy available elsewhere in law. Colorado has no rent escrow and no pay-into-court requirement, so there is no mechanism by which you can hold the money while you argue. The practical answer is the boring one: answer notices the day they arrive, start remedial action within twenty-four hours where life, health or safety is in play and seventy-two hours otherwise, keep the records, and never let a repair notice sit for ten days.

title: Colorado Protects Tenant Organizing — Do Not Restrict or Penalize It
bodyText: Colorado does not give tenants a general statutory right of access to your property to organize, but it does protect organizing from anything you might do about it, and that protection is what binds you. You may not retaliate against a tenant because the tenant organized or became a member of a tenants' association or a similar organization. Retaliation is defined broadly: raising rent, cutting services, terminating or refusing to renew without the tenant's written consent, bringing or threatening a possession action, intimidating, threatening, discriminating against or harassing the tenant, and charging or seeking to collect any fee, cost or penalty. Organizing is also defined broadly, and it covers lawful concerted activity for mutual aid as well as forming or running a tenants' association. Do not put a term in your lease that bans tenant associations or meetings, requires your permission to organize, or charges a fee or penalty for organizing activity: a lease term that waives or modifies a tenant's rights under Colorado's habitability part is void, and so is a term charging a cost, fee or penalty because the tenant exercised one of those rights. A tenant who proves retaliation recovers the greater of three months' rent or three times actual damages, plus attorney fees and costs, and may end the lease; the tenant need only show the protected activity was a motivating factor, not the only reason, and may raise retaliation as a defense to your possession action. You keep your ordinary rights: you may still enforce reasonable, evenly applied rules about use of common areas and about solicitation by people who are not tenants, and nothing stops you from serving a notice to terminate or to vacate where the law otherwise allows it. The cautious course is to document a legitimate, documented business reason for any rent increase, nonrenewal or charge that follows organizing activity, and to keep the file. A city or county may require more. Mobile home parks have their own parallel rule and are not covered by this row.

title: Colorado Tenant-Screening Rules — Look-Back Limits, Portable Reports and the 2027 Notice
bodyText: Colorado regulates how you screen applicants, and none of it belongs in the lease: it governs your application form, your advertising and your decision letter. Where you use rental or credit history, you may not look back more than seven years before the application date. Where you use criminal history, you may not consider an arrest record from any time, and you may not consider a conviction older than five years, with four carve-outs you may always consider: methamphetamine manufacture or distribution offenses, possession of materials to make methamphetamine or amphetamine, any offense that required sex-offender registration, and any homicide or related offense in part 1 or part 6 of article 3 of title 18. Colorado does not require you to wait for a conditional offer before running criminal history, and it sets no other look-back period. On income, you may verify that the applicant's annual income is at least twice the annual rent and nothing more; where the applicant is using a housing subsidy, the test runs only on the applicant's own share of the rent, and you may not consider or ask about a credit score, an adverse credit event or a lack of credit score unless federal law makes you. Breaking either income rule is treated as income discrimination under Colorado's anti-discrimination act, which carries its own penalties and a minimum damages figure. You must accept a portable tenant screening report the applicant supplies, you may not charge any fee to access or use it, and you may not charge an application fee at all to an applicant who gives you one; you must also advertise that right in at least twelve-point bold-faced type in your advertisements, on your website home page or in the application itself, or give it orally with written confirmation. There is a narrow exemption from the portable-report rules for a landlord who takes only one application fee at a time per unit or per applicant group and refunds it within twenty calendar days of either side declining the lease. If you deny an application you must give a written denial notice stating the reasons, within twenty calendar days of deciding, and where you pulled a consumer report you must include a copy of it and tell the applicant about the right to dispute its accuracy; if a proprietary system means you cannot cite the criteria, give the screening company's report with only the proprietary information redacted. The applicant may insist on paper. From January 1, 2027 you must also put a notice in every rental application saying what information and data you will try to access when you screen, giving a general description of the factors you will weigh (credit history, rental history, income and criminal background, where they apply), and saying whether you use a third-party screening service and naming it; you are not required to adopt or publish fixed disqualifying criteria. Build that notice into your application template before 2027 rather than after. Two things Colorado does not give you: there is no statute shielding you from a negligence claim for renting to a person with a criminal record, and there is no statute letting a tax-credit or other subsidized-property owner impose lease conditions based on prior felony convictions. Federal fair-credit and fair-housing law applies on top, and a city or county may require more. Take advice before adopting a blanket criminal-history policy.

title: What Colorado Law Already Makes the Tenant Responsible For
bodyText:
Colorado gives you a statutory tenant-duty list that applies whether or not your lease repeats it, and it is worth repeating in the lease anyway, because a breach of the lease is a lease remedy and a breach of the statute on its own is not.

The duty is to use the part of the premises within the tenant's control in a reasonably clean and safe manner, and the statute says a tenant fails that duty by substantially failing to do any of six things:
- Comply with tenant obligations in building, health and housing codes that materially affect health and safety.
- Keep the unit reasonably clean, safe and sanitary so far as the unit's condition allows.
- Dispose of waste lawfully and sanitarily.
- Use the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, elevator and other facilities and appliances reasonably.
- Keep the tenant's own household and anyone in the tenant's control from disturbing the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment.
- Promptly tell you if the premises is uninhabitable or has a condition that will make it uninhabitable if it is not fixed.

A separate duty forbids destroying, defacing, damaging, impairing or removing any part of the premises knowingly, intentionally, deliberately or negligently, or knowingly letting someone in the tenant's control do so.

Note the word "substantially": an isolated lapse is not a statutory failure, so do not treat every untidy inspection as a breach.

Three limits matter when you enforce.

- Nothing in the tenant-duty section lets you shrink your own habitability obligations, so a duty clause cannot be used to shift a repair you owe onto the tenant; the one exception is a single-family premises you receive no governmental subsidy for, where you and a tenant who actually has the skills may agree in a separate signed writing, supported by consideration, that the tenant performs specified repairs, and never work that would endanger the tenant's health or safety.
- From January 1, 2026 you may not assign the tenant any fee or charge for repairs, cleaning or other necessary work due to normal wear and tear, or for damage or a defective condition that existed before the tenancy: such a provision is void, not merely unenforceable as to the charge.
- You may not penalize a tenant for calling the police or for emergency assistance, so a conduct or disturbance duty must never be written or applied in a way that does.

Keep your remedy on the lease side, document the condition with dated photographs before and after, give written notice of the specific failure and a chance to correct it, and do not deduct wear-and-tear or preexisting-condition amounts from the deposit.

A city or county may add duties. Mobile home parks are governed by their own part of the statute and are not covered here.

title: Colorado Has No Notice Rule for Changing a Non-Rent Lease Term
bodyText: No Colorado statute tells you how much notice to give before changing a term of a residential tenancy other than the rent. The code has a sixty-day written notice rule for a rent increase, and only where there is no written agreement between you and the tenant; a bar on increasing rent more than once in any twelve-month period of consecutive occupancy, whatever the length or type of tenancy and whether or not there is a written agreement; and a one-business-day notice duty if the identity of the landlord or the authorized agent changes. For everything else — a parking rule, a pet rule, a utility arrangement, a house rule, a smoking rule, a fee the lease already provides for — the state leaves the mechanics to the lease and to general contract law. That has three practical consequences. First, during a fixed term you cannot unilaterally change a term at all unless the lease itself gives you that power; a lease provision letting you adopt or amend rules is what makes a mid-term change possible, and without one you need the tenant's agreement. Second, for a periodic tenancy the ordinary route is a written notice to terminate the tenancy, served before the end of the period and expiring at the end of it, offering a new tenancy on the new terms: Colorado's notice periods are at least ninety-one days for a tenancy of a year or longer, twenty-eight days for six months or longer but under a year, twenty-one days for one month or longer but under six months, three days for a tenancy of a week or longer but under a month or a tenancy at will, and one day for less than a week. Third, and this is the trap, that route is closed for most tenancies once the tenant has been in the premises twelve months: Colorado requires cause to terminate or refuse to renew, and wanting different terms is not one of the statutory causes, so you cannot force a term change by nonrenewal. You also cannot use a termination notice whose primary purpose is to raise the rent in a way the rent-notice section does not allow. Changing a fee is narrower still than changing rent: a fee, charge or amount may not increase by more than two percent over the course of a rental agreement of one year or less, utilities excepted, so a lease-provided fee is effectively frozen within a one-year term however much notice you give. The cautious course is to put a clearly drafted rules-and-regulations provision in the lease saying how you will adopt or change rules and how much notice you will give, to give at least the same notice you would need to end the tenancy, to make any change prospective only, and to get a signed addendum for anything that touches money. Mobile home parks have their own rule-change notice provision. A city or county may require more.

title: Towing a Vehicle From Colorado Rental Property — What You Must Have in Place First
bodyText:
In Colorado a tow from your property is lawful only if you have done your part first, and most of the duties that make it lawful are yours, not the tow company's.

You must have posted signs before any vehicle can be towed without consent.

Each sign must be at least two square feet with lettering at least an inch high, contrasting sharply with its background and with the structure it is on; it must state the parking restriction, then the times and days it applies (or say "Authorized Parking Only" if it runs around the clock), then the name and telephone number of the towing carrier you have authorized; it must be printed in English and Spanish; it must be permanently mounted both at the entrance facing the street, visible before and on entering, and inside facing the parking area; it must not be obstructed; and it must sit between three and ten feet from the nearest surface.

Because the sign names your towing carrier, changing carriers means changing your signs.

You must also give notice of your parking regulations, and a warning that a vehicle in breach may be towed at the vehicle owner's expense, to the driver on entering and parking; if you have tenants, the statute says the way you do that is by issuing each tenant a written document containing the applicable parking regulations, before the regulations are adopted or changed or before the person agrees to become a tenant.

The towing carrier then needs documented permission, not automated and not pre-approved, for each individual vehicle, given in the twenty-four hours before the tow and signed on the commission's form. You or your leaseholder, a common-interest-community person within its area of operation, or an employee of either or of a property management company retained to collect rent and perform residential services may give that permission.

Two traps: if you would earn income from the tow, that carrier may not do it, and an employee with a financial interest in the carrier or in a parking manager that earns income from tows may not give permission. The carrier may not patrol or monitor your property looking for violations.

A twenty-four-hour written notice on the windshield is normally required before the tow, stating that the vehicle will be towed if it stays parked inappropriately, describing the inappropriate parking, giving the time it will be towed, and warning that repeating it may lead to a tow without notice.

That notice is not needed where the driver has already had two notices for the same thing, for a repossession, a court, administrative or peace-officer order, a vehicle blocking a driveway or roadway, a disabled space without a valid or recently expired placard or plate, a marked fire zone, a vehicle occupying or blocking a resident's own designated, rented or purchased space, or a vehicle parked without authorization in a lot marked for the exclusive use of residents or invited guests.

A vehicle is parked inappropriately if it breaks the procedure for getting authorization to park, fails to comply with your signs or with the tenants' agreements, or breaks a statute, rule, ordinance or resolution. No one may tow from private property because a plate check shows the registration has expired, unless a peace officer ordered it; the carrier may not charge a drop fee once the car is hooked up but still on the property, must stop a tow in progress if asked, and must release the car for fifteen percent of the fees up to sixty dollars.

None of this applies to a tow ordered by a peace officer, or to a parking space serving a business on commercial real estate.

Abandoned vehicles are a separate route: a vehicle left unattended on your property for twenty-four hours or longer without your or your lessee's consent, or left without consent and not collected from the impound lot within forty-eight hours after a tow you requested, counts as abandoned, and you, your lessee, or an agent of either authorized in writing may have it towed and impounded by a licensed operator. The operator then carries the notification, reporting, appraisal, lien and sale machinery; do not try to sell or dispose of a vehicle yourself. Your city or county may set a different abandonment period, and nothing in the towing or abandoned-vehicle statutes preempts local towing ordinances, so check local rules.

A towing carrier may not pay you or anyone else money or other valuable consideration for the privilege of towing, so do not accept a per-tow payment or a share of tow revenue.

Your practical checklist: compliant bilingual signs naming your current carrier, a written parking-regulations document issued to every tenant before signing and reissued before any change, a signed per-tow authorization every time, and no financial interest in the tow.

title: The One Colorado Exemption You Must Claim in the Lease Itself
bodyText: Colorado has no tenant-protection act of the kind that makes a landlord serve a notice to claim an exemption from a rent cap or a just-cause rule. It has one exemption that behaves that way, and it is easy to lose. If you own five or fewer single-family rental homes and you are letting a single-family home, your lease can be an exempt residential agreement, and the practical benefit is that the demand for unpaid rent runs five days rather than ten. But the exemption exists only if you give notice in the agreement that the ten-day notice period does not apply to the tenancy. No notice in the lease, no exemption: the ten-day period applies whatever your portfolio looks like. Do not treat it as something you can assert later, in the demand or in court. Count your single-family rental homes honestly, and if you acquire a sixth the exemption is gone even though the lease still says otherwise, so do not rely on the clause once you cross the line. Colorado's other exemptions work differently and need no notice at all. The for-cause eviction rules in part 13 do not apply to a short-term rental, to an owner-occupied or master-tenant-occupied single-family home, duplex or triplex that is not a multifamily property of four or more units, to a mobile home space leased to a home owner or under a lease-to-own or purchase-option agreement, to employer-provided housing, to a tenant who has not been a tenant of the premises for at least twelve months, or to a tenant you do not know to be a tenant; none of those requires you to tell the tenant you are exempt. The lease statement about source-of-income discrimination does not apply to a landlord with five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five rental units in all, again with no notice required to claim it. Mandatory mediation before an eviction does not apply to a landlord with five or fewer units, with no notice required. The cautious course is to say nothing in the lease about any exemption you are not sure of, to include the exempt-residential-agreement notice only where it is genuinely true, and never to recite an exemption as if it reduced your other duties. A city or county may require more.

title: Colorado Has No Tenant-Protection-Act Notice to Serve
bodyText: Colorado has nothing like the statewide tenant-protection acts that cap rent increases and require just cause, and so it has no notice telling the tenant those protections exist or that your property is covered by them. There is no rent cap: no Colorado statute limits how much you may raise the rent, only how often, and the general assembly has declared rent control on private residential housing a matter of statewide concern and forbidden every county and municipality from enacting an ordinance or resolution controlling rent on private residential property, with narrow carve-outs for a voluntary agreement with the local government and for a deed restriction placed under one. So do not expect a local rent-cap notice either, and do not copy a rent-cap or just-cause advisory from another state's lease into a Colorado lease: a notice that misstates the law is worse than no notice. Four real Colorado duties sit in the space a tenant-protection-act notice would occupy, and those you do have to get right. Your written rental agreement must include a statement that Colorado law prohibits source-of-income discrimination and requires a non-exempt landlord to accept any lawful and verifiable source of money, unless you are a landlord with five or fewer single-family rental homes and no more than five rental units in all. Your written rental agreement must state the name and address of the landlord or the authorized agent, and you must notify tenants of a change within one business day. You must give the tenant a signed copy of a written agreement within seven days of signing. And if you are starting an eviction for nonpayment, Colorado has written the federal thirty-day notice to vacate into state law; how far it reaches beyond federally backed and subsidized housing is not settled, so see the separate note on it. Separately, Colorado does limit rent increases to one in any twelve-month period of consecutive occupancy and does require cause to evict most tenants once they have been in the premises twelve months, but neither comes with a notice you must serve in advance to claim or to disclose. During a declared disaster a separate consumer-protection statute measures an unconscionable rent increase, so check that before raising rent in a disaster period. A city or county may require disclosures of its own, so check local rules.

title: Colorado's Tenant-Protection Statutes Have No Expiry Date
bodyText: None of Colorado's landlord-tenant statutes is written to expire. The warranty of habitability, the security deposit rules, the prohibited-lease-clause list, the retaliation bar, the rent-increase frequency limit, the for-cause eviction rules, the rental application rules and the domestic-violence protections all run indefinitely, and there is no repeal date in the statute you have to diary. That means you cannot plan on a protection lapsing, and it also means you do not have to date-check the law you are relying on for an expiry. Two practical consequences. First, the right question for a Colorado landlord is not when a protection ends but when a new one starts: Colorado amends its landlord-tenant law most sessions, and several changes have recent or future start dates, so check whether a rule has changed rather than whether it has expired. Second, two statutes a landlord does touch are on review clocks even though no tenant protection is. The public utilities commission's regulation of towing carriers, which is what governs towing from your property, is scheduled for sunset review and then repeal on September 1, 2030; the state collection-agency and debt-collection article, which governs a collection agency you might use for unpaid rent, is repealed effective September 1, 2028; and the asbestos control provisions carry a repeal date of September 1, 2027. If any of your lease text or procedure depends on one of those, diary the date and check whether the general assembly has extended it before you rely on it. Do not read any of those sunsets as ending a tenant's rights; they are reviews of regulatory programmes, and the general assembly routinely extends them. Nothing in a lease can shorten a Colorado tenant protection either: a provision purporting to waive or modify the for-cause eviction rules is void, and so is a provision waiving or modifying the habitability part or the security deposit part.

title: When Colorado Makes You Write in Spanish — or in the Tenant's Own Language
bodyText: Colorado does not require you to translate the whole lease, and it has no rule that advertising or negotiating in another language forces you to supply a lease in that language. What it does have is three specific translation duties and two type-size floors, and they are easy to miss because they sit in three different places. First, in the lease: since January 1, 2025 every rental agreement must carry, in English and Spanish and in at least twelve-point bold-faced type, a statement giving an address where the tenant can mail or hand-deliver written notice of an uninhabitable condition and an email address or accessible online tenant portal for the same notice. Both channels, not either. Second, in your portal: if you give the tenant an online tenant portal or platform, the same English-and-Spanish statement must be posted conspicuously inside it. Third, and this is the one with the widest reach, in your notices: a written demand or notice to terminate under Colorado's eviction statute, or under the for-cause eviction part, must be written in English, in Spanish, or in any other language that you know, or have reason to know, is the tenant's primary language. That is a conditional duty keyed to your own knowledge, so it bites when you have corresponded with the tenant in another language, when the application or the tenancy file shows it, or when your staff has interpreted for them. Keep a note in the file of the language you have used with the tenant and serve in that language as well as English when you have any reason to think it is their primary language; a demand in the wrong language risks the whole eviction. Separately, a lease statement about the warranty of habitability and the ban on retaliation must appear in at least twelve-point bold-faced type, and your portable-tenant-screening-report advisement must appear in at least twelve-point bold-faced type in advertisements, on your website home page or in the application. Those two are type-size rules with no translation requirement. Signage is a fourth place: the parking signs that make a tow or a boot lawful on your property must be printed in English and Spanish. Two cautions. Colorado prescribes the content, language and type size of the lease statements but not their exact wording, so a translation you supply is your translation and not a state form; have it checked by someone who reads Spanish before you use it at scale. And nothing in Colorado law lets a translation reduce what the English text says, or lets a lease provide that the English version controls in a way that waives a tenant's rights under the habitability part. Mobile home parks have a much broader language-access regime of their own, including a rental agreement in English and, on request, in both English and Spanish. A city or county may require more.

title: Barring Someone From Your Colorado Rental Property
bodyText: Colorado has no no-trespass-notice form, no registry and no statute telling a landlord how to bar someone from a rental property. What it has is a criminal trespass statute whose definitions do the work, so the mechanics are yours to get right. Knowingly and unlawfully entering or remaining in or upon the common areas of a hotel, motel, condominium or apartment building is second degree criminal trespass, a petty offense, and so is unlawfully entering or remaining on premises enclosed in a manner designed to exclude intruders or fenced; unlawfully entering or remaining on premises generally is third degree criminal trespass; and knowingly and unlawfully entering or remaining in a dwelling of another is first degree criminal trespass, a class 1 misdemeanor that rises to a class 6 felony if the dwelling is inhabited or occupied. Everything turns on the word unlawfully. A person enters or remains unlawfully only when they are not licensed, invited or otherwise privileged to be there, and someone on a part of your property that is at the time open to the public is there with license and privilege unless they defy a lawful order not to enter or remain that was personally communicated to them by you or by another authorized person. So three defenses are built into the statute: the person was licensed or invited, the area was open to the public at the time, or no lawful order was personally communicated to them. A license to be in a building only partly open to the public does not extend to the part that is not open. There are separate posting rules, but they apply to unimproved and apparently unused land that is neither fenced nor otherwise enclosed, not to an apartment building. The practical consequence is that a sign alone will rarely do it for a common area used by residents and their visitors, and a letter to an address you do not know is not personal communication. Deliver the order to the person face to face if you can, have a witness, record the date, time, place and words used, keep a copy signed or at least initialed by whoever delivered it, and say plainly which areas the order covers and that it is not time-limited unless you say so. Three limits you must respect. A tenant's own guest or invitee is normally on your property with the tenant's license, so barring a person the tenant still welcomes puts you in conflict with the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment and with the broad statutory meaning of tenant, which reaches household members and anyone with your explicit or implicit permission to occupy; take advice before doing it. You must never bar a person, or take any adverse action against a tenant, because the tenant called for police or other emergency assistance in a situation involving unlawful sexual behavior, stalking, domestic violence or domestic abuse, and no agreement may waive that right. And you cannot create a new ground for eviction by lease: for a tenancy Colorado's for-cause part covers, cause exists only as the statute describes it. Barring a stranger, a former tenant who has been evicted, or a person with no connection to any resident is the straightforward case; barring a resident's visitor is not. A city or county may have its own ordinance, so check local rules.

title: Colorado Has No Truth in Renting Act — but It Does Void Bad Lease Terms
bodyText: Colorado has no Truth in Renting Act and nothing like one. There is no statute making it an offence to put a misleading or legally void provision in a lease as such, no statutory penalty for doing it, and no duty to hand the tenant a tenants' rights handbook, booklet or statement of legal rights at signing or at any other time. So do not look for a state-published tenant handbook to attach; there isn't one you are obliged to give. What Colorado does instead is void the bad term and, in places, require specific text in the lease. Your written rental agreement must not include a clause assigning a penalty stemming from an eviction notice or an eviction action resulting from a lease violation; a one-way fee-shifting clause; a waiver of a jury trial (except in a possession hearing), of joint, class or collective claims, of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment (with a narrow third-party carve-out), or of mandatory mediation; a provision affixing a fee, damages or penalty for failing to give notice of nonrenewal, beyond your actual losses; a provision calling any amount other than the set monthly occupancy payment "rent" for which rent remedies including eviction are available; a provision requiring the tenant to pay a markup or fee on a third-party-billed service beyond the narrow allowance, or any fee that violates Colorado's landlord pricing statute; a provision letting a voucher or subsidy provider sue for possession solely for unpaid utilities; and a clause letting you recoup mandatory mediation costs. Anything included in breach of that list is void and unenforceable. Three affirmative requirements run the other way: a written agreement must state the name and address of the landlord or the authorized agent; it must carry a source-of-income statement unless you are a small landlord; and it must carry two habitability statements, one of them in English and Spanish, both in at least twelve-point bold-faced type. There is also a prescribed radon warning statement that must go in a separate signed document before signing, not in the lease. Separately, Colorado's consumer protection act reaches a false representation about the characteristics or uses of property and a failure to disclose material information intended to induce the consumer to enter the transaction, but that nondisclosure limb carries an intent-to-induce element, so mere silence is not a violation and you should not treat the act as a general lease-honesty statute. The practical upshot: Colorado will not fine you for a bad clause, but it will strike it, and a void clause in a lease you are relying on is worse than no clause. Run your lease against the prohibited list, delete anything that fails, and do not pad the lease with terms borrowed from a state that has a truth-in-renting regime. A city or county may require disclosures of its own.

title: Removing a Squatter in Colorado — and Why It Almost Never Covers a Tenant
bodyText: Colorado has a fast squatter-removal route that sits outside the ordinary eviction statute, and the whole point for a landlord is knowing when it does not apply. The route is a county-court complaint and a verified motion for a temporary mandatory injunction restoring possession, which the court must hear as soon as practicable and no later than the next court day, after which the sheriff removes the person within twenty-four hours and orders them to stay off the premises on pain of arrest for criminal trespass. It works only against an unauthorized person, which the statute defines as someone occupying an uninhabited or vacant residential premises with no current or prior agreement or consent of the owner or an authorized agent, written or oral, about the use of the premises. Three exclusions take most real situations out of it. It does not reach a relative of the owner or of an authorized agent, including a spouse, descendant, stepchild, parent, stepparent, grandparent, brother, sister, uncle or aunt, by whole or half blood or by adoption. It does not reach a person from whom the owner or an authorized agent has accepted money or anything of value. And it does not reach a person who was previously given permission to enter and remain on the premises. So a current tenant, a former tenant, a holdover, a guest the tenant let in, an unapproved occupant who has paid you anything, and an adult child of yours are all outside it: for any of those you must use the eviction statute, and for most tenancies of twelve months or more you also need statutory cause. The premises must also be uninhabited or vacant, which a let unit with a tenant in it is not. Do not use this route to shortcut a difficult tenancy. The motion is sworn under penalty of perjury and asks you to initial each of eight statements, including that you have never had an agreement with the person, never accepted money from them, are not related to them, have demanded that they vacate, and have told them you are going to court; a declarant who swears falsely faces sanctions, contempt and prosecution for perjury or false swearing. If the court decides the occupant is not an unauthorized person it denies the motion, and you are then free to bring an ordinary eviction. Whatever the situation, do not remove or exclude anyone yourself. Colorado makes it unlawful for a landlord to remove or exclude a tenant without resorting to court process, and that includes willfully cutting utilities or removing doors, windows or locks other than for repair or maintenance; the only exceptions are a cleanup consistent with the illegal-drug-laboratory rules, mutual consent, and a genuine abandonment evidenced by returned keys, substantial removal of the tenant's property, notice, or an extended absence with rent unpaid that would make a reasonable person believe possession was permanently surrendered. A tenant who proves unlawful removal recovers actual damages plus the higher of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, with fees and costs, and the court can restore possession. Colorado's forcible-entry rules also forbid entering real property other than peaceably even where entry is allowed by law. None of this belongs in your lease: the removal route is a court procedure and a lease clause cannot create or shorten it. If you find someone in a vacant unit, call law enforcement about the trespass, document the vacancy and the absence of any dealing with the person, and take advice before filing.

title: Charging Separately for Parking in Colorado
bodyText:
No Colorado statute tells you whether parking must be bundled into the rent or may be charged for separately, and none caps what you may charge for a parking space. The question is left to the lease, but three general rules bound it tightly and the first one is new.

- Since January 1, 2026 you may not offer, display or advertise an amount a person may pay for the property unless you clearly and conspicuously disclose the total price as a single number, without separating that total price into separate fees or charges, and that single number must be more prominently displayed than any other pricing information. Total price means the maximum total of all amounts a person must pay, including any additional mandatory goods or services, and it expressly includes amounts that must be paid to use the property and amounts that are not reasonably avoidable. So if parking is mandatory, or if the unit cannot practically be used without it, the parking charge belongs inside the advertised single number; if parking is genuinely optional and the tenant can take the unit without it, the better view is that the charge is reasonably avoidable and sits outside the total price, but you must still clearly and conspicuously disclose, before the tenant consents, the nature and purpose of that pricing information, including whether it is refundable, what it is for and who receives it. That boundary has not been tested, so the cautious course is to advertise an all-in figure that includes parking whenever parking is required, to make optional parking visibly optional in the advertisement and the lease, and never to split a figure in a way that makes the headline rent look lower than what the tenant must actually pay.
- **The charge itself must survive Colorado's list of forbidden landlord charges.** You may not charge for a good, service or property that is necessary to comply with your own obligations, or for one not actually provided, or above the total price of what you are charging for, or for the maintenance of common areas — so a charge for the use of a designated space is defensible, but a charge dressed up as parking-lot upkeep is not. You may not charge a fee that increases by more than two percent over the course of a rental agreement of one year or less, so a parking charge is effectively fixed within a one-year term. And you may not charge anything related to the overdue payment of a fee that is not rent, so no late fee on late parking money.
- **A parking charge is not rent, and this is the one that catches landlords out.** Your lease must not characterise any amount other than the set monthly payment for occupancy as rent for which the rent remedies including eviction are available, so you cannot evict for unpaid parking money, and you cannot recover it by deducting from a rent payment and then calling the rent short. You can recover it as a lawful charge listed in the lease, including from the security deposit, but only if the lease actually lists it.

Two more things.

- You may not restrict parking because a vehicle is a plug-in hybrid or an electric vehicle, and in the electric-vehicle-charging context the statute allows a reasonable fee to reserve a specific parking spot, which is the only express statutory blessing of a parking charge in Colorado.
- Whatever you charge, you must have issued every tenant a written document containing the applicable parking regulations before they agreed to the tenancy.

A city or county may regulate parking minimums or charges, so check local rules.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms in Colorado — Five Routes, None of Them a Lease Statute
bodyText: Colorado has no statute saying a residential lease or a lease term is void for unconscionability. Unconscionability for leases is common-law doctrine in Colorado, and because no court decision has been looked at for this library you should treat the doctrine as live but unmapped and not rely on any particular formulation of it. What Colorado does have is five statutory routes that reach the same ground, and most of them are more dangerous to you than a bare unconscionability argument. First, and the only one written for a tenancy, you may not increase a tenant's rent in a discriminatory, retaliatory or unconscionable manner to circumvent Colorado's for-cause eviction rules — so an eye-watering increase aimed at making a tenant leave is attacked as unconscionable by statute, not by doctrine, for any tenancy those rules cover. Second, the prohibited-clause list: anything on it that appears in a written rental agreement is void and unenforceable without any court finding about fairness, so the list, not the doctrine, is what actually strikes most bad lease terms. Third, consumer protection: it is a deceptive trade practice to knowingly or recklessly engage in any unfair, unconscionable, deceptive, deliberately misleading, false or fraudulent act or practice in the course of your business, which gives a tenant a statutory claim without proving a classic unconscionability case. Fourth, pricing: since January 1, 2026 a landlord who breaks Colorado's landlord pricing rules is treated as engaging in a deceptive, unfair and unconscionable act or practice, with a fourteen-day written-demand route and eighteen percent annual interest compounded annually on top of actual damages. Fifth, and this one is easy to overlook, if the property is in a common interest community — a condominium, a planned community or an HOA-governed subdivision — a court may refuse to enforce a contract or contract clause relating to that community on finding it was unconscionable when made, may enforce the rest without the clause, or may limit the clause to avoid an unconscionable result.
