Whether a lease of a unit is a contract relating to a common interest community has not been decided, so treat it as a real risk rather than a technicality; the court will look at the commercial setting of the negotiations, whether you knowingly took advantage of the other party's inability to protect their own interests through physical or mental infirmity, illiteracy, inability to understand the language of the agreement or similar factors, and the effect and purpose of the clause. Those factors are the practical checklist. Do not present a lease on a take-it-or-leave-it basis to someone who cannot read it or cannot read English; do not bury a money term; keep every charge proportionate to an actual cost and actually disclosed; and remember that Colorado separately makes any waiver or modification of the habitability part, the security deposit part or the for-cause eviction part void, so you cannot get the same result by consent. If a term feels like something you would not want read aloud in court, take it out.

title: Interest on What a Colorado Tenant Owes You
bodyText: Colorado already gives you interest on money a tenant owes, without anything in the lease. Where there is no agreement and no other provision of law setting a different rate, interest on money runs at eight percent a year compounded annually. More specifically, a creditor receives eight percent a year compounded annually on money or property wrongfully withheld, or on money after it becomes due, from the date it was withheld or became due to the date of payment or judgment, whichever comes first; and that interest is allowed even if the amount was unliquidated when it became due, so an unquantified damages claim still carries it. There is an alternative measure for wrongfully withheld money, at the claimant's election: an amount that fully recognizes the gain or benefit the person withholding it realized. After judgment, interest runs at the rate specified in a written contract if there is one, and otherwise at eight percent a year compounded annually. You can stipulate for more than eight percent, but only in writing, and not above forty-five percent a year; the statute also says the public policy of the state does not prohibit agreeing in advance to interest on interest or compound interest. Before you write any interest term into a lease, note four Colorado limits that make it more trouble than it is worth for most landlords. You may not require a tenant to pay any amount of interest on a late fee, and a lease provision that breaks the late-fee rules is void and unenforceable, with a fifty-dollar penalty per violation, a seven-day cure window and then a civil action for compensatory damages, a penalty of between one hundred fifty and one thousand dollars per violation, costs and attorney fees. Since January 1, 2026 you may not require a tenant to pay any fee, charge or amount related to the overdue payment of a fee, charge or amount that is not rent, which on its face reaches interest charged on an unpaid non-rent amount, and a fee that breaks those pricing rules is a prohibited lease clause and void. You may not characterise anything other than the set monthly payment for occupancy as rent for which the rent remedies including eviction are available, so interest is never rent and can never support an eviction. And a charge may not increase by more than two percent over the course of a rental agreement of one year or less. So the cautious course is to rely on the statutory eight percent rather than stipulating a rate, to claim interest when you sue or counterclaim rather than adding it to a running ledger the tenant receives, never to add interest to a late fee or to an unpaid non-rent charge, and never to treat interest as rent. If you want a contractual rate above eight percent, take advice first and keep it to amounts that are plainly rent or plainly damages. Nothing here is affected by a city or county ordinance, but local rules may add disclosure duties.

title: Colorado Has No Usufruct — Letting Property You Hold for Life or for a Term
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law idea and Colorado does not use it. The word appears six times in the entire Colorado Revised Statutes, every one of them in the water-law title describing the usufructuary nature of a water right, and not once anywhere in landlord-tenant law or property law. So there is no Colorado statute telling you what happens to a lease granted by someone who holds the property only for their own life or only for a limited term, and nothing setting out a usufructuary lessor's duties to the owner or to the tenant. Colorado's nearest equivalent is a life tenant, and the statutes confirm only the obvious: a life tenant's record interest in real property terminates on the holder's death, which can be proved for the land records by a death certificate and a sworn supplementary affidavit, or by a two-person affidavit where no certificate can be procured. What follows from that is general property law rather than statute, and the practical point is the one to act on: you cannot grant a lease that outlasts the interest you hold. If you hold a life estate, or you are a master tenant subletting, or you hold under a contract that will end on a date, a lease that runs past the end of your own interest leaves the tenant without a landlord and leaves you exposed to the tenant. Three things to do. Match the lease term to your own interest, and never grant a fixed term that ends after yours does; if you need a longer tenancy, use a periodic tenancy so it can be ended within your own term. Tell the tenant in writing who the landlord is and give an address, because Colorado requires a written rental agreement to state the name and address of the landlord or the authorized agent and requires notice of a change within one business day. And plan for the deposit: Colorado's definition of landlord reaches the owner, manager, lessor, sublessor, successor in interest or agent of the owner, and from January 1, 2026 where your interest in the premises ceases the person holding the deposit has sixty days to transfer it to your successor or return it to the tenant, so a succession must be arranged rather than left to happen. A tenant may also have a claim against whoever actually holds the deposit and whoever is the landlord at the time, so do not assume the end of your interest ends your exposure. None of this is settled by any Colorado statute and no court decision was consulted for this library, so take advice before granting a lease out of a life estate, a sublease or any other limited interest.

title: Charging Tenants for Utilities That Are Not Metered to Their Unit
bodyText:
Colorado does not make a lease term unenforceable simply because it charges a tenant for utilities that are not separately metered to the unit. Since March 26, 2026 the state has instead set out exactly when you may allocate utility costs among the tenants of the same premises by formula, and if you meet all four conditions the allocation is lawful.

- The total you bill across all tenants must not exceed what the utility provider charged for service to the entire premises, so you may not recover more than you paid.
- You may not apply any markup, surcharge, administrative fee or other amount in excess of the actual charges from the utility, except as otherwise permitted by law — and the one thing the law otherwise permits is the narrow third-party-billing allowance, which lets a written rental agreement require either a markup or fee of no more than two percent of the amount you were billed, or a markup or fee of no more than ten dollars a month, but not both.
- Utility costs for common areas or shared facilities must be excluded from any tenant allocation. That is the condition landlords most often get wrong: corridor lighting, a shared laundry, an irrigation system, a pool pump and a leasing office all have to come out of the pool before anything is apportioned, and you may not charge any fee for the maintenance of common areas either.
- You must clearly and conspicuously disclose the method of allocation for the dwelling unit in the tenant's rental agreement or in an addendum to it; a method you can describe only on request is not disclosed.

Four further rules sit on top.

- You may not charge anything for utilities above what the utility provider charged for service to the tenant's own unit, except under the third-party allowance or the allocation rules.
- **A utility charge is not rent:** You may not characterise it as rent for which the rent remedies including eviction are available, and you may not evict for unpaid utilities as if it were rent.
- Your lease must not let a voucher or subsidy provider sue for possession based solely on unpaid utilities.
- Nothing excludes utilities from being counted as rent when a voucher or subsidy programme calculates the housing costs it will pay.

Finally, plan ahead: for premises constructed with permits applied for on or after July 1, 2027, gas, electric and water service delivered to the premises must be metered either directly by the utility provider or by a submeter, so a new building cannot use a formula at all. If you are building or substantially permitting after that date, budget for meters.

Mobile home parks have their own water-usage disclosure and landlord-utility-account rules and are not covered here. A city or county may require more.

title: A Utility Deposit Is Part of the Security Deposit
bodyText:
Any money you take from a tenant to cover utilities is a security deposit in Colorado, whatever you call it on the lease, because the test is what the money secures and not the label you give it.

Three things follow.

- It counts inside the two-month deposit ceiling along with every other deposit you hold, so calling part of it a utility deposit buys you no extra headroom.
- **It comes back on the same clock as the rest of the deposit:** Within thirty days after the lease ends or the tenant hands the unit back, whichever happens last, unless your lease sets a longer period, and the lease cannot set more than sixty days.
- You may keep part of it only for a reason on the statute's closed list, on which unpaid utility charges appear, so a real unpaid utility bill is recoverable from the deposit — but only if you send the written statement listing the exact reasons, with the documentation the deposit rules require, and pay the balance at the same time.

Miss the deadline or the statement and you forfeit the right to keep anything at all, and a retention the court finds wrongful costs three times the amount withheld plus the tenant's attorney fees and costs.

Never label a utility deposit non-refundable or treat it as the tenant's last month of utility service; a nonrefundable utility charge collected before the tenancy also runs into the application-fee cap. A deposit the utility itself holds because the tenant is the utility's own customer is not yours: you cannot claim it, you cannot require it be assigned to you, and if the tenant never claims it the utility pays it into a state low-income energy assistance fund.

Your city or county may add requirements, so check local rules.

title: When a Utility Disclosure Must Be in the Lease
bodyText: Colorado has no general utility disclosure form or attachment you must hand a tenant. There is one case where the disclosure has to be in the lease or in an addendum to it: if you allocate shared or master-metered utility costs among tenants by a ratio or formula rather than by a meter for each unit, the method of allocation must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously in that tenant's rental agreement or an addendum, and it is one of four conditions you must meet for the allocation to be lawful at all. Outside that case, a separate utility addendum is lawful but optional, and this library covers the ordinary case in its utilities clauses instead. What is not optional is the pricing side. Before the tenant agrees to pay, you must disclose clearly and conspicuously the nature and purpose of anything the tenant will pay that is not part of the single advertised total price, including what the charge is for, who receives it and whether it is refundable. The actual cost a utility provider charges for service to the tenant's own unit does not have to be folded into your advertised total price, which is why utilities are the usual example of a charge that needs this separate explanation. Keep the explanation accurate: misdescribing what a charge is for, who gets it or whether it comes back is itself a violation. Mobile home parks have their own annual water-billing disclosure and posting rules that do not apply to a site-built rental. Your city or county may require more, so check local rules.

title: Learning That a Tenant's Utilities Are About to Be Shut Off
bodyText:
Colorado gives you no statutory right to be told that your tenant's gas, electric or water is about to be shut off. There is no provision letting a tenant name you, in a separate document or anywhere else, as a party the utility must notify, and no provision requiring a utility to warn the owner before it disconnects a unit for the tenant's nonpayment. The disconnection rules the state does have are directions to the Public Utilities Commission to write rules for regulated gas and electric utilities, and those rules speak to the utility and the customer, not to you.

That leaves three practical routes, none of them a statutory entitlement.

- Ask the utility directly whether it offers a third-party or additional-contact notification on a customer's account; that is a matter of the utility's own rules and tariff, so the answer varies by provider and you should get it in writing from them.
- Ask the tenant to sign whatever authorization the provider requires and to keep you in the loop, which you can make a lease obligation.
- **Keep your own eye on the risk:** In a building you master-meter or where the account stays in your name, you are the customer and get the notices anyway.

Do not respond to an unpaid tenant utility bill by cutting service off or letting it lapse. Willfully terminating utilities is treated as an unlawful removal of the tenant in Colorado and the statutory damages are severe, and losing heat, water or electricity is also a habitability breach with its own remedies.

Mobile home parks have their own rules.

title: You Cannot Shut Off a Utility You Bill, Submetered or Not
bodyText: If you meter or allocate a utility yourself and the tenant does not pay the bill, you still may not interrupt the service. Colorado treats willfully terminating utilities as removing the tenant from the unit without court process, and the damages are not a slap on the wrist: the tenant's actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, plus attorney fees and costs, and a court may order the tenant back into possession. Losing heat, running water, hot water or electricity is separately a habitability failure, which gives the tenant the right to terminate, to hire a professional and deduct, and to claim the rent back for the period, and a condition that materially interferes with life, health or safety starts a twenty-four-hour clock. Nor can you turn an unpaid utility charge into a nonpayment eviction: unless the amount is part of the single monthly payment for occupancy, your lease may not characterize it as rent for which rent remedies including eviction are available. So your remedies for an unpaid submetered bill are the ordinary ones for a non-rent debt: pursue it as a debt, retain it from the security deposit if the lease lists it, and in a subsidized tenancy remember that the lease cannot let the subsidy provider sue for possession on unpaid utilities alone. On the billing side, if you buy gas or electricity from a regulated utility and pass it on through a master meter you can ask the Public Utilities Commission to exempt you from rate regulation, but only on terms: no charge above the actual cost the utility bills you, the sum of what you bill all the end users must not exceed the utility's bill, and you must pass refunds and rebates through with a written notice giving ninety days to claim them. A ratio or formula allocation is lawful on its own four conditions. And for premises built on permits applied for on or after July 1, 2027, gas, electric and water must be metered directly by the provider or by a submeter.

title: When the Utility Account Is in Your Name
bodyText: Keeping the utility account in your own name is lawful and often sensible, but it moves the whole risk of nonpayment onto you. You are the utility's customer, so you get the bills and the notices and the tenant has no standing with the provider; and if service stops because you did not pay, the unit becomes uninhabitable. Lack of running water, hot water, heat during the colder months or landlord-caused loss of electricity is presumed to materially interfere with the tenant's life, health and safety, which gives you twenty-four hours from notice to start putting it right. The tenant can then end the lease without penalty, hire a professional and deduct the cost from rent, and claim that the rent for the period was worth nothing. If you let the service lapse deliberately to make the tenant leave, you are treated as having removed the tenant without court process, and the damages are the tenant's actual loss plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars. Three further things are worth knowing. If you buy gas or electricity wholesale and pass it on through a master meter, you may bill the tenants no more in total than the utility billed you, you may add nothing for your own metering, billing or administration beyond the small statutory markup, and you must pass refunds and rebates through. A municipal water or sewer bill the tenant does not pay is your problem too: inside municipal or county limits the provider generally cannot disconnect the user, and instead certifies the unpaid charges as a lien on the property itself, collected like taxes; special-district charges are a perpetual lien that can be foreclosed. And no tenant can have a receiver appointed over your building: that application belongs to the attorney general or to a county, city or municipality, on evidence of a pattern of neglect, which expressly includes inadequate heating or sanitary facilities. Colorado gives a tenant no express right to pay your utility bill and deduct it from rent, so the cautious course is to assume a tenant who restores essential service will be allowed to deduct what it cost and to not let the account fall behind. Mobile home parks have their own remittance rules.

title: Utility Shutoffs: What Colorado Law Actually Says
bodyText: Two different rules get called the utility shutoff law, and only one of them is about you. The one that binds you is short: willfully terminating a tenant's utilities, or willfully causing heat, running water, hot water, electricity or gas to be cut off, counts as removing the tenant without court process. The tenant can sue for actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, with attorney fees and costs, and the court can put the tenant back in possession. The same conduct is also a habitability breach, and willfully removing doors, windows or locks is treated the same way. The only recognised exception to the no-self-help rule has nothing to do with utilities: it is an exclusion carried out under the state board of health's rules for cleaning up an illegal drug laboratory. The other rule binds the gas or electric utility, not you. Colorado directs the Public Utilities Commission to write standard practices for disconnecting service for nonpayment, and the statute lists what those practices must cover: no shutoffs on Fridays, weekends or holidays, none during an emergency or safety event, limits on afternoon shutoffs, payment plans, referrals to energy assistance, protections for customers whose electricity is medically necessary, bans on disconnection during extreme heat or cold for the area, no remote disconnection without a real attempt to reach the customer, and same-day reconnection in defined cases. Note what that is: a direction to a regulator, so the detail lives in commission rules and the utility's tariff rather than in the statute, and it applies to regulated gas and electric utilities. There is no statutory winter moratorium in Colorado and no added winter notice period. Two statutory holds do exist, both on the utility: a pending low-income energy assistance application that was denied for incomplete paperwork puts a sixty-day disconnection hold on an investor-owned utility, and a customer enrolled in a percentage-of-income payment plan cannot have service terminated for the old arrears. Municipal and county water and sewer providers generally cannot disconnect a user inside their limits at all; they certify the unpaid charges as a lien on the property instead, which is your exposure, not the tenant's. Mobile home parks have their own rules, and your city or county may add more.

title: When a Tenant Does Not Put the Utilities in Their Name
bodyText:
Colorado has no statute about transferring utility accounts at the start of a tenancy. There is no statutory deadline by which a tenant must put service in their own name, no notice you can serve to force it, and — this is the important half — no opt-in right to cut the service off if the tenant does not. Some states give a landlord exactly that: a few days' notice and then permission to have landlord-name service disconnected.

Colorado gives the opposite. Willfully terminating utilities is treated as removing the tenant without court process, and it exposes you to the tenant's actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, attorney fees and costs, and an order restoring possession; it is a habitability breach as well. Letting your own account lapse so the provider disconnects is the same conduct by a slower route.

So the transfer obligation has to come from your lease, and your remedy has to be money rather than darkness. Put the duty in the lease with a date, make the tenant responsible for reimbursing you at cost for service you keep paying for in the meantime, and keep that reimbursement clearly separate from rent — a Colorado lease may not treat a utility charge as rent for which eviction and the other rent remedies are available, and you may not add a markup, an administrative fee or a late charge to it. Keep paying the bill while you sort it out, and pursue the money as an ordinary debt or from the security deposit if your lease lists the charge.

Mobile home parks have their own rules, and your city or county may add more.

title: Renting to Veterans: No State Incentive, and a Protected Class
bodyText: Colorado runs no landlord incentive for renting to veterans. There is no tax credit, no risk-mitigation or damage-reimbursement fund, no signing bonus and no pilot programme that pays you for taking a veteran tenant or a veteran's housing voucher, and nothing in the code gives a private landlord a veterans-specific benefit of any kind. The one place veterans appear on the housing side is municipal: a city or town may create a veterans' housing authority and give veterans preference in housing that authority builds, buys or leases. That is a power for the municipality, not for you. What does bind you is the other direction. Veteran or military status is a protected class in Colorado housing law, which covers members and veterans of the armed forces, the reserve and the National Guard, but not someone dishonourably discharged. You may not refuse to rent, make housing unavailable, or treat anyone worse in the terms, conditions or privileges of a tenancy because of that status — and the statute goes further than most people expect: making or causing a written or oral inquiry or keeping a record about an applicant's veteran or military status is itself an unfair housing practice. There is one exception, and it is narrow: the inquiry or record is allowed where its purpose is to determine eligibility for veteran or military housing or for a veteran or military housing benefit. So if you take part in a veterans housing programme, or you offer a veterans benefit yourself, you may ask what you need to verify eligibility for it and nothing more. Before you advertise a veterans-only discount or preference, take advice: the exception covers asking, and whether the favourable treatment itself is lawful is not spelled out, so the cautious course is to run any veterans preference through a recognised programme and document it. Separate federal protections for servicemembers also exist, and Colorado has its own military service relief statute.

title: Accepting Rent After a Breach or a Notice
bodyText:
Colorado has no statute telling you what happens when you take rent after a tenant has broken the lease or after you have served a notice. The one acceptance-of-rent rule in the statute books applies to mobile home parks, where accepting rent during the ninety-day cure period does not waive the right to terminate for the noncompliance; there is no equivalent for an ordinary rental. That leaves the question to the courts, and the common-law waiver doctrine is real: a landlord who keeps taking rent as though nothing happened can be found to have given up the breach, or to have created a new tenancy on the old terms. Colorado court decisions are not covered here, so treat the risk as live rather than measured.

Two statutory points do help you.

- For unpaid rent, you do not have to demand the rent on the day it falls due; the statute says so expressly, and it is the failure to pay after the demand that works the forfeiture — so a delay in demanding does not by itself cost you the right.
- Your lease cannot contain a tenant waiver of the statutory notice period that precedes a nonpayment eviction, which is ten days, or five for an exempt residential agreement and three for an employer-provided housing agreement (C.R.S. 13-40-104(1)(d)).

Practically: put a reservation-of-rights term in the lease, and then back it up each time. Reserve your rights in writing when you accept any payment after a breach or after serving a notice, say what the payment is applied to, and keep the notice alive on its own terms.

Never use the lease to try to waive the tenant's statutory rights: a term waiving or modifying any right, remedy, obligation or prohibition in the habitability rules is void, deposit rights cannot be waived, and for a tenancy covered by the for-cause eviction rules a waiver of those requirements is void too.

A payment that cures a rent demand within the time the law allows ends that nonpayment case whatever your lease says.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule in Colorado
bodyText: Colorado does not tell you what temperature to set a water heater to. There is no maximum, no minimum, no requirement to check or reset the thermostat between tenancies, and no anti-scald provision anywhere in the statutes — the word scald does not appear in the Colorado code at all. What the habitability rules require is supply rather than temperature: the unit must have running water at all times and hot water in an amount sufficient for the tenant to do everything ordinarily needed to stay clean and healthy, and inadequate running or hot water is presumed to interfere materially with the tenant's life, health and safety, which starts a twenty-four-hour clock once you have notice. The boiler inspection article, which does carry temperature and pressure limits, expressly exempts service and domestic-type water heaters, and it exempts boilers in private residences and in apartment houses of fewer than six units as well. Where a temperature requirement does exist it comes from a code rather than a statute: the state examining board of plumbers establishes the Colorado plumbing code as the minimum standard for installing, altering and repairing plumbing equipment statewide, local governments may adopt amendments at least equal to it, and your lease's habitability obligations include compliance with applicable building, housing and health codes where a violation would materially interfere with the tenant's life, health or safety. So the practical course is to set the heater as the manufacturer's instructions and the applicable plumbing and building code require, keep hot water genuinely available, and have the installation permitted and inspected where the code calls for it. Check your city or county rules, which may set a figure the state does not. Do not treat the absence of a statutory temperature as permission to ignore one.

title: Waterbeds: No Colorado Statute
bodyText:
Colorado says nothing about waterbeds. The words waterbed, flotation and liquid-filled do not appear anywhere in the statutes, so there is no provision requiring you to allow one, none letting you refuse, none setting a deposit or an insurance requirement for one, and no notice you have to give.

The point is left to your lease and to ordinary contract law, which means you can decide it — but only in the lease, and only before the tenant signs. If you want to prohibit waterbeds and other liquid-filled furniture, say so; if you want to allow them on conditions, set the conditions in writing, and consider requiring a proper frame and liner, installation on a floor that can take the weight, and proof that the tenant carries renter's or liability insurance covering water damage.

Do not try to charge a separate waterbed fee or a non-refundable deposit: Colorado's fee rules bar a charge above the actual price of what you provide and a charge for something you do not actually provide, any deposit you take is a security deposit inside the two-month cap whatever you call it, and a nonrefundable charge taken before the tenancy runs into the application-fee cap.

If a waterbed does cause damage, the deposit rules are your route, and they have tightened: you may retain only for damage beyond normal wear and tear that did not pre-exist the tenancy, or for another lawful charge your lease actually lists, so list it. A clause assigning the tenant a charge for work due to normal wear and tear or a pre-existing condition is void as against public policy.

Your city or county may have a rule the state does not.

title: No Window Guard Requirement, and the One Window Rule That Binds You
bodyText: Colorado has no window guard law. Nothing requires you to install guards or fall-prevention devices in a unit where children live, nothing obliges you to offer them on request, and there is no prescribed lease notice or model text about them — the words window guard appear nowhere in the statutes. What the habitability rules do require about windows is different: unbroken windows as part of the weatherproofing of the building, and locks or security devices in good working order on every exterior window designed to be opened, with a missing or broken window lock presumed to interfere materially with the tenant's life, health and safety. Willfully removing windows or locks is treated as unlawfully excluding the tenant. There is one window rule that reaches your lease, and it runs the other way. A tenant who has given you notice that they are a victim-survivor of domestic violence, domestic abuse, stalking or unlawful sexual behaviour, with the documentation the statute lists, may change the locks and take other reasonable safety precautions, and the statute names installing window bars as an example. You may not prevent it, charge a fee for it, retaliate or take any adverse action over it, and any lease provision that prohibits it is void and unenforceable; you also have an affirmative duty to take all steps reasonably necessary to make the unit safe in response to the tenant's safety concerns. Doing the opposite is expensive: the tenant can recover statutory damages equal to actual damages plus the greater of three times the monthly rent or five thousand dollars, with fees and costs. So read any no-alterations clause as subject to that right, and if you do choose to install guards, treat the installation as yours to maintain in working order. Your city or county may require guards where the state does not, so check local rules.

title: Which Colorado Notices Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Colorado has no single provision saying every notice must be written; the requirement is scattered, and so is the meaning of the word. These must be in writing. A notice ending a periodic tenancy or declining to renew a fixed term: it has to describe the property, state the exact date the tenancy ends, and be signed by you or your agent or attorney. A demand for unpaid rent before an eviction, on the statutory notice period, which is three days for most tenancies and five under an exempt residential agreement — and your lease may not contain a tenant waiver of that notice requirement. Your statement of the exact reasons for keeping any part of a security deposit, with the supporting documentation, delivered with the balance. Notice to each tenant when your identity or your agent's changes, which may be written or electronic and is due within one business day, or you may post it conspicuously instead. The signed copy of the lease you owe the tenant within seven days, electronic unless the tenant asks for paper. The two habitability statements your lease itself must carry in twelve-point bold type. And for a victim-survivor's early termination, your written statement of actual damages within thirty days after the tenant vacates, which you forfeit future rent by missing. Two traps. First, what counts as writing differs: in the habitability rules a writing includes paper, electronic and digital records, but that definition expressly does not apply to the notices and demands in the eviction article, so serve those on paper in the statutory manner. Second, your lease can give away your own right to written notice: if your lease or your property rules say a tenant may give notice of an uninhabitable condition verbally, that waives your right to receive it in writing, and the twenty-four or seventy-two hour clock then starts on a phone call. Keep every notice route in the lease written, name the address and the electronic address for notices, and remember you cannot force a tenant into electronic-only dealings — a party who agrees to transact electronically keeps the right to refuse to do so for other transactions, and that right cannot be waived by agreement.

title: Federal 30-Day Notice, Now Also Colorado Law
bodyText:
The federal row explains the CARES Act 30-day notice to vacate for properties with a federally backed mortgage or in covered federal housing programs. In Colorado it is no longer only a federal rule. Since May 29, 2025, Colorado law requires a landlord who starts an eviction for nonpayment of rent to comply with the notice requirements of that federal section as it read on March 27, 2020, whatever has happened or happens to the federal law since (C.R.S. 38-12-1502(1)).

Two consequences.

- The federal court disagreement about whether the 30-day notice still applies does not help you in Colorado: the Colorado duty stands on its own, frozen at the 2020 text.
- A later federal repeal or narrowing would not release you either.

What is not settled is how far the Colorado duty reaches. The statute speaks of any landlord who files a nonpayment eviction and does not repeat the federal limit to covered properties, but the federal notice it adopts applies to covered dwellings, and the same law asks the state housing division to help landlords work out whether a property is a covered dwelling, which suggests the federal scope carries over. Colorado court decisions are not covered here.

The course that works under every reading: before any nonpayment eviction in Colorado, give the tenant a written notice to vacate and do not require them to leave until 30 days after you give it, alongside Colorado's own demand for payment.

The duty covers nonpayment evictions only, and it applies to mobile home park landlords as well. Take advice before filing if you have not given the 30-day notice.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Colorado follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (C.R.S. § 4-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (C.R.S. § 4-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Colorado's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (C.R.S. title 38, article 12 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Colorado law does forbid a written rental agreement from waiving the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing (C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3)(a)(III)(C)), so a lease cannot take that covenant away. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Colorado's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
